Microsoft goes quiet after church groups ask for 1% of data center costs

Ars Technica Long form September 28, 2026

“Microsoft claims to want to be a good neighbor, but the jury is still out.”

Microsoft has spent all year telling communities that when it brings a new data center into their area, it is committed to being a “good neighbor.” It will pay local property taxes that support local hospitals, schools, parks, and libraries, and it will invest in “vital services the community cares about,” the company promised. And it has sent liaisons into those communities to learn what those needs are.

But ask those liaisons how much the company is willing to invest, and the answers can be hard to come by.

At community meetings, Microsoft representatives have seemed unprepared to answer questions that go beyond the company’s “good neighbor” campaign materials, Ars has learned. The company has acknowledged in public-facing documents that simply matching its employees’ charitable donations—which totaled $229 million across 29,000 nonprofits in 2024—isn’t enough. But it has been vague about what more substantial local investments might look like. And to critics, Microsoft’s local investments seem especially small compared with the estimated hundreds of millions in state-level tax breaks that data center developers get in 38 states—exemptions that often last more than a decade.

In Georgia, a recent audit found that the state “gave up $474 million in sales taxes in one year—and got back just $41 million from the industry,” journalist Ronan Farrow reported. Why Georgia is willing to give away so much in tax breaks is unclear, Farrow noted, since “by the state’s own estimate, 70 percent of the data center construction would have happened anyway.”

Some communities are starting to question that logic. In Indiana, for example, big firms like Microsoft can buy data center equipment without paying the state’s 7 percent sales tax. The exemption could apply to as much as $13.2 billion in projected equipment purchases. Without the exemption, up to $900 million could have been added to the tax base supporting state programs, Indy Mirror estimated. And the exemption can last for 50 years, which has some residents wondering how much their communities are giving up to attract data centers.

While Microsoft stands to benefit enormously from such tax breaks, the community living around a 900-acre Granger data center in St. Joseph County is suffering, according to We Make Indiana, a local nonpartisan group of about 25 congregations and community organizations.

Last year, the state passed a property tax savings bill that reportedly hamstrung local governments’ ability to raise revenue for community services. As vital services deteriorated, We Make Indiana spent the past six months trying to alert Microsoft to the most urgent community needs in areas like health care, child care, elder care, transportation, and affordable housing.

Recently, it became clear that Microsoft was not prepared to meaningfully help address the bigger issues plaguing South Bend. We Make Indiana was disappointed to learn from a company liaison that Microsoft will only approve a series of one-time nonprofit donations totaling up to $1 million. We Make Indiana believes that maximum budget is not proportionate to the tax savings or improved profit margins Microsoft will get from operating the Granger hyperscaler.

When it comes to community investments, Microsoft appears to be no better or worse than other companies building data centers. Amazon, another big player in the field, may not have offered environmental commitments as strong as Microsoft’s, but it has also provided one-time grants of hundreds of thousands of dollars to a handful of local charities, We Make Indiana members told Ars.

If Microsoft really wants to become a role model for responsible data center development, it could do much more with its “community-first AI” platform to benefit its neighbors over the long term, We Make Indiana argues. The group has even offered a vision for how that could work. In May, it sent the company a proposal calling for Microsoft to negotiate directly with community members on a binding agreement under which Microsoft would agree to donate a small portion of its data center costs to the county each year.

“Microsoft has publicly stated that it wants to be a good neighbor,” the group’s proposal said. “This is an opportunity to demonstrate what that means.”

Through the proposed “Fair Share Agreement,” Microsoft would establish a fund to address social and environmental impacts from its $1 billion data center. An independent board would oversee payouts from the fund to ensure maximum community impact. Over the lifetime of the data center, including during construction, Microsoft would be expected to contribute a fair percentage of its annual costs to the fund, We Make Indiana proposed.

Their idea is not new, but it hasn’t caught on widely yet.

Most prominently, US Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) has introduced a plan for a national “sovereign wealth fund” that would force AI firms to donate as much as $7 trillion to benefit Americans. But Sanders’ proposal is far broader than what We Make Indiana is asking for. A closer parallel is the Data Center Fair Share Act, a bill introduced in Pennsylvania by Democratic state Sen. Lindsey M. Williams.

That bill would require data center developers to enter into legally binding “community benefits agreements” with community organizations. Those agreements would require firms to share “at least 10 percent” of the project’s total cost with a fund prioritizing investments in areas like workforce development, environmental improvements, public safety, infrastructure, affordable housing, energy consumption, or other beneficial uses.

Ryan Juskus, a leader with We Make Indiana, told Ars that his group believes asking for 10 percent “is very much on the high end.”

Initially, We Make Indiana planned to ask for as little as 1 or 2 percent, as the group estimated that even a 1 percent share could add approximately $30 to $40 million annually to community programs. But instead of approaching Microsoft with a firm offer, their proposal asked Microsoft to assess what percentage might be fair.

Additionally, they asked Microsoft to agree to meet higher environmental standards, particularly on issues related to water/energy use, air quality, sustainability, and workforce protections.

In South Bend, such binding commitments from Microsoft would make a substantial difference and set a high bar for other data center developers negotiating with local governments in the state, We Make Indiana suggested.

“It’s kind of like asking Microsoft to help us solve our challenges when the state has abandoned us,” Juskus told Ars.

“We would love to see Microsoft show leadership in an area that needs real leadership right now around doing data centers better, and who better to do that than Microsoft in partnering with a community like ours that has been a very struggling community for a long time?” he added.

But Microsoft has gone silent since receiving the proposal, despite the company’s bold promises to support “the entire community.” A spokesperson told Ars that the company considers the proposal an important part of its community listening process but said it’s too early to discuss it because Microsoft is still engaging other community leaders.

“Microsoft remains committed to developing our data center project in Granger in partnership with the community,” Microsoft’s spokesperson said. “This process will include investments in areas that reflect local priorities. We appreciate the community’s efforts to share their priorities with us—their input, including the community proposal we received, is an invaluable part of this process. At this early stage of development, investment decisions have not yet been made.”

Still, the company has approved some initial grants. Microsoft’s announcement did not detail how much each group will receive, but so far, the company has prioritized educational nonprofits and a community college, with the goal of building digital skills and helping people feel more comfortable with using AI. The company has also set up a land trust that “preserves and restores natural lands and waters in northwestern Indiana” while donating to groups dedicated to hunger relief and community volunteering.

These donations, Juskus told Ars, are “completely not proportional, not ongoing,” and “entirely” on Microsoft’s terms. Accepting these one-time investments when the community knows developers are extracting much more value from building in their location seems short-sighted, he suggested.

“It frankly just kind of buys silence,” Juskus said.

To Juskus’ group, which is built on community relationships, it seems “easy to be a ‘good neighbor’ when you get to set the criteria and evaluate your progress all by yourself. A real neighbor discerns what’s to be done through relationships and accountability,” Juskus said.

Responding to Microsoft’s statement, Juskus expressed doubts that the data center investments will help South Bend residents where they need it most.

“Efforts by County Council members and the community to get binding commitments related to water, energy use, and decommissioning plans to reduce the harm of this project are met with vague and noncommittal public relations responses from Microsoft,” Juskus said. “The community enhancement donations that Microsoft is pledging to nonprofits in our county are miniscule, given the project’s scale.”

To drum up local support for their proposal, We Make Indiana is planning a series of public demonstrations to highlight the contrast between the tax breaks data center developers stand to receive and the cuts to basic services like bus lines and health care the community faces. They hope to make enough noise to convince county officials to use upcoming negotiations over additional tax incentives as leverage to secure a binding commitment from Microsoft to invest in community well-being over the long term. They also expect such messaging could make it harder for officials seen as favoring corporate interests to win elections as data center backlash mounts nationwide.

“In a fast-changing local and national environment, we will continue to organize our community and elected leaders to use every piece of leverage we have to bring Microsoft to the table for real conversation and negotiation,” Juskus said. “Microsoft claims to want to be a good neighbor, but the jury is still out.”

We Make Indiana first presented its proposal at a meeting with Microsoft’s liaison in a church.

“What we have is a concept,” the group told Microsoft’s representative. “And what we want is for Microsoft to enter into negotiation,” Juskus said. That way, “we could work out something that isn’t just imposed from above.”

The rep—whom Microsoft declined to connect Ars with despite a month of back-and-forth—promised We Make Indiana that she would check back in after admitting that the group’s request was “way beyond her or even her boss’s purview,” Juskus said.

The next week, Microsoft held an open house, and We Make Indiana showed up with 75 community members to prove there was community support for their proposal. But the open house seemed more like a PR campaign than a sincere attempt to engage the community, attendees told Ars.

“The specialists Microsoft brought out to the open house here in the county had talking points with little substance,” Juskus said.

For example, when a We Make Indiana team member with expertise in environmental policy asked how Microsoft planned to recycle all decommissioned materials, Microsoft’s rep “did not have any answers to those questions,” Juskus said.

During an interview with a local radio station, a different Microsoft rep confirmed that the proposal was not on his radar, said Andre Stoner, a former pastor and peace activist who leads We Make Indiana. He is not optimistic that Microsoft will ever directly address their proposal.

“We have very little confidence that there’s been any robust conversation inside,” Stoner told Ars.

Nathan Taft, a senior campaigner for the nonprofit environmental advocacy group Stand. earth, has been working with We Make Indiana, as well as groups in other areas where Microsoft is building data centers. He told Ars that each community must negotiate its own deals to fulfill local needs but that the fair share agreement in Indiana offers one way to ensure that environmental safeguards and community investments continue over the long term.

Taft told Ars that communities are “specifically looking at Microsoft because, to be fair to them, they’ve been a big leader in the climate space and community benefit space. They’ve done a good job in the past, and we want them to be that leader again. But increasingly, there’s been a big gap between what Microsoft is saying and what Microsoft is actually doing in public spaces and in communities.”

At town hall meetings, Microsoft seems to rely on “diffusion techniques” to avoid answering residents’ questions transparently, Taft told Ars. Rather than host a single speaker or panel addressing all questions in the room, “we’ve seen in multiple different places, they’ll have five or six different reps scattered across a room, and people come up and talk in little clusters,” Taft said. “And they’ll be like, ‘That’s a good question. Let me write this on a sticky note and put it on the wall.’ And it seems very rote and kind of like they’re ticking a box. It doesn’t seem like they want to hear real dissent.”

“It seems like what’s most important to them is getting as much compute online as quickly as possible,” Taft said. “And the communities are an afterthought.”

Stoner thinks other communities should consider pressuring data center developers to enter fair share agreements. The Better Data Center Project provided key assistance to his group when crafting their proposal, he said.

Juskus worries that northern Indiana may be developing “a unique significance in Microsoft’s eyes” after the company recently broke ground on a second data center there.

“As I understand it, we’re in a data center sweet spot, with abundant land and water, state-level tax incentives, and our location at a junction point in the electrical power grids,” Juskus told Ars.

Stoner told Ars that We Make Indiana is working to convince local officials to back the fair share agreement, potentially by using a county economic development director’s plan to create a “tax increment financing” (TIF) district around the Microsoft site as leverage. Microsoft has not publicly supported the TIF, but locals believe the company would benefit from the additional incentives and worry that it could use the TIF to expand the site.

“We are exploring whether the TIF can be leverage with Microsoft, with a message like ‘No TIF without a Fair Share,’” Stoner told Ars.

Microsoft seems to think that We Make Indiana shouldn’t speak for the entire community. But Stoner told Ars that engaging decision-makers on issues affecting the wider community is what his group does. Developing the fair share agreement involved “many, many, many conversations with our community leaders, with people in our congregations, with our leaders, to think about what it is we’re asking for and how and why,” Stoner said.

Some group members oppose AI, while others are neutral, but We Make Indiana has already won at least one major battle since entering the fight. A rumored Meta data center was blocked after the group rallied hundreds to pressure officials to vote against it at a public meeting that lasted until 4 am. The fight with Microsoft is not about stopping the data center, which is set to begin construction this fall and could be operational by 2029. It’s about building it better, Stoner said.

“We want development that doesn’t threaten our environment and our electric bills and that invests in a decent way, a proportional way,” he said.

Microsoft may be underestimating We Make Indiana. Stoner said the group has been organizing since 2024, building on work from a 2018 group called Faith in Indiana and using its community connections to secure bipartisan support for policies it favors. The Microsoft fight is the first time that We Make Indiana has engaged a corporate partner, Stoner said, and if they refuse to listen, the group stands ready to “mobilize hundreds of people from faith communities.”

“Basically, this is a question of power: Do they need to talk to us or not?” Stoner said. “Or do they think they don’t need to?”

To Stoner, giving tax breaks to AI firms while cutting funding for buses and childcare amounts to elected officials taking from the poor to benefit the wealthiest corporations. In the long term, he hopes to put an end to sales tax exemptions in his state. But in the meantime, he wants the fair share agreement to “be one of the big issues that’s debated in this election this fall,” Stoner said.

From impulse purchase to pocket studio: The M-Vave FM-1

Ars Technica Long form October 26, 2026

M-Vave’s cheap FM-1 pocket synth has exploded as a community firmware playground.

The M-Vave FM-1 is exactly the kind of device I have a weakness for. I may not have an intended use for the frequency-modulation synthesizer, but when a low price meets a high coolness factor, I’m powerless to keep it out of my cart.

Initially billed as a pocket cousin of the famous Yamaha DX7 synthesizer, the FM-1 is a bargain at only $59.72 after fees. At release, it was a cool device that did what it said on the box, but not much else.

But in July, some intrepid tinkerers on Reddit’s r/synthdiy board began reverse-engineering the FM-1’s stock firmware to expand the device’s abilities. By September, custom firmware began appearing. We’re not even through October, and there are already more community firmware projects available to install on the FM-1 than I could ever hope to cover.

I decided to check a few of them out. And just in case you were wondering: Yes, it plays Doom.

On October 17, M-Vave announced FM1 Open, a software package that encourages FM-1 owners to develop custom firmware for the synth-turned-whatever-else-you-can-imagine. Alongside the FM1 Open package came an SDK, a browser-based workbench, and version 15 of the stock firmware, now an open platform you can flash and build on. The unit’s 27 physical piano keys and modest 1.54-inch TFT display lend themselves well to a host of projects, musical or otherwise.

Normally, when an enthusiast community reverse-engineers a closed device, an official patch quickly follows. M-Vave has taken the opposite approach, though. The application source is published under GPLv3, and the company even includes an in-browser emulator to test custom firmware prior to flashing actual hardware. There’s a caveat, however: The underlying synth engine that powers the stock FM-1 package is still distributed as a closed binary, so it’s the application layer of the stack that’s actually open. I don’t think that diminishes M-Vave’s gesture toward the community, but it’s worth noting.

Before you rush to AliExpress, be aware that flashing custom firmware comes with risks. The JieLi chip powering the FM-1 keeps firmware in a single flash bank, so an interrupted update can leave the device in a difficult-to-recover state. As long as the flashing process completes without interruption, you should be fine. But nothing is foolproof, and there’s always a risk of bricking a device if something goes wrong.

Flashing will also wipe all information on the device. Before you try to load a new firmware package on the synth, back up your saved projects and settings because they will disappear. I was starting from a blank stock canvas, so there was no real risk.

The unit I received was running stock v14 firmware, and community guides repeatedly warn users to update to the stock v15 firmware before attempting to install custom firmware. Guess who didn’t listen? I blindly assumed that since I’d just received my FM-1, it would be running the latest firmware package (v16 now). I was wrong.

Caught in the excitement, I tried to flash Doom directly onto the v14 firmware package, and the installation failed about 80 percent through. Still, it wrote something. The synth worked, but the device stopped speaking the same language as the installers. Thankfully, M-Vave anticipated careless users like me and thoughtfully included a “force-flash” tool in the FM1 Workbench. It restored my unit to stock v15 in about 10 seconds, saving me a huge headache.

The lesson is simple: Always check your current firmware version.

The development scene around the FM-1 is exploding, and new options are appearing all the time. You can browse the listings to see what you might like to try, and a community tip from the fm1-custom-fw GitHub offers some good advice:

While not an absolute hard rule, there is a prominent community recommendation to avoid flashing one custom firmware directly over another. To minimize bricking risks, some users suggest rolling back to the official stock firmware (v15) via M-VAVE’s official updater first, and only then flashing the next custom firmware build. Alternatively, you can use TransitFM1—a dedicated lightweight bridge firmware by Quixotic7 designed with crash-guarded boot stubs and stock V15 identity emulation to safely transition between custom builds.

Some other tips I picked up along the way from community discussions and my own mistakes:

Here are some projects to try.

What better way to measure the value of any electronic device than asking, “will it run Doom”?

The FM-1 already has several Doom-related projects up and running. Playing on a 240 x 240 display with mini piano keys will never be my preferred way to take down demons with a shotgun, but that doesn’t make it any less cool to see the game running on a $60 synthesizer clone. It’s a novelty, but the clone version played surprisingly well. The short draw distance means enemies occasionally pop out of nowhere, but who doesn’t love a jump scare while demon hunting?

You can explore community Doom options through the fm1-editor directory.

While the stock firmware aims to re-create the Yamaha DX7 experience, Melodee takes its cues from the mid-’80s Casio CZ-1, a full-featured synthesizer that uses phase distortion to create a sound modern artists are still chasing. Melodee comes with four engines: a CZ-1 emulator, a DX7-style engine, a percussion engine for the 808s, and my personal favorite, a Commodore 64 SID sound chip emulator.

As a child of the 8-bit era, I’ve always had a soft spot for the amazing soundtracks built around the technological limits of the day. Composing chiptunes always seemed like an interesting hobby, but I never had the right tools. Now, thanks to Melodee, I have a pocketable chiptune keytar I can take anywhere.

Want to re-create that classic Cash Money sound on a $60 budget? The FM-1 now has you covered—this could be your chance to become the next Mannie Fresh.

This is where a capable device becomes the deal of the year. Felucca is the foundation for many other community firmware projects, transforming the FM-1 into a true multi-engine synth. The stock firmware lets you select different instruments, but you can play only one at a time. Felucca runs independent instruments simultaneously, letting you create a full-band sound all by yourself.

Felucca includes more than a dozen sound engines, from phase distortion to virtual analog, plus a built-in sampler. Other highlights include a RAW in-browser web editor that makes arranging tracks less painful than working on the FM-1’s tiny screen, and a full multi-track pattern sequencer built into the device. If you want to make music, this is a great place to start.

SLOOP is the FM-1’s groovebox solution. Cards on the table: Before writing this article, I wasn’t familiar with what a groovebox was. In a nutshell, it’s a self-contained music studio that can be operated without a PC. SLOOP turns the FM-1 from an instrument you play into one you compose with. You program drums and bass on a grid, chain loops together, and let the machine keep the beat going while you layer other sounds on top.

SLOOP adds drum machines and synth layers to the FM-1, running on Felucca’s sound engines. The result is a legitimate eight-track, battery-powered beat maker that fits in your pocket. Unlike Felucca, SLOOP is designed more for live performance, letting you build and stack layers of sound as you go. I didn’t always fully understand how I arrived at the results I produced in SLOOP, but I was having too much fun to care.

After exploring some of the available custom firmware packages, I decided to take my own advice and try Felucca as a starting point for actual recording. I connected the FM-1 to my PC using the same USB connection I’d previously used for flashing. Audacity recognized Felucca immediately, and I was able to select it as a recording device. From there, I could select any instrument or effect on the device and record it live over USB to Audacity tracks.

That’s all well and good if you’re sitting at a desk with a PC, but what if inspiration strikes while you’re out and about? That’s where Felucca’s self-contained recording process shines.

Creating music entirely on the FM-1 was more intuitive than I expected. Once I pulled up the Felucca controls cheat sheet, the process was smooth: use the Algorithm knob to switch between recording tracks and Presets to switch instruments. From there, I could build and layer my creation track by track.

I put together a four-track beat loop after about 15 minutes of fiddling with the firmware. I just felt my way around in the dark, auditioning sounds and slipping them in wherever I thought they fit. It was about as simplistic as it gets, but with some time and practice, I think I could churn out something worthwhile. If it was this straightforward for me, just imagine what someone with actual musical talent could achieve.

I’ll admit that my fingers were occasionally too big for the task. The FM1’s soft-touch keys feel great, but my index finger sometimes slipped off the intended note and onto an adjacent key. It’s not a dealbreaker, but there were a few times I had to retry a part due to hitting a wrong note.

Since there doesn’t appear to be an on-device export function, transferring the track to my PC was as simple as opening Audacity and hitting record while playing a beat on the FM-1. I retained live control throughout recording, too. Toward the end of the sample below, you can hear me fading out the audio by turning down the master volume knob. The same approach would let you weave any number of live modulations into a recording. You can hear my modest attempt at a quick beat below.

The FM-1 is the type of technology I love. I’m the furthest thing from a professional musician, but the price is low enough and the device is versatile enough that I can play around without feeling guilty about a $1,500 synth setup gathering dust in the corner.

My 10-year-old has been taking piano lessons for a few years now and has clearly inherited my urge to tinker with tech. The FM-1 could be the perfect holiday gift he never knew he needed. I’ll probably order another one for him since I still want to play with mine. At this price, I don’t have to sweat it.

M-Vave didn’t send this unit for review; checkout curiosity just got the better of me. I’ve since ordered the company’s SMC-PAD sampler, too, but that’s another article for another day.

Would I buy the FM-1 again tomorrow? In a beat.

DIY VR: How to build your own headset, and why you probably won’t want to

Ars Technica Long form October 19, 2026

A primer on the joys and pains of building your own head-mounted display.

Virtual reality is in a bit of a weird place right now. After a lot of unfulfilled promise in the 1990s, it came back strong with the 2016 release of the Oculus Rift. For a while, it looked like VR, AR, XR, the metaverse, or whatever you wanted to call it, was going to be huge. Mark Zuckerberg was certainly convinced, and even Apple got in on the hype with its Vision Pro.

But by then momentum for alternate realities of every acronym was already in steady decline, and it only dwindled from there. The rate of development of new headsets has slowed, with many companies (including Apple) scaling back or shelving their efforts. While new releases like the Steam Frame and Pimax Dream Air are still happening, many of the most interesting developments in the space these days are on the enthusiast front.

That’s right, DIY VR is a thing, and with a couple hundred dollars in components, plus many hours of your time, you too can enter the immersive world of virtual reality while also experiencing the highs and lows of soldering, firmware flashing, and 3D printing. I rode that rollercoaster myself and learned why this is still a decidedly niche movement.

I stumbled into this space about a year ago. I primarily use VR for sim racing to practice driving the world’s greatest cars on the world’s greatest tracks while at home in my pajamas. At that time, I was using an HP Reverb G2, a virtual reality headset built around the Windows Mixed Reality (WMR) standard.

As part of its own cooling on VR tech, Microsoft was nixing support for WMR, and I feared that I might need a new headset. (I need not have worried. Many talented folks have kept WMR headsets alive through third-party drivers like OASIS on Steam.)

That’s when I found YouTuber CNCDan’s video on building a VR headset for $150. The price was certainly compelling, and as someone with a particular set of electronics skills developed over years of disassembling and repairing pinball machines, I thought it sounded kind of fun.

That opened the door to a rich landscape of DIY VR development, complete with software tools and hardware advice on how to get started.

The best starting place is Relativty VR. This project, started in the late 2010s by Jonas Ceccon, Gabriel Combe, and Maxime Coutté, includes all the code, configurations, and guidance you’ll need to get started.

But there are others, like OpenVR Arduino HMD, Project North Star, and the full-body tracking SlimeVR. There are plenty of ways to piece together your headset. As my first attempt, I kept it simple, sticking with the Relativty software and relying on the 3D headset models provided by CNCDan as part of his build. First step: the hardware.

A DIY VR headset is a mixture of hardware and software, and while you can have the software ready to go in just a few clicks, chances are it’s going to take some time to get the hardware you need. That’s doubly true given the uncertainty in global shipping.

The biggest and potentially most important piece of hardware is a 3D printer. Although I’ve seen some compelling DIY VR headsets made out of repurposed VR phone holders—Google Cardboard among others—most projects fit in shells that come out of a 3D printer. If you don’t have access to one, services like Formlabs can handle it via mail order, but given the amount of tinkering here, it’s certainly advantageous to print at home.

Regardless, you need to buy quite a few things. Let’s start with the most expensive: displays. You might think a pair of panels small enough and good enough for a VR headset would be difficult to find and prohibitively expensive, and you can certainly spend a lot here, but the standard option is a set of 2.9-inch LCDs, which can be purchased with the necessary controller for about $125.

Each has a 1440×1440 resolution. They offer 150 nits of brightness and a contrast ratio of 600:1. Not exactly world-class specs, but plenty enough for this application, and though they’re pretty ugly to view from odd angles, since you’re literally going to be sticking them a few inches from your eyeballs, that’s not really an issue.

The next missing piece is a sensor module containing an inertial measurement unit, or IMU. This device detects the headset’s position. You’ll want a GY-91, a sensor board that has an onboard accelerometer, gyroscope, magnetometer, and barometer. You can find one for around $5, but buyer beware for reasons I’ll explain shortly.

Next is the circuitry that ties it all together. Some DIY VR projects call upon custom PCBs riddled with components. The Relativty project just relies on an Arduino Pro Micro, which can be bought at any number of electronics retailers for $5 or less.

You’ll also need a pair of 34 mm-diameter lenses to focus those tiny displays, some miscellaneous hardware to connect the pieces, and a nylon strap to hold the thing to your head. Oh, and a pad from an HTC Vive, because nobody wants the sharp edges of layered plastic extruded from a 3D printer rubbing against their face.

My total spend for all that came to just under $180.

Before you break out the soldering iron and fire up your 3D printer, I suggest you start with a breadboard and some patch wires. Wiring on this project is on the simple side, but trust me when I say it will be much easier to figure out why your firmware isn’t flashing with a few components on your workbench than when they’re all crammed inside a headset.

I won’t include all the wiring details here, as it’s best to follow the guide in the GitHub above, but in general, you need to connect your IMU to your Arduino to provide both power and data.

You can also optionally connect the display controller to the Arduino for power, as suggested in the video above. That’s what I did for my testing, but be advised, this isn’t necessarily a good idea given the power requirements of the displays vs. the capabilities of the Arduino. You’re better off running a separate USB cable to the display or a USB splitter inside the headset.

Once you’ve wired everything and powered it on successfully, you’re ready to start with the software.

Flashing the firmware to the Arduino should be the easy part, but this is when things started falling apart for me. In theory, you install the Arduino IDE on your desktop, download the FastIMU project, connect your Arduino via USB, and then click compile. Easy.

Mine just kept failing. I got a basic error message, e:-1, again and again. After a bit of research and tinkering, I finally figured it out, and the news wasn’t good.

Although I ordered and paid for a GY-91 with an onboard 9250 IMU, and that’s what it identified as, in actuality, it was a basic, cheaper 6500 IMU, one that lacks the magnetometer.

As I learned (the hard way), this is a disconcertingly commonplace experience. Many shady electronics companies are happy to sell you the wrong component for the wrong price. The two devices are compatible and operate much the same way, but without the magnetometer, tracking performance drops substantially.

Once I updated the code to reference the 6500 I had and not the 9250 I thought I had, everything flashed beautifully, and I was instantly up and running. I calibrated my IMU through the Arduino IDE, and I was ready for final assembly.

You can find various shells online for custom VR headsets, many of which are designed to accommodate this specific set of boards used in Relativty. I decided to use CNCDan’s files, as it looked like a clean and clever design, even allowing for adjustment of the distance between displays, known as interpupillary distance, or IPD.

That makes for a complicated assembly process, requiring numerous printed parts, a handful of threaded receivers melted therein, plus rods and screws to hold it together. You’ll also need a pair of eye boxes, each one holding a lens on one side and the display on the other.

This was where I made a painful mistake. The design’s eye boxes contain small clips, and the instructions suggest you just pop the displays in there.

This is not what you should do. The exposed LCDs are extremely fragile, and by clipping them in, I managed to break both. The small amount of pressure required was enough to shatter them, and the damage was invisible until I turned them on.

Given that, I highly recommend modifying those boxes, either by printing them without the clips or by breaking them off after the print is complete. I used a few strips of thin painter’s tape to hold mine in place.

With all the wires jammed into place, I screwed the headset together, stuck on the face pad, threaded on the head strap, and proceeded to spend about five minutes trying to get a comfortable fit. I never quite succeeded.

I booted into SteamVR’s living lounge space and was immediately discombobulated. For one thing, I was staring straight at the floor. For another, turning my head just sent the view spinning in different directions in a way that quickly threatened nausea.

I had forgotten to recalibrate the headset after mounting all the components, and my cut-rate IMU was now oriented differently than it had been when it was on my workbench.

After recalibrating and a little more firmware fiddling, I got back into SteamVR’s setup room and could tell I still had a problem. Holding my head perfectly still, I could see the perspective slowly spinning.

Additionally, the IMU axes seemed slightly crossed, so the perspective change didn’t quite match my head movement. I verified the IMU was mounted correctly in the case and recalibrated a few times with no improvement.

I soldiered on, booting into iRacing, my favorite SteamVR-compatible racing sim. Before I was even out of the pits, my perspective was drifting. I mapped the recenter view command to a button on my steering wheel, and had to reach for it quite often.

Still, the image quality was not nearly as bad as I expected. Those cheap plastic lenses work surprisingly well, and though I could make out the pixels on the displays (the dreaded “screen door” effect of VR), it didn’t bother me. Brightness and contrast were more than adequate, and the refresh rate of 60 Hz was enough for casual practice.

But sensor drift and headset comfort were real issues. Without a proper cable-routing solution, the headset kept tugging to one side, and despite the padding, it was smashing my nose and cheeks.

I’ve done hourslong endurance races in multiple mass-market VR headsets. After 15 minutes in this one, I was ready to quit.

My total outlay for this project was $239.93. But that includes the extra $62 I had to spend on a second set of displays. Avoid that expensive gaffe, and you’re looking at around $180 in components.

That makes it roughly half the cost of a Meta Quest 3S, one of the cheapest headsets on the market right now. That’s a substantial savings, but I’d certainly recommend that most people pay the extra. The tracking issues in my headset are maddening, the image quality is middling at best, and this is far and away the least comfortable headset I’ve ever worn.

All that can be fixed, though. Some projects use a MinIMU-9 IMU, which looks miles more accurate and is less likely to be faked, but it’s also substantially more expensive at $35. You can also step up to higher-quality LCDs or even tiny OLED panels that come with all the color and contrast you could ever want. There are options for onboard battery packs, wireless adapters, and of course you can spend as much time as you like designing an ultra-comfortable housing for it all.

But even if you ignore the time commitment, once you start adding those upgrades, you’re not far from the cost of that Quest, a far-from-perfect headset that still works effortlessly and comfortably out of the box.

As always with these projects, it depends on what you want. If you just want a cheap, easy, reliable headset for your next-gen immersive gaming fix, this probably isn’t it.

If, however, you want a fun project that will help you appreciate the industrial design required to make a good-looking and comfortable wearable device, this could be it. I learned a lot and, despite the frustrations, I’m glad I embarked on this journey.

That said, while I’ll keep tinkering and likely throw a few more upgrades at this thing, I can’t see it replacing my other headset for regular racing duties, deprecated though it may be.

Amazon has over 1 million robot workers. What’s next for human employees?

Ars Technica Long form October 12, 2026

The second-largest corporate employer has bet big on robot workers to scale.

No organization in the world operates more robots than Amazon. The company already has more than 1 million robots working in warehouses around the clock to make tens of millions of same-day and one-day package deliveries happen on a daily basis—and Amazon is poised to significantly grow that robotic fleet in the coming years as it establishes new factories to churn out increasingly more capable robot workers.

Despite deploying so many robots, Amazon is also the second-largest corporate employer in the world, with more than 1.5 million full-time and part-time human workers, according to its 2025 annual report. Amazon executives say that the growing robot fleet has eased the burden on its human workforce by taking on the toughest fulfillment center tasks that carry the greatest risks of physical fatigue and injury. But labor advocacy groups and independent researchers point to evidence suggesting that warehouse automation driven by AI is not all upside for the humans who work alongside robots.

“For the last 100 years, most of the automation that we’ve seen usually happens away from workers—you’re taking that high-risk task away from the worker, and you’re doing so in a way that is not physically proximate,” Brad Greenwood, professor of business at George Mason University, told Ars. “The rise of collaborative robots really changes that dynamic for two reasons: one is that it is physically proximate, and two, the robot has the ability to dictate the pace of work.”

In many ways, robotics and AI are well suited to the relentless pace of work that is already happening inside e-commerce fulfillment centers. Amazon’s promise of speedy deliveries for its 200 million Prime subscribers in particular requires hundreds of thousands of human employees to speedily assemble and ship out customer orders that often combine a dizzying array of products.

Much of the work in fulfillment centers also frequently involves “dull, dirty and dangerous” tasks that people may prefer to hand over to robots. The injury and illness rate for workers in the US warehouse sector has typically been more than double the average across all industries, according to the US Occupational Safety and Health Administration.

“You have almost 2 million people working in the warehousing sector in the United States, and it’s characterized by very high turnover and very high workplace injury rates,” said Greenwood.

But robots are still far from capable of handling the many different tasks that human workers can perform. So Amazon still has a massive human workforce working in tandem with the company’s growing fleet of wheeled robots and robotic arms—and workplaces can get complicated when humans are expected to keep pace with robotic counterparts.

Amazon has rapidly built its robotic fleet following the pivotal decision to acquire the robotics company Kiva Systems in 2012. Kiva was among the earliest companies to pioneer wheeled mobile robots that bring racks of items to warehouse workers, instead of requiring people to continually walk around grabbing items off of shelves inside fulfillment centers.

Since the acquisition, Kiva was renamed Amazon Robotics and has focused on deploying an array of mobile robots and robotic arms that Amazon primarily manufactures in-house at facilities in Massachusetts. This year, the company also announced it would build additional production factories in Austin, Texas, and Greenwood, Indiana, to churn out even more robots in the future.

“There’s a theme of how we look at the challenges that we can help our associates and our employees with, and how we can make our customers’ lives better through these technologies,” Scott Dresser, vice president of Amazon Robotics, told Ars. “Each step of the way, [we are] tackling a hard or deep set of technical challenges to achieve that goal.”

Most of Amazon’s million-robot fleet still consists of those wheeled mobile robots. The company claims that its robotic Sequoia system can identify and store items up to 75 percent faster at fulfillment centers by coordinating swarms of such robots. Hercules and Titan robots, the size of a pool table or a baby grand piano, respectively, roam warehouse aisles to retrieve tall fabric shelving units called pods packed with plastic tote crates and bring them to human employees at various workstations.

Such mobile robots typically follow grid lines of stickers laid out on the floor and stay within fenced-in areas away from human employees. But the newest mobile robot, called Proteus, has sensors that allow it to operate safely around humans and other objects in a more free-roaming role.

Those swarms of mobile robots traveling through narrow lanes between rows of storage pods can also sometimes create robotic traffic jams. That is why Amazon began coordinating its robots using a suite of AI foundation models collectively named DeepFleet, which can help predict potential robot congestion ahead of time.

More recently, Amazon has been deploying a growing number of robotic arms that can grab items stowed high up inside inventory pods, sort packages and place them in carts or on top of mobile robots, and handle the many different individual products that Amazon customers order when shopping online.

The company expects to more than double its existing fleet of robotic arms this year, according to Amazon CFO Brian Olsavsky in a July earnings call. When Ars sought clarification, Dresser described the current number of deployed robotic arms as being in the single-digit thousands.

Amazon first bought third-party robotic arms to help lift and stack heavy pallets and bins inside its fulfillment centers. But the first robotic arm developed in-house by Amazon Robotics to sort individual mailer envelopes and boxes from cluttered piles, called Robin, began testing in 2021 before debuting at a facility in Lakeland, Florida, in 2022.

“With Robin, it was really that first attempt at taking a number of customer orders all in a jumble and building the advanced robotics to identify the items in that scene, to strategize on how to pick them up and build a motion plan that would be successful in placing it down on one of our mobile drive units,” Dresser explained.

The robotic arm uses eight suction cups to pick up individual packages. But before it takes any action, the robot’s software analyzes a top-down view of the conveyor belt cluttered with packages and quickly ranks possible picking actions.

In a 2023 research paper, the Amazon Robotics team described having developed several picking strategies for the robots to follow early on—but each had its own limitations. One strategy that prioritized picking larger packages encountered challenges when smaller packages lay on top of or overlapped with larger ones. Another strategy that favored picking up packages near the top of piles would fail in practice to retrieve “unreachable picks” and partially buried packages.

Improvements came from replacing such hand-crafted algorithms with an AI approach known as machine learning. The machine learning model initially trained on more than 394,000 picking actions from deployed robotic arms to estimate pick probabilities of success, and then used an online pick ranker to prioritize optimal actions for the Robin robots.

The best machine-learning method in that trial achieved a 93.73 percent success rate compared to 92.28 percent success for the best-performing traditional algorithm. That may seem trivial at first glance, but it meant the machine-learning method resulted in about 16,500 fewer failed picks than the traditional method during a work period involving more than 1 million total picks. That matters for an operation like Amazon’s that prioritizes speed and efficiency at scale.

The Amazon Robotics team further showed how such a machine-learning method could reduce the failed pick rate by 20 percent during an experiment involving 2 million picks by robotic workstations set up to resemble the operations of Amazon’s Robin fleet. They presented this work at the International Symposium on Experimental Robotics in July 2025.

Next up was Cardinal, a robotic arm that can place packages weighing up to 50 pounds into wheeled carts that are eventually brought to Amazon trucks waiting in loading docks. These robots first began operating at a facility in Nashville, Tennessee, in November 2022.

“Think of it as a game of Tetris: You’re sorting packages, and you’re placing them into the cart, and you want to be able to pack that as densely as you possibly can,” Dresser told Ars. “Dense containers are great from a sustainability perspective and from a transportation cost perspective.”

Cardinal built on lessons learned from Robin’s development in picking up and manipulating packages, while adding the capability to densely pack customer orders into the carts. Amazon has just started to deploy Cardinal in larger numbers and will continue to do so over the next several years, Dresser said.

Robin and Cardinal can handle several dozen package variations. But the newer Sparrow robotic arm was developed to tackle an even more challenging task—handling the hundreds of millions of products of varying shapes and sizes that can go into customer orders.

Specifically, Sparrow focuses on consolidating items from partially filled container-size totes to create densely packed totes. When items get picked out as customer orders are being fulfilled, Sparrow continually refills the totes.

“When we think about how AI applies to the physical space in robotics, Sparrow was really the first place where we truly deployed foundation models that enabled us to deal with that high diversity of products,” Dresser told Ars.

Such foundation models have helped the Amazon Robotics team to efficiently identify and classify those hundreds of millions of items to develop new robotic strategies for grasping them, Dresser explained. They also eliminated the need for manually coding every single item.

More recently, the Amazon Robotics team has created a foundation model for robotic perception that can handle new, never-before-seen products that may end up in Amazon fulfillment centers. The team also developed a generalized action model compatible with different types of robotic arms that may use varying combinations of suction and finger grasping.

“If you need to build ad hoc perception models for every such task and embodiment, that just doesn’t scale,” Kapil Katyal, a senior applied science manager at Amazon Robotics, said during a presentation attended by Ars at the Intelligent Robots & Systems conference held in Pittsburgh on September 29.

“So one of the initiatives we took up in our team was to design a foundation model which could work for any new embodiment of robots that we deploy, and across all of the perception tasks that we need to perform over those,” Katyal said.

Most of the robotic arms have relied primarily on vision. But Amazon’s newest robotic arm, Vulcan, is the first to combine vision with force feedback sensors capable of providing a sense of touch. This enables the robot to accurately pick out or stow away items within the fabric-covered inventory pods.

“You need to be able to insert an item, create space, or pull something out,” Dresser said. “Those are really hard things to do with traditional non-touch-based systems today, like the suction-based systems that are part of Sparrow.”

Vulcan initially began operating at Amazon fulfillment centers in Spokane, Washington, and Hamburg, Germany, starting in 2025. It is not widely deployed yet, but Dresser said the company expects to scale up use of this robotic arm in 2027.

Each new robot has benefited Amazon’s human workforce, according to the company. For example, Vulcan focuses on picking and stowing items located in the top rows of inventory pods that would otherwise require a person to use a step-ladder, along with handling items located just above the floor. That enables employees to focus on picking and stowing items that are within more comfortable reach.

But investigations by labor advocacy groups, journalists, and the US Congress have painted a less rosy picture of Amazon’s automation drive over the years. The Strategic Organizing Center (SOC), a coalition of trade unions headquartered in Washington, DC, published reports in May 2021 and April 2022 showing higher injury rates at Amazon’s robotic warehouses compared to non-robotic warehouses. That analysis drew on injury data reported by companies to the US government from 2017 through 2020.

“Amazon likes to talk about its latest robots because it doesn’t want to talk about the tens of thousands of Amazon workers who are injured every year due to Amazon’s obsession with maximizing speed and minimizing costs,” Joan Moriarty, director of strategic research and Campaigns at SOC, said in an email to Ars.

The organization also gathered nearly 1,000 responses from Amazon workers in an online survey conducted in February 2021. “Workers consistently report that the presence of robots increases the pace of work expected in Amazon facilities, forcing them to make fast, repetitive motions, substantially increasing the risk of injury,” Moriarty said.

The US Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) also conducted a 2024 investigation led by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt). The committee’s report noted how Amazon’s internal data also suggested a link between robotic productivity and increased pressure on human workers, leading to higher injury rates.

Amazon has described these reports as flawed and being reliant on older data predating the deployment of its most modern robots, including the robotic arms that became operational over the past several years. The company also touted improvements in its overall workplace injury rates without detailing any potential differences between robotic and non-automated warehouses.

“All of these claims ignore the fact that since 2019 our Global Recordable Incident Rate has improved 43 percent and our Global Lost Time Incident rate, which includes the most serious injuries that require employees to take time away from work, has improved 70 percent,” an Amazon spokesperson told Ars. “Our consistent year-over-year improvements have worked in parallel with our robotics growth across our operations network.”

The most nuanced findings on Amazon’s automation drive may come from a research study published in the journal ILR Review in April 2025. That analysis showed Amazon’s robotic warehouses had a 40 percent decrease in severe injuries compared to legacy fulfillment centers—which suggests some benefits from having robots take on the most physically challenging and risky tasks.

However, the same study also found that robotic fulfillment centers had a 77 percent increase in less severe injuries associated with physical strain from repetitive motions.

“At least one of the mechanisms by which this appears to be manifesting is through the pace of work, in that pick rates for the robotic fulfillment centers are off the charts higher,” said Greenwood at George Mason University, who was one of the paper’s coauthors.

A faster pace of work driven by partial automation could mean “the robot is dictating the pace of work” and spurring human employees to perform certain repetitive actions more quickly, Greenwood told Ars. “That appears to be what’s driving the strains and the sprains that we observe,” he said.

The study drew in part on Amazon company data obtained by journalists at Reveal and The Center for Investigative Reporting, covering weekly data at more than 150 Amazon warehouses from 2016 through 2019. Although the data is older, Greenwood said the findings are still relevant to Amazon’s ongoing automation efforts.

“I haven’t seen a tremendous amount of evidence to suggest that these dynamics are changing, inasmuch as you still have a tremendous amount of turnover in the warehousing context—and that’s not just Amazon,” Greenwood said.

Greenwood and his colleagues also analyzed online comments posted on Reddit by Amazon fulfillment center employees. In those comments, Amazon employees described work at robotic fulfillment centers as being less physically stressful but also mentally exhausting because of the physical repetitiveness and faster pace associated with higher productivity expectations.

An obvious question is whether automation efforts by Amazon and other companies will end up replacing some potential human hires with robots. For its part, Amazon has touted the robotics push as providing new job opportunities for human employees. Fulfillment centers with advanced robotics typically require 30 percent more employees working in reliability, maintenance, and engineering roles, and the new facilities for manufacturing additional robots will also supposedly bring more than 300 jobs each.

“As we recognize that each of these robotics [developments] can change the nature of work, we’re providing opportunities for our employees to upskill and learn some of these things,” said Dresser at Amazon Robotics. “We’ve actually increased the number of robotic maintenance technicians that we have in the network by over 30 percent, and that is a much higher-skilled, higher-compensated job.”

The company has also described its automation efforts as going hand in hand with a growing business that needs more human employees. “As we’ve deployed robots over the past decade, we’ve seen our operational footprint grow, creating hundreds of thousands of jobs as we expanded our network,” the Amazon spokesperson told Ars.

However, there are apparently internal discussions within Amazon about robots potentially reducing the need to hire humans. In October 2025, The New York Times reported on internal strategy documents suggesting that the robotics push could allow the company to reduce projected hiring needs in the United States by more than 160,000 people by 2027 and 600,000 people by 2033. (An Amazon spokesperson responded at the time by saying the documents reflected the views of just one group inside the company.)

Even as Amazon looks to build out its robotic fleet beyond the million-robot mark, discussions about the company’s workplace safety and working conditions are unlikely to go away. Although just a very small fraction of Amazon’s hundreds of thousands of employees have unionized in the United States, labor unions have “traditionally served a very good role in terms of improving worker safety,” Greenwood said.

“Now, obviously, I understand that firms are not always excited to engage in that conversation, and I can’t say that would solve the problem here,” Greenwood told Ars. “But developing a better relationship between management and labor is usually the best path forward to try to figure out how to reduce these injury rates, which would have benefits for Amazon as well.”

The first Amazon Labor Union that was organized among workers at a warehouse in Staten Island, New York, in April 2022, has been pushing what it describes as a Safety Bill of Rights that outlines changes it would like to see to make their workplace safer. The image that accompanies the document declares: “We are not robots.”

This story was updated on October 13, 2026 to correct the name of Brad Greenwood.
