Israel's election deadlock is a sign of the country's deep divisions

BBC News Wed, 28 Oct 2026 20:53:02 GMT

"Democracy is the worst form of government except for all those other forms that have been tried." So said Winston Churchill in the House of Commons in 1947.

His aphorism came to mind as Israel's election results filtered through on Tuesday night - exit polls blending with ballots that were cast to dash or fulfil people's hopes and fears.

This election has, in some ways, been a celebration of democracy. Voters turning out in record numbers, Jews and Arabs alike. Many spent thousands to fly in from abroad to cast their ballot.

At polling stations across the country, we saw the passion of campaigners, as they used every minute to try to change that last mind and win that last vote.

President Isaac Herzog said the election was a "badge of honour" for Israeli society. "It is remarkable to see how deep the desire for democracy is in Israel," he exclaimed.

Yet this election left the most established democracy in the Middle East without a clear path to a new government. It produced an inconclusive result where neither opposing bloc will have a majority in parliament.

Some might say this was business as usual.

Israel has never had a one-party government. Its fragmented, proportional representation system is almost designed to govern by coalition.

Yet many commentators warned this election had revealed the fundamental and perhaps growing divisions that scar this nation. This was not a plebiscite in which an electorate united around a single cause.

Some of these fissures are not new. There were divisions over judicial reforms that led to mass demonstrations in the early years of this government.

There were also divisions over how to respond to the deadly 7 October 2023 attacks - whether to save hostages or destroy Hamas. The casualties suffered by Israeli reservists in the fighting in Gaza that followed deepened tensions over the exemption of ultra-Orthodox young men from military service.

But has this election put in even sharper contrast the deep fault-lines that lie within Israeli society?

There are the tensions between the religious and the secular, divides not just of faith but of society.

Should Israel's government subsidise religious study? Should some parents sacrifice their sons and daughters to defend Israel when others do not? The ultra-Orthodox now make up almost 15% of the population. Their world-view is poles apart from that of denizens of high-tech, modern neighbourhoods of Tel Aviv.

There are divisions over fundamental politics.

Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party suffered significant losses, but is still on track to be the largest in the Knesset. All this for a prime minister accused of corruption, which he denies; a leader also accused of failing to protect Israel before 7 October, something he will not allow to be investigated.

Some 10% of voters backed the Jewish supremacist far-right: politicians like Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who even as results were being announced was promising to establish Jewish settlements in Gaza.

The Arab parties, which represent about a fifth of Israeli citizens, made huge gains, winning some 15% of the vote, potentially giving them seats numbering in the high teens.

And then there was the opposition bloc, a mix of centre, left and right led by Gadi Eisenkot who fell short of winning the change they wanted - change that many believed was existential for the future of this country.

How these vastly diverging views coalesce into some form of government is now the unenviable task facing Israel's body politic - the choices and compromises they may have to make could involve fundamental decisions about the country's future.

Would Netanyahu be ready to abandon his religious allies and form a coalition with right-wingers from the opposition bloc? Would they be ready to swallow their hostility towards the prime minister and sit in his government?

Is the opposition bloc ready to abandon much of its campaign promises and co-operate with Arab parties to force Netanyahu out of office? Are the Arab parties ready to risk joining a government that could fall within months?

Yair Golan, the left-wing Democrat leader, urged the opposition bloc to form a partnership with Arab parties. "We must no longer accept Netanyahu's racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes," he said.

But are the people of Israel ready for such a reality?

Amit Segal, an Israeli commentator sympathetic towards Netanyahu, said the high turnout among Arab Israeli voters "reminded Jews on both sides that, after years of division, they may have to learn to sit together after all".

The risk is that this election, instead of putting Israel on a new path, has instead raised further doubts about what it is that unites its citizens. What are the common factors that bind this complex, varied collection of peoples into one polity?

Autocratic governments, which are growing in number, have long criticised democracies for producing weak and temporary governments, often fragile coalitions that struggle to hold together, let alone deliver what the people wanted.

Israel may now struggle for months to form a government. It might even fail and have to hold another election.

President Herzog acknowledged this risk head on as he prepared to open coalition negotiations: "We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections."

For years, Israel has focused on defending itself against its external enemies. But must it also now be ready to defend itself from perils within, if the divisions writ large by this election become unmanageable?

In another speech, Churchill once said democracy was not just "insurance against dangers from abroad". It was also, he added, "insurance against dangers scarcely less grave and much more near and constant which threaten us here at home".

Can Israel's democracy live up to this challenge?

Netanyahu's bloc leading Israel election but short of majority, partial results show

BBC News Wed, 28 Oct 2026 20:24:39 GMT

Partial results from Israel's general election show veteran Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is leading his rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, but is still short of a majority in parliament.

With 85% of ballots counted, Netanyahu's Likud party and its far-right and ultra-Orthodox Jewish allies were on track to win 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset. Eisenkot's Yashar party and three other Jewish opposition parties in his bloc were set for 48.

Both leaders have said they will try to form a governing coalition.

Arab-led parties, who are on course to win an unprecedented 19 seats, could emerge as kingmakers, but all but one of the Jewish parties have pledged not to work with them.

With between 430,000 and 480,000 absentee ballots from groups including soldiers, diplomats and hospital patients yet to be counted, it could still take a day or two for the final election results to emerge.

Once they are confirmed, President Isaac Herzog will hold consultations with all the political factions and invite the leader whom he believes has the best chance of success to form a government - a process that could take weeks.

If they fail, then ultimately there would have to be another election.

During a meeting at his residence in Jerusalem, Herzog praised the 77.7% turnout in Tuesday's election, which was the country's highest in more than two decades.

"It is a badge of honour for Israeli society, and it was remarkable to see how deep the desire for democracy is in Israel," he said.

He added that he expected to receive the official results next week, after which he would begin discussions with every faction.

"We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections. So, I expect everyone who comes here to come with an open mind."

Both the prime minister and his main rival have insisted that they should be tasked with forming a governing coalition.

Eisenkot declared that the public had "spoken in favour of change", after initial exit polls published by three Israeli broadcasters projected that his "Change Bloc" would emerge with between 52 and 53 seats in the Knesset, compared to 50 seats for Netanyahu's bloc.

"The coalition of failure has lost the people's trust," he told supporters at Yashar's election headquarters in Tel Aviv. "I will work with my partners to ensure that the people's decision is translated into a Zionist government."

Later, the broadcasters updated their exit polls, with two projecting that the rival blocs would be tied on 51 seats and one giving Netanyahu's bloc a narrow three-seat lead.

Netanyahu then appeared at Likud's headquarters in Jerusalem and declared that his right-wing bloc had won a "great majority".

"We must put in place a strong right-wing national government," he said. "It is forbidden, simply forbidden, to endanger Israel by forming a government that relies on anti-Zionist Arab parties."

As the votes were counted on Wednesday, it emerged that his bloc had done better than the exit polls predicted and was on course to win 53 seats. However, that figure is 15 seats fewer than it had once controlled in the last Knesset.

Tuesday's election was the first since the deadly Hamas-led attacks on Israel on 7 October 2023 and the wars that followed in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.

It was also seen by Israelis as one of the most consequential in the country's history, because it could decide not just their leadership but whether the country continues on its current hard-line, religious-nationalist trajectory.

Key campaign issues included accountability for the security failures that led to the 7 October attacks, the conduct of regional wars, conscripting ultra-Orthodox Jewish men into the military, judicial reforms and Israel's international standing.

Avigail Levine from Kfar Saba, who voted for former prime minister Naftali Bennett's opposition Beyachad party, told the BBC that she was disappointed with the election results.

"I was hoping for new leadership. I feel we need it as a nation," she said. "The people in power on 7 October should not be in power now."

She said people were frustrated that Netanyahu had not shouldered responsibility for what happened three years ago, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage. Her husband's grandmother was among those who died in Kibbutz Be'eri.

Gal from Ramat Gan said he voted for Netanyahu because Israelis "cannot relax and live in peace with neighbours when all they want is to erase us from the map".

He also said he was "afraid of the strengthening of the Arab political parties".

Likud complained on Wednesday that they had "stolen" the election. It alleged that they had resorted to "bribery, threats, violence, fraud and the use of prohibited software to encourage voters", without providing any evidence. The Central Elections Committee said it would examine the claims as part of a post-election review.

The two Arab parties - the United Arab List and the Joint List - are set to almost double their representation because of a surge in turnout among Arab Israelis, who account for about a fifth of the population and often describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel.

Mahdi Kabaha from the Arab-majority city of Umm al-Fahm, who campaigned to get out the Arab vote, described the result as "historic".

"Arab citizens came out and said clearly: we want a real say in this country," he said.

The head of the Joint List, Yousef Jabareen, told the BBC that Arab voters had been motivated in part by the opportunity to remove far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir from office, whom he accused of racism and "provocation against our community".

Ben-Gvir, the leader of the Jewish Power party, has called for the annexation of the occupied West Bank, Jewish settlement of Gaza, and the "voluntary emigration" of Palestinians. Several Western countries have imposed sanctions on him for incitement against Palestinians.

United Arab List leader Mansour Abbas, who served in a short-lived governing coalition formed after the 2021 elections, said on Tuesday night that he hoped "the numbers will work out and we, the Change Bloc and the UAL, can ensure that there are 61 Knesset seats".

The leader of the left-wing Democrats party, Yair Golan, told his partners in Eisenkot's bloc that there was an "opportunity to form a change government in partnership" with the Arab parties and replace Netanyahu's coalition.

"We have no future here if we don't stop being afraid. And if we don't put an end to racism," he wrote on X.

Eisenkot has previously raised objections or attached conditions to that kind of alliance, including recognising Israel as Jewish and democratic, and Hamas as a terrorist organisation that must be destroyed. The right-wing parties in his bloc, meanwhile, have flatly rejected it.

"The opposition parties cannot dictate any conditions," Jabareen said. "If the opposition in Israel are willing to afford real and substantive change, and an alternative for the dangerous, extreme-right-wing government... they will have to negotiate with us."

Flávio Bolsonaro lands in Miami after defeat in Brazil's presidential election

BBC News Wed, 28 Oct 2026 20:22:49 GMT

Brazilian Senator Flávio Bolsonaro has flown to Miami after losing the country's presidential election on Sunday.

His arrival in Florida ends days of confusion over his whereabouts, after he was reported to have travelled to Argentina, and then prematurely reported to have already entered the US on Tuesday.

The US has said it would grant visas to Bolsonaro and his family, who travelled with him. Brazil cancelled his passport, after he failed to surrender it to authorities, due to an ongoing criminal investigation. He has denied any wrongdoing.

In a statement, Bolsonaro cast himself "as the true elected president of Brazil", and thanked the American government for granting entry to his family.

Newly reelected President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has criticised the departure, saying "those who have nothing to hide have nothing to fear".

In a statement, distributed by the right-wing Brazilian influencer Paulo Figueiredo, Bolsonaro thanked both the presidents of Argentina and the US, and the American public "who share the same values ​​as the good people of my own country".

"It was never my intention to leave my homeland, but I know exactly where this is heading," he said.

He repeated unfounded allegations of "electoral fraud" which he said allowed a "mathematical impossibility" to occur in the election.

He called himself a victim of a coup d'état and political persecution, and said his travel to the US was to protect his family.

"I want to tell not only my 60 million voters, but the entire Brazilian people, that I am the elected president," he alleged.

"The criminals who stole Brazil's election are part of a criminal organization that has established a tyranny."

After Bolsonaro won the first round of Brazil's election, Lula won the second round by more than four million votes, which was attributed to significantly higher turnout, and swaying more undecided voters.

The result was confirmed by the president of Brazil's top electoral court, himself appointed by Jair Bolsonaro. He said that an extension to voting hours did not impact the count or result.

Speculation about Bolsonaro's whereabouts was first triggered by a report on an Argentine news site, which claimed that he had crossed the land border between Brazil and Argentina and then boarded a private plane en route to the US.

Brazilian police took the rumours seriously. Early on Tuesday, they checked border crossings but found no evidence that Bolsonaro had left the country, and Argentine officials said they had no reports of him crossing.

For a little while, it seemed like Bolsonaro may just be keeping an uncharacteristically low profile after being unexpectedly beaten by his left-wing rival in the presidential run-off vote on Sunday.

When he failed to surrender his passports in time to meet a 24-hour deadline, Brazilian authorities cancelled the documents and ordered police to make checks at border posts.

With Bolsonaro's lawyers saying they did not know where he was, speculation quickly grew again that he might have left the country.

Then, several sources told the BBC and other broadcasters he was on his way to the US.

The US State Department confirmed that it would issue Bolsonaro and his family visas to enter the country.

There were even reports that he had already landed. BBC Brasil and BBC Mundo were informed by three people close to the Bolsonaros that the senator had arrived in the US.

A cousin, who is close to Flávio Bolsonaro and his younger brother Eduardo, told BBC Brasil that the defeated right-wing candidate had arrived in Miami.

Another close aide to Eduardo Bolsonaro told BBC Mundo that Flávio was with his younger brother in Miami.

Neither Flávio nor Eduardo Bolsonaro could be reached directly for comment at the time.

Hours later, however, Argentine migration authorities posted a tweet saying that Flávio Bolsonaro, his wife, and two daughters had only just crossed into Argentina over land on Tuesday night local time.

At around the same time, US President Donald Trump told reporters who quizzed him over the matter: "I heard he was in Argentina."

Flight tracking data verified by the BBC suggested the Bolsonaros departed from Puerto Iguazú in Argentina at 12:18 local time (03:18 GMT) on Wednesday to head to Guayaquil in Ecuador.

After a brief stop, the same private jet took them to Miami-Opa Locka Executive Airport, where they were pictured disembarking just before 09:30 local time (13:30 GMT).

Photographers, who had been waiting for his arrival to finally put an end to all the speculation, swarmed around Bolsonaro as he left the airport in Miami, while his team tried to cover him with umbrellas.

Flávio Bolsonaro is not the first member of his family to travel to the United States.

His father, Jair Bolsonaro, also left Brazil for Florida in December 2022 before his successor, Lula, was inaugurated.

Jair was still in the US when his supporters stormed Brazil's government buildings and Supreme Court on 8 January. He later used his absence as part of his defence in his coup trial, which led to a conviction and 27-year sentence.

Eduardo Bolsonaro, meanwhile, has been living in Texas after taking leave from Brazil's Congress. While in the US, he lobbied officials there in an attempt to influence the coup trial of his father, which led to the US imposing punitive tariffs on Brazil and sanctions on key officials.

Eduardo was convicted in absentia over this by Brazil's highest court earlier this year.

It is not yet clear what Flávio Bolsonaro's ultimate destination will be, nor how long he plans to stay in the US.

He is the subject of two investigations currently pending before Brazil's Supreme Federal Court.

One is regarding possible irregularities in the transfer of nearly $70m (£53m) from private bank Banco Master to the film Dark Horse – a biopic about his father.

The second investigation relates to alleged money laundering, both of which Bolsonaro denies.

He is set to lose his parliamentary immunity on 31 January, when his eight-year Senate term ends.

What we now know about the UK economy in four charts

BBC News Wed, 28 Oct 2026 20:08:45 GMT

The UK may have no involvement in the US-Iran war, but the country is feeling the full force of the conflict on its economy.

Soaring energy prices are set to dent growth in the short term, push up inflation and leave living standards in a "grim" place, according to the latest official forecast from the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR).

Interest rates are also predicted to rise, making borrowing more expensive, along with government debt repayments.

Chancellor John Healey warned the nation faces "real challenges ahead" as he announced policies that he said would offer "breathing space" for households in the coming months.

"What we face today are global economic storms," he said. "We can't wish them away. We must choose the course we steer through them."

In its first assessment of the UK economy since the Middle East conflict started, the OBR said rising energy prices were the biggest risk to the economy in the near future.

Despite raising its growth forecast for this year, it sharply cut its prediction for next year from 1.6% to 1%.

Growth is then set to rebound in the following years.

When an economy grows, businesses tend to invest more, create more jobs and give pay rises to workers, which leaves people feeling better off on average, though it can take time and not everyone necessarily benefits.

Companies making higher profits also pay more in tax, which can enable the government to spend more on public services. When there is slow economic growth, or the economy shrinks, the opposite can occur.

Inflation can weigh on growth and the OBR has forecast that prices are set to rise at a faster pace as higher energy bills filter through supply chains and to consumers, especially in 2027.

High global oil prices have already hit drivers at the pumps, with petrol priced at almost £1.73 per litre on average, while diesel is near £1.99.

Elevated oil prices over time can lead to prices edging upwards across a host of goods, such as food, as companies pass on the higher expenses they face to consumers.

Goods are typically transported to destinations by lorries and vans, so high fuel prices can have far-reaching consequences.

The OBR now thinks inflation will stay higher for longer than previously forecast, peaking at 3.8% in 2027.

Despite the cost-of-living support announced by the government, economists at Pantheon Macroeconomics said the measures were "small beer given the surge in inflation we expect over the winter".

High inflation paints a bleak picture when it comes to living standards and the OBR has forecast a dip next year as energy bills hit the spending power of households.

Those on lower incomes are set to be hit harder, however, because energy costs eat up a bigger share of their monthly budget and disposable income.

Real household disposable income, a measure of living standards, is forecast to grow from 2027, but not by as much as previously thought.

"It's a pretty grim picture," according to the OBR's David Miles, who says there has been "virtually no growth" for individuals since before the Covid pandemic.

"It's been a dismal period in British economic history."

Inflation is expected to average 3.4% next year, before falling to the Bank of England's 2% target towards the end of the decade.

The Bank is widely expected to raise interest rates next week due to higher inflation in recent months. Rates are currently at 3.75%, but the OBR now forecasts they could rise to as high as 4.5% in the coming years.

It had previously forecast two interest rate cuts this year.

Higher rates makes borrowing money more expensive but can boost returns on savings.

Inflation also raises the cost of borrowing for the government, with spending on debt interest set to rise.

Such repayments are also predicted to increase the overall amount the government borrows, which is set to increase every year by more than had been previously forecast by the OBR.

Higher spending on welfare and pensions due to inflation is also expected to increase borrowing, though it is forecast to fall as a share of the economy over the next five years.

However, forecasts are only a best guess at what might happen in the future. Given the way the conflict in the Middle East has upended previous predictions, the future of the war could alter inflation expectations.

US President Donald Trump has suggested the war will end after the mid-term elections next month.

The OBR admitted there remained "significant uncertainty" around its predictions due to the changing situation in the Middle East.

What the Budget offers for under 25s - and what it leaves out

BBC News Wed, 28 Oct 2026 20:02:38 GMT

Chancellor John Healey has announced his Budget, which includes changes to minimum wage and help for people trying to get onto the housing ladder.

Here is how the Budget could affect you if you are under-25.

If you are an 18-to-20 year-old earning the minimum wage, your pay will go up by 3.9% from next April.

However, the increase may be lower than you had expected. That is because Healey reversed course on how his Labour predecessor, Rachel Reeves, had been increasing the minimum wage for young people.

Labour had promised to do away with "discriminatory age bands", with all adults entitled to the same minimum wage. This year, 18-20 year-olds will see the same increase as older workers, meaning the disparity will remain. So, for 18-to-20 year-olds, your pay will rise to £11.27, while over-20s will be paid a minimum of £13.21 an hour.

The increase also means a 21-year-old, who is working full time on the minimum wage and took out a student loan after 2023, will now earn enough to meet the £25,000 repayment threshold, over which they will start paying back 9% of their earnings.

The Budget contained plans to help people get onto the housing ladder, including the introduction of a "First Time Buyer Isa". This is an account in which savers can build up a deposit, with the government topping up contributions of up to £4,000 each year with a 25% bonus.

The new savings account will be introduced in 2029, replacing the existing Lifetime Isa, which has been criticised by some for imposing harsh penalties on those buying homes for more than the £450,000 cap.

The cap will remain, but the new "First Time Buyer Isa" will ensure savers are not penalised by losing their own money when making withdrawals. Savers will only lose contributions made by the government when making withdrawals which are not eligible for the account.

The penalty for withdrawals from existing Lifetime Isas will be lowered, too, to address concerns about savers being punished.

The government had already revealed a £4.7bn scheme for first-time buyers in England dubbed Your First Home. It is aiming to help 70,000 individuals and couples get on the housing ladder

The scheme will allow people to buy a new-build home with a deposit of 2.5%. It will provide them with a loan worth 20% of their property's value to help pay for the purchase.

Capped at £110,000 outside London and £140,000 in the capital, it is aimed at those hoping to get on the housing ladder without help from "the bank of mum and dad".

If you are a young person hoping to start a business in England, the Budget contained good news for you.

The chancellor wants to level the playing field for young entrepreneurs who have bright ideas, but who might not have the same family financial backing as others.

In an attempt to encourage more young people to start their own businesses, the government will pilot a "Young Entrepreneurs Allowance" in England.

The allowance will see your living costs partly covered by the government for the first year your business is operating. Healey hopes it will encourage more young people to take the plunge and become entrepreneurs.

Details of the scheme are thin at the moment, however, only that it will be rolled out "shortly".

If you are one of more than a million 18-to-24 year-olds not in employment, education or training (Neet), Wednesday's Budget may have been a frustrating watch.

The chancellor acknowledged the scale of the crisis facing young people, but said solutions would not come yet. Ministers are waiting on a series of recommendations from Alan Milburn, who has been looking into why so many young people are Neet in the UK.

Milburn has warned Britain is "at risk of a lost generation" due to the crisis, saying a "round of ammunition" is needed rather than a silver bullet. He will make recommendations to the government later this year.

Healey said he refused to write off young people during his Budget speech and the government was looking forward to Milburn's final report.

Another group left hanging were those with outstanding student loans, particularly the controversial Plan 2 loans taken out between 2012 and 2023 - which many fear they will never be able to pay off.

If you have student loans, the government has said it is looking at ways to reform the repayment system. But action was not forthcoming at the Budget, despite expectations in the run up that the issue might be addressed.

After the statement, Chief Secretary to the Treasury Emma Reynolds said the loan repayment system is "under review".

"We inherited a system that is difficult and unfair on young people, but we weren't able to move on that today," she told the BBC.

Dharshini David: Healey buys himself some time, but big questions still unanswered

BBC News Wed, 28 Oct 2026 19:51:01 GMT

John Healey talked of charting a new course for Britain, but this Budget was more about course-correcting than charging down a new path.

It was abundantly clear that the financial fallout from that conflict in the Middle East has hampered the finances of households and businesses – and the government's ability to help.

While the government targeted those impacted by higher energy and fuel bills, the "breathing space" it aimed to provide was limited; it is a pill that doesn't fully alleviate the pain.

The most telling evidence was that official forecasters predict that while earnings will rise, that is not compensating for higher prices and taxes.

Even after the extra help is taken into account, households' incomes after inflation and tax are set to be typically lower across the next two years than the start of the parliament. On that basis, it could be the second worse parliament for living standards, after the last one, since the 1950s - a sign of how far the war has blown prosperity off course.

But it can't be all be blamed on the war. Taxes haven't helped. Although there were few major measures aimed at households, the policy of previous chancellors of freezing the thresholds at which different rates of tax on income apply - fiscal drag - has been maintained in the background, scooping more money out of pay packets.

Overall, this Budget has the tax burden - the proportion of the nation's income going to the tax office - rising to a new historic high of 38.6%

However, a more generous package of help would have been hard to pull off. The impact of higher inflation and debt have increased borrowing costs by £14bn in the past year alone.

The Chancellor had to prove to the markets which lend the government money that he has a plan to bring down future debt to avoid those costs climbing further.

As it stands, debt interest repayments are due to be £160bn in 2032, more than double the amount spent on schools in England.

And the plans Healey has unveiled already eat into wiggle room he has within the public finances. He says he was right to do so - that's what such safety margins are there for - in times of strife. But the great uncertainty that remains made going further very risky. Energy prices remaining high, for example, could easily chew up all the spare cash.

So the result was what some have termed a beige, safe Budget. As Healey strove to prove his fiscally sound credentials, there wasn't even the customary rabbit pulled out of the hat, the end-of-speech sweetener.

The markets seem reassured – even if some of his tax raising plans involve clamping down on loopholes and those not paying the right tax, which is always highly uncertain.

So the chancellor appears to have bought himself some breathing space. But that means some big questions have been postponed until another day, not least on public services.

Higher-than-expected inflation may mean that if areas such as health and defence are prioritised, budgets for some other "unprotected" areas – justice and higher education for example – are set to lag behind inflation after 2028.

There was a hint too from John Healey that he'd tap into some of those budgets to help out defence spending. To maintain those budgets in 2030 would means finding tens of billions of pounds.

And issues around the other big area of spending – welfare – remain unresolved. Between 2025 and 2032, spending there is set to increase by £100bn.

The official forecasters also noted the rapid rise in sickness and disability caseloads since the start of the pandemic. They warn if that trend continued, spending on such benefits would rise by a further £13bn.

Any suggestion of welfare reform has been postponed until the forthcoming review into the plight of workless young people.

Then there's the issue of boosting growth. There was a bit more detail on the plans for devolution – but there is much to be fleshed out.

And on another key part of the growth strategy, housebuilding, there was disappointing news. Even though first-time buyers are set to get more help, their first home may be more elusive.

Between regulation and higher costs – in part, related to the war - the OBR estimates that 190,000 fewer homes will be built by 2032 compared to what it thought in March, a significant setback.

So the chancellor may have unveiled 98 (relatively small) measures but the to-do list gets longer.

With his official forecasters warning that, in a very uncertain world, his finances face exceptional risks, playing a wait-and-see game feels like a prudent move.

The risks go both ways: the OBR points out that a swift resolution to the war and an improvement in the economy could spell a significant boost to the public finances.

So the chancellor has more reason than most to keep his fingers crossed that happens rapidly.

For as it stands, the official forecasters say incomes after inflation, living standards, are set to be only 1% higher at the end of the decade than at the start.

A series of economic shocks outside out control could thwart plans to turbo-boost prosperity . And as today shows, breathing space only extends so far.

He said he would set out how the UK would reach the 3% target by 2030, as well as 3.5% of GDP by 2035, at next year's spending review.

Government departments have yet to decide what will be cut from their capital budgets.

Capital budgets are focused on long-term investments, rather than day-to-day spending. For example, earlier this year, when departments had to make capital budget cuts to fund the initial defence spending rise, a number of major road improvement schemes were scrapped.

Badenoch criticised Healey for not using his Budget to explain how he would boost defence funding to 3%.

"And today, I am getting work under way to get there in a fiscally sustainable way."

In addition to looking at public spending, Healey said he also wanted to use "more innovative financing alongside the private sector and our international allies".

The chancellor said this would include:

The Office for Budget Responsibility estimates that the UK government's target to increase defence spending to 3.5% of GDP by 2035 will cost £35bn.

Helen Miller, director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said: "Increasing investment in defence companies may contribute to the target but it is unclear how much this will lead to an increase in UK defence capabilities.

"There is much further to go to get to 3% of GDP on defence and it is hard to believe that this government will want to get there without topping up spending totals."

In his Budget speech, Healey also announced £10bn of economic and military support for Ukraine, in the form of loans and export guarantees.

The funding includes £5.5bn of loans through World Bank guarantees and a grant contribution to the World Bank International Development Association's crisis facility.

A further £3bn will be made available to Ukraine through loans facilitated by UK Export Finance, a government export credit agency.

Healey told the House of Commons that the week had started with Russia launching a "brutal ballistic missile attack" and that the extra money would send "a clear message to Moscow".

Later on social media, Zelensky welcomed the money, saying: "Every step to strengthen Ukraine brings Russia closer to realising that it must end this war of its own making."

US civil rights leader Dolores Huerta dies aged 96

BBC News Wed, 28 Oct 2026 18:48:15 GMT

Pioneering US civil rights leader Dolores Huerta, who advocated for poor farm workers, has died at the age of 96, her family has announced.

The prominent labour organiser campaigned alongside fellow labour leader Cesar Chavez for farm workers' rights in the 1960s and 1970s, founding the transformative United Farm Workers Union (UFW) with him.

Huerta continued her advocacy work on immigration and voting issues through her foundation.

"As you can imagine, this is an incredibly difficult time for us, and we ask for privacy as we grieve this incredible loss to our family," family spokesman Erik Olvera said on Wednesday. The BBC has confirmed that Huerta died of cancer.

Born in New Mexico, Huerta grew up in Stockton, California, in the heart of the state's large agricultural industry. She was raised by her mother, who at one point worked at a cannery.

Huerta first became a teacher after graduating from university before turning to organising workers and shepherding the Chicano power movement. She became the emotional throughline of several revolutionary movements rallying for better wages, and living and working conditions for the poor.

She later worked on civil and women's rights and gender equality, as well as environmental issues, all while raising 11 children. She continued that work into her 90s.

"I would like to be remembered as a woman who cares for fellow humans," she is reported by multiple sources to have once said. "We must use our lives to make the world a better place to live, not just to acquire things. That is what we are put on the earth for."

Earlier this year, Huerta said Chavez, who died in 1993, had "manipulated and pressured" her into having sex and on another occasion forced her in the 1960s.

That was after the New York Times published an investigation detailing allegations from Huerta and two other women, who said Chavez groomed and sexually abused girls involved in the labour movement.

Huerta said the two encounters with Chavez resulted in pregnancies that she chose to keep secret, arranging for the children to be raised by other families.

Chavez's family said in a statement at the time that they were "devastated" by the reports and praised the women's "courage to come forward".

The UFW was among those paying tribute to Huerta, saying in a statement posted to social media that she had coined its motto - "Si Se Puede!", Spanish for "Yes, we can!" - which became a familiar rallying cry for activists seeking better working conditions for Hispanic farm workers.

"Her life's work was to empower her community to face and overcome injustices, and she has left farm workers and the entire Latino community stronger and more organised than she found it," the UFW said.

"Her commitment to civic engagement and bringing political power to disenfranchised people is a lesson we all should carry to the ballot box."

Huerta spent much of her life recruiting members to the union, protesting and picketing for various causes and helping negotiate the first farm worker contracts in North America.

Former US President Bill Clinton, who awarded Huerta the Eleanor Roosevelt Human Rights Award in 1998, said in a statement that he and former US Secretary of State Hillary Clinton "lost a dear friend" and that "we've all lost a stalwart champion of working Americans".

"To see her in action was to witness a living legend who never stopped pushing for progress and seeing every new obstacle as a fresh opportunity to educate, to organise, and to uplift—even as those efforts sometimes brought her grave consequences," Clinton said.

California Governor Gavin Newsom said on Wednesday that Huerta "represented the best of us". He praised her "resolute spirit, her passion for justice and fairness, and her commitment to those overlooked and forgotten".

Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass remembered Huerta as an "icon" and "fearless leader", who inspired many to activism and helped secure landmark protections nationwide.

Bass highlighted Huerta's work to amend laws to require overtime pay for farm workers after eight-hour days and her contributions to the first comprehensive standards to prevent heat deaths in California.

"Dolores reminded us that no matter the odds, no matter the obstacle, we can build a greater life for ourselves, our community, our city, and our country," she said.

Huerta also helped end what was known as the Bracero Program, where Mexican men were brought to work temporarily into the US, and helped negotiate the 1986 Immigration Reform Act, according to the union.

The president of the voting group Voto Latino, María Teresa Kumar, called Huerta a "civil rights giant" who gave "her entire life, until her final days, to championing and fighting injustice for everyone, no matter who they were or where they came from".

The Congressional Hispanic Caucus, made up of Democrats from the Senate and House of Representatives, said in a statement on Wednesday that "Dolores Huerta defied definition".

"A national and international icon, her legacy is woven into the fabric of our history," they also said. "Her fight for justice will continue to inspire generations. Rest in power, hermana."

Healey unveils £100 for energy bills and bank tax in first Budget

BBC News Wed, 28 Oct 2026 18:45:09 GMT

Millions of households will get £100 to help with soaring energy bills to be paid for by a tax on bank profits, John Healey has announced in his first Budget.

The chancellor said he wanted to give hard-pressed families "breathing space now" and "hope for the future" as the UK economy is battered by "global economic storms".

He also unveiled tax breaks to boost high street businesses - but confirmed that many big decisions, including on defence spending and welfare, will not be made until next year.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said Healey's plans were "not bold enough" and the government was "overspent, overborrowed, overtaxed and drowning in an out-of-control welfare system".

In an hour-long speech to a packed House of Commons, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham and other frontbench colleagues cheering him on, the chancellor unveiled a string of measures aimed at cutting the cost of living.

These include:

Healey increased the tax on the profits of big banks from 3% to 6%, which will last from January next year to April 2028, and increased taxes on high-stakes gambling machines.

As part of a package to help business, Healey increased the point at which High Street shops in England start paying business rates from £12,000 to £18,000, with vape shops and adult gaming centres excluded from the relief.

But he had little scope for big giveaways as the public finances remain stretched, with the UK set to spend £14bn more on debt interest payments this year.

Income tax thresholds will remain frozen and the tax on income from savings and property rental will rise to 24% for basic rate taxpayers from April 2027, after it had been scheduled to go up to 22%.

But a cut to the cash ISA allowance from £20,000 a year to £12,000, announced last year by Healey's predecessor Rachel Reeves, will be axed.

The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) downgraded its growth forecast for next year to 1%, with slightly higher increases predicted for subsequent years.

In its latest assessment, the OBR said British households were set to be little better off than before the Covid pandemic even a decade after Covid-19 hit, a situation the watchdog's boss David Miles described as "pretty grim".

In his Budget speech, Healey repeatedly stressed that the UK economy was being battered by "global uncertainties" and soaring oil prices caused by conflict in the Middle East.

"Those are the storms we face. We can't wish them away. We must choose the course we steer through them," he told MPs.

Healey also used his speech to announce plans to allow regional mayors to keep 20% of business rates and a share of income tax to spend on local priorities.

The aim was to allow mayors to retain 100% of business rates raised in their areas by the end of the decade, he added, in "the most radical act of devolution in a generation".

And he sought to address opposition claims the Labour government is unwilling to cut benefits, insisting that both he and Burnham were committed to bringing down the welfare bill in a "Labour way".

But he said no decisions would be taken until reviews by Alan Milburn, into young people not in work or training, and Stephen Timms, on Personal Independence Payments, had been published, with legislation to follow next year.

The £4.7bn black hole in the defence investment plan will be funded, the chancellor revealed, in part through taking money from capital budgets across Whitehall.

Healey said he will set out how the government plans to meet its commitment to spend 3% of the national income on defence by 2030, and 3.5% by 2035, at next year's spending review.

But Badenoch said he "should have set out a plan for 3% today," highlighting his claim when he resigned as Sir Keir Starmer's defence secretary in June that UK forces were at risk due to a lack of cash.

"So now he is the man who is increasing risk to personnel on operations, he is the man who is making our country less safe, he has failed his own test," the Conservative leader said.

"This is on him and no-one will ever forget. If he had any decency he would resign again today."

The Tory leader said that with the UK heading for a record tax burden and "spending more on debt interest than on the army and schools combined", Healey's Budget was "not good enough, not strong enough, not bold enough".

Helen Miller, director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said the Budget "has a raft of fiddly measures but very little that will move the dial on growth".

Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey said that until the government has "the courage" to fix the UK's trading relationship with the EU any Budget will just be "tinkering around the edges" and will not provide the growth the country needs.

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said the Budget was full of "little giveaways" but "doesn't overall do very much" and did not offer "anything of any value on defence whatsoever".

Healey also faced criticism from the left, with the general secretary of the Unite union, Sharon Graham describing the cost of living measures in the Budget as "baby steps".

"Scrapping standing charges on gas and a £100 energy payment for households in council tax bands, A to D, whilst welcome, will not touch the sides, when many forecasts show bills set to jump over £400 in January," she added.

Green Party leader Zack Polanski said it was a Budget "that betrays the future for young people and the planet they inherit".

He added: "The chancellor didn't mention climate once but praised bankers repeatedly."

Last week the 29-year-old became the first Welsh artist to top the UK singles chart in 15 years with the viral TikTok hit.

The singer, who is originally from Pontprennau in Cardiff, said his dreams had "come true" and life would "never be the same again" after a challenging few years in which he even had to give up on music for a time.

Miller made history when he became the first Welsh artist to top the singles chart since Sian Evans' feature on DJ Fresh's Louder.

He is also the first solo male Welsh artist in 41 years to top the singles chart, after Shakin' Stevens' 1985 timeless festive hit, Merry Christmas Everyone.

"It just doesn't feel real. To actually live my dreams the way that it's coming about right now," he said.

The song found fame on TikTok when actress Jennifer Love Hewitt posted videos featuring the track. But Miller said the "genuineness" of the track also made it stand out as his first song since his hiatus.

"I went through a really, really hard few years in my personal life, and I took two years off music," he said.

"There's a genuineness to how I sound in the song. The world's in a little bit of a dark place right now so maybe that's why it's made people come together."

Miller's song has shot him to stardom but, of course, life carries on as normal for his loved ones.

He said his parents were "finding it a bit mad" with his dad going back to work as an Uber driver in Cardiff.

"None of us know what's going on," he said.

He added: "It felt fulfilling to go up to her and say that I made something of myself.

"I've watched Strictly Come Dancing growing up and that's obviously been such a dream of mine to perform on the show."

Miller said now he wanted to "marry the two worlds of dancing and singing" in his career.

Babydoll led to a viral dance that has become synonymous with the song, but Miller said he was relaxed about his future hits, saying "if it becomes a trend, it becomes a trend".

After being depressed for a "long time", Miller said he was now feeling "genuine joy".

Addressing his fans, he added: "Thank you from the bottom of my heart for changing my life and giving me my dreams."

He is currently planning a world tour, and as a proud Welshman, he intends to put on some of the shows in Wales.

"It's really exciting. I'm definitely coming back to Cardiff baby."

Miller said he felt "weird" giving advice to his fans after his meteoric rise, but believes the key is to be "delusional with your dreams".

"Don't worry about the street you grew up on, the financial situation you got brought into," he said.

"If you don't believe in you, no one's going to believe in you."

Miller said he was a prime example of someone who had made the "impossible possible" as he never imagined it could happen to him.

"I was always scared that I would never be something of myself," he said.

"Put your heart out there because one day it's going to click."

Tax thresholds remain unchanged - here's what it means for your pay

BBC News Wed, 28 Oct 2026 18:12:24 GMT

Income tax thresholds, which have been frozen under successive chancellors, will stay at current levels until April 2031 as planned. But after that they are expected to start to rise again with inflation.

John Healey may not have mentioned the end of this policy in his Budget speech - after all, it is still some way off - but according to the documents released by the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) the freeze, which has been shaving additional tax off people's take-home pay for the past five years, is scheduled to end.

The proportion of your income that is taken in tax will continue to go up over the next four years in line with decisions made in previous Budgets.

But then the personal allowance - the point at which you start to pay tax - and other thresholds, where you tip into paying a higher rate of tax, will rise again with inflation, meaning you keep more of what you earn.

Freezing thresholds is often dubbed a stealth tax because, unlike raising the headline rates, it is not as obvious on your payslip.

It has been a useful way for chancellors from Rishi Sunak onwards to raise more money to help pay for things like defence, the NHS, schools and support for the sick, disabled and the elderly.

The amount of extra money brought in by freezing tax thresholds has risen steadily every year, and is due to reach £58bn by 2030-31, more than the UK government spends on transport and not far off current defence spending.

They hit you hardest if your income is close to one of the tax thresholds, but anyone who gets a pay rise is affected, as long as you earn enough to pay tax. Only people earning under £12,570 - the personal allowance threshold - pay no income tax.

By 2031 an extra 6.8 million people will be paying tax who wouldn't have if the personal allowance had not been frozen, the OBR calculates.

The state pension is currently just below the personal allowance threshold, and pensioners looked set to be drawn into paying tax from next April, when the basic state pension rises to £13,036.

However, the chancellor is putting in place a new separate Pension Tax Allowance, which will ensure that low-income pensioners, with income up to the value of the full new state pension, will not pay income tax.

The personal allowance threshold is set for the whole UK, so people in Scotland will also be affected, although other tax bands there vary.

National Insurance Contributions (Nics) are levied according to the same thresholds.

Wages usually go up year-on-year to cover the rising cost of living. Normally tax thresholds would also be raised in line with rising prices. Currently that isn't happening - the thresholds have been "frozen" at 2021 levels.

So, as your pay rises, a bigger proportion of it ends up above the threshold where you start to pay tax.

If the personal allowance had risen with inflation over the last five years, you would now be able to take home the first £16,070 of your salary without paying any income tax. Instead you pay 20% on anything you earn above £12,570.

As incomes rise, frozen thresholds also mean more and more people are dragged into the higher, 40%, tax bracket.

An extra 5.4 million will be higher rate taxpayers by 2031, thanks to the freeze, according to the OBR.

If thresholds had risen with inflation you would have had to be earning £64,470 this year before you tipped into the higher tax bracket.

As it is, with thresholds frozen at 2021 levels, you pay the higher rate on anything you earn over £50,271.

If you were already earning more than the threshold and you get a pay rise, a bigger proportion of your earnings will be taxed at the higher rate.

Almost one in four taxpayers will pay some of their tax at the higher rate by 2031, according to the government's official forecaster.

The same principle - that rising income can push you into a new tax bracket - applies to the additional, 45%, rate that is charged on a person's income over £125,140.

Wages have risen sharply to keep up with inflation in recent years, making the impact of the first five years of this policy quite noticeable, and that is set to continue.

The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) says if Healey had unfrozen the personal allowance this week, instead of keeping it in place until 2031, basic rate taxpayers would have saved up to £198 in tax a year.

Higher rate taxpayers would save £395 a year.

However, for people in the middle of the earnings range, a cut to Nics introduced in 2024 has offset the higher income tax bill.

How much of a difference "unfreezing" thresholds will make in four years' time depends on how fast wages are going up at that point.

There is no fundamental principle at stake, no point that is the "right" level for tax thresholds. Before the financial crisis the personal allowance was much smaller than today, and it was allowed to grow until the pandemic hit. Even in 2031 you'll be able to take home a bigger proportion of your earnings before income tax than you could back in 2008.

Will I get the £100 energy payment and when will I receive it?

BBC News Wed, 28 Oct 2026 17:47:37 GMT

Up to 20 million households in England will get a £100 payment to help with their energy bills this winter, Chancellor John Healey has announced in his Budget.

Here's what you need to know about the payment.

For many people, the £100 on offer is a lot of money, but it's worth considering the context.

A typical yearly energy bill is forecast to jump by £276 in January, according to consultants Cornwall Insight.

And some more recent forecasts suggest a typical annual bill could rise by £400 or so to £2,100 in January.

Therefore many people will still feel worse off despite the payment.

Those living in properties which are in council tax bands A to D in England will get the payment, the government has said.

As such, it's worth checking which council tax band your home is in. If you live in England, you can use the search function by typing your postcode into the box.

If you get a paper council tax bill, your band will also be printed on there.

The chancellor said the policy was for England but that funding would be given to Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland to make the payment as well.

He urged the devolved governments to follow suit to "give people of all nations in the UK breathing space on their energy bills this winter".

The Welsh government has said that it will also make a £100 cost-of-living payment to all households in council tax bands A to D.

The Scottish government said it would "seek to replicate" the £100 energy payment.

Meanwhile, the Northern Irish government does not have the legal authority to make the £100 payments unless it agrees its budget, which it has failed to do since the start of this financial year.

If you pay your council tax by direct debit, the money will be paid directly into the bank account that you use to pay it, from the start of January.

Students living in halls will not get the payment because student halls are not in council tax bands A to D.

However, if you're a student living in a property that is in council tax bands A to D, as in a private home or flat let out by a landlord, then you will get the payment.

Students do not pay council tax so the local authority will be responsible for finding a way of giving them the payments.

This is also the case for those who do not pay council tax because of another kind of exemption, or if you do pay council tax but you do it by cash or some other way.

The government said it would give councils guidance on how local authorities should do this in due course.

The government has said the support is to help households with the cost of energy.

But the money will appear directly in people's bank accounts. As such, people could choose to spend it on something else.

The chancellor said the money for the £100 cash payments is coming from a tax rise on banks.

The surcharge on banks' corporation tax will rise from 3% to 6% for 15 months from 1 January 2027 to 31 March 2028.

He said: "I do recognise I have been a very determined and focused man.

"With women, of course, which is the subject of my trial, I've been persuasive, seductive, begging and flirting, and dedicated a lot of my life to what seems now beyond reckless philandering, and idiocy."

He told the jury: "Regrettably I've had a lot of consensual sex, which I see has caused harm."

After Brand entered the witness box on Wednesday morning, defence barrister Ian Winter KC began by taking him through the indictment, asking him if he had committed the offences.

After each question, Brand replied "no" loudly towards the jury.

Brand was then asked about the Channel 4 documentary and the impact it had on his relationships with friends and colleagues. "It was devastating," Brand said.

Winter questioned whether Brand had been able to persuade any friend or acquaintance who might have been able to give evidence on his behalf to appear in court.

Brand replied: "I have not." Winter asked: "Will they touch you with a bargepole?" Brand said: "No."

Brand also claimed in court that he was told he could not stay with his son at Great Ormond Street hospital in London when the child was having open heart surgery, following the documentary and a newspaper investigation.

He told the court: "Due to material that had been published in the public eye they had to bar my attendance and presence."

Brand told the court: "My entire life has been consumed by these allegations," adding that he had "devoted myself to these matters".

Winter asked Brand if he recalled meeting the first complainant, who alleges he raped her at the Labour Party conference in Bournemouth in 1999.

Brand said yes, explaining that he found her "loquacious" and "interesting".

When asked if there was any truth in the allegations that he raped her, he said: "No."

Under cross examination, the prosecution suggested Brand "just didn't care whether she was interested in having sex with you or not". Brand rejected that, saying he did care "very much".

Asked whether he was sure he "didn't think no means yes", he replied: "I know what no means."

Brand was then asked about another woman, who alleges that the entertainer grabbed her breasts before dragging her into a toilet and raping her.

Brand said he recalled been invited to a party in London at a bar in 2004, and said a friend had introduced him to the complainant by saying "something like 'there's a bird here who really wants to meet you mate'."

When asked if he remembered what he said to her upon meeting, he told the court: "I would have said something like, 'You're really, really beautiful'."

The barrister asked whether he had grabbed her breasts. "Absolutely not," Brand replied.

When questioned if he would have behaved in the way that had been alleged, he said it would have amounted to "disgusting behaviour".

"I was increasingly focused on my promiscuity," he said. "That's not the way I would have behaved because it's not only criminal but vulgar."

Brand said he remembered going into the toilet with her but said "no" when asked if he had dragged or forced her there.

"Did your penis enter her mouth at all whilst in the cubicle?" Winter asked. "No," said Brand.

Another complainant, who worked at MTV, alleges that Brand tried to drag her into a toilet at work in 2001.

At the time, he was one of the channel's star presenters. She said she managed to wrench herself away.

Asked if he had intended a non-consensual sexual encounter, Brand told the court: "Absolutely not."

In relation to another woman, who accuses Brand of anal rape, he said he remembered her being in his dressing room at the Hammersmith Apollo theatre in London in 2009 after his comedy show.

He said after a "memorable" sexual encounter, he contacted her again to try to meet, adding: "I was excited and enthusiastic about it."

Brand also said he had saved her number in his phone using a code, saying: "That was what I used to denote casual hook-ups and women I met I could hook up with."

After inviting her to his house in Hampstead, he said they had consensual sex in his room.

When asked if he committed anal rape, he said no. When asked if she had asked him to stop, he said no.

Asked by the prosecution later if his memory was "a little selective" in what he could remember, Brand replied: "No."

Brand was also asked on Wednesday about his wedding to singer Katy Perry in October 2010 and whether it brought a "sea change" to his life. He said the marriage brought him "staggering fame".

Being cross examined, Brand agreed with the prosecution's suggestion that he blamed Channel 4 documentary programme Dispatches for the allegations.

Asked if the media had been fair to him, Brand said he "would reject that suggestion strongly".

Under intense questioning from Karmy-Jones, Brand denied pretending to be gay in his pursuit of women, after one of the complainants said they assumed he was gay and that she had felt "sexually safe with him".

Brand also told the jury he had an obsession with sex as a younger man but denied giving himself a "goal" to sleep with 5,000 women.

From the witness box, he said consent was "non-negotiable".

The trial continues.

Police believe dissident republicans may be responsible for a "viable postal device" which was delivered to a hotel in Londonderry.

They carried out a controlled explosion on the device, which was later taken away for a forensic examination.

Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) Chief Supt Gillian Kearney condemned it as "shameful and utterly abhorrent", adding that "those responsible clearly do not care who or what they harm".

"We are keeping an open mind as to who is responsible, and we are working through a number of lines of enquiry, one of which, at this time, is that dissident republicans may be responsible," Kearney said.

She said the investigation was at an early stage and has appealed to anyone with information to come forward as "it could make all the difference".

A number of people were evacuated from The Ebrington hotel, along with staff from neighbouring premises.

The chair of a local policing watchdog said he believed it may be linked to the Ministry of Defence (MoD) having a stall at a careers fare at the same hotel last month.

A Halloween funfair had been taking place a short distance away from the hotel.

It remained open during the security alert.

Toni Collins said the targeting of The Ebrington was a "disgrace" especially in the run up to Halloween when thousands would be in the city.

"No-one wants it and no one supports it," she said.

Teresa Boyle from Enniskillen is visiting the city. She said the community had moved on and no-one wanted to return to the conflict of the past.

"That's what people want, peace," she added.

Mayor of Derry City and Strabane District Council councillor Grace Uí Niallais said her "thoughts are with the staff and anyone impacted".

"This was a serious and reckless incident which has no doubt caused trauma to all involved. We will not go back to the past but instead look forward to the fantastic four days of Halloween celebrations ahead," she said.

She paid tribute to the police officers who responded to the incident, "once again putting themselves in harm's way to ensure the safety of the public".

Secretary of State for Northern Ireland Sir Chris Bryant said it was "very worrying".

He added: "This is absolutely despicable. Whoever has been involved in this, I very much hope that we'll be able to track down who it is, and they should face the full force of the law."

Ulster Unionist councillor Darren Guy, who chairs the local policing and community safety partnership, believes the incident was timed to cause maximum disruption.

He also said it may have been linked to the MoD being represented at a careers event at the hotel in September.

"Recently, there was a careers event held in that hotel where I believe an RAF [Royal Air Force] stall was there for the careers event at that time.

"This was specifically done this week to cause as much disruption as possible during the 40th Halloween celebrations with thousands of international visitors visiting the city and the amount of families, especially young families going out to enjoy the many things on offer.

Sinn Féin councillor Christopher Jackson said it was too early to "speculate" about any link between the alert and the jobs fair.

"There is no justification whatsoever for carrying this out and putting people in danger, especially when the city is gearing up for the 40th anniversary of the Halloween festival," he added.

"Derry is a warm and welcoming place and it's disgusting why someone or some organisation did this."

Julie Middleton, Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) assembly member for Foyle, told BBC Radio Ulster's Good Morning Ulster programme on Wednesday that she was "deeply disturbed and disgusted".

The Police Federation for Northern Ireland (PFNI) described sending a viable device to a hotel as "the height of madness".

Labuschagne's form hits record low but Australia hint at future

BBC News Wed, 28 Oct 2026 17:33:41 GMT

Marnus Labuschagne has not scored a Test century since the 2023 Ashes

Third Test, Cape Town (day two of five)

South Africa 329: Ackerman 95; Starc 6-72

Australia 330-4: Inglis 85*; Jansen 2-37

Australia lead by one run

Scorecard

Marnus Labuschagne has been front and centre for an era of Australian cricket.

Chirping, chewing and, with bat in hand, often appearing to idolise and mimic his team-mate Steve Smith.

Smith has been ruled out of the enthralling decisive Test against South Africa with a neck injury.

Without him, Australia wanted their number three to feast at last chance saloon, where he has been perched for an eternity, on day two in Cape Town.

The 32-year-old lasted five deliveries and did not score a run.

Labuschagne failed to scored a Test century for the 48th time in a row - a new record for the number of consecutive innings a batter in Australia’s top four has waited to raise his bat at three figures.

"That will never be broken," said former Australia quick Jason Gillespie on ABC.

"I say that because, respectfully, I don't think anyone will be given that length of time again."

There was a time when, from his insertion into the 2019 Ashes as a concussion substitute until the end of England's next quest to win back the urn, Labuschagne averaged 65 in Test cricket.

Repeat that over a Test career and only Sir Donald Bradman's mark of 99.94 would be ahead.

Instead, since his last Test century at Old Trafford in 2023, he averages 24.77.

Labuschagne may get one more chance in this Test, should Australia not progress from their position of 330-4, leading by one run, and dismiss South Africa before needing to pad up again.

Even that may not be enough.

"I just feel it is too far gone now," Gillespie added. "It is a very big sample size. Australia are at a point where they need to look elsewhere."

Labuschagne's technique has been pored over again and again as his slump progressed.

In August, the great Ricky Ponting, one of his predecessors as Australia's number three, called for the axe to fall.

"He can't score off the back foot," was Ponting's cutting remark.

Having batted nicely in three or four innings in this series only to give it away after reaching 30, here he was stuck on the crease, playing back to a full ball and nicking spinner Simon Harmer to slip.

"That's nerves and the pressure the selectors have put him under for an extended period of time," said former Australia batter Simon Katich on SEN Radio.

"They put him in this position by not making the decision to give him a breather."

It felt like all of Labuschagne's issues collapsing into one.

But if his pained stare down the pitch signalled the end of something, what followed hinted at their future.

With Travis Head already out and Labuschagne following, the score 58-2 in reply to the Proteas' 329, there was no Smith to steer Australia out of this tricky spot.

Matt Renshaw, Cameron Green and Josh Inglis, three of the junior members of this side, instead made fifties and put their side in the ascendancy.

Renshaw is one of those who has been kept out by the selectors in the hope Labuschagne could rediscover his best form.

Had he been picked to open in the World Test Championship final against South Africa in 2025, rather than Australia's decision to try Labuschagne as opener, he may have spent the following 17 months ending the debate over who should replace David Warner.

Having got his chance in this series, initially as number five before the Nic Maddinson experiment was cut short after two Tests, the Middlesbrough-born Renshaw looks like being a fixture for this winter and beyond.

His 74 here, which followed a career-best 190 in Durban, suggests a return to England next summer awaits.

Green is one who has not lacked opportunity. Long viewed as Australia's golden boy, the 27-year-old has flicked across 39 previous Test without ever truly appearing comfortable.

In making 65 below Table Mountain, the towering all-rounder played with the composure and authority he has often lacked.

Most impressive, though, was Inglis - another Aussie who spent his early years in Yorkshire.

He had not faced the red ball since March, has had his preparations limited by a broken finger, and came in with South Africa buoyed by Marco Jansen dismissing Renshaw and Green in successive overs before tea.

The 31-year-old finished 85 not out in an unbroken partnership of 145 with Alex Carey. There would be no late-evening South Africa fightback, like the one Mitchell Starc inspired on day one to bowl South Africa out.

This is not to say everything has fallen into place for Australia. Smith will return, meaning Green and Inglis would likely move from their current batting positions of four and five for their next Test against New Zealand in December.

Smith has avoided batting in Labuschagne's position before, and a four-Test trial of Green in that spot in 2024 and 2025 was aborted after he returned 188 across eight innings.

Leeds-born Inglis, meanwhile, has three first-class matches worth experience at number three, in which he averaged 12.66 and has a best score of 29.

But if ever a day showed Australia there is merit in moving from one generation to another it was this.

Three of their less experienced players, albeit two of them have celebrated their 30th birthdays, stood up to take Australia to a position from which they can control this Test.

Labuschagne did not. His days look numbered.

Inglis was particularly effective cutting and sweeping South Africa's spinners

Australia fight back to keep Cummins out of unwanted club... for now

Bloodied, dazed and angry - how passengers' rail journey turned to disaster in Spain

BBC News Wed, 28 Oct 2026 17:16:03 GMT

It was approaching 09:00 (08:00 GMT) and two high-speed trains were travelling south from the Spanish capital, Madrid, to Seville.

One, run by state-owned operator Renfe had 397 passengers on board. Ahead of it on the same line was a train of Iryo private operator with 147 passengers. A reported issue with the automatic signalling system - a computer failure - had forced all trains to halt on the affected stretch.

Then the impossible happened, Spain's transport minister said, as the Renfe train was ordered to proceed in "error".

It crashed into the back of the other train between municipalities Mora and Orgaz, about 140km (87 miles) south of Madrid.

Spanish journalist Roberto Gómez was dozing on the high-speed Renfe train, when it stopped and an announcement was made to passengers that there was congestion on the tracks.

The train eventually began to move again, he explained, and then the crash happened.

"The impact was terrible," he told Onda Cero radio. "You can imagine, the carriage is completely destroyed. All the suitcases are all over the wrecked carriage."

Gómez suffered only minor injuries but described another passenger falling on top of him and sustaining a deep gash on his head.

"We were able to help people who had suffered severe blows to their chest and ribs," he said.

Rafael Barcelo was in one of the worst-affected carriages. A bruise on his forehead makes him one of the lucky survivors. He was having a coffee at the time of the crash and "felt a huge impact".

"We were all thrown into the air," he told Reuters news agency at the site of the crash.

"I am reasonably OK, my friend is quite worse."

"I was travelling in coach seven, which is the one with more victims and the one most destroyed. I at least counted eight victims in that coach," he said, visibly shocked.

In the last carriage of the Renfe train, Miguel Ángel Pérez saw a similar scene.

"It was a terrible crash. The carriage partially overturned," he told Spanish TV program La Hora de La 1. "Luckily there were few people standing," he said.

Despite being in one of the carriages least affected, Salvador Arriza said "everything was completely destroyed inside - the seats were detached, and most of the people who were travelling facing the same direction as the train were thrown into the air".

"I was lucky, because I was sitting facing the opposite direction and the crash pushed me into my seat. But it was something brutal."

As some people tried to break windows to jump out, he said others could not move "because they were trapped between the seats".

Once out, he saw how bad the situation was.

"What caught my attention is that in one of the coaches there was a piece of train track that went through the roof of the coach, and I think that might have helped to stop or reduce the inertia of the train."

The train that was hit from behind was one of six to have been ordered to halt at 08:30. It was still stationary when the order was given to the Renfe train to proceed.

Transport Minister Óscar Puente appeared in front of the cameras to say an employee had ordered the resumption of travel at 08:36 and some 17 minutes later the "truly unbelievable" had happened.

Sebastián Herrero from Seville was on the Iryo train and experienced the crash first hand.

He felt a "terrible, terrible impact" and was thrown on to the seats in front of him, he told El Mundo newspaper.

"After we fell, there were many people with broken noses, broken arms... We started seeing smoke everywhere."

Another man, who was not identified, told Reuters news agency: "Everything was overturned. Some people were thrown into the air. They are very badly injured."

Eduarda was also on the stationary train, travelling with her two cats.

She told Cadena Ser radio how the crash had thrown her forwards. Once outside, the chaos hit her. She heard screams and saw people under the train who she said had died, and a carriage was on fire.

For Fernando Seco the worst came after he left the train and saw a "horrible scene".

"There were many injured people, a lot of blood and many dead," he said.

Some of the fortunate passengers who escaped injury in the crash began helping others. Even injured and bloodied passengers did their best to help.

It was not long before local people arrived, followed by the police and ambulance services of the Guardia Civil.

"People from neighbouring towns brought water," a volunteer told Reuters.

"We are distributing it, especially to be taken to the accident site where people are in worse condition."

Some residents brought cars to help with the evacuation to the nearby town of Urda, he explained.

Spain was already reeling from the Adamuz high-speed rail disaster outside Córdoba in January, in which 46 people died.

It happened on the same high-speed rail line, but much further south. So Wednesday's accident has raised many questions for the authorities.

The Spanish transport minister said the circumstances were "inexplicable".

According to regulations, under such circumstances, a train driver would be required to proceed at what is known as "sight speed" - about 40km/h (25mph), a speed that allows them to stop in time if they encounter an obstacle.

Officials will investigate what order the Renfe train got, if it was travelling at the usual speed for that section of track - "around 200km/h" according to the minister, and, more significantly, why did the operator not stop its journey when his screen would have displayed that another train on the same line was stationary.

Affected passengers were visibly angry.

"It isn't possible that our train was stopped for five or 10 minutes and that the other train wasn't told to stop," one of them said.

"How can this happen with the technology we have?," he added. "It's not normal. We weren't told anything. The person who should have been told something was the driver of the other train. We wouldn't have cared as long as the other train had been warned. I don't understand this."
