Why can’t we cool water as quickly as we can heat it? part 3

New Scientist October 28, 2026

Why can’t we cool water as quickly as we can heat it? (continued)

Graham SmithMelbourne, Australia

Advertisement

The rate of heat transfer to, or from, water is determined by three variables. The first factor is the difference in temperature between the heating source and the water. The second factor is called the heat transfer coefficient. The third is the contact area between the water and the medium that is doing the heating or cooling.

Heating is generally accomplished by an electrical element, or some form of flame. The heating source can be hundreds of degrees hotter than the water. In contrast, cooling is generally accomplished with a liquid refrigerant or with ambient air, both of which are usually less than a few tens of degrees cooler than the water.

The heat transfer coefficient (HTC) is a measure of the conduction and convection that is occurring in the particular physical system. Water isn’t a very good conductor, but it can be a very good convector, because water density changes with temperature, which sets up currents that carry heat away from the heating surface. The convection occurring with boiling water results in an extremely high HTC, because the turbulence carries more of the heat away, and because the steam transfers huge amounts of latent heat. Therefore, the observation of faster heating is due to a combination of greater temperature difference and a higher HTC.

Water isn’t a very good conductor, but it can be a very good convector, because water density changes with temperature

However, in industrial cooling towers or your home evaporative cooler, the water surface area can be increased enormously by the water being broken into small drops and being in contact with air. The HTC is also high because the evaporated water carries away the latent heat. In this case, it is quicker to cool than to heat.

Kevin HeskethPreston, Lancashire, UK

We can engineer systems that cool water as quickly as we can heat it. Think of the coolant system for a car. The coolant is pumped into the coolant channels in the engine and is rapidly heated up by the engine block. Then it passes into the radiator, which has multiple thin channels where it is cooled by air flow.

When the system reaches its running temperature, it reaches an equilibrium temperature governed by the thermostat. The heating time is the time the coolant spends in the engine block coolant channels, and the cooling time is the time the coolant is in the radiator. These don’t necessarily match, but they could be engineered to do so by resizing the radiator channels.

Why do dogs usually follow instructions, but cats largely ignore them?

New Scientist October 28, 2026

Humans have domesticated both cats and dogs. Why do dogs generally follow instructions, whereas cats largely ignore them?

Caroline PetersWokingham, Berkshire, UK

Wolves are pack animals. Therefore, as they were domesticated, human owners took on the role of the pack leader. The dogs would naturally obey commands given by the surrogate pack leader – hence the term “master” for the owner of a dog.

Advertisement

Domestic cats, on the other hand, evolved from a wild species that was naturally solitary. Such animals would therefore be used to making their own decisions. It is possible to train cats to respond to human instructions, but this has to be done in a way that is advantageous to the cat in order for it to want to comply.

The current trend for “adventure cats” is a case in point – if the cat enjoys trips out with its owners, it will quickly learn to follow the instructions that lead to this reward.

Cats moved into areas around human grain stores during the Neolithic agricultural revolution, attracted by rodents

We taught our own cat (who was acquired as a rescue at age 11) to respond to a hand held up like a stop sign so that she would not immediately jump onto people who don’t like cats. She very quickly understood what was required by this gesture. She also learned that the sound of the bell from one of her toys was a command to heel and would come in immediately if this was shaken, whether or not a food reward was given on her return. We even had one cat who had been taught to play fetch just like a dog.

As with all domestic animals, the key to success in training is to be absolutely consistent in the message that you’re trying to convey. All human members of the household must expect the same result from the same message and, especially when dealing with cats, the animal must see the benefit in obeying the command.

Pam LunnKenilworth, Warwickshire, UK

It may be a category error to suggest that we have domesticated cats.

Cats moved into areas around human grain stores during and after the Neolithic agricultural revolution. The concentration of rodents drawn to grain stores proved a convenient attraction for cats. The “domestic” cat genome has changed very little since then: they retain their wild characteristics.

There may be an argument for saying that cats have domesticated us, exploiting us for our willingness to feed and pamper them.

The law in the UK says that cats have the right to roam, and their owners cannot be held liable for trespassing or property damage they cause.

This is in contrast to the legal position of dogs, whose owners remain liable for any injury or damage caused by them.

Simon McLeishLechlade, Gloucestershire, UK

Domestic dogs and cats have both been companions to humans for a long time, and they have both adapted to live with us.

The two animals are descended from very different ancestors and, accordingly, their behaviour is very different. Genetic testing indicates that the closest relative of domestic cats is the African wildcat (Felis silvestris lybica), while dogs are most closely related to wolves (Canis lupus) – so close, in fact, that domestic dogs are classified as a subspecies of the wolf, not a separate species.

Their behaviour is very different. Wolves themselves are pack animals, with a distinct hierarchy. Their place governs their behaviour and, to them, a human is a dominant member of the pack in a way that no domestic cat would recognise. For millennia, dogs descended from wolves have been bred by humans to enhance traits such as trainability.

Having said that, with patience, it is possible to train domestic cats to carry out taught actions, but it generally needs more work and time than it does with dogs.

Peter Meehan London*, UK

I used to walk down a quiet lane and my pet cat enjoyed strolling along the other side of a hedge, jumping back to me when it suited him. A cat hears instructions, but will make the decision to act on things more interesting to them.

*Editor’s note: We would like to point out that Peter’s actual address is in Catford.

Neil SutcliffeGlossop, Derbyshire, UK

There is an error in the initial suppositions: humans have indeed domesticated dogs, but cats have domesticated humans, hence the reversed master-servant relationship.

Kevin CraigArvada, Colorado, US

Clearly the questioner has never owned a greyhound!

Why the world’s first spinal cord transplant is so controversial

New Scientist October 28, 2026

The virologist Jonas Salk said that “hope lies in dreams, in imagination and in the courage of those who dare to make dreams into reality”. Salk was certainly daring – he risked paralysing himself, his wife and their children while testing his polio vaccine. Thankfully, it paid off. None of them experienced any ill effects and his work is credited with saving millions.

Risks have to be taken for medicine to advance, and someone is always the first to receive a treatment. But there are risks, and then there are risks.

Salk tested his vaccine on cells, monkeys and children who had already had polio before turning his unexposed family into guinea pigs. His approach is far from standard protocol today, but he did a lot to reduce the risk of something going wrong.

Advertisement

There is less evidence to justify an operation that took place this month in Russia. Details are scant, but the procedure involved cutting out a section of spinal cord from someone with a complete spinal cord injury and gluing in a replacement piece from a donor. The transplant was a world first, but there is little evidence to believe it will have worked or that now was the time to try it.

The transplant was a world first, but there is little evidence to believe it will have worked

History tells us that acting ahead of medical evidence can have catastrophic results. Take the first synthetic organ transplants, which replaced tracheas with plastic tubes. The surgeon who fitted them admitted they hadn’t been tested on large animals because they “didn’t have the time”. Complications and deaths followed.

With new medical procedures, the gold standard is randomised controlled trials, which are costly and take time, but they aren’t the only route. When someone is critically ill, there are compassionate-use protocols that make interventions available before they are fully tested. Pig kidney transplants are currently being trialled this way, for example.

The dream of spinal cord transplants will surely become a reality one day, but only if the science underpinning them is built first. Courage, dreams and imagination are of course good, yet with experimental surgeries, evidence is better.

Christchurch double homicide: Rodney Fallowfield enters guilty pleas

New Zealand Herald October 28, 2026

Rodney Fallowfield pleaded guilty at the High Court in Christchurch today. Pool photo / RNZ

Rodney Fallowfield has today admitted murdering two men in Christchurch last month.

Fallowfield, 58, appeared in the High Court at Christchurch this morning charged with the murders of former Devils Henchmen Motorcycle Club president Glen Tukaki and Nigel Robinson.

The courtroom was packed when a member of the public stood and yelled “You gutless piece of s...” as Fallowfield was led into custody, after entering guilty pleas.

He will be sentenced on April 10 next year.

It is not the first time Fallowfield has killed.

In 2021, he was jailed for more than four years for strangling his wife Shirley Reedy to death.

Fallowfield, then 54, killed Reedy at a Te Anau motel while on a belated honeymoon after they had married in April the preceding year.

After a trial in the High Court at Invercargill, Fallowfield was found not guilty of murder but guilty of manslaughter.

During the trial, the Crown argued Fallowfield strangled Reedy because he wanted to silence her when she threatened him with a rape allegation, while the defence said he “snapped” but did not mean for his actions to be fatal.

Fallowfield admitted responsibility for Reedy’s death but denied he intended to kill her.

At a parole hearing in 2022, Fallowfield was said to be “genuinely remorseful”.

“He confirmed to the board that he was truly sorry for what had happened, and he will have to live with his guilt forever,” said Parole Board panel convenor Serina Bailey.

The board heard that Fallowfield had a lengthy criminal record featuring assaults, attempted arson, driving matters, dishonesty and burglary.

The Otago Daily Times, after Fallowfield’s sentencing, revealed evidence about a previous strangling that the jury did not hear.

The woman involved said Fallowfield attacked her after she had problems sourcing drugs, verbally abused her, then choked her.

She recalled coming to as he stood over her.

“He told me he thought he’d killed me. He told me I lost consciousness and began to have a seizure. I don’t know how long I was unconscious for.”

Fallowfield was initially denied parole but released in 2023. He told the Parole Board he wanted to “move on” with his life.

The board met with one of his victims, who said her family had “forgiven” the killer.

“But what they really wanted to know is why he committed the manslaughter, not just the details of the offending,” the board decision said.

“She reiterated that the family miss their sister and daughter greatly.”

He was released on parole with a number of conditions that were in place for six months.

“This board considers he is no longer an undue risk considering the work he has done in the prison, his presentation today, his future planning and the support he will have in the community and the conditions which are to be imposed,” the decision said.

“It is noted he is considered as low risk of re‑offending.”

Contact the Open Justice team

Al Williams is an Open Justice reporter for the New Zealand Herald, based in Christchurch. He has worked in daily and community titles in New Zealand and overseas for the last 16 years. Most recently he was editor of the Hauraki-Coromandel Post, based in Whangamatā. He was previously deputy editor of the Cook Islands News.

Managed retreat on the cards for long-term storm recovery on East Cape

New Zealand Herald October 28, 2026

A report identified bridge realignments and managed retreat in Punaruku (pictured) as the preferred long-term option. Photo / Corey Fleming

Some East Cape communities could face relocation as Gisborne grapples with storm recovery.

Gisborne District Council’s emergency management committee received reports on Wednesday outlining recovery work needed in Wharekahika/Hicks Bay, Onepoto Bay, Punaruku and the Wairenga Stream near Tokata Rd since January’s Tropical Depression 5F.

Recovery manager Naomi Whitewood said the reports were commissioned to understand the storm’s impacts and identify potential solutions.

Council principal scientist Dr Murry Cave led the project using a protect, adapt, retreat or avoid framework established by the Ministry for the Environment.

Both assessments concluded the January event was driven by landslide sediment and debris, and was a one-off flood that could be resolved with stream clearing and road repairs.

The assessments recorded 619 landslides across the Pukeamaru Range, including 183 in the Wairenga catchment.

Sediment and debris could continue moving for years.

Council noted communities held strong ancestral connections to the whenua, so decisions carry weight.

A Tonkin and Taylor report, supported by Massey University geomorphologist Professor Ian Fuller and risk specialist Professor Tim Davies, identified an ongoing threat to life in Hicks Bay, Punaruku and Onepoto Bay, where boulders, sediment and woody debris were carried through streams and rivers, causing flooding and property damage.

An area of concern was Punaruku, where 24 people were evacuated and one whānau had to be rescued from their rooftop.

The report suggested large structural protection works, such as stopbanks, should not be relied on and could worsen conditions downstream at the Te Araroa motorcamp and surrounding houses.

Short-term options included improved flood warnings, monitoring and community emergency management.

Planning controls, updated hazard modelling and mapping could help prevent further development in hazard zones.

The report also identified maintaining stormwater drainage near State Highway 35 at Onepoto Bay and addressing bridge alignments in Punaruku.

For the most exposed properties, managed retreat was identified as a long-term option, alongside bridge realignments in Punaruku.

However, the report did not identify which properties might need to relocate, who would be responsible for relocation or property acquisition, or how much the work would cost.

The central government co-funded Category 3 buy-out programme, due to expire in March 2027, has no equivalent for the January storm.

The report noted the Tāmaki Makaurau Recovery Office in Auckland had also been told central government would not support buy-outs based on pre-storm market values.

Whitewood said some whānau were considering leaving, while others were concerned about losing their only piece of whenua.

“We have whānau that are considering whether they need to leave. We have whānau that have decided that they want their whānau to stay in the area for the rest of their lives there, and then we have whānau that really have no idea what they need to do.”

She said some landowners wanted to progress short-term solutions, particularly in Punaruku, while others needed more time and support to consider their options.

Councillor Rawinia Parata said the report outlined potential solutions but lacked clear next steps.

“It doesn’t tell us who’s responsible for supporting, navigating, implementing, engaging. It kind of goes halfway.”

The findings needed to be considered alongside the communities’ cultural and historical connections to the land, Parata said.

“It doesn’t tell us anything about the history of the community, it doesn’t tell us where the sites of significance are, it doesn’t tell us how much it hurts to be told to move.”

Whitewood said the report provided expert information for communities, iwi and hapū to consider, but did not assign responsibilities or prescribe solutions.

When asked by Parata, Whitewood said the report had not been peer-reviewed, but some landowners were seeking peer reviews independently.

Cave said an international peer review was planned. The report’s completion had been delayed until findings from retired High Court Judge Paul Davison’s external review into the Mauao landslide in Tauranga were released.

Engagement with local groups meant feedback about history and culture was taken into account and community action for long-term solutions was added to the report, he said.

The report did not determine what properties might need to relocate or the cost of works.

Wairenga Stream, near Tokata Rd outside Te Araroa, changed course in January and again in June, causing recurring flooding on farms, an orchard and nearby properties.

There was no current risk to life or affected public lifeline assets, so redirecting the stream for $50,000 to $75,000 was identified as a preferred option.

The work would require an engineered design, resource consent, agreement from affected landowners and funding.

The land involved was primarily Māori freehold land and adjoining properties.

The council assessment found the circumstances did not meet the threshold for emergency works under the Resource Management Act.

With no council budget or external funding available, the report recommended council support landowners through the consent process and help explore funding options.

Councillor Rob Telfer said the situation would set a precedent in the region, because redirection could happen in any gully in the community.

Telfer asked what resource consent and monetary boundaries were stopping the work from progressing as quickly as possible.

“The cost is falling on a small number of individual landowners, but we as a council can facilitate that process as much as possible. But we do not manage every single stream and river in the region. Quite a lot of land is private land, and so it is their responsibility to do that.”

Whitewood said the review was critical information before moving to next stages, but meetings were planned with landowners to discuss obstacles.

Telfer asked if it would be possible in future to provide information and modelling for future events where work on private land could be undertaken as soon as possible.

Cave cautioned that each stream or river change was different and section 330 of the RMA restricted emergency works powers to specified authorities and operators.

Chief executive Nedine Thatcher Swann said clearer information about what work was permitted, who could undertake it and what support council could provide would help reduce reactive decision-making.

Councillors Telfer and Jeremy Muir moved the overall recovery report.

Election 2026: Latest poll has National so low it stretches credibility. What does the trend show?

New Zealand Herald October 28, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

If this morning’s RNZ-Reid Research poll is to be believed, voters are less enamoured with National now than they were in 2020, when Labour won a historic majority.

The poll has National on 24.8%, almost 6 percentage points behind Labour (30.6%).

It’s not surprising that National has dismissed it.

It was conducted over a similar period to this week’s 1News-Verian poll, which had National on 28.9%, 1.6 percentage points ahead of Labour.

Both canvassed 1000 eligible voters, though Reid Research used online panels, while Verian uses both phone calls and online.

Those Reid Research panels seem to favour Labour. Its previous poll, at the end of September, had Labour 5 percentage points up on National when most other polls had them neck and neck.

It also had Labour’s advantage at 3.1 points in August, 5.3 points in July, 4.8 points in March, and 3.1 points in January.

So what can we take from the RNZ-Reid Research poll, if anything?

The trend is good news for Act, which rose 1.1 points since the end of September, and for Opportunity, which was 1.7 points higher.

That upward direction for Act is mirrored in the 1News-Verian poll over the same period, but not for Opportunity, which barely moved (from 6% to 6.3%).

The trend for the other parties in the RNZ-Reid Research numbers follows other polls in showing how little the dial has shifted during the campaign.

That includes for Labour, which will find stability encouraging considering the Mongrel Mob focus over the polling period.

Labour will also be pleased to be in the 30s in this morning’s result (30.6%), and able to form a government with the Greens (14.5%) and Opportunity (7.2%).

The caution for Labour is not only the grain of salt it should take with the Reid Research numbers.

In 2023, Labour’s election night result was lower than Labour’s support in all of the major polls’ final pre-election numbers.

The exception was Roy Morgan, which appears to be the counter to Reid Research in that it tends to favour National. Roy Morgan has National ahead of Labour by an average of 7 points since July.

The Herald, as a general rule, has refrained from using Roy Morgan’s political polling in any of its reporting for years.

Derek Cheng is a senior journalist who started at the Herald in 2004. He has worked several stints in the press gallery team and is a former deputy political editor.

Central Hawke’s Bay shed fire likely started by bird’s nest in tractor

New Zealand Herald October 28, 2026

Waipukurau deputy fire chief Glen Millar said a bird’s nest in a tractor likely started the fire. Photo / NZME

A bird’s nest in a tractor likely started a large fire that swept through a Central Hawke’s Bay farm shed.

A Fire and Emergency New Zealand spokeswoman said crews were called to the fire at Farm Rd, near Landfill Access Rd, about 10am on Wednesday with two water tankers.

On arrival, crews found a 17m by 8m shed fully involved, and stopped it from spreading further.

The spokeswoman said the fire was not considered suspicious.

Waipukurau deputy fire chief Glen Millar said the fire was likely started by a bird’s nest in a tractor after machinery had been used to clear waterways on the farm.

He said tractor engine bays should be checked before and after each use to avoid fires like it.

Millar said the farmer had a shoulder injury at the time of the fire and was unable to make the check under the bonnet as a result.

Contact our newsroom

Rural insurer FMG said birds’ nests accounted for about $1.2m in tractor fire claims annually.

It said this week that it wanted to remind machinery operators to stop and pop the bonnet before and after work.

Over the past three years, FMG had received more than 100 tractor fire claims linked to birds’ nests, accounting for 32% of all tractor fire claims during that period.

The majority of tractor fire claims caused by birds’ nests that FMG saw were during the starling breeding season, which typically ran from September to December.

FMG loss prevention manager Abby France said starlings in particular squeezed into surprisingly small places and built nests much faster than expected.

“With dry grass readily available on farm, a bird can build a nest in the time it takes you to stop for smoko or have a cup of tea.

“It’s not just tractors. We’ve seen nests cause fires in quad bikes, side-by-sides, cars, utes and other machinery as well.”

FMG encouraged farmers and machinery operators to make checking under bonnets part of their routines.

France said leaving bonnets up on parked machinery could discourage birds from nesting and fitting machinery with easily accessible fire extinguishers operators knew how to use.

It said it had free stop-and-pop reminder stickers, which could be ordered from its website.

The 1News Kaupapa Māori Debate is taking place this evening at 7.30pm. We will bring you live updates.

Opportunity Party leader Qiulae Wong says she's "really encouraged" by this morning's RNZ-Reid Research poll putting her party on 7.2%.

Opportunity recorded the biggest gain out of all parties, rising 1.7 points.

National was on 24.8%, Labour on 30.6%, the Greens on 14.5%, Act on 10.1%, NZ First on 9.9% and Te Pāti Māori on 1.9%.

"Really encouraging that we continue to be well clear of the 5%", Wong said this morning.

"It is a very close election, and we hold the balance of power on most polls. I believe that the safest vote this election is for Opportunity because voters know that we will achieve those five bottom lines and we will bring some stability to the next term of government regardless of whether it's Labour or National. Voting for Opportunity is a vote to change NZ politics for good."

Opportunity Party leader Qiulae Wong is leaving the door open to negotiating with NZ First after the election - if leader Winston Peters changes his behaviour.

Peters yesterday refused to entertain the idea of working with Opportunity when asked by Newstalk ZB Wellington Mornings host Nick Mills.

"I'm not gonna waste my time with questions like that," he said.

"I'm talking about the people who are going to survive this election."

Asked this morning if Wong would consider forming a government with NZ First, she said the ball is in their court.

"At this point it's about the behaviour of Winston Peters and NZ First. There are policy areas where we could work with them on things like competition and energy market reform but it's very difficult to see working with a party that is intentionally trying to sow division in New Zealand at a time when we actually need to come together on some big long-term issues.

"We're not ruling them out, if we do we'll make that really clear. At this point it is just a big consideration for us in terms of what the next Government looks like."

Wong said her party had been very clear with its bottom lines and the kind of future they want to build for New Zealand, and that is what will be prioritised in any coalition talks.

She said it's important in an MMP environment to remain flexible and be able to work with other parties.

"In saying that, New Zealand First has made remarks that are incredibly divisive, very dangerous rhetoric that we don't believe belong in politics. If they can put that kind of behaviour aside and actually focus on the policies and issues that matter, then there's a chance of working with them. At the moment that seems unlikely, but that's a choice for them, not for us."

Asked what Wong made of Peters calling her "the new media darling" at a public meeting last night, she said it was not the kind of politics she participates in.

"I think it's sad that they're spending so much time trying to tear other people down rather than just focus on what we need to take New Zealand forward.

"I think that's just their style of doing politics. It's easier to criticise others than to talk about your track record, to talk about where you want to take the country, to talk about a vision that people can get behind.

"But I think New Zealanders are really sick of that. They're sick of the bickering, they're sick of the political point scoring, they want something different and they really want some hope and optimism for the future."

National leader Christopher Luxon believes there is a lot of variance in polls as he responds to the RNZ-Reid Research poll which has National on 24.8%.

"I think there's lots of polls roaming around saying lots of different things," he told RNZ's Nine to Noon programme.

He repeated his view that it would be a very tight election.

"Stick with the plan that's starting to work, don't put it at risk."

Asked how National could buck a declining trend in the polls, Luxon responded: "All you can do is make the case, make the choice very clear to New Zealanders."

The Electoral Commission has referred two people to the police after they claimed to have voted multiple times.

"It is an offence under section 215 of the Electoral Act 1993 to vote more than once," the commission outlined in a statement.

"As these matters are now with the Police, the Electoral Commission will not be commenting further."

New Zealand First Party leader Winston Peters on the Mike Hosking Minor Leaders Breakfast. Photo / Alyse Wright

New Zealand First leader Winston Peters, speaking on the Mike Hosking Minor Leaders Breakfast, says he believes the election campaign is the worst he's ever seen.

Peters also agrees potential coalition negotiations with National and Act would go more smoothly given the two parties had more experience in Cabinet.

Speaking to host Mike Hosking, Peters echoed Green co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick when he said voters were sick of the campaign's pettiness and he believed it was "about the worst campaign I've ever seen".

Peters' campaign has largely consisted of public meetings across the country. Asked why he valued that forum, Peters rounded on mainstream media, saying outlets had changed to take sides politically and as such, it left social media and public meetings as his preferred way to get his message to the electorate.

Peters expressed frustration New Zealand wasn't an export "powerhouse". Challenged on the relative success of New Zealand's exports, Peters argued the country should be more successful and reinforced the need to double the value of exports in the next decade.

Asked for his proudest moments of the last term, Peters referred to retaining provincial investment, getting rid of "woke legislation" and increasing New Zealand's respect on the world stage through his efforts as Foreign Affairs Minister.

On another round of potential negotiations with National and Act, Peters expected they would progress more smoothly than in 2023 as the two party leaders had experience in Cabinet.

He reinforced the party's policies designed to retain workers and businesses in New Zealand as opposed to losing them to Australia, noting his proposal to cut the corporate tax rate for small businesses would see a "galvanising of business".

Peters again declared the Waitangi Tribunal would be scrapped within three months of the next government forming, which he believed was supported by a "significant proportion of the coalition" despite National being of the view that the tribunal had a role to play.

He emphasised the need for National supporters to split their vote by voting for a National candidate but giving their party vote to NZ First or Act, saying that approach would make it more likely the coalition could be re-elected.

Act Party Leader David Seymour on the Mike Hosking Minor Leaders Breakfast. Photo / Alyse Wright

Act leader David Seymour, speaking on the Mike Hosking Minor Leaders Breakfast, says proposals by potential coalition partners for compulsory KiwiSaver are a "non-starter" while predicting smoother coalition negotiations.

Speaking to host Mike Hosking, Seymour said he believed coalition talks between National and NZ First, should the parties be able to form a majority, would be smoother this time around.

"I think so, everyone knows each other and everyone knows what its like to work together."

Seymour, like Swarbrick, acknowledged compromise was necessary to form a coalition but referenced the party's policy to remove tax from KiwiSaver as an important aspect of its policy platform.

He reiterated that while describing National's compulsory KiwiSaver policy as a "non-starter".

He didn't express regret when asked about the level of reform the Government had been unable to progress, again pointing to the need for compromise.

When asked if this morning’s RNZ-Reid Research poll putting National below 25% was an outlier, Seymour didn't provide a direct answer although noted Reid Research in 2023 had National lower than what it ended up on on election night.

Seymour argued Act had "come of age as a party", lauding the efforts of his ministers in Government.

He believed Act candidate James Christmas would win the Tāmaki seat and likened National's current candidate to Simon O'Connor, who lost the long-time National seat to Act's Brooke van Velden in 2023.

Auckland's mayor Wayne Brown is doubling down on his want for council to control the city's motorways.

Brown yesterday released his Manifesto 2026, outlining goals nine days out from the election, despite not running for mayor this campaign.

It included wanting the council to take control of Auckland's motorway and rail network from central government, as well as wanting the next prime minister to also be the Minister for Auckland.

He told Ryan Bridge TODAY "process-orientated" perspectives on roading hold the country back.

"We're in a country short of cash, particularly short of cash for roading and transport issues, and so every dollar competes with every dollar.

"If some unelected group in NZTA squander $3.2 billion on a motorway entirely within my district that I've yet to be shown the root of, that makes no sense."

Brown said he believed there was a culture of "over-safety" and mandated processes in New Zealand that "get in the way" of roading development.

"I come from a business background; I'm totally outcomes orientated.

"So it's 'what is the outcome I want?' and 'how do we adjust the process to get there?'

"Less cones, less traffic lights that annoy people... "

Green Party co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick on the Mike Hosking Minor Leaders Breakfast. Photo / Alyse Wright

Speaking on the Mike Hosking Minor Leaders Breakfast, Green co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick believes any dip in the polls as a result of the party's association with gangs would have already been seen, arguing voters are more interested in other issues.

Two polls this week show the Green Party holding its 14-16% vote share of recent months. The polling period of both polls captured in its final days the saga concerning last week's resignation of Labour candidate Kerrin Leoni for campaigning at a gang event, which came after MPs from Te Pāti Māori and the Greens did the same.

Swarbrick said she would have expected any impact to have been seen in polls this week but she believed voters were interested in other issues, such as the cost of living.

Asked about Labour leader Chris Hipkins ruling out many Green Party tax reform policies and ruling out giving the party some ministerial positions, Swarbrick insisted the relationship between the two parties was good and "collaborative", noting she and co-leader Marama Davidson had regular conversations.

However, she acknowledged the declining "direction of travel" for the two major parties, which she believed made the rule-in, rule-out conventions nonsensical.

Swarbrick didn't provide a clear answer when questioned on what her party might be able to secure in coalition negotiations regarding tax reform. Labour has promised no new taxes aside from its capital gains tax, whereas the Greens have proposed extensive tax reform, headlined by a wealth tax. While she encouraged people to vote for what they wanted, Swarbrick said "of course we're going to compromise".

Swarbrick appeared confident her party would retain the three electorate seats it won in 2023, but also felt it likely the Greens would win Te Tai Tokerau and Christchurch Central, which was a long-time Labour seat.

On Opportunity, Swarbrick wasn't sure how much of the Greens vote had been lost to Qiulae Wong, saying the party's support seem to be "flowing in from everywhere", reiterating how Opportunity could support the current governing parties and how it wasn't a guaranteed vote to change the Government.

She observed that voters were "exhausted" and sick of the "tit-for-tat nonsense".

A sharp drop in the New Zealand dollar following yesterday's Reserve Bank decision to leave the Official Cash Rate unchanged wasn't unexpected, according to the Bank's Governor Anna Breman.

The NZD fell about 75 basis points to US56.07c after the Monetary Policy Committee voted 4-3 to hold the OCR at 2.75%.

"We did think that the New Zealand dollar could weaken, but you have to remember that this decision to hold at this meeting came after two consecutive OCR hikes," Breman told Herald NOW's Ryan Bridge Today.

There were different estimates on how much the NZD would react, but the committee also considered factors other than the exchange rate when looking at how the NZ economy would be affected.

A weakened exchange rate was good for exporters but made importing more expensive. It also wasn't great for inflation but that depended on how long-lasting the effect was on the exchange rate, Breman said.

"If you have temporary volatility in the exchange rate, we had a bit of a stronger Kiwi dollar before earlier in the year, we tend to see through temporary volatility."

A weak exchange rate also didn’t tend to have a big inflationary impact if demand was also weak, as is currently the case.

"Currently we're seeing that households are still being cautious, so it's difficult for firms to pass on cost increases onto households."

Nicola Willis has dismissed the National Party's low poll result as being "completely out of whack".

The latest RNZ-Reid Research poll has National at 24.8%, 1.1 percentage points lower than the last poll three weeks ago and behind Labour on 30.6%.

Willis told Ryan Bridge TODAY the poll is "completely out of whack with other public polls", citing the 1News Verian edition, which had the party on 29%, ahead of Labour on 27%.

"My read is it's very close out there. We have an election which is going to be very consequential. There are still a lot of votes to be won, and so we're working every day to grow that party vote."

Teenager rescued after getting stranded while fishing in East Auckland

A teenage fisherman was rescued by emergency services at Musick Pt near Bucklands Beach. Photo / File

A teenage fisherman was rescued by emergency services in east Auckland after being stuck on rocks.

Police received a 111 call just after 8pm yesterday at Musick Pt near Bucklands Beach.

Senior Sergeant Garry Larsen, officer in charge of the Marine Rescue Centre, said the boy had been fishing.

“He realised the tide was coming in quickly, putting him in a tricky spot with the terrain meaning he could not climb out,” he said.

“The Auckland Maritime Unit coordinated the response, deploying the Police Search and Rescue high ropes team to the area.”

He was rescued and able to return home safely.

Larsen said the teenager did the right thing in calling 111.

“Our advice for anyone heading out on the water or going fishing is to be prepared.

“It’s a good reminder with lighter evenings and summer around the corner to play close attention to tides and conditions on the water,” he said.

Police advice for the warmer months is to know your limits and have a few modes of communication if something goes wrong, Larsen said.

Always tell someone where you’re going, and when you’re due back, he added.

Surge in people injecting peptides prompts Health NZ needle exchange kits

New Zealand Herald October 28, 2026

Medsafe says many unapproved peptides are illegal and potentially dangerous.

By RNZ Morning Report

Health New Zealand has started providing pharmacies with peptide-injecting kits as part of its needle exchange programme for people injecting peptides without a prescription.

In the six weeks since the programme began, 2300 kits have been handed out to 190 participating pharmacies – and it has been suggested users include parents administering peptides to their children.

But Medsafe has warned many of the unapproved peptides are illegal, untested and potentially dangerous.

“Peptides are small substances made naturally in the body that act as signals, helping to regulate things like growth, healing, hormones and our metabolism,” Bronwyn Petrie, Health NZ group manager of population health as part of the needle exchange programme, told Morning Report today.

“I don’t think we know the size and scale of the unapproved peptides in New Zealand, but what we do know is that internationally and here in New Zealand, there has been a huge spike in people injecting peptides.”

She said unapproved peptides were being promoted “widely” on social media, with claims they could slow ageing and help with muscle-building and losing weight.

There had been a massive rise in the number of people approaching needle exchange services – set up in the 1980s to help drug users get their fix in a safer way – to inject peptides. It is funded by Health NZ, and considered one of the country’s most successful harm reduction initiatives.

“And so they have [pulled] together a free pack for those providers and for our pharmacies to provide for those people,” Petrie said.

“But critically, I really want to point out that this shouldn’t be seen as an endorsement of unapproved peptides. It’s about supporting our providers, responding to the demand, meeting people where they are, and ultimately preventing potential harm.”

In May 2026, Medsafe warned against anyone using them if they were not prescribed or sourced from a pharmacy.

“There is a very real risk that these products may be of poor quality, not contain the substance claimed on the label (if they are labelled), contain other harmful substance not on the label or not be sterile (and so may contain substantial quantities of germs or mould).

“These products ... are illegal and potentially harmful. Using them can cause serious and potentially life-threatening reactions.”

Specific products mentioned by Medsafe included BPC-157, CJC-1295, GHRP-6, Ipamorelin, Kisspeptin, KLOW, melanotan II, retatrutide, sealank, seamax, TB-500 and thymosin.

“Even if these products actually contain the advertised ingredient, there is no good scientific evidence that they work as advertised or that they are safe. Neither is there any evidence that these products are sterile, and because they are injected, it means there is a high risk of a life-threatening infection from using them.”

Petrie said that warning was “pretty clear”.

“I guess our role from Health New Zealand was really supporting our providers, making sure that they had information and the packs to provide. And really our key messages are if you are injecting peptides, you know, speak to a health professional, but also please use sterile equipment, never share needles and dispose of it safely.”

Petrie said needle exchanges offered confidentiality to encourage their use, so records of who accessed the services were not kept.

“But anecdotally we have heard you know, whether it be a gym user or whether it be a mother coming in wanting something for their child, it’s a really wide range of people and I think that’s what makes it even more challenging in many ways.”

She said she did not know the specifics in the case of a mother needing peptides for her child, but it “could be associated with growth or muscle healing or a whole range of different things”.

“The proliferation of peptides and their use is widespread and potentially growing. So this is just something that we wanted to do proactively ... and it’s only one thing that we’re doing as well. [Health NZ has] just released a peptide podcast ... and we’re also working closely with the Ministry of Health and others thinking about how to respond to this.”

Another supermarket chain might not fix our problems, NZIER says

New Zealand Herald October 28, 2026

Smaller retailers face barriers including wholesale access and suitable sites. Photo / 123rf

By Susan Edmunds of RNZ

Adding another brand to New Zealand’s grocery market may not necessarily reduce grocery prices, the New Zealand Institute of Economic Research says.

It has released a new report that argues other factors could be holding back competition.

The supermarket sector has become a key election issue, with National proposing to break up Foodstuffs, Labour wanting vertical separation and the Green Party proposing to buy supermarkets.

NZIER senior economist Susie McKenzie said the debate about the sector often treated high grocery prices and weak competition as the same problem.

“High grocery prices are a real concern for households, but they reflect more than just the level of competition between supermarkets. Production, transport, distribution and other underlying costs all contribute to what consumers pay.”

She said there were some barriers to competition that policy could help address, including limited wholesale access, purchasing advantages for established supermarket groups and difficulties in securing suitable retail sites.

“We need to tackle the barriers to competition not just focus on the number of supermarkets.”

But she said underlying structural constraints arose from New Zealand’s relatively small market, geography and economies of scale.

“Improving wholesale access could make it easier for smaller retailers to compete without having to establish their own expensive distribution networks,” she said. “But it won’t necessarily overcome the other challenges of operating in a small and geographically dispersed market.

“There seems to be evidence about wholesale access being a problem. Smaller retailers need to be able to obtain groceries at competitive prices and without that they can’t really establish distribution networks of their own, it’s not really competitive for them to do so.”

She said Commerce Commission reforms that introduced a regulated wholesale access regime requiring the major supermarket groups to supply competitors had little result.

“It sounds like under 0.03 percent of sales have actually gone through that regime, so there’s more room to look into why it hasn’t been delivering the intended outcomes and what more could be done in that space.

“It’s an important, unresolved barrier. We need to understand why those existing arrangements aren’t delivering competitive supply for smaller retailers.”

Other direct interventions such as separating existing supermarket businesses or wholesale and retail operations could increase competitive pressure but could also involve significant costs, she said.

“At the heart of the supermarket puzzle lies a tension between economies of scale and competition,” McKenzie said.

“Large supermarket groups can operate more efficiently by spreading their costs across extensive networks. But those same advantages can make it difficult for smaller competitors to enter and expand. The challenge is to strengthen competition without unnecessarily sacrificing those efficiencies.”

She said it was common for other small economies to have highly concentrated grocery markets.

“More supermarket chains won’t necessarily mean cheaper groceries. What matters is whether competition becomes more effective, and whether the benefits of intervention outweigh the costs. Ultimately, success should be measured by better outcomes for consumers, not simply by the number of supermarket chains.”

She said voters needed to know that there were no simple fixes.

“All the different proposals come with some benefits, some trade-offs. At the end of the day, we want stronger competition. The Commerce Commission has said that competition isn’t sufficient and it’s not working well for consumers. But we also don’t want to lose the efficiencies that we currently have in the supermarket industry that are also benefiting consumers. So it’s a fine line there.”

One has overcome bone cancer and the loss of a leg. The other turned a traumatic first rugby experience into a lifelong passion for the game.

Today, Canterbury youngsters Ava Lyall and Zara Lamperd were rewarded with a moment they’ll never forget, helping unveil the Crusaders’ 2027 squad alongside the players they have spent years admiring.

While today’s event celebrated the club’s future stars, it also highlighted the profound impact the Crusaders can have off the field, inspiring young supporters, creating lifelong connections and helping families through difficult times.

Ava and Zara were among 38 people chosen from across the Crusaders community to take part in the club’s squad launch, where supporters and local heroes could announce the 2027 playing roster themselves.

One by one, guests stepped on to the stage, opened sealed envelopes and revealed a player’s name, creating an emotional twist on the traditional squad announcement.

“It’s about getting excited… people love the team and love to be involved,” he said.

“The passion people have for this team is great.”

Among those presenting were Ava, whose battle with bone cancer has inspired her family and community, and Zara, whose unwavering devotion to the Crusaders began after a frightening introduction to rugby that could easily have ended very differently.

Among them were Ava, whose battle with bone cancer has inspired her family and community, and Zara, whose unwavering devotion to the Crusaders began after a frightening introduction to rugby that could easily have ended very differently.

Ava was nominated by her mother Tracey Lyall, who said she was “an incredibly special young girl who has shown more courage, strength and determination than most people face in a lifetime”.

“At just 9 years old, Ava was diagnosed with bone cancer. She has endured chemotherapy, long hospital stays and amputation of her leg,” she said.

“Despite everything she has been through, she continues to push herself, embrace new challenges and prove that nothing will stop her.

“She has taken up wheelchair basketball and recently competed in the Halberg Games, where she was named MVP for her team.”

Lyall said having her daughter involved in the naming of the team was “a special and unforgettable experience” for her.

“Sport has always been a huge part of Ava’s life, and her love for the Crusaders is something that brings her much happiness,” she said.

“She deserves the chance to be part of something she loves and create another amazing memory. We couldn’t be prouder of Ava, and we can’t think of anyone more deserving of this opportunity.”

For Zara, the road to the Crusaders stage began with a traumatic moment that could easily have turned her away from rugby altogether.

Her father James Lamperd explained that in 2024, when Ava was 6, she walked on to Apollo Projects Stadium to play her first game of rugby as part of a Crusaders curtain raiser.

“She didn’t make it to full time. A collision left her battered, bloody and all but missing her two front teeth,” he said.

“What could’ve been a terrifying intro to rugby became something entirely different. The care shown by the Crusaders support crew turned one of the worst moments of her young life into one of her fave memories.

“They made her feel safe, brave, valued, and maybe part of something bigger than herself.”

Lamperd said because of that, Zara “wasn’t scared to play again”.

“Because of that day, she fell in love with rugby. And, because of that day, she fell in love with the Crusaders,” he said.

“Ever since, they have been HER boys. She even insists on hunting down [Crusaders medic] Hamish at games to ensure his signature is on her new merch too, given that was who treated her that very first day.

“She’s proudly stood as part of honour guards, attended kids’ days, treasured every signed item, and can identify basically every player at a glance.

“She feels every win, loss, injury, and departure deeply, because it is happening to her family.”

Lamperd said the Crusaders had “helped raise” his little girl.

“What makes her special is her unwavering loyalty. When we attended the final this year, all she wanted to do after the game was get on to the field and hug the players so they knew their supporters still loved them,” he shared.

“Her support doesn’t depend on the scoreboard. She loves fiercely, celebrates wholeheartedly, and always makes sure she can find a way to lift those around her.

“The values she sees in the Crusaders’ resilience, commitment, connection and whānau are the same values she carries in her own life.

Lamperd said his family was “blessed by the Crusaders’ mana”.

“If anyone embodies “One of Us”, it is this little girl whose heart has been red and black since the day the Crusaders wrapped their arms around her,” he said.

“The Crusaders have helped raise someone who lives the values they represent and we’re so grateful.”

Among the other supporters to announce squad members was Jason Hampton, nominated by his wife Erika as a special treat for their 19th wedding anniversary on October 21.

She said Hampton was “without a doubt, a diehard Crusaders fan” who “bleeds red and black”.

Hampton had faced “struggles” in his life, but his wife said no matter what he encountered, he was “always the person who puts everything aside to be there for someone else”.

“He gives so much of himself to other people, often without expecting anything in return,” she said.

“Rugby has also been a huge part of his life. He played the game for many years before hanging up the boots and continuing his love for rugby through becoming a referee for a number of years, so for him, rugby isn’t just something he watches on a Saturday night; it’s a part of who he is.

“He is the kind of person who lives and breathes the game, loves the Crusaders with a passion, and is always in the corner of people he cares about.”

Richard Prokopavicius was nominated by his son Luke.

“He represents so much of what Christchurch is about: resilience, community, hard work and rebuilding,” he said.

“My father migrated to Christchurch and quickly embraced the new city as his home, became a proud New Zealand citizen and, more importantly, a true Cantabrian.

“Christchurch became the place where he built his life, career and family. Following the devastating earthquakes, my father played a meaningful part in helping Christchurch rebuild. As an architect, he was involved in designing and helping deliver many of the newly constructed buildings and developments that contributed to the rebuilding of Christchurch CBD. He dedicated years of his professional life to helping the city find its feet again.”

Luke Prokopavicious said his father would argue he was “just doing his job”.

But he felt the contribution was much more special.

“I have seen the sacrifices he made and the connection he has to Christchurch first-hand,” he said.

“He wasn’t simply rebuilding a city – he was also trying to rebuild his own life. I watched him lose so much of what he had worked his entire life to build for our family in Christchurch.

“Despite that, he continued working, contributing and putting the city and the people around him first.”

At the end of the ceremony, superfan Jenny Greenwood was honoured with a special Crusaders jersey-themed cake to mark her 67th birthday.

RNZ-Reid Research poll: National below disastrous 2020 result as Opportunity surges

New Zealand Herald October 28, 2026

National leader Christopher Luxon and Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong.

By Craig McCulloch of RNZ

The National Party has dropped below 25% in the latest RNZ-Reid Research poll, while Opportunity has reached a new high and could decide the next Government.

National has dismissed the result as “out of step” with other polls, just nine days before voting closes.

Christopher Luxon’s party is on 24.8%, down 1.1 percentage points since the last RNZ poll three weeks ago. That puts National below its disastrous 2020 election showing, though still above its historic low in 2002.

Labour remains the most popular party on 30.6%, down 0.2 points, while Opportunity records the biggest gain, rising 1.7 points to 7.2%.

The result differs sharply from the 1News-Verian poll released on Tuesday, which put National ahead on 29% and Labour on 27%. It also showed Opportunity slipping one point to 6%.

The two surveys were conducted over almost identical periods, with Reid Research surveying voters from October 20 to 26 and Verian from October 21 to 25.

Both canvassed 1000 eligible voters, though Reid Research used online panels and Verian split its interviews evenly between phone and online.

The RNZ-Reid Research poll puts the Greens on 14.5%, down 0.3 points.

Act has overtaken New Zealand First, rising 1.1 points to 10.1%, its strongest result in this poll since the 2023 election. New Zealand First is down 0.7 points to 9.9%.

Te Pāti Māori has slipped 0.1 points to 1.9%, leaving it entirely dependent on winning electorate seats to return to Parliament.

Just 3.3% of respondents said they were undecided or would not vote, down from 5.6% last poll.

On these numbers, Labour and the Greens could form a government with Opportunity’s support, without needing Te Pāti Māori.

The poll projects 37 MPs for Labour, 18 for the Greens and nine for Opportunity, giving them 64 seats in a 120-seat Parliament.

The current coalition would win just 54 seats, with 30 going to National and 12 each to Act and NZ First.

Opportunity’s nine MPs could give them a majority too, although Luxon has repeatedly ruled out working with the party.

Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong has promised to negotiate first with whichever party wins the most seats, giving Labour the first chance on these projections.

The seat calculations assume Te Pāti Māori wins one or two electorates, giving it two MPs. Further electorate victories would expand the size of Parliament.

National could also cause an overhang if it wins more electorates than its projected 30 seats. Either scenario could change the numbers required to cobble together a majority.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins has strengthened his personal ratings, even as his party’s support remains largely unchanged.

He remains the preferred Prime Minister on 23.3%, up 1.4 points, while Luxon is unchanged on 17.1%.

Another 12.7% of respondents selected no preferred Prime Minister or said they did not know.

Hipkins’ performance rating has also turned positive, with 39.7% saying he is doing well as Opposition leader, compared with 34.7% who say he is doing poorly.

Luxon’s assessment remains firmly negative: 53.8% say he is performing poorly as Prime Minister, compared with 30.1% who say he is doing well.

About half of respondents, 50.5%, believe New Zealand is heading in the wrong direction under the current Government, while 30.5% believe it is heading in the right direction.

Another 17.4% say neither right nor wrong, while 1.6% do not know.

Speaking to RNZ, National’s campaign chair Simeon Brown acknowledged the election would be “very close” but cast doubt on the poll’s accuracy.

“Ultimately, it’s out of step with most of the other polls that we’re seeing, including our own,” he said.

Brown rejected suggestions that National had fumbled its campaign strategy, either by ruling out Opportunity or focusing heavily on gangs.

“No, it’s a very clear message,” Brown said. “If you want a National-led Government with no new taxes to grow our economy and to stop Labour and [Greens’ co-leader] Chlöe Swarbrick putting a wrecking ball through the New Zealand economy, you have to party vote National.”

Act leader David Seymour also described some of the poll’s movements as an “outlier”, though he said he was “grateful” to those giving Act their support.

“Look, I try not to be the rooster taking credit for the sunrise,” he said. “It’s important not to try measuring up the curtains before you’ve looked out the window, where you’ll see that people are just starting to vote and make up their mind.”

Hipkins said the result reflected the “real momentum” from the public for change: “They’ve seen three years of this Government. They don’t want to see three more.”

Swarbrick said the polls suggested New Zealanders were sick and tired of National’s “childish” attack politics.

She said political parties had an opportunity to present a vision for the country, but the Government had instead chosen to spend more time attacking the Opposition and her personally.

Wong told RNZ she was encouraged by Opportunity’s jump in support but cautioned that “nothing is guaranteed”.

“We’re just going to keep working hard right up until election day,” she said. “We still need every vote that we can get. We are making history here.”

NZ First and Te Pāti Māori declined requests for interviews.

Reid Research surveyed 1000 eligible voters online from October 20-26, 2026, using quota sampling and weighting by age, gender and geography. The poll had a reported maximum margin of error of +/- 3.1 percentage points at a 95% confidence level. Party-vote figures excluded the 1.9% who were undecided or did not know and the 1.4% who said they would not vote.

Could a cute alien called Allen be the next Bluey? Its creator hopes so

Sydney Morning Herald October 29, 2026

The team behind the world’s favourite TV show have made their first movie - and they’re aiming for the stars.

Daley Pearson has a deadpan response when I suggest that his film Allen – in which a cute-ugly alien comes to Earth and befriends a young boy – reminds me just a little of a certain sleeper hit from the 1980s.

“I’ve not seen it,” he says of E. T. The Extraterrestrial, just about managing to keep a straight face as he does so. “I’m going to stick to that line as well. Everyone keeps telling me about it. I have to check it out. It’s Steven Spielberg, right?”

He is, of course, joking. The first feature from Brisbane-based Ludo Studio, the makers of Bluey, is a veritable showbag of references big and small to the movies and TV shows, the music and the games of the 1980s and ’90s, the decades that shaped the 42-year-old who co-wrote (with Sophie Miller) and co-directed (with Jeffrey Walker) the live-action movie.

“I wanted to do something funny about nostalgia,” says Pearson, who co-founded Ludo with Charlie Aspinwall in 2012 (the pair serve as executive producers of Bluey, which was created by Joe Brumm and is officially the world’s most-watched show). “It started with a funny idea, what happens to the kids in those movies … when they grow up to be not as special as they were told they’d be.”

The sense of disconnect between the promise and the reality can leave you, he says, “in a state of arrested development”.

That is very much where we find Petey (TJ Power), who still dreams of reconnecting with the funny creature from outer space who disappeared back into the ether before he’d even hit puberty.

The adult Petey lives in a flat beneath the home of brother Jaden (Josh Helman) and his wife Carly (Charlotte Nicdao). Though they too met Allen when they were kids, they’ve long since put aside such childish things – unlike Petey, who has never really moved on.

Though it’s a family-friendly comedy, Pearson readily admits there’s also a sense of sadness and loss about Allen. Everyone has, he says, a moment that “pops you out of that childhood bubble” – and Petey’s is the disappearance of the best friend he’d ever had.

2:33

Allen - official trailer

The studio behind Bluey has made its first movie: a family-friendly comedy about an alien named Allen.

“It could be a death, or it could be divorce, or you move away [from friends], or your dog runs away. It could be something small or big,” he says.

In Pearson’s case, it was very much at the bigger end of the scale.

“I had a brother who passed away when I was 14, and that was what popped me out of childhood,” he says. The nostalgia in his film is, he admits, “about missing this part of your childhood and wanting it back … I hope there’s a little bit of a real heart beating, a real feeling of loss and longing that gives the film a bit of an anchor.”

In littering his film with tokens of a certain time – the Jenga sets, the Michael Jackson songs, the video board game Nightmare (created, he proudly informs me, in Brisbane, just like Bluey and Allen) – the filmmakers were sowing it with mnemonic triggers.

“We wanted things in there that you’ve forgotten you remember,” he says. “There was a bit of nostalgia porn to it, but it’s more that those things really meant something to us. When I see those things, or play with those things, or listen to those things, I do remember my brother or my family. It’s a little portal key to that sort of stuff.”

In a sense, he continues, nostalgia is both an element of the film and its subject matter: “It’s about missing the past, but it’s also about missing the things that this stuff gives us access to so easily – like smelling the perfume of a former partner or something. You just get hooked back into that time and place.”

Pearson’s take on the deep soak of nostalgia is a little more complex than merely basking in the rosy glow, though. “It’ll drown you if you keep hold of that past too much,” he says. “It’s an anchor that’ll keep carrying you down. But if you can hold on to it and let it float you up, then it’s so special.

“The real path to happiness begins in relaxing and letting go.”

If that all feels like a lot of weight for a family film to carry, it is. But Allen isn’t weighed down by it. It’s bright, buoyant and busy. But above all, it has a brilliant conceived and executed alien at its centre.

Whenever Allen is on screen, the film comes to life. He’s cute, but not cloyingly so. He’s also a bit mischievous, and at times has an air of menace akin to the pocket-sized monsters of Joe Dante’s Gremlins (1985). He is, in short, a star. But getting him there took some trial and error.

Allen is a mix of CGI and puppetry. There was also an animatronic version, though he didn’t make the final cut.“It came out looking a little like Allen’s mean older brother,” says Pearson. “It would definitely have tipped the scales into some sort of horror. We said we’d use it for a sequel if we needed the bad version of Allen to come back because it was quite severe.”

And what about a second coming for the alien? Could we see a sequel? A series? Games? Is there scope for Allen to become the content machine, and merch monster, that Bluey is?

“We’ve got some ideas, it would be incredible, but we’d better see what people say first. We can’t get ahead of ourselves,” says Pearson. “But I would love it. It always felt like once Alf [TV’s favourite alien of the 1980s] left, there was just an open space for a vehicle like this, and it would be a dream.”

Allen is streaming on Netflix from November 12.

Chiefs sign Justin Tucker in wake of sexual misconduct allegations as Butker struggles

The Guardian Wed, 28 Oct 2026 19:59:56 GMT

Tucker was banned under NFL’s conduct policy

Butker has missed five of 16 FG attempts this season

The Kansas City Chiefs have signed the former Baltimore Ravens kicker Justin Tucker to their practice squad after Harrison Butker’s poor start to the season.

Tucker was widely considered one of the best kickers in NFL history until the Ravens released him in May 2025. The Ravens said his departure was a “football decision” after a slump in form, but the move came months after he was accused of inappropriate sexual behavior by massage therapists. Tucker denied the allegations and never faced criminal charges but he served a 10-game NFL ban for violating the league’s personal conduct policy.

More than a dozen massage therapists from spas and wellness centers in the Baltimore area accused Tucker of inappropriate sexual behavior. One therapist who spoke to the Baltimore Banner, which broke the story, described Tucker’s alleged behavior as “really degrading”. Another said: “I can’t watch sports anymore. I see his face everywhere.”

The 37-year-old has not played in the NFL since he was released by Baltimore. During his time with the Ravens, he made seven Pro Bowls and won the Super Bowl in his rookie season. His final season in Baltimore, in which he made just 73.3% of his field goals, was statistically the worst of his career. Tucker’s career average for field goals is 89.1%.

On Wednesday, Chiefs head coach Andy Reid said he was not worried about Tucker joining the team.

“He’s done his suspension, took care of that business there,” Reid said in response to a question about what message the move sent to the team’s female fans. “I’ll leave it at that.”

The Guardian Wed, 28 Oct 2026 19:58:27 GMT

Israel election – live updates

Israel election: what we know so far

Analysis: Rise of Palestinian parties in Knesset will redraw Israel’s political landscape

Israel’s future hung in the balance on Wednesday as it became clear that Benjamin Netanyahu had lost his governing majority. His political fate now depends on whether opposition Jewish parties are prepared to forge a common front with Palestinian parties, whose support surged in Tuesday’s elections.

The leader of the Jewish opposition bloc, the retired general Gadi Eisenkot, appeared to rule out such a broad coalition in a premature declaration of victory overnight for what he called a “Zionist majority”.

As the vote count proceeded on Wednesday, initial exit poll projections that Eisenkot’s bloc would have a narrow lead over Netanyahu’s coalition looked increasingly in doubt as the prime minister’s bloc edged ahead, with the votes of deployed soldiers and other absentee ballots – about 14% of the total electorate – yet to be fully counted.

With the remaining 86% of the votes tallied, both Jewish blocs looked certain to fall short of the 61 Knesset seats needed for a majority government, leaving Eisenkot and his allies facing a clear choice: either make a pact with Arab Israeli parties heading for a record result of 16-19 seats, or hand Netanyahu a political lifeline in the form of new elections or a unity government.

On Wednesday night, Netanyahu reacted to the high Palestinian turnout and the success of Arab Israeli parties by claiming they had “stolen the election”. He did not offer evidence, but said on X that his Likud party had sent “hundreds of testimonies and pieces of evidence” to the central elections committee and the Shin Bet internal security agency.

Both those agencies have been politicised under Netanyahu’s government. The elections committee had sought to ban Arab Israeli parties before the poll, but the attempt to exclude them was overturned by the country’s supreme court.

Donald Trump took credit for Netanyahu’s better than expected performance so far, claiming his overt backing in the run-up to the vote had made the difference. “When the endorsement went out, it helped him a lot,” Trump said, adding that the result appeared to be heading for a stalemate or a Netanyahu win.

Yair Golan, the leader of the centre-left Democrats, a junior partner in Eisenkot’s Change bloc, urged Eisenkot to negotiate with the two Palestinian parties, the Joint List and Ra’am (the United Arab List).

“We have no future here if we don’t stop being afraid. And if we don’t put an end to racism. We can no longer accept Netanyahu’s racist distinction between Jewish and Arab votes,” Golan wrote on X.

“Anyone who tries to erase the votes of Arab citizens is surrendering to Netanyahu and giving up on Israel,” he added, pointing out that Netanyahu relied on ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties that were non-Zionist and opposed conscription for their constituents.

Noa Landau, a commenter writing in Haaretz, argued that by making Zionism the test for forming a coalition, excluding potential partners, while the prime minister had not, Eisenkot had fallen “into the trap Netanyahu laid for him over the course of the election campaign”.

The Joint List leader, Yousef Jabareen, said its strong performance meant it “can’t be ignored under any political scenario”. He said Netanyahu’s government, especially its extremist national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, “has made life bitter for every Arab citizen”.

“We will be ready to pave the way to oust the government of Netanyahu, Ben-Gvir and Smotrich – and send them home,” Jabareen said. Another Joint List official described the choice facing the Jewish opposition as “supremacy or building democracy”.

Counting all the votes could take another few days, with absentee ballots the last to be tallied. Most of those are from deployed soldiers. The army vote usually swings right, but that broad picture may be complicated by the fact that a lot of older, more moderate reservists are now on active duty.

Once all the votes are accounted for, it will be up to Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, to give one of the party leaders six weeks to form a government. If the first choice fails, the opportunity passes to their rival. In the weeks of political wrangling likely to ensue, both Netanyahu and Eisenkot are expected to lure defectors from each other’s camps.

Netanyahu would remain in office in a caretaker capacity until a new majority is formed. He might expect to benefit if the deadlock leads to another round of elections. Tens of thousands of diaspora Israelis who returned to vote on Tuesday, and were mostly opposed to the governing coalition, might not return for another vote, for example.

The Palestinian parties and Jewish centre-left have been urging the opposition to focus on finding common cause in the Knesset, replacing the speaker and pursuing legislation that the factions can agree on, such as ordering an independent review into the security failures that led to the 7 October attack by Hamas in 2023.

On Wednesday, Herzog urged all parties to keep an “open mind” in trying to build a new government coalition.

“We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections,” he said.

The election happened in the midst of Israel’s war in Gaza – barely mentioned in the course of the campaign, despite the fact that Israel has been accused of committing genocide in Gaza and ethnic cleansing in the West Bank, and Netanyahu is wanted by the international criminal court for alleged war crimes.

A UN commission of human rights experts reported on Monday that Israel had continued to commit genocidal acts against Palestinian civilians in Gaza after a ceasefire was declared in October 2025. Since then 1,431 Palestinians have been killed by the Israeli military, including 300 children.

The report, by the Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, said: “Israeli authorities and forces continue to commit genocidal acts with the genocidal intent to destroy, in whole or in part, the Palestinians in Gaza.”

Israel’s ambassador to the UN, Daniel Meron, rejected the report as an “attempt to destroy the Jewish state” and “to undermine Israel’s ​legitimacy and deny its fundamental right to exist and defend itself”.

Eisenkot and much of his bloc support the war in Gaza, and sought to make the election a referendum on Netanyahu. The turnout was nearly 78%, the highest since 1999, with marked increases in the number of serving military members voting.

Political deadlock has led to repeated votes in the past. Between 2019 and 2022, Israel held five elections.

Netanyahu is Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, governing for 19 of the past 30 years, and its most tenacious political survivor. Entangled in a long-running corruption trial, he and his far-right coalition had stoked xenophobic fears and suggested Israel would be vulnerable to a nuclear attack without him.

The campaign, febrile even by Israeli standards, included Netanyahu posting a picture of a nuclear explosion devastating Tel Aviv on the eve of the polls opening.

Since the deadly attack launched by Hamas on Israel’s southern communities on 7 October 2023, Israel has devastated Gaza and killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, fought Hezbollah in Lebanon, occupied new territory in Syria and launched a war alongside the US against Iran.

During his opening statement, Paxton showed a CCTV clip of a passenger, Stephen Crean, attempting to wrestle a knife from Williams. He said Williams told Crean: “Do you want to die?”

“We say, clear evidence of the defendant’s intention to kill, as was the use of the knife to stab so many, and to stab and cut Mr Crean in his hand, head and lower back,” Paxton said.

Paxton described the “terror” of the attack, which led some train passengers to run “for their lives” and hide away in toilets, store cabinets and under seats.

The prosecutor also praised the “extraordinary bravery” of the passengers who tried to wrestle the knife off Williams.

This included Scott Green, who was stabbed while he attempted to grab the knife from Williams. A member of the train crew, Samir Zitouni, was also stabbed multiple times as he tried to use a frying pan to stop Williams, jurors heard.

“In the face of that threat and the defendant’s sheer brutality some stood tall to protect others trying to de-escalate his rampage, defending themselves and putting themselves in harm’s way to protect strangers,” Paxton said.

Paxton also praised the train driver for his decision to make an emergency stop in Huntingdon.

Williams, of no fixed abode, previously admitted a series of offences, including the wounding of 12 people, but denies 14 counts of attempted murder.

Paxton told the court Williams posed a “dangerous threat” to the people he encountered before the train attack on the evening of 1 November.

Jurors heard Williams had approached a 17-year-old boy on the Docklands Light Railway in London in the early hours of 1 November and asked him if he was “beefing the devil” before he knifed him in the face and hand.

Williams also attacked three people in Peterborough on the evening of 31 October, the court heard, including a 14-year-old boy.

“Across the Halloween weekend last year, to the many people he encountered, the defendant, Anthony Williams, posed a dangerous threat, marauding through towns and cities, on streets and trains alike, armed with a knife,” he said.

“He stabbed many, seeking to end their lives with deadly intention, striking out at them when they were defenceless and in fear.”

The trial continues on Thursday.
