Labour is still searching for an energy fix for a new world

The Guardian Wed, 28 Oct 2026 19:11:36 GMT

The chancellor is right to focus on pure affordability, but £100 handouts and delayed decisions won’t shield consumers from the next wave of price hikes

Amid the myriad of small measures, virtually everything in John Healey’s budget came back to the cost of energy. The higher energy prices that have resulted from the Iran war have pushed up inflation, are eating into households’ incomes, are a drag on businesses – and are the main reason why the forecast for GDP growth next year was cut from 1.6% to just 1%.

And energy was the focus of Healey’s sole surprise in his consumer-facing policies – the £100 payment to 20m households in A-D council tax bands to help with fuel bills this winter. It will be funded, in effect, by tapping the banks for a few quid for 15 months via the bank surcharge.

But the chancellor will know that £100 won’t look generous when the bills land. Gas prices are still rising, and leading supplier EDF’s latest prediction is that the regulator’s price cap will be hiked by £466 in January, pushing the annual rate for an average household to £2,189. When Labour took office in July 2024, talking naively about taking £300 off bills over the life of the parliament, the cap was £1,568.

No surprise, then, that the messaging on energy is shifting. Here is the passage in Healey’s speech that hinted at big changes ahead: “Today I’m setting a new course on energy: to get UK energy costs down in line with Europe. From this point, our Labour government’s priority is first and foremost cheaper energy, with clean power key to achieving this.”

Thank goodness for the reset towards affordability. It is long overdue. The biggest impediment to economic growth, including the prime minister’s longed-for “reindustrialisation”, is the cost of energy in the UK. There is little Healey can do about international gas prices, but he can do “deep reform of our energy system”, as he put it. So what’s the plan?

That, unfortunately, is where the “new course” turned blurry. Take the promise to introduce “a new cost control framework to drive down all aspects of energy bills”. The ambition is laudable, because energy bills have become littered with levies and charges – everything from socialising unpaid consumer energy debt to funding Sizewell C – that should more naturally be funded from general taxation. It’s about time the Treasury took an interest in such hidden taxes.

But the costs don’t disappear just because they are placed within a new framework. The tough question is how much a chancellor is willing to fund from Treasury coffers in the interest of lower upfront bills for consumers and business. It is not a small question, because wide-ranging definitions of levies can produce figures as high as £15bn.

It’s good that Healey is demanding no new levies (unless they bring down bills), but that’s not the same as hacking into the existing thicket. Funding for green hydrogen projects is being taken on by the Treasury, which is a start. But come back in next year’s spending review, it seems, to discover the size of Healey’s scythe. More urgency is needed.

There was a bit more clarity on the electricity generation side. “This government will only buy and build new projects when they lower bills and when they can connect to the grid,” said Healey. That reads as a strong hint that offshore wind commissions will be slowed until prices fall (which probably requires a fall in borrowing costs for developers) and the upgrade of the grid is more advanced. Very sensible: sequencing matters, as the alarming costs of “wasted wind” demonstrate regularly.

But Healey’s ambition to “break the grip of international gas prices” by switching older renewables projects on to lower fixed-price contracts is not new. Ed Miliband, when energy secretary, said the same. The test is how hard ministers are willing to twist the arms of renewables owners, who are very attached to arrangements that give them jackpot revenues when gas prices are high. The basic tension remains: for consumers to win, somebody has to be paid less than they were expecting.

So, yes, one can applaud the change of tone and direction. A reset in energy policy to prioritise affordability was bound to arrive eventually. The drive to clean power also had to be a drive to cheap power. But one cannot yet say the new approach is joined-up. Policies to drive the electrification of homes and transport were not turbo-charged, which they need to be to reduce long-term dependency on gas and oil. And “deep reforms” to the electricity market are, to put it gently, a work in progress. More urgency needed.

The Guardian view on Labour’s budget: bold ambitions and welcome first steps

The Guardian Wed, 28 Oct 2026 19:01:30 GMT

Banks, landlords and gambling firms will pay more as the chancellor begins building a fairer economy and a more active state in a cost of living crisis

John Healey’s first budget was a Rorschach test. Supporters saw dozens of measures offering “breathing space” to a public worn down by rising prices. Critics admitted to a slew of announcements but countered that each was modest in value. Underlying both views is that the budget was more ambitious on how a state can do more to protect the public than on how much it spends. The chancellor has taken a small step in the right direction – a tricky feat in a turbulent world. But an economy marked by entrenched inequality and more than a decade of stagnation will need a bigger stride.

The Office for Budget Responsibility’s “pretty grim picture” of living standards exposes the budget’s central weakness: its relief is temporary, while the squeeze on households persists. As the government deficit shrinks and company profits recover, households are expected to move from saving roughly £50bn in 2026 to borrowing roughly the same amount in 2031. By then, mortgage repayments are expected to reach 4.25% of household disposable income – the highest level since 2009. The OBR expects growth to recover from 1% in 2027 to 1.8% in 2029, while weak worker “bargaining power” allows firms to rebuild profit margins. That sits uneasily with Mr Healey’s promises to working people.

Admittedly, the budget’s ambitions – shaping energy markets, ending rough sleeping, devolving tax and spend decisions – go beyond its winter relief package. Mr Healey is also right to ask banks, gambling companies and landlords to contribute more. Preventing hardship is better than repeatedly paying for its consequences. In ringfencing homelessness prevention in local government spending, even though the savings are experienced in the NHS, he is making both moral and financial sense.

The problem, however, is not that Mr Healey’s budget lacks ambition, but that it lacks firepower. The bank tax raises just £1.5bn over 15 months, against the projected £11bn that a Thatcher-style levy on interest-free deposits could have yielded. The Resolution Foundation has a point when it says that 80% of homes get a £100 energy payment, while 1.4 million poor families miss out. Relying on revenues from the giant Rosebank oilfield before its approval is settled would be reckless. So would treating the export of its oil as an answer to the climate damage caused by burning it.

The choices that Mr Healey makes all too often reflect the fiscal constraints he opted to retain. Is it really “credible” to claim that there will be £11bn of cuts to “unprotected” budgets (those that aren’t defence, the NHS, schools or international aid) in 2031-32? Many experts think not. Should the defence budget be funded by “reprioritising” other departments’ capital spend? Mr Healey thinks so. The prime minister called the 2009 Marmot review his bible on reducing inequalities – it advocates for widescale economic rebalancing. But devolving tax revenues without adequate redistribution risks giving the wealthiest places the most to spend, rather than giving the poorest the help they need. Mr Healey has yet to explain how he will prevent that.

Global events could make Mr Healey’s life much tougher. Prolonged disruption in the strait of Hormuz would further squeeze real incomes. But the chancellor has in his budget sketched the outline of a social-democratic active state: taxing rentiers, protecting vulnerable people and investing in prevention. The question is whether those commitments have enough resources to succeed.

The Guardian view on Israel’s elections: Netanyahu lost his mandate. If opponents unite, he’ll lose power too

The Guardian Wed, 28 Oct 2026 19:01:16 GMT

His chief rival should reject the prime minister’s anti-democratic vision and work with Palestinian Israeli parties

Benjamin Netanyahu has lost his mandate but not, so far, power. While final votes are still being tallied, most voters picked his opponents on Tuesday. His bloc’s share of seats remains the largest, but appears to have slumped by around 10, leaving it below the 61 needed for a majority in the Knesset. Palestinian Israeli parties surged, and are projected to almost double the 10 seats they held. The result is that Mr Netanyahu’s main challenger, Gadi Eisenkot, a former head of the military, now faces a choice: fall into line with Mr Netanyahu’s racist fearmongering or work with Arab-led parties.

The prime minister who oversaw shocking security failures ahead of the Hamas atrocities of 7 October 2023 still pitches himself as “Mr Security”. On trial for corruption, he has persistently attacked democratic institutions, especially the judiciary. He embraced and then indulged the ultra-right as they cheered on brutal settler violence in the occupied West Bank. (Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich lost ground in these polls, but perhaps due to their vision’s permeation of mainstream politics more than a revolt against it.) Mr Netanyahu’s war on Iran has destabilised the region. The tens of thousands of Palestinians killed by his government’s genocidal war on Gaza have barely featured in the election campaign, but its cost for Israeli hostages and international support for Israel have been noted by voters.

Mr Netanyahu relied on fear, campaigning with the slogan “the right or Palestine” and accusing Palestinian citizens of Israel, around a fifth of its population, of trying to “steal the election”. They have often boycotted their democratic right, in a system stacked against them, with politics moving rightwards. Mr Eisenkot’s bloc gives them little reason for optimism; Tuesday’s turnout testifies to their desperation to see an end to the most extreme government in Israel’s history. Millions of Palestinians living under illegal Israeli occupation got no vote at all.

Mr Netanyahu, the consummate survivor, may pin his hopes on another election. For now, as incumbent, he holds extra cards. The greatest danger is that he pushes Donald Trump into a renewed offensive on Iran after the midterms, seeing perma-war as political salvation.

Mr Eisenkot, one of many burned by their dealings with the prime minister, is unlikely to risk a “unity government”. His bloc could remove Mr Netanyahu “if it is brave enough”, observed Ahmad Tibi of the Joint List ticket of Palestinian parties. In campaigning, most opposition Israeli politicians ruled out a coalition with the Joint List or Ra’am (the United Arab List) – except on terms that they will not accept. But the Palestinian parties have made clear that they are open to cooperation and there is precedent. Mr Netanyahu himself reportedly made overtures to Ra’am in 2021; instead it joined the coalition that unseated him.

“We can no longer accept Netanyahu’s racist distinction between Jewish and Arab votes,” wrote Yair Golan, head of the centre-left Democrats – noting that Mr Netanyahu talks of a Zionist majority but relies on the support of non-Zionist Haredi parties. Mr Eisenkot may fear that supporters will not tolerate a deal but they will not thank him for failing to boot out Mr Netanyahu when given the chance. That would also allow the prime minister to turn this result into an ideological victory. Israel defines itself as Jewish and democratic. Mr Eisenkot and his partners should accept every vote and citizen as equal.

Vladimir Putin praised Elon Musk’s genius and said he was in touch with Starlink’s controlling shareholder as Russia develops its own satellite communications for its military to use against Ukraine.

The Russian president, speaking at a summit with African leaders in Moscow, was comparing the Earth-orbiting network built by Musk’s SpaceX with Russia’s gradual efforts to build its own Rassvet constellation.

“Elon Musk is a genius, a true genius,” the Russian leader said, according to the Tass news agency. “How many of these [satellites] does he have in orbit? More than 5,000, and we’re only taking the first steps.”

The true number of active SpaceX satellites is estimated at about 10,000, which provide the high-speed internet service that has been the subject of a diplomatic row between Musk, the US and Ukraine earlier this month.

A military version of Starlink, called Starshield, was suddenly restricted one night in the middle of October, preventing Ukraine from conducting medium drone attacks and hampering some of its anti-drone air defences.

Initially, Musk, an ally of the US president, Donald Trump, denied that he had ordered a throttling of the internet connection, before saying at the end of last week that he had closed a loophole in which the civilian Starlink had been used by the military.

Putin appeared to be trying to flatter Musk, whose control of the communications technology has raised questions about the US billionaire’s leverage over the White House and the impact he is able to have on Ukraine’s war effort.

“We are in close contact with our American partners – including Mr Musk – because it is very important, in orbit, not to get in each other’s way and ​to maintain a certain level of discipline and order,” Putin said.

Starlink does not work in Russia and its use by Russia inside Ukraine was restricted earlier this year. Meanwhile, Moscow has begun to develop an alternative system, though, with an estimated 26 working satellites, its capacity is limited.

Last week, after about 10 days of restriction, Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, announced that “Starlink and Starshield operations have been restored” and that the speeds were “now where they need to be”.

Few believe the issue is permanently settled, with relations between Zelenskyy and Trump fraught in the run-up to the US midterm elections next Tuesday. Trump has also reached out to Putin, agreeing to buy diesel from Moscow early in October in an effort to reduce the oil price before Americans go to the polls.

Zelenskyy said on Wednesday that he hoped proposed trilateral peace talks, involving Ukraine, Russia and the US, would take place between 6 and 10 November in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the UAE, shortly after the midterms.

“We are waiting for the American side. I think that they’ll be ready with all the answers after the elections,” the Ukrainian leader said at a press conference in The Hague with the Dutch prime minister, Rob Jetten.

Earlier, Zelenskyy said he had spoken to Andy Burnham, the UK prime minister, as it emerged that Britain would provide £10bn in extra financing for Ukraine over the next three years – and an immediate £500m for air defence systems.

The additional aid was, Zelenskyy said, “a truly strong and very timely step” that came “as Russia needs to see and feel that Ukraine will not be left alone” as the war heads towards what is expected to be its most difficult winter yet.

John Healey, the UK chancellor, announced the extra funding as part of the government’s annual budget. “The prime minister and I called President Zelenskyy to tell him about our commitments in the budget today. He told us: ‘You’ve made my day’.”

The Dutch government also said it would provide €500m in military support for the winter, and a further €1.2bn in non-military aid, partly to help fund urgent repairs to Ukraine’s utilities and manufacturing.

Kyiv has been relentlessly attacked by Moscow this autumn as Russian forces fail to make progress on the frontlines in the east of Ukraine.

Russia had launched more than 100 ballistic missiles against Kyiv and the surrounding region since the middle of October, Zelenskyy said overnight, hitting power plants and other key targets in an effort to cause a humanitarian crisis in the capital.

But the Conservatives have criticised the government for postponing big decisions, including on defence and welfare. Lucy Hough speaks to economics editor Heather Stewart

Read original article

He promised fresh hope and delivered doom, but Dr Death’s budget succeeds in doing no harm

The Guardian Wed, 28 Oct 2026 18:21:37 GMT

Armed with 98 measures, a rictus grin and a decidedly comedy-free speech, the chancellor at least offered us – and Labour – some breathing space

It was as if John Healey was taking the Hippocratic oath. First do no harm. For your first budget, this may be no bad thing: we can all think of plenty of chancellors who have done untold damage. Take a bow George Osborne. It might just have been better if the doctor that Healey had chosen to impersonate was not Dr Death.

John can’t help looking like the last man you would want to stop by your hospital bed. Not everyone can have a naturally sunny disposition. His face seems to be carved out of despair. But it would be a big help if, when called upon to make his most important speech of the year, he didn’t reinforce the impression when he opened his mouth. A one-way journey to the slough of despond.

“I’m very sorry to let you know, Mr Crace,” he would say with Voldemort delight. “But your cancer is now terminal. You have months to live.” And just when you are trying to process what he’s said and are preparing to say your goodbyes, he would let you know he had made a mistake. You only had weeks to live after all. He would then smile wanly, pat you on the shoulder before moving on to kill off his next patient. You wouldn’t be seeing him again.

Healey began with a few cheery words. Cheery by his standards, that is. This was a budget for working people. People often talked about global headwinds. John was here to let us know that these headwinds were more like a storm. Make that a hurricane. One we’d all be lucky to come out of alive. The wars in Iran and Ukraine, the rising cost of energy. The whole world was basically screwed. He knew the government had suggested we all stockpile food and water ahead of the apocalypse, but frankly we might as well not bother. Why prolong the agony?

“Fresh hope for Britain’s future,” he said. The word hope died on his lips. Only Healey can send you into a vortex of existential futility with an attempt at optimism. Even the normally upbeat Andy Burnham who was sitting next to him looked lost in his own sense of pointlessness. Not even a glimmer of a smile. The main reason he had appointed Healey was because he could be relied on to do his bidding. To deliver the kind of budget Andy had in mind. Ed Miliband was far too much his own man. But Burnham hadn’t factored in the aura of gloom.

The one consolation was that even John couldn’t be as depressing as Rachel Reeves. But Healey was working on it. Give him time. Most budget statements try to tell a story. To create a coherent narrative of the state of the economy, the government’s plans to stimulate growth and fix the problems they inherited. Even when the problems the chancellor is inheriting are the ones they created. But Healey was going to try a different approach. Just a series of unstructured, random spending announcements. Dr Death’s Seven Last Words on the Cross.

Most budget speeches also contain the odd joke. Or what passes for a gag in the minds of MPs. None of them are going to get gigs at the Edinburgh fringe. But on the few occasions that the mirror cracked and Healey’s mouth tried to form a rictus grin, his words fell flat. Turns out that not everyone finds telling people they have nothing to live for quite as funny as John. Worse still, he is a man with no sense of timing. He makes Ed Balls sound like a comedy giant.

There was the obligatory reference to Liz Truss’s mini-budget, and the hand that the shadow chancellor, Andrew Griffith, played in it. That should have been fertile comic ground as it has the benefit of being true. Four years on, we are all still suffering PTSD. Everyone apart from the Trusster, who believes the real problem was that she was forced to reverse £70bn of unfunded tax cuts. But Healey couldn’t land the punchline. Labour backbenchers were willing him to succeed, but they still couldn’t bring themselves to laugh.

The only really funny moment was completely unintentional, when Healey said that the energy secretary had opposed Jackdaw. That was supposed to be kept an open secret, not broadcast to the world. The Tory benches couldn’t contain themselves with forced laughter. The chancellor tried to redeem the situation by ad-libbing that at least the opposition was still awake. Which was more than could be said for many Labour backbenchers.

Fresh hope and breathing space, Healey said again. It had become his only leitmotif. And, yet again, it felt like another nail in the coffin. The world was in turmoil, the country bouncing from crisis to crisis and the chancellor was doing not very much. Or rather he was doing a lot – he announced 98 different measures – but none of them amounted to a lot. Not that anyone was going to complain about getting £100 off their council tax or not having to queue up at the post office for your Amazon returns. These things do make a difference.

It was just that we were waiting for the big reveal. The major surprise. But time passed. And passed. And none came. There was a promise to spend 3% of GDP on defence by 2030, but no details of how. It was the miserabilist’s dream. Growth baked in at less than 2%, living standards predicted to fall.

A sense of drift. But maybe it was all deliberate. A country put on palliative care because it wouldn’t survive extreme surgery. Healey had said he had called an early budget because it was time to inject some urgency into the public finances. But many of the really big decisions had been kicked into the long grass. He had said the budget was to give the country some breathing space. It felt as if the government were the ones who needed the breathing space.

Kemi Badenoch’s response was similarly underwhelming. Then she had rather shot herself in the foot by admitting that the country had been paralysed and miserable under the Tories. She even found herself agreeing with some of Healey’s measures but her overall assessment – Was that it? – was echoed by many Labour MPs. Not that Kemi had any answers herself. None to be taken seriously, at least. At his own press conference, a disinhibited Nigel Farage had just sounded mad. There is no appetite for the Tories or Reform. So a breathing space it is.

Burnham promised big change – where was it? Instead we got the Martin Lewis budget

The Guardian Wed, 28 Oct 2026 18:19:15 GMT

The financial guru’s fingerprints are all over John Healey’s red book – but Lewis is not a politician. His everyday fixes can’t meet this turbulent moment

Was this Andy Burnham’s budget – the bold vision of a new prime minister who burns with a passion to topple “40 years of neoliberalism”? Fat chance. Was it John Healey’s budget – the repair job of a cautious chancellor fretting about record-high taxes, £3tn of public debt and an economy stuck in first gear? Little sign of that.

This budget was cast in the image of a man who isn’t in Burnham’s government or even a Labour politician – but who appears almost every day on TV, on podcasts and is probably better known than 649 of the MPs at Westminster. Today’s budget was the Martin Lewis budget.

Lewis is the MoneySavingExpert, whose weekly Money Tips email advises 10 million British subscribers on cheap mortgages, Black Friday deals and how to score two pizzas for £10. Tips and tricks to stave off rising prices and make the most of the money you have. Given that the Bayeux tapestry is French, and the Koh-i-noor is Indian, Lewis may be the closest thing Britain has to a genuine national treasure.

Over the past four years, since Russia launched its full-scale war on Ukraine and sent energy prices soaring, Lewis has become more political and wielded greater influence in Westminster. His fingerprints were all over this “red book”. This morning, before the cabinet had even had its traditional pre-budget pep talk, Lewis had gone to Downing Street for a personal briefing from the chancellor on its key measures. On Radio 4’s Today programme, he was the big budget interview, rather than any politician or BBC editor.

No wonder, because the most eye-catching of the budget’s measures had been written by the money saving expert. Scrapping standing charges on gas bills, shielding more pensioners from income tax and fixing energy bill credit against council tax bands – all of these came from Lewis’s wishlist. Beyond policies, he has also informed Burnham’s politics. At last year’s Labour conference, Lewis advised any new prime minister to “pick a hundred things that piss people off and fix them at one a day for the first hundred days”. Et voilà! The King of the North has vowed to end loudcasting on public transport, crack down on unfair parking fines and introduce more drop boxes for the post … and more and more.

For Labour ministers, government by MoneySavingExpert may seem a no-brainer. After a wretched couple of years under Keir Starmer, they can pose as the people’s champion, for ever on your side. Best of all, all these micro-policies cost micro-money. Today’s budget had 98 measures – more than any I can remember in decades of covering fiscal events, yet they all cost trifling sums.

Which brings us to the killer problem: Lewis is one of the most trusted people in Britain. But he’s not a politician. He’s never claimed to be. He speaks the language of terms and conditions, not financialisation – and he knows his limits. To quote a New Statesman essay last week on the new MoneySavingPolitics: “As governments have embraced retail policies and suggestion-box-style politics in his image, Lewis has been raising the alarm that there are too many people who can no longer help themselves and it is time for structural change.”

The difference was clear today. In her first budget, Rachel Reeves announced extra spending worth £74bn by the end of the period. By comparison, Healey announced a grand total of £380m. For all Burnham’s grand ambition and soaring rhetoric, his first budget was only 0.5% of Starmer’s first budget.

This is obviously not how the King of the North wants you to see him. Listen to Burnham speak, and you hear a changemaker, an ideas man, a leader with a 10-year plan. But does he put his money where his mouth is? Does he heck. The anxiety I have heard for months from so many of his advisers and MPs was borne out in this budget: he’s big talk and small stick.

The best line of the day came from Kemi Badenoch. “The prime minister came to power promising to end 40 years of neoliberalism, and instead we got 4p off gherkins,” the Tory leader said, while Burnham and Healey frowned like men caught bang to rights. What’s the point of cut-price marmalade when a few months ago you promised to nationalise Thames Water?

Why, for that matter, chuck out the old boss when the new one is less ambitious? Whacking banks with a tax in order to cut energy costs is good politics, but this new government should have been much more ambitious. A hundred pounds is a token saving when the typical household’s fuel bill is about to top £2,000. Given how harsh this El Niño winter is likely to be, I imagine the government will have to cobble together another intervention before the new year.

Ministers are now caught in a pincer movement between Badenoch to their right, who can argue they aren’t tackling the really big problems and, to their left, the Greens and Plaid, as well as the Scottish nationalists, who will keep on saying they aren’t doing enough for their own voters. In a day of grim economic forecasts, perhaps the worst was from the Office for Budget Responsibility, which said that in the face of high inflation, earnings will not rise at all next year – while 2030 would see households with take-home pay just 2% above where it was before Covid struck in 2020. Put those two figures together and – despite all the Westminster chat – you can forget about a snap election that delivers Labour a new majority.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

If ministers can’t offer any protection against an economic outlook that bleak, they will face an angry and mutinous public. If the Labour party wants to be re-elected, it needs to give people a reason to go out and vote for it. Pointing to bond markets isn’t a defence, because markets aren’t in open rebellion. Yes, government borrowing is a lot more expensive than it was in the post-crash years of cheap money and the interest bill on the nation’s debt is high. But no one thinks Britain is France. Gilt traders today looked at a government running down its financial buffer and were completely unruffled. Had Healey borrowed much more to invest in social and cheap housing, he could have argued that such spending would soon enough bring down benefit bills – and markets would have believed him.

I write this as someone who wants Burnham to do well – and certainly to do better than today’s tiny raft of tweaks. Unlike many Labour politicians, he can talk sincerely about where disastrous rightwing politics have led this country. When he promises a new economic and political model, I – and many others – am up for it. In contrast to Starmer he doesn’t act as if he hates 80% of his own party members. Unlike Starmer’s advisers, his team doesn’t subsist on a diet of received wisdom and petty vindictiveness. But at some point, the grand rhetoric and the romantic notions need to cash out into a programme of change. Otherwise, voters will draw the conclusion that this summer’s coup against a recently elected prime minister had no grand motivation apart from saving the skins of Labour MPs and fanning a few egos.

A Martin Lewis budget is fine, but Labour chose Andy Burnham as its leader and the public were promised a Burnham budget. They’re still waiting.

Aditya Chakrabortty is a Guardian columnist and the Guardian’s senior economics commentator

Budget 2026: what it means for your wallet, your mortgage and your pay

The Guardian Wed, 28 Oct 2026 18:14:08 GMT

How the chancellor’s measures on tax, benefits and pensions will affect your personal finances

Healey offers £100 payment to households to help navigate ‘global economic storms’

Budget 2026: key points at a glance

Budget 2026 calculator: find out if you are better or worse off

Josh graduated two years ago from an English university and is back home in London. He earns £28,500, out of which he pays £3,186 in income tax and £1,274 in national insurance (NI) contributions a year. This results in take-home pay of £2,003 a month or £24,040 a year. Despite an outcry, the salary threshold for repaying his plan 2 student loan will remain frozen at £29,385 for three years from next April, so any pay rise is likely to trigger payments. Graduates must repay 9% of earnings over the threshold.

Layla earns the UK’s typical (median) wage of £41,000 as a nurse. She pays £5,684 in income tax and £2,274 in NI contributions. This results in take-home pay of £2,753 a month or £33,041 a year.

Traditionally income tax bands keep pace with inflation, but they have been frozen until 2031. This means a greater proportion of pay is taxed than would otherwise be expected.

With no changes to the “big three” – income tax, NI and VAT – her finances will look much the same in 2027.

She qualifies for the £100 energy payment for English households in council tax bands A-D (council tax is devolved). Her energy bill will also be reduced by the decision to abolish standing charges on gas bills and the extension to the VAT cut on electricity to July.

Simon is an accountant earning £65,000, and Maria earns £28,000 as a part-time teacher. Some of their child benefit is clawed back through the high-income child benefit charge, which is a tax penalty that kicks in at £60,000. As a result the couple have combined take-home pay of £6,141 a month or £73,690 a year.

With no big tax changes this budget has not transformed their finances. Like other Britons they benefit from the energy bill shake up and their band D home qualifies for the £100 payment.

Tom and Martha work as teachers in London, earning £45,000 and £50,000 respectively. They have combined take-home pay of £6,287 a month or £75,439 a year. They rent a flat and are desperate to get on the property ladder. With a combined income of £95,000 they are eligible for the Your First Home scheme to help first-time buyers purchase a new-build home in England with a deposit of as little as 2.5%. Applications open in February, but only those with a total annual household income of £110,000 or less outside London, or £140,000 or less within London will qualify.

Lawyer Lucy earns £98,000 and civil servant Robert £48,000. The couple have combined take-home pay of £8,790 a month or £105,477 a year after tax. At this level, all the family’s child benefit entitlement is clawed back. Any pay rise for Lucy has big tax implications as she is close to the £100k “cliff edge”. For every £2 of income over that, you lose £1 of the £12,570 annual tax-free personal allowance so any earnings between £100,000 and £125,140 are effectively taxed at 60%.

Their suburban home is in council tax band G so they miss out on the £100 energy payment. On the plus side, the keen savers will benefit from the cancelling of a plan to cut to the annual cash Isa allowance for under-65s from £20,000 to £12,000 a year from April.

The Cooper family have three children and live in a rented property in Leicestershire, paying £995 a month. Paul works 35 hours a week in a distribution centre and is paid the ”national living wage” (NLW) for older workers, which is currently £12.71 an hour. His partner Hannah is not working. After tax, NI and his pension contribution, his take-home pay is £1604 a month. This is topped up with a monthly universal credit (UC) and child benefit payment totalling £1,989 a month. They will benefit from the 2027 rise in the NLW to £13.21 per hour and will also receive the £100 energy payment.

Maxine drives 25,000 miles a year delivering parcels and earns £40,000 on a self-employed basis. Earlier this year the government upped the tax-free mileage allowance for people who drive for work from 45p to 55p for each of the first 10,000 miles which equates to a £200 saving for a basic-rate taxpayer. After tax – and that relief – she has take-home pay of £2,939 a month or £35,273 a year. From April 2027 the government is increasing the tax deductible rate above 10,000 miles from 25p to 35p a mile which will result in an additional £300 tax saving. The 5p increase in fuel duty which was to have kicked in next year has also been delayed again.

When the new state pension increases in April next year it will reach £13,036, exceeding the £12,570 annual personal tax allowance. Peter’s only income is the new state pension and it looked as if he might owe £93 of income tax. However, to remove this liability the government is creating the new “pension tax allowance” which will be applied automatically.

Bob and Margaret have a combined income of £60,000 from their state pensions and interest on savings. After paying tax of £4,572 they have a combined income of £4,619 a month or £55,428 a year.

The big news for them is the tax rate on their savings income is increasing by 4 percentage points to 24% in April. Their additional state pension income will also be subject to tax. As a result of both changes their net income will fall by £1,101 a year.

The couple is yet to access Bob’s private pension. From April any money left unspent in a defined contribution (AKA money purchase) pension after death will be included in inheritance calculations for the first time, so he is planning to withdraw some of the cash.

Mo has been running his successful chain of florists for 30 years and wants to retire. He hopes to sell his business, crystallising a £1m gain that will attract capital gains tax. He is eligible for business asset disposal relief which reduces the rate from 24% to 18% on his £1m. However, from April the chancellor has cut this allowance to £500,000 which would increase his CGT bill by £30,000 to approximately £210,000.

‘It all happened in a split-second’: survivors recount details of deadly train crash in Spain

The Guardian Wed, 28 Oct 2026 18:12:01 GMT

Passengers describe carriages full of seriously injured people after crash that has claimed at least 68 lives

At least 68 killed in Toledo train crash – full report

Josimar Medina woke a little before 9am on Wednesday to find himself airborne and hurtling through his carriage on the fast train from Madrid to Seville.

“I remember flying through the air and looking for my girlfriend, who was also shooting through the air,” said Medina, a 37-year-old tourist from the northern Peruvian city of Chiclayo.

Once he landed, he looked around and realised just how lucky he and his girlfriend, Vitoria Maia, had been.

“I saw people with cuts, people covered in blood, people missing limbs, and I saw one person who had nothing left below the chest,” said Medina. “I saw people with their heads crushed and people with mutilated arms.”

The Peruvian stood recounting the details of Wednesday’s deadly rail crash, in which at least 68 people were killed and dozens more were injured, wearing a light brown T-shirt stained with the blood of a young American man he had helped move to safety.

Medina and Maia had been in the seventh carriage of the state-operated Renfe train that smashed into the back of a train run by the private Iryo company on the same line from the capital to the south of Spain. Had they been any further forward, they could well have been among the accident’s fatalities.

As it was, the couple climbed out of the train and helped the injured while they waited for medics and Guardia Civil officers to arrive at the scene of the crash, which took place amid vineyards and olive groves near the small town of Urda in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha, near the city of Toledo.

Within hours of the crash, Urda had been transformed into a frantic emergency response centre, with a local sports centre pressed into service as a triage post for the walking wounded. Cars, vans and trucks from the emergency services in Castilla-La Mancha and neighbouring Madrid crowded the streets.

Fredrich and Arabella Barilea, a couple from the Philippines who now live in Dubai, were on the Iryo train, and Fredrich was sent flying by the impact.

“One guy was shouting: ‘Get out! Get out! Another train could hit!” said Fredrich. “We saw all the people were also getting off. Many of them had head injuries and were covered in blood. We just got as far away from the train as we could.”

Eventually, buses arrived to ferry the lightly injured survivors to Urda – although the Barileas said they were too shocked and confused to know where exactly they had been brought.

“It all happened in a split second,” said Arabella. “The table we were sitting at just disappeared in the crash. I feel like we’re on our second life. You never know what could happen. We’re very grateful.”

Around the couple, people queued patiently on the street as they waited to board coaches. Wearing torn and bloodstained clothes and, in some cases, bandages on their heads, they stared, mute and uncomprehending. Spain may have been in mourning, as the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, said during his visit to Urda, but many of those fortunate enough to survive Spain’s second major rail crash in less than a year were still too deep in shock to begin grieving.

Ata Yelkaya, a young tourist from Turkey, usually takes the bus when he travels around Spain. On Wednesday, however, he had decided to try the Iryo. Sleepy and assuming his train had come to a halt at a station, he had switched off his tablet and pulled up his hood in preparation for a nap. At 8.53am, he felt what he would later learn was the impact of the Renfe train smashing into the carriages behind him.

“I woke up with a bump and hit my head on the seat in front of me,” he said, “I looked across at an elderly couple near me and saw that the woman had a cut in her eyebrow. That’s when I knew something serious had happened.”

When he looked out of the window, he saw the carriages behind his – carriage No 5 – had come off the track and that many people had been killed or injured.

“Everyone was in shock but I tried to help other people get off the train,” he said. “I’m from Turkey and I lived through the 2023 earthquake there, so I stayed calm and tried to think about what to do and how to get out. It was only when I got out and saw some of the dead people that it hit me. I think everyone was in shock; too shocked even to panic or to scream.”

Wednesday’s disaster stirs memories of the Adamuz rail crash in January, in which 46 people died. Once again, a small town has found itself at the centre of a national disaster and, once again, local people have rallied to help, bringing food and water to a hall that had been set up as a centre for those searching for their relatives.

But, as also happened at Adamuz, the solidarity and kindness on display is likely to turn to anger over the coming hours as people seek answers as to how one of Europe’s most modern and extensive high-speed rail networks could experience two deadly collisions that have between them claimed at least 114 lives in the space of just 10 months. With a snap general election just a month away, many voters could use their votes to register their fury over another rail disaster. The “inexplicable circumstances” that led to the crash – as Spain’s transport minister has called them – will need to be explained as swiftly and thoroughly as possible.

For all the rush to action and unity on display, there was also a sickening sense of deja vu. One woman from Urda, who had spent the morning driving people to town from the crash site, had few words to describe what she had seen and heard.

“Mejor no verlo,” she said – “it’s better not to see something like this”. Again.

Howe, Nagelsmann, Pochettino: can anyone end Manchester United’s doom loop?

The Guardian Wed, 28 Oct 2026 18:00:09 GMT

Even an elite coach would surely struggle at Old Trafford amid the executive chaos and with an unfit, uneven squad

In January 2014 the 13th series of Celebrity Big Brother aired in the UK, the show so popular that its run time was extended by five days before a public vote anointed Jim Davidson the winner. Then, two years later when Brexit happened, people wondered where their tolerant country had gone, lamenting the ephemeral spirit of London 2012 as though the 2011 riots were some kind of fever dream, not a desperate response to decades of structural and institutional racism exacerbated by the cruelty of unnecessary austerity.

The truth is that if security is quickly upended, it was built on quicksand to begin with. Which brings us to Manchester United, easing effortlessly from an uplifting third-place finish to some of the worst football in their history.

It is entirely possible that Alex Ferguson made a deal with the devil to the effect that United would be great until he retired and hilariously dreadful thereafter. But assuming not, his l’état, c’est moi mentality was busy setting up the post-him fall even at the height of the success – itself a consequence of what had gone before.

A day after the Munich air disaster, Louis Edwards – later a seller of condemned meat to schools – joined the board, eventually assuming control thanks to a dodgy rights issue. He bequeathed the club to Martin – his substellar son – who floated it for personal gain, turning an institution that sought to win, entertain and unify into a business legally compelled to return value to shareholders.

This left United vulnerable to acquisition by anyone and, when Ferguson fell out with two directors – a horse, a horse, his kingdom for a horse’s ejaculate – they sold to the Glazers, who loaded the purchase price and accordant interest obligation on to the club, with government and football authorities waving through a move since outlawed. Ferguson, meanwhile, must have feared exactly what the takeover would entail and known that without his support the banks might not have lent the money, while the chief executive David Gill admitted opposition to it but stayed in his role anyway, and so the pillaging began.

The English game then exploded, with investment in United left available only to those of wealth so extreme it necessarily casts aspersions over their character – such as arch polluter and anti‑immigration zealot, Jim Ratcliffe. Proclaiming inaccurate and divisive rhetoric contrary to the inclusive, cosmopolitan spirit of Manchester and United, jobs were culled and fights picked with fans, Old Trafford’s most desirable seats socially cleansed so the club could sell them to day-trippers for astronomical prices, with longstanding supporters banned after trumped-up charges of touting – a deeply principled stance the club fails to apply to itself.

Not untypically for a billionaire, Ratcliffe seemingly believes that correct opinions reflect exchequer not expertise, giving himself final say on footballing decisions. And rather than the “best in class” executives he promised, his United operate according to what political analysts call the “Boris principle”, no‑marks in thrall to their own self‑image given jobs for which they lack the ability and character, the consequent chaos being effective sabotage.

So the patterns continue: Champions League qualification is missed, insufficient funds are released; a new unsuitable manager spends heavily on players below requisite standard; Champions League qualification is achieved via unsustainably reactive style; the manager is denied necessary funds amounting to less than the bounty of Champions League qualification; the manager imposes a proactive style without the necessary materials; the manager is belatedly fired for a fee far exceeding that saved by cutting jobs; a new unsuitable manager, with entirely different requirements to his predecessor, is appointed; executive accountability is absent.

It is thus no surprise that Michael Carrick remains unfired, despite exuding the vibe of a man who’s mentally fired himself. Perhaps it’s a stay of execution, but more likely there’s bizarre hope of a turnaround, partly to save paying him off, partly because the relevant executives can’t achieve consensus on a replacement, and partly because surely even Omar Berrada and Jason Wilcox accept that, following another catastrophe, after dismissing Carrick they are honour-bound to dismiss themselves.

Except they and United don’t work like that.

So, just as they failed Carrick by not recruiting properly; failing to add experience to his coaching team; failing to replace outgoing fitness and set-piece coaches and failing to interrogate details of his new game-model, they are now failing him by having him continue in a job that is too much for him, destroying a season that remains salvageable. Meantime, the Glazers’ dividends continue unabated.

As such, the question isn’t so much who should be United’s next manager as can anyone manage United? Increasingly, it looks like the answer is – to quote Don Logan in Sexy Beast – “No”.

There are immediate on‑pitch issues: the team are unfit and their collective mentality weak; after years being lied to, the captain has finally broken; and the players hate the suits, the package toxic. Those are the minor problems.

Sign up to Football Daily

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

after newsletter promotion

Roughly, football management comprises five aspects: coaching, tactics, talent ID, pastoral care and presence. And, though no manager excels in every department, at this version of United surely they must. Moreover, given this is no job for a novice, track record is also important – and it might be here that Unai Emery’s candidature falls down, his brilliance in transforming mid‑ranking clubs undermined by failures at two high-profile basket cases.

Which brings us to pastoral care and presence. In the postwar era, only Erik ten Hag has won a trophy at United without tangible charisma, the size of the club now demanding it more than ever. This is not a quality associated with Eddie Howe, while Antonio Conte does not scream pastoral care and, brilliant though his career has been, he failed miserably at Spurs, the only environment he has inhabited that is remotely similar to United.

Should United miss Champions League qualification, financial strictures will make an elite coach and tactician essential. But in any event, football has changed such that the alchemic art of combining players and personalities no longer guarantees success.

Which leaves us with talent ID, player quality and intelligence being the best coaching and tactics there are. Of the 78 players purchased post-Ferguson, only Bruno Fernandes and perhaps Zlatan Ibrahimovic could be classed as cast-iron successes, so the next man – assuming United don’t target Emma Hayes, who embodies more of the right stuff than almost anyone else – must have a keen nose. Even Jürgen Klopp, the other manager who fulfils these criteria – and of all the damage Ed Woodward wreaked on United, turning him off was most costly – benefited from a department which delivered the greatest run of transfers ever.

Which leaves Mauricio Pochettino, who built something at Tottenham despite the environment, and Julian Nagelsmann. But had Pochettino not signed a new contract with the USA men’s team, the sense is that, as when Mourinho arrived at Old Trafford after years of speculation, he’s past his magical best, while Nagelsmann may be the free-thinking genius of his own imagination, just as he may be an emperor’s new clothes bluffer.

All of which is to say that failure has many fathers and, once ingrained, is not easily eradicated. Yet just as society has too much going for it to ever move quite beyond the pale, so too does Manchester United. Even the longest journey starts with one step; but does anyone have the nous to ensure it’s taken in the correct direction?

I’ve been watching the 7 Up TV series. One change in our behaviour really struck me

The Guardian Wed, 28 Oct 2026 17:59:27 GMT

Before mobile phones, being filmed was very rare – and if you were, you acted naturally. Today, our relationship to the camera is very, very different

Not for the first time, I got something wrong. As someone who made a living being on camera, I developed theories about what it takes to be yourself on screen. My main thought was that everyone in the world would soon be able to do it, because they’d be getting so much practice.

Once upon a time, hardly anybody was filmed or videoed. When the head of my middle school announced in assembly one morning that there would be television cameras in the dinner hall at lunchtime, every child woke up. For once the headteacher had our full and undivided attention. Consternation was in the air. This would have been about 1979. Regional television news probably needed pictures to cover a story about school dinners or something. Nobody, but nobody, in the school that day missed that evening’s edition of Midlands Today. It was a big deal. I saw the back of my head, and was agog.

In the home, being filmed was just as rare. Before smartphones, before camcorders, moving pictures of domestic life were few and far between. Growing up in the last decades of the last century I was aware of the existence of cine cameras but knew of no one who owned such an exotic, perhaps even vaguely sinister piece of kit.

By the time I first appeared on television in the mid-90s, the dam was starting to burst. Not only did I stand as proof that any Tom, Dick or Harry could have a go at TV presenting, but camcorders were proliferating. Babies bawling, toddlers toddling, kiddies doing “shows”, teenagers sulking, grandads snoozing – all were preserved for posterity, or at least until the tapes were lost for ever in some dark corner. Now there can’t be a human being in the UK of whom there isn’t some video footage on a smartphone, in the cloud, or wherever these things exist.

The ubiquity of video cameras surely means we’re more natural in front of them. But looking natural is different to being natural. It might even be the opposite.

This dawned on me when talking to the remarkable Tony Walker, who 63 years ago was one of the seven-year-olds featured on the longitudinal documentary series which started with Seven Up! and has now concluded with 70 Up. From the back of Tony’s black cab I listened as he told me how this little East End rascal had barely seen a TV, let alone a TV camera, before the day Michael Apted’s crew came bowling into his life. I went back and binge-watched the series from the beginning – 7, 14, 21 Up and so on – and, while this group obviously gained experience of television every seven years, from the outset it’s striking how naturally everyone speaks. This is not despite, but because of, their lack of practice. They’re blisteringly honest and are being – dread phrase – their authentic selves. They’ve yet to learn how to be anything else.

The same thought is provoked by Chris Terrill’s seminal BBC series, Soho Stories, now repeated 30 years after it first went out. Chris, embedded in the Soho area of central London for a year, mines a rich seam of characters: Gwen the student/burlesque dancer, Mark the tailor, Danny the wannabe actor and so on. Even as recently as 1996 it’s noticeable that they don’t have enough of a grasp of the grammar of television to be able to do anything other than reveal an unvarnished, unmediated version of themselves. The lack of guile is at the heart of their honesty.

Fast forward to 2026 and it’s guile galore. Influencers, vloggers, clever dicks, dicks, whoever – all are talking to camera with disarming competence, entirely at home with the form and quite coruscatingly natural. Yet natural is the last thing they are. To see what natural really looks like, examine people’s expressions on very old black and white photographs, back before they’d worked out what faces to pull. Compare and contrast with today, in which everyone’s acquired the knack of presenting a carefully, if unconsciously, curated version of themselves. The level of naturalness is a lot of things, but the one thing it isn’t is natural. If you want natural, go back to the days before folks had worked out how to pretend to be natural.

Adrian Chiles is a broadcaster, writer and Guardian columnist

The Jackdaw gasfield, net zero and climate adaptation

Andy Burnham writes that his determination to tackle the climate crisis is “unwavering” and that the transition must not leave communities behind (We will make the net-zero transition work for Britain – approving the Jackdaw gasfield is part of the plan, 22 October). Whatever one thinks of Jackdaw, the test of that pledge is whether people are also protected from climate impacts that are already here.

The research that you reported on last week attributed two-thirds of the heat deaths that it estimated – 4,354 of them in the UK – to climate change.

The numbers from that study were not available when the health secretary took questions in the Commons last Tuesday, but the signs were – stretched ambulance services, cancelled operations and overheated wards. Heat was barely mentioned.

The prime minister says that he will not be “so careless with people’s lives” as oil and gas workers face the transition. He is right, and the same care is owed to older people in care homes, pregnant women, patients on hospital wards and outdoor workers facing the next heatwave.

So the government must commit to practical action before next summer. That means effective cooling and heatwave plans in hospitals, maternity units and care homes, stronger early warnings, welfare checks for isolated older people, and protections for workers in dangerous temperatures. The Climate Change Committee has shown that the investment needed is manageable and the cost of inaction far greater.

Net zero and adaptation are not alternatives. Mr Burnham should say what he will deliver, and when. Emma Howard Boyd Chair, National Heat Risk Commission

The idea of using fossil fuels as a “bridge” to green energy has been touted by polluters and politicians since the 1980s. It’s mind-boggling that we’re still at this point.

Energy security, national security and avoiding climate catastrophe all come with rapidly expanding green technologies such as heat pumps and renewables. The benefits there far outweigh those produced by gas drilling, and it’s these that should be Andy Burnham’s full focus when he talks of a green transition. After decades of delay, the world’s transition now needs to be fast.

Thanks to the failure of the politicians who came before, we need heaps of gas to heat our homes this winter, but the idea of baking that in for more decades isn’t just stupid – to myself and my peers who look ahead with fear at an increasingly precarious future, this decision is an insult. Gwydion Elliott Sheffield

Andy Burnham – “not a climate guy”, according to one of his MPs – argues in his opinion article that an increase in CO2 emissions is required to bring down CO2 emissions. George Orwell would appreciate that. Douglas Currie Edinburgh

The BBC’s education editor role should not be scrapped

The Guardian Wed, 28 Oct 2026 17:58:56 GMT

The broadcaster’s decision speaks volumes about BBC priorities and the state of public dialogue, says David Blunkett. Plus a letter by Richard Bourne

Can I add my voice to the expression of considerable disquiet at the BBC’s proposal to eliminate the post of education editor, instead combining responsibility with that of social affairs (BBC News to axe education editor role in cost-cutting move, 22 October). These two distinct areas of public life are critical to our understanding – under the remit of the BBC charter – to educate and inform, as well as entertain.

The requirement to take education seriously surely requires someone with deep understanding of this complex area, which affects every single person in the country: from the moment they’re born, all the way through lifelong learning and the current challenges of artificial intelligence and robotics.

Some readers will remember the great Mike Baker, who was a practitioner as well as an informer; an experienced and extremely erudite broadcaster who brought alive the elements of the education debate which, when I was the education and employment secretary, were described as the then-government’s top three priorities: “Education, education, education.”

The proposition to downgrade the standing and the acquired experience necessary to present to the public speaks volumes not only about BBC priorities, but about the state of our public dialogue. David Blunkett Labour, House of Lords

It is retrograde of the BBC to downgrade its education coverage. Educational changes and debates are news. They need nuanced analysis. While it is true that they fit into a wider spectrum of social issues, all electors deserve journalists devoted to this coverage.

When I was the Guardian’s education correspondent from 1968 to 1972, when debates raged on comprehensive schools and there were student sit-ins and a teachers’ strike, it would have been inconceivable if there had not been a full-time BBC education correspondent.

People as different as Margaret Thatcher, then education minister, and Jack Straw, then a student leader, became household names thanks to TV, radio and journalism. The BBC should think again. Richard Bourne London

The controversial Daily Telegraph columnist Allison Pearson is understood to be in negotiations about leaving the broadsheet as the newspaper’s new owner makes significant newsroom cuts.

Sources told the Guardian that Pearson – firmly on the right of the Telegraph’s roster – is preparing to announce her exit imminently and is crafting a statement about her future plans.

The news comes after the German media company Axel Springer, which completed a £575m takeover in June, warned that as many as 100 journalists’ roles were at risk of redundancy as it transitioned into being “a global, AI-powered premium media and intelligence business”.

One insider said the Brexit-backing columnist had been “in some sort of negotiation to make an elegant departure” after discussions with management about her future at the title.

But they said rumours of her expected exit had been circulating within the newsroom for a number of days, and were not a surprise after a column she wrote in September had raised some eyebrows internally, particularly among senior management.

Pearson wrote in an opinion piece that the far-right activist Tommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, had “the rough-diamond charisma to pull a large, enthusiastic crowd”.

She also wrote: “Every single person who marched in the rain to Unite the Kingdom, every decent person hanging our beautiful flags from lamp-posts and motorway bridges and on village greens, is making patriotism respectable again. Step by step, inch by inch, we are taking our country back from those who hate it.”

Pearson has been the Telegraph’s chief interviewer and a columnist since 2010. But her relations with some senior editorial figures were said to be strained over a number of subjects she raised in her columns, particularly around immigration.

Other managers did not welcome the attention she brought to the title when she was investigated by police in Essex in 2024 for allegedly stirring up racial hatred with a social media post.

The force was criticised by Pearson and her supporters when officers knocked on her door on Remembrance Sunday over a photograph she retweeted amid heightened tensions over the policing of Gaza protests. Pearson deleted the post and the police investigation was dropped, but a review concluded the force was right to look into the allegations.

When the Telegraph’s purchase was announced – ending three years of uncertainty over its future – Mathias Döpfner, Axel Springer’s chief executive and controlling shareholder, said he planned to invest in the title as he wanted to make it the “leading centre-right media outlet in the English-speaking world”.

The Telegraph will also focus on increasing its audience globally, “particularly in foreign affairs, defence and business”, according to an email to staff from the chief executive, Carolin Hulshoff Pol.

Ensuring prisoners can’t refuse to attend court

The Guardian Wed, 28 Oct 2026 17:54:12 GMT

One prison officer says existing rules on offenders making court appearances should be enforced rather than introducing fresh sanctions

The report on judges being given powers to punish prisoners who refuse to attend court raises a question about why we appear to have abandoned a straightforward approach that once worked (Criminals who refuse to attend sentencing face losing prison privileges under new rules, 22 October).

When I joined the Prison Service as an officer more than 30 years ago, prisoners were not permitted to decide whether they would attend court. If they refused to go voluntarily, they could be escorted under restraint where necessary.

The result was predictable: few prisoners refused, because they knew their refusal would not prevent them from appearing.

There is a wider lesson here for the administration of justice. When noncompliance becomes a means of delaying or obstructing the system, introducing additional punishments may be less effective than ensuring that lawful instructions are carried out in the first place. Prisoners have rights, and the use of restraint must always be lawful, proportionate and justified. But those rights do not extend to exercising a veto over the judicial process.

After more than three decades, I find it difficult to understand why a principle that was once routine now appears to require a fresh solution. Sometimes, effective public administration is not about creating new sanctions but about having the resolve and resources to enforce existing rules. Name and address supplied

Bone of contention: why dog trainers are at war

The Guardian Wed, 28 Oct 2026 17:44:49 GMT

It’s the canine equivalent of gentle v tough parenting – and there is no sign of a ceasefire. So what is the correct way to get man’s best friend to behave?

Name: Dog training wars.

Age: Puppy to 14 months, and beyond.

Appearance: Aggressive.

Is this about dogs fighting? No, it’s the trainers who are fighting.

What are they fighting about? There are two camps: “positive” trainers, and “balanced” trainers. The former rely on rewards, the latter on a range of disciplinary stimuli, which might extend to prong collars that dig into a dog’s neck when it pulls.

What do the balanced ones say about the positive ones? “It’s all treats, treats, treats, so help me God,” the dog trainer Brian Lee told the Wall Street Journal. “It’s no different than giving your kid a BMW on his 16th birthday.”

And how do positive trainers address these allegations? “I kind of laugh at this whole idea that using treats in training is somehow going to spoil dogs,” says another dog trainer Victoria Stilwell.

I don’t see this getting resolved any time soon. Rewarding dogs with too many treats is “the biggest problem with dog training at the moment,” says the animal behaviourist Dr Ian Dunbar, despite standing in the positive camp.

If I’m honest this war of words doesn’t sound that heated. But it’s getting worse thanks to social media.

To be fair, everything is getting worse thanks to social media. Positive trainers call balanced trainers cruel; balanced trainers call positive trainers “treat-slinging wieners”.

Is this the dog version of the “gentle parenting” v Fafo parenting debate from earlier this year? It’s similar, but I don’t think anybody was recommending prong collars in that instance.

Is treat-slinging v discipline the only issue? There’s also a parallel war about the virtues of online training versus in-person training.

Which is best? Some say in-person is the only way. “You can’t resolve temperament issues over the phone,” Dunbar told the Times recently. “It’s insane.”

I see Dunbar has more than one dog in this fight. But Siobhan Dunn, who runs online courses, disagrees. “We’re working with owners all over the UK, many of whom would never have been able to reach us in person,” she says.

I’m confused – who’s right? It may help you to know that in-person training can cost £150 an hour.

Any signs of a ceasefire in the training wars? Lee has already called for calm on Instagram. “The criticising culture has been exhausted,” he wrote. “It’s time to put down the ‘dog training approach’ pitchforks.”

Did people respond positively to his message of calm? Not so far. “There is literally NOTHING in your bio that tells me you actually have an education in canine behaviour,” wrote another trainer.

Do say: “Dog rewards don’t have to be food-based – what about a trip to the theatre?”

Don’t say: “DOWN BOY.”

‘Like Saddam opened a Cheesecake Factory’: how did the restaurant end up in a Maga fight over ‘elitism’?

The Guardian Wed, 28 Oct 2026 17:41:49 GMT

Obama has been accused of ‘snobbery’ over his Trump diss, as people rush to defend the restaurant chain’s ‘affordable opulence’

Around lunchtime on Tuesday, a Rolls-Royce stopped at the intersection of Beverly Drive and Dayton Way in Beverly Hills, California. Local people in athleisure walked past Balenciaga, Dior and Prada boutiques, as visitors on Hollywood bus tours ogled nearby Rodeo Drive, where Burberry and Louis Vuitton shops meet at a celebrated street corner.

Up the street, across from the upmarket Erewhon grocery store – home to $21 smoothies – a few diners sat outside an American landmark: the Cheesecake Factory.

The beloved restaurant chain began here in Beverly Hills in 1978; now it has hundreds of locations across the US and Canada. And this week, it’s become the US’s latest surreal culture-war touchstone.

It started when Barack Obama, campaigning for Democrats in Ohio, made a joke that hit Donald Trump right in the real estate. Referring to his successor’s remodeling obsession, the former president said: “He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory. Just gold everywhere.”

The joke was about maximalism: Saddam had 100 palaces and loved gold plating, and the Cheesecake Factory, while affordable for many, offers swanky surroundings that a curmudgeon might describe as over the top. While the Beverly Hills restaurant has a fairly staid interior, a nearby location at Los Angeles’s Grove mall has a grand staircase, floral paintings on the ceilings and an ornate balcony.

Obama’s comments got a laugh at the rally – which surely contained many Cheesecake Factory customers – and went viral. It’s likely the former president knew he would touch a nerve, given Trump’s twin fixations on remodeling and on Obama himself.

Then the backlash began.

Asked by a reporter whether he had a response to Obama, “who made fun of the Cheesecake Factory, comparing it to the White House”, Trump spent nearly two full minutes explaining that the work had been done by the “finest artisans”, that Obama “doesn’t notice dirt and filth” – a racist trope – and that Trump himself only spends “five minutes a day, 10 minutes a day” addressing the problem. (Later that day, he spent another 10 minutes talking about it.)

But the framing of the question – posed by a reporter for LindellTV, founded by the Trump-supporting My Pillow founder Mike Lindell – pointed to what has become a rightwing talking point: the out-of-touch Obama, these critics claim, was mocking restaurant for regular people. The Cheesecake Factory isn’t cheap – a burger will run you about $20 – but it’s positioned as a treat that won’t break the bank.

The conservative political strategist Corinne Clark Barron tweeted: “KEEP THE CHEESECAKE FACTORY OUT OF YOUR ELITIST MOUTH.” On CNN, the New York Post columnist Lydia Moynihan said the remarks showed “how elitist he and the party that he continues to lead has become”. On Fox News, a chyron announced: “Obama criticized for Cheesecake Factory ‘snobbery’.”

This seems to deliberately misconstrue the joke’s primary target, which was the president, not the restaurant. It also conveniently forgets the first half, about Saddam Hussein, who was not known for minimalist taste. Nevertheless, the pitchforks were out, and the Trump administration deployed a true man of the people – the treasury secretary and hedge fund founder Scott Bessent – to dine there.

In fact, he “always” does, as he was at great pains to point out. “I had a great meal, always have a great meal,” he told a Fox Business reporter. He ordered “what I always have: the French Dip Cheeseburger”. Bessent, whose net worth is roughly $600m, said he would “tell the Martha’s Vineyard set to give it a try”.

The median home price in Beverly Hills, home to the first Cheesecake Factory, is $4m; the restaurant itself is far more affordable than the 90210 zip code might suggest. But as Bessent himself proved, the restaurant’s clientele includes plenty of elites: Jennifer Lawrence, Miley Cyrus and Drake are all reportedly fans. It’s a stretch to suggest Obama was punching down here.

That said, given the fierce devotion the restaurant inspires, Obama was perhaps taking a risk even mentioning it – especially at a time when the cost of living is on the ballot. “I think it’s a little bit sad that the pettiness of politics would create that soundbite, knowing all our challenges going on in the country today,” Rick McCormack, who helped create the restaurant’s decor, told CNN’s David Mack. Odes to the restaurant and its “affordable opulence”, as Mack puts it, abound.

In the Atlantic, Elaine Godfrey praises its “sumptuousness: the orange, inviting glow from the knobbly chandeliers; the floral frescoes and painted columns; the generous fountain pops and the dense wedges of cake”. A Redditor puts it more simply: “I can eat the whole plate of food like a savage and waddle to my car afterward with a piece of cheesecake to go.” The food is indeed good, and plentiful: the chain is known for its enormous and diverse menu, with items ranging from fried mac and cheese to avocado egg rolls to vegan cobb salad. There’s also, of course, lots of cheesecake, including but not limited to the mind-boggling Oreo Dream Extreme. On Tuesday, the chain reported third-quarter revenue of $1.03bn, up from $907.2m a year before. It’s routinely named among Fortune’s 100 best companies to work for.

In short, everyone loves the Cheesecake Factory, from Birmingham, Alabama, to Des Moines, Iowa, to Beverly Hills, where the autumn sun shone this week over warm baskets of complimentary bread. Surely it can take a joke.

Budget winners and losers: pensioners and households gain as banks and betting shops hit

The Guardian Wed, 28 Oct 2026 17:37:02 GMT

How the Burnham government’s first attempt to ease cost of living pressure pans out for key stakeholders Budget 2026: key points at a glance

Every budget has its winners and losers, and John Healey’s first as chancellor was no exception. While some gained from tax breaks and rule tweaks, others will either pay more, or had their hopes of reforms dashed. Here are some of those with reason to cheer, or sigh:

Everyone in a band A-D property: A £100 payment to help towards this winter’s energy costs. The payment is guaranteed in England from January. Other parts of the UK have been given funding to do the same.

Pensioners: The state pension will go up to £13,036 next April, and pensioners will get a new matching personal allowance at the same time. The allowance will lift all income they receive to that level out of tax.

Teenage tech bros – and other young entrepreneurs, in England: They will gain from a new allowance, which will give them support towards their living costs in the first year of their business.

Independent cider makers, and brewers: More generous tax reliefs for small alcohol producers will help 2,000 businesses, and a new “guest beer” rule will mean that tied pubs in England and Wales must offer their drinks.

EV drivers – but only those who use lower-powered public chargers: The government will give £100m in subsidies for on-street charging, saving people without home charging about £150 a year.

First-time buyers with small savings: The Your First Home scheme will help those with a deposit of as little as 2.5% to buy a newbuild home. It will be open to households earning up to £140,000 in London, and £110,000 everywhere else in England.

Cash Isa fans: Savers under 65 will not have their cash Isa allowance cut next April after Healey reversed an announcement made in last year’s budget. They will, however, be encouraged to try their hand at investing with a new, yet to be announced, incentive for those buying stocks and shares for the first time.

Self-employed fathers: Two weeks of paternity pay, currently worth up to £194 a week, will be available from April 2029 to those who work for themselves.

Paddington Bear: The small bear from Peru is a well-known consumer of marmalade and could see the cost of his favourite spread fall by 20% as a result of the removal of tariffs from more than a 100 products, which also included gherkins and garlic.

Banks: A temporary increase in the bank corporation tax surcharge, from 3% to 6% for 15 months, will mean they pay a combined £1.5bn extra to the Treasury over the period. But it had been suggested that the levy would be raised to 8% and bank shares rose after the budget, so maybe they are actually winners.

Betting shops: Tax on slot machines with stakes of £1 or more will increase from 20% to 25% from April 2027. Shares in gambling companies also rose, as investors had feared the hike may be bigger.

Students: They may have hoped for a change in the repayment thresholds to ease the pain felt by those on plan 2 loans, but there was no movement. Instead the thresholds are set to be frozen from next April.

Savers who have money outside Isas: The tax on interest was set to go up next April and Healey added another two percentage points to the rates that had already been announced. Once a basic-rate saver has used up their tax-free allowance on interest they will pay 24% on returns, while a higher rate taxpayer will pay 44% and an additional rate payer 49%.

Buy-to-let landlords: Taxes on property income will also go up by more than had been expected, and to the rates outlined for savers. For this, however, there are different rates in Scotland.

Private renters: The increase in taxes on landlords could lead to a steady rise in rents, according to the Office for Budget Responsibility. It says, together with other measures introduced in recent years, the extra cost means landlords may leave the market and potential new investors stay out.

Poor families in bands E and above: The £100 energy rebate is being distributed using council tax bands, but this means 1.4 million of the poorest families miss out, according to the Resolution Foundation.

People in urban communities hoping to access nature: The budget included exemptions for biodiversity net gain (BNG) on brownfield sites. BNG requires developers to build in nature gains when developing plots but Healey is removing this requirement for plots up to 1.5 hectares (3.7 acres) in England.

Additional reporting by Jasper Jolly and Sandra Laville

British racing chief warns budget tax hike may have ‘devastating’ impact on sport
