Call for urgent talks after gaming machines tax increase

Brant Dunshea: ‘thousands’ of betting shops may close

Brant Dunshea, chief executive of the British Horseracing Authority, said on Wednesday that the sport’s ruling body will “urgently engage with the government to establish how we can work together to reduce the impact” after John Healey, in his first budget as chancellor, raised the duty on the profits from fixed-odds gaming machines in betting shops from 20% to 25%.

The widely expected rise in machine games duty (MGD) was well below the doubling of the rate, from 20% to 40%, recommended this year by the Social Market Foundation thinktank, but Dunshea warned that the move could “still prove devastating for our sport” since it presented a “clear risk” that “hundreds, if not thousands” of betting shops nationwide faced closure as a result.

There are about 5,500 betting shops in the UK and the average shop contributes approximately £25,000 to racing annually via the levy and rights payments for live coverage and data.

“British racing derives nearly a third of its £350m annual income from betting via high street shops,” Dunshea said, “[and] is now set to potentially lose £57m a year, based on independent modelling that was shared with the Treasury before today’s budget.

“While the MGD rate increase is not as severe as some called for, this change could still prove devastating for the future of our sport, impacting prize money, the viability of racecourses, thousands of jobs and vital horse welfare projects and research.

“[Closures] will also significantly impact a large part of the sport’s fanbase for whom a visit to their local bookie is the primary way they engage with horse racing.”

The Prem is aiming to expand from 10 to 12 sides in time for the 2029-2030 season and English rugby’s governing bodies insist their priority is to back domestic teams.

“Resources are currently focused on supporting English clubs throughout the pyramid who aspire to join the league,” they said in a joint a statement. “The Prem is an attractive league and responsibility for its expansion sits with the Men’s Professional Rugby Board, which has established detailed entry criteria that any prospective club would need to satisfy.”

Joining the Prem could cost an interested club up to £23.5m, made up of the P-share that secures a percentage of central income and voting rights and the requirement to fund a Premiership Women’s Rugby programme.

Carey and Inglis counterpunch to put Australia on top in South Africa

The Guardian Wed, 28 Oct 2026 17:12:49 GMT

Keepers rebuild the innings to reach 330-4 at the close

Green sparkles but Labuschagne duck must be the end

If Cape Town’s first day was a rollercoaster, the second was some more sedate form of transport, though it continued with ups and downs fitting its mountainous backdrop. Twice, South Africa produced double strikes to stall promising Australian positions; twice the Australians rebuilt. Finally, Josh Inglis and Alex Carey pushed Australia in front, 330 for four to South Africa’s all out 329, ready to surge on through day three with those six wickets left in hand.

While Travis Head was there, Australia’s first session threatened to match South Africa’s the day before, when Aiden Markram and Marques Ackerman had piled on 140 against a bewildered attack. Head threw his hands at width, mixing luck with skill for seven boundaries. His new foil Matthew Renshaw showed contrasting temperament for the opening role, leaving and defending the new ball with the clarity he had shown in the middle order in Durban, underlining why he was the original candidate to replace Jake Weatherald at the top before the selectors’ brief and ill-fated Nic Maddinson excursion.

Head’s contribution of 41 out of 58 will continue debate about his batting position. It’s clear at a glance, given an opener’s average of 49 is titanic by modern standards, but the detail is stark: that average breaks down to 23 in the first innings of a match, 43 in the second, 71 in the third, and 60 in the fourth. Head smashes up teams later in games set up to suit his approach, but hasn’t batted time when doing so is essential in tricky early conditions. Having more of a shield up top, leaving Head to plunder in the middle, may still be the best use of a precious resource.

There is also his current problem with chopping on to his stumps, today via an awkward cut against Simon Harmer’s off-spin. That makes eight times bowled in his last 15 dismissals, up from 20 out of 66 before that span. Harmer struck again in the same over, teasing Marnus Labuschagne into a catch at slip on what must be Labuschagne’s last chance at Test cricket before the opportunity comes to blood a replacement during the Australian summer.

Labuschagne’s problem is not so much the duck, which can happen to anyone, but its tentative provenance: a player who has trained so hard to move dynamically against spin had both feet in cement, poking uselessly at a ball that would have carried on past the stumps. In theory, he has one more innings left to save himself, but that was the shot of a player who is in no state to use it.

Cameron Green arrived for a rebuild, but South Africa were fuming after the third umpire denied a catch from Gerald Coetzee’s bowling. Harmer at second slip was convinced, and replays looked identical to precedents where a player with fingers flat on the ground gets the ball to bounce up into their palms. This time it wasn’t given. Australia added 85 before the stand ended, including an explosive over when Green hooked the returning Rabada’s bouncer barrage, with some risk, for a consecutive six, six, and four.

Harmer also had Renshaw given not out to a gorgeous ball that drifted across the left-hander, spun back past the edge, and hit his back pad, but was umpire’s call for height. It was Marco Jansen who ended the frustration, needing third-umpire recourse to prove that extra bounce had nicked the top edge of Renshaw’s half-hearted uppercut, then in Jansen’s next over, Harmer at slip inked in the Green catch that had been whited out. Just before tea, Australia’s set pair had been removed for 74 and 65. Still trailing South Africa by 144, at 185 for four, more was needed.

It came from Inglis and Carey, both wicketkeeper-batters, though Inglis adopted the traditional counterpunching style of their kind, while Carey tended more to defence between moments of creative scoring. Again a partnership grew with both contributors heading towards half-centuries. Harmer was milked, Rabada remained ineffective, and as Inglis opened out after passing 50, he hit a six off both, and consecutive fours cutting Coetzee.

There were moments of peril mixed in, like Harmer spinning one back to Inglis that almost took off-stump, and a couple of top edges that landed safe, but Australia’s scoring kept the field spread, and unlike Mitchell Starc’s demolition derby with the new ball the previous evening, South Africa’s use of it just sped up the scoring. By stumps the stand was 145, with Carey 51 and Inglis 85, and after captain Pat Cummins was sufficiently unsure of his batting that he chose to bowl on day one, the new configuration had come good on day two. Next is whether day three sees Australia move into a decisive lead, or whether South Africa can rein them in.

‘This isn’t supposed to happen’: giant-slaying Fleetwood revels in fairytale Arsenal win

The Guardian Wed, 28 Oct 2026 16:52:23 GMT

Fishing town in disbelief the morning after its footballing minnows beat mighty Arsenal on penalties

On a wet and windy night on the north-west coast of England, a League Two side sensationally knocked the Premier League champions out of the Carabao Cup. But this is not just a fairytale story of giant-slaying: Fleetwood Town and Arsenal have an unlikely history that stretches back long before Tuesday night’s game.

Arsenal played at their iconic Highbury stadium until 2006, and Fleetwood’s ground has the same title, being named after Highbury Avenue, the adjoining street.

Fleetwood also play in red shirts with white sleeves in the style of the classic Arsenal kit. Nobody is exactly sure why, but according to Ray Curtis, a barman in the town’s King’s Arms: “Fleetwood’s first ever kit, the home kit, was given to them by Arsenal.”

And in the 2000s, not long after Patrick Vieira captained Arsenal, Fleetwood boasted a namesake star: a Brazilian striker called Magno Vieira.

At the 5,300-capacity Highbury on Wednesday morning, the floodlights that Fleetwood had hired for the occasion were being packed away. “It’s back to reality, back to being a League Two team, that’s our normal,” said Zsofia Wright, the ticket office and retail manager.

On Tuesday, the excitement and anticipation started early. “We started getting what team had turned up, who’d flown in, and the whispers started, and it’s like, ‘oh, they’ve gone quite strong’,” Wright said.

“So we were all planning to just enjoy the occasion. And then obviously, we went 1-0 up and everyone was kind of looking at each other, like this isn’t supposed to be happening.”

She said it was back to reality when Arsenal equalised except that “the clock kept on going and the score didn’t change”.

Wright said everyone was on the pitch after the dramatic penalty shootout that saw the Premier League champions and Champions League finalists ousted from the competition. The next stop for players, fans and management was the stadium bar.

“Just incredible,” Wright said. “We were here till about half one last night. It was brilliant, amazing.”

“The atmosphere was crazy,” said Chris Newman, 33, who was at the match with his son. He returned to the club shop on Wednesday to pick up two souvenir programmes. “Everything happened so quick,” he said. “I just didn’t expect it at all.”

The shop has done a roaring trade over the past 36 hours, with half-and-half Fleetwood and Arsenal scarves proving especially popular. One buyer with a London accent said: “I’m a Spurs fan, it’s brilliant.”

Wright said the town was abuzz the morning after: “Bars, pubs that are struggling, they were open till God knows what time yesterday. We just hope it can continue throughout the season, just hope that attendances start to pick up, and get consistency back again through the gates.”

The club’s nicknames – the Cod Army, the Fishermen, the Cods and the Trawlermen – all derive from the Lancashire town’s fishing industry.

Sharon Brooks, who was visiting a fishmonger by the harbour, said: “We thought it’d be three, four or five nil, but they did so well to get a draw and then win on penalties, and five brilliant penalties. It’s nice for a town like Fleetwood, and [against the] Premier League winners last season, they just surprised you didn’t they?”

Her 12-year-old son, Ryan, who is an Arsenal fan, said: “Even though I wanted [Arsenal] to win it, I’m pleased for them.”

In the King’s Arms, everyone was eagerly awaiting Wednesday night’s draw, which will decide who Fleetwood plays next.

Donald Maclean, who missed the game because he was on duty at a nursing home, said: “I saw the goals this morning and I was delighted, over the moon, imagine Fleetwood taking down the Gunners! Never been heard of before, so yes, we’re all delighted about it. Brilliant!”

The Cod Army’s victory has delighted fans partly because it was so unexpected – Fleetwood sit 84 places below Arsenal in the football league pyramid.

Michael Houton said he had thought the result impossible “because Arsenal shouldn’t have got beaten should they? Not against Fleetwood.”

Paul Dagger was so pessimistic about his team’s chances that he had staked £200 at half-time on Arsenal to win at odds of 10/7. “Gyökeres [of Arsenal] scored within five minutes of the start,” he said. “I thought, oh here we go, money’s coming in now. You live and learn.”

Fleetwood fans hope it will be the start of something bigger than just a victory for lovers of the game. “The town needs it,” Dagger said. “As you can see, it’s full of charity shops and vape shops.”

Garry Gill, a retired crane operator, said: “I am a Fleetwood fan and I think it’s fantastic for the town. It’s going to bring coin.

“If they play with the determination they did last night, any team that comes to play now is going to be frightened. And normally, that’s not the case, they think it’s an easy win.”

Jim Buckley said: “It’s magic. We’re a Mickey Mouse town of 25,000 people, there’s no train station. I mean at the Emirates, they can fit three towns the size of this town in there.”

He was not far out – Arsenal’s stadium can hold 60,000 fans.

The drinkers in the King’s Arms said the travelling Arsenal fans had had a good day out despite the embarrasing defeat.

Dagger said: “Two pound twenty a pint in here, two pound fifty a pint over the way. They couldn’t believe it, they were going, facking ‘ell, it’s eight quid where we are.”

Back near the harbour, at the Shark Chippy, there was a lunchtime rush. Dishing up cod and chips, Bethany Taylor said she lived near the ground and could tell the result from the roar of the crowd and the flares. “It was good, brilliant,” she added. “We weren’t expecting it.”

“It’s an incredible result isn’t it?” said her colleague Louisa Smith.

But do they think Fleetwood can lift the Carabao Cup? “It’d be a struggle, but hopefully they will,” Smith said. “We wish them luck.”

Healey gives households £100 to help navigate ‘global economic storms’

The Guardian Wed, 28 Oct 2026 16:40:50 GMT

Payments to 20m homes part of package to cut energy bills and ease cost of living crisis, paid for by bank windfall tax

‘A pretty grim picture’: outlook for UK living standards slashed despite Healey’s budget

Budget 2026: key points at a glance

John Healey promised to steer Britain through “global economic storms” as he announced an energy giveaway of £100 to 80% of households in England, funded by a smaller than expected windfall tax on banks.

In his first budget, the chancellor said 20 million households in council tax bands A to D would receive a £100 payment – a measure he said would cost £2.6bn.

That includes equivalent funding for Scotland and Wales, whose governments can decide whether to replicate the measure. The policy will help a large number of middle earners, reaching houses worth up to about £600,000 in London.

“I know that with the conflict in the Middle East, rising energy bills are a real worry. I know that people look to government at times like this, not to solve all their problems, but to give them a bit of breathing space,” he said, announcing the payment.

The relief on bills comes at a cost to big banks via the banking surcharge rise, and to savers and landlords, who were hit with an unexpected tax rise.

Healey said his budget would shape Britain’s future on defence, energy, welfare and entrepreneurship. “This Labour government has set a course for fresh hope, good growth and support for those who need it.”

The chancellor also extended the VAT cut on electricity bills until next July, and as widely expected, cancelled fuel duty rises pencilled in by Rachel Reeves.

Healey said this would help businesses as well as consumers. “For millions of people, the cost of living and the cost of doing business are the same. The home is the office. The van is the family car,” he said.

He blamed the war in the Middle East for the deterioration in the economic outlook since Reeves’s spring statement, but insisted he would keep Labour’s deficit-reduction plans on track.

“Analysts like to speak of economic headwinds, but what we face today are global economic storms,” he said, describing his statement as “a budget built on fiscal discipline, which matches immediate action today with clear direction for the future”.

He said higher inflation as a result of the Iran war was expected to cost the government £14bn more in interest costs and the Office for Budget Responsibility had downgraded its growth forecast to 1% for next year, from the 1.6% it expected in the spring.

Healey nevertheless promised to meet Labour’s first fiscal rule, on balancing current spending with tax receipts by 2029-30, but with diminished headroom of £15bn – against the £24bn that Reeves set aside in March. He said the cushion would be rebuilt to £22bn by 2030-31. “That is what a buffer is for. Use it when you need it, rebuild it when you can.”

The chancellor said the energy package would be funded by a windfall tax on Britain’s banks and the unexpected two percentage-point income tax rise for landlords and savers.

He is doubling the additional levy the banks pay on their profits to 6% from the current 3% for 15 months from January. That fell short of the rise to 8% that many industry figures had expected.

Healey lavished praise on the sector as he announced the measure. “I want to say directly to our banks: I celebrate and I am grateful for the role that you play,” he said. Bank share prices rose after the announcement, with NatWest and Standard Chartered up by more than 4%.

Healey announced several measures intended to cut businesses’ costs – including raising the rates relief threshold from £12,000 to £18,000 for companies in the retail, hospitality and leisure sectors. The change would be funded by higher taxes on gambling and vape shops, he said.

There was a package of policies that Healey said would tackle the “moral mission” of homelessness.

There will be no easing of fiscal drag, however, despite Andy Burnham previously expressing concern at the rate at which households were being pulled into higher rates of income tax.

Forecasts show that the freeze on tax thresholds will drag an extra 6.7m people into paying income tax and push 5.4m more into the higher rate band by 2031–32. The minimum wage will increase by 3.9% to £13.21 an hour, an increase of £910 to the gross annual earnings of a full-time worker.

Pensions will also rise thanks to the triple lock, but with new tax relief to keep pensioners from paying income tax as the state pension rises above the personal allowance for the first time. About 500,000 pensioners are to benefit.

Healey also announced sweeping new powers for regions, pledging all mayors would be given a share of income tax revenue from 2028. He said he intended that local and regional government would retain 100% of business rates income before the end of the decade.

He said the devolution package would be “new powers to the people who know their areas best, not sentimentality but supply-side economics”.

Guardian and ITN have ‘duty to public and sources’ to publish sexual allegations against well-known figure, court hears

The Guardian Wed, 28 Oct 2026 16:40:36 GMT

Individual known in court as PPT is seeking a permanent injunction, with lawyers citing his risk of suicide

Two news organisations have a duty to the public and their sources to publish allegations of exploitative sexual behaviour by a well-known figure despite claims he is “highly likely” to attempt suicide, the high court has heard.

The anonymous individual, known in court simply as PPT, is seeking an injunction against the Guardian and ITN to stop them publishing the allegations, which he denies.

His legal team have argued that publishing would be likely to lead to his death, after two previous attempts to take his own life.

However, the legal team for the media groups told the high court there were powerful “countervailing” considerations compelling them to publish the claims.

Gavin Millar KC, the lead barrister for the media outlets, said they had “not just the responsibility, but the duty to publish information we believe to be in the public interest”.

He argued the claimant had not taken the impact on the sources involved in the investigation “sufficiently into account”.

“They have made a substantial commitment to being contributors, and were extremely anxious for the publication and the broadcast to go ahead as soon as possible,” Millar said.

Many of the women making the allegations have been traumatised by PPT’s alleged conduct and have suffered mental health crises and mental illness as a result, according to a written submission from the media groups.

It states: “They believe that it is important that their allegations are publicly aired so that other women are protected and the full nature of his conduct is disclosed, and in order to assist the sources to recover from their own experiences.”

It said the media outlets had credible evidence of seriously improper conduct “towards a large number of women over a prolonged period”, including potential criminal conduct.

Millar said if publication of the allegations were blocked, “our women contributors and others we are aware of” were likely to find “other ways to make their stories known publicly”.

He added that proceeding with publication through the Guardian and ITN would be the “best way to put the information into the public domain”.

The well-known figure is seeking to block publication of the allegations by citing article two of the European convention on human rights (ECHR), which relates to the right to life; article three, relating to “inhuman or degrading treatment”; and article eight, which protects the right to respect for private and family life.

However, the media companies argue that the European court of human rights, which enforces the ECHR, has never ruled in such a way that would cause these articles to apply in this case. They also argue countervailing rights under article 10, which protects the right to freedom of expression.

Millar said the investigation into PPT had spoken to more than 100 people, including 30 who gave first-hand accounts.

He told that court that since the Guardian and ITN first contacted PPT in May so he could respond to the allegations, deadlines had been repeatedly extended and unusual measures put in place in order to act responsibly, given PPT’s medical issues.

Millar said that “recognising the difficult and unusual nature of the case”, the media companies had then agreed to delay publication so that PPT could seek an injunction and have his case heard before a judge.

PPT’s legal team has previously told that court there was evidence his life would be endangered should the allegations be published.

A summary of an assessment of the claimant’s current wellbeing by an independent expert stated that he could not conclude either that suicide was inevitable if publication went ahead, or that psychiatric treatment could eliminate all risk.

The expert said that the risks could be lowered should the allegations be published while PPT was in an inpatient psychiatric setting.

The trial has now concluded, with Mr Justice Nicklin retiring to come to a ruling.

Spain’s Sánchez declares three days of mourning after at least 68 killed in Toledo train crash

The Guardian Wed, 28 Oct 2026 16:39:15 GMT

High-speed service travelling from Madrid to Seville ran into back of another, knocking two carriages off track

The Spanish prime minister has declared three days of mourning after at least 68 people were killed and dozens more injured in a collision between two high-speed trains in central Spain.

The trains were travelling in the same direction on the line that stretches from the Spanish capital, Madrid, to Seville on Wednesday when one of the trains ran into the tail of the other that had stopped, knocking several carriages off the track.

The tragedy marked the second deadly train accident this year in Spain. “All of Spain is in mourning,” the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, said from the scene in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha. It was “unacceptable for a country like Spain to suffer two high-speed train accidents in the same year, as we have”, he said.

Footage broadcast by the regional channel CMM TV ​showed a derailed train with at least one carriage remaining on an elevated section of track. Twisted metal, broken panels and wreckage could be seen strewn across an embankment beneath the line.

Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, Spain’s transport minister, Óscar Puente, said such rear-end collisions were “highly unlikely” as he suggested that the accident may have been caused by human error made in “inexplicable” circumstances.

He said the LZB signalling system, which automatically halts a train if the line ahead is occupied, had gone down at about 8.30am local time due to a computer malfunction. As a result, an estimated six trains had been halted along a stretch of around 63km, he said.

The task of monitoring the rail lines then fell to a 24-hour command centre in Madrid. The centre instructed at least two of the trains to continue as normal, despite the fact that there was still a “stop signal” in place on the line, said Puente.

“It was the control centre, through its operators, that made the decision to resume traffic, under circumstances that, from our point of view, are inexplicable,” he said. “Clearly, it was a wrong decision … I am not attributing responsibility to anyone, I am just stating the facts.”

The Castilla-La Mancha regional government said on Wednesday afternoon that the death toll had risen to 68 as rescue ​teams continued to ⁠search ​through the wreckage ​of ​the derailed ​carriages. Castilla-La Mancha’s leader, Emiliano García-Page, told reporters that more victims were likely as “it has not yet been possible to reach the bottom of the carriages”.

Another 73 people needed medical treatment in hospital, he said, including 15 who were in serious condition.

Miguel, ‌a passenger travelling with several colleagues in the rear car of one of the trains, described the moment of the accident to Cope radio. “We heard a massive roar, a truly enormous thud that went on for 10 seconds, as if the train were ‌about to derail,” he said. “Through the right-hand window, we could see a wrecked train – I imagine it must have been ​the other one.”

The transport minister on Wednesday confirmed that the collision involved a train from Spain’s state-owned Renfe company and the private rail company Iryo – the same two companies whose trains were also involved in a crash in Adamuz in January in which 46 people were killed.

In Wednesday’s disaster, the Iryo train was travelling ahead on the tracks and had been sitting stationary when the Renfe train was told by the control centre to resume its journey. The Renfe train then travelled approximately 25km before colliding with the Iryo train about 17 minutes later.

The speed at which the Renfe train was travelling remains unknown, the transport minister told reporters, though the section of rail on which it was travelling allows for speeds of up to 200km/hour.

Puente said that similar erroneous instructions had been given to at least one other train on Wednesday morning. “And it was the engineer of one of the trains who corrected the command centre and told them he can’t resume normal operation – it has to be [an] on-sight operation,” Puente said, citing a protocol that allows trains to advance but at a greatly reduced speed in order to ensure that there are not other trains sitting on the tracks ahead. “The operator said: ‘OK, on-sight operation.’”

Sánchez said the causes of the accident were under investigation. If it emerged that it was due to failures in the security system or negligence, these shortcomings would be addressed with the “utmost severity”, he added.

“Everything strongly suggests that the causes of the two accidents [Wednesday’s and January’s] are completely unrelated, but it is not up to me to say so,” he said. “But what is clear is that, if we need – as we certainly do – to further strengthen safety in order to rebuild confidence in our high-speed rail system, it will be done.”

Manuel Galán, the mayor ​of ​Urda near the city of Toledo, said he had ​been ‌asked by ​emergency ​services to prepare a sports hall to accommodate the injured.

Spain’s main political parties, which are gearing up for next month’s general election, suspended their planned activities for the day.

The opposition People’s party leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, said on X: “Very concerned about the information we are getting about a new rail accident. The priority now is to attend to the victims and support their families. My full support to the emergency teams working on the ground.”

Spain’s football federation postponed all 24 Copa del Rey games scheduled for Wednesday.

Skulls, bulls and someone peeing in her own eye: four great exhibitions to see for free

The Guardian Wed, 28 Oct 2026 16:28:34 GMT

Andy Warhol’s skulls and Pierre Bonnard’s fruit have more in common than you might think. Plus: the world’s rudest cartoon character is up to dirty tricks again

Andy Warhol’s skull leers at Francisco de Zurbarán’s trussed-up little lamb from across the length of the gallery. Separated by hundreds of years – Warhol’s painting from the 1970s, Zurbarán’s from the 1630s – it’s an intergenerational conversation about still life’s staying power, and the inevitability of death.

This brilliant little show brings together still life paintings from way back in the past right up to the present day. There’s a gorgeous 1610-19 Dutch flower painting by Osaias Beert the Elder, and a vast vision of meats and cheeses with a pair of animal lungs hung grossly on a hook behind by Giovanni Battista Recco from the 1650s. There are piles of 19th-century French apples, vases of undulating 18th-century flowers. And then that little Zurbarán lamb – one of six he painted – glassy-eyed and morose, so laden with religious symbolism.

When we hit the modern era, there’s a lovely Pierre Bonnard painting of grapes and apples in sickly yellow and orange, a genuinely amazing Nicolas de Staël composition of stark, blocky bottles, lumps of pink rock by Philip Guston that look like cheese. Ignore the crap Picasso and the lumpen Juan Gris, and you get to come face to face with Warhol’s grim, grinning neon orange skull.

The whole show reinforces the idea that still life painting is terribly named. Because it’s not about life at all, it’s about death. Every fruit and vegetable in these works is about to rot, every flower is wilting, every animal carcass is about to go fetid. These are paintings of life’s fragility and precariousness. This is about how time is fleeting, how life is temporary. Mortality is written into every brush stroke.

Is this the greatest still life show ever put on? Does it have a tight curatorial concept? Does it tell an important story about the history and evolution of the genre? No, no and no. It’s just a bunch of really good, historic paintings. See, still life isn’t all just flowers and fruit. And even when it is, it’s pretty good.

Robilant, London, until 18 December

Panting, his grey tongue hanging out, blood streaming down his back, the bull is on the verge of death. Paul Pfeiffer’s newest film captures the moment a matador plunges a sword into that bull’s back, but with no fanfare, no drama, no judgment. This is a film about ritual and spectacle, not about animal cruelty or cultural violence.

This isn’t Pfeiffer at his most attractive or impressive. Instead, this long, awkward, often ugly piece of art cinema zooms in on the faces of the crowd at a corrida, the hands of the saxophone players in the band, the colours of the walls, the patterns on the matadors’ clothing. It’s all the tiny details of this spectacle, the intricacies that make it tick.

It is, essentially, a film about how humanity creates spectacles to lose ourselves in, and how we repeat actions, sounds and movements to create some kind of meaning. The film is outwardly about bullfighting, but more widely about all rituals, religious or cultural. Is the corrida any different from going to church or a concert or a football match? In the end, we’re all just trying to find meaning by taking part, by belonging, by coming together and cheering as one. Throughout the film, people cheer, drink and eat, the band plays, a bull dies. That’s life, I guess. Joy and sorrow with some snacks in between.

Thomas Dane Gallery, London, until 19 December

Ebecho Muslimova has gone through the looking-glass, and what she has found on the other side is more worrying and uncomfortable than any kind of horror fantasy land. She’s found reality.

In every painting and installation here, Muslimova’s cartoon alter ego Fatebe is navigating a world turned upside down, spun on its head and inverted. Fatebe is a lewd, rude, nude comic book character, her naked body able to twist and contort, her face always plastered with a grin and her orifices always on display. One painting finds multiple Fatebes bent over, gleefully scrubbing parquet floors (a nod to a Gustave Caillebotte painting, this show is drowning in art history references) while another Fatebe makes a paper chain out of fabric she’s yoinking out of her nethers. Yet another work sees hundreds of Fatebes filing up the stairs of the gallery itself, but the plaster is crumbling and the print is peeling.

Fatebe is trapped under a glass like a spider, or she’s turned herself into the legs of a table. In one drawing she has grown two heads, one peeing into the other’s eye, the other defecating back in return.

All this gross-out weirdness and art historical density isn’t about fantasy and escape though. I think it’s about feeling pulled in endless directions, it’s about being stuck between the place you came from and the place you’re in now, it’s about discomfort and alienation. Or it’s about being able to wee in your own eye. Who knows, really. Either way, it works.

Bernheim, London, until 28 November

Back in 2013, a Palestinian fisherman found an ancient Greek statue of Apollo poking out of the sand. Thinking it was gold, they cut off a finger, but it was just beautiful, mottled green bronze. They tried to sell it on eBay, posting pictures of the sculpture laid carefully on Smurf bedsheets, but the authorities stepped in and confiscated the sculpture. No one knows where it is now, but Rosalind Nashashibi has painted it here, preserving its strange, almost magical history in hazy visions of green limbs on cartoon-covered sheets.

Not all the works are good, and the images of nudes and landscapes feel either like a distraction or filler. But the Apollo images are great. They’re like paintings of an autopsy, stark and unsettling. They’re filled with narratives – a clash of ancient art and modern cartoon, a beleaguered people finding hope of salvation in a gift from the gods, an act of care as those people gently try to preserve this sculpture on their softest bedsheets. Hope and despair, history and the present, all colliding in some often beautiful, washed-out painting.

Grimm, London, until 21 November

Even with the residual winds from Storm Boelo still buffeting the ground, we presumed Arsenal’s second string would have enough about them to record a comfortable win at Highbury, over 20 years after they left a London stadium of the same name to begin their residency at the Emirates. It was not to be and almost five months to the day since exiting a cup competition on penalties following a curiously flat and uninspired display, Mikel Arteta’s side exited a cup competition on penalties following etc, and so on.

Considering their team came into this game on the back of consecutive defeats by Cheltenham and Exeter, Fleetwood’s Cod Army would almost certainly have settled for seeing their players avoid embarrassment but after watching them go ahead against a team of Fancy Dans who were visibly labouring in the miserable conditions expectations were duly raised. Arsenal equalised courtesy of a scrambled Viktor Gyökeres effort that is unlikely to trouble the Puskas Award jury, before all hell broke loose when young Max Dowman was sent off for retaliation following a Harrison Neal challenge that – depending entirely on what team you support – was a potential career-ender or wasn’t even a foul. While he is not yet old enough to drive, get a tattoo or vote, Dowman has apparently been around long enough to earn himself a stinging rebuke from his manager, who conveyed the impression the 16-year-old could look forward to being sent to bed without any supper and having his screen-time vastly reduced.

A penalty shootout in which yet another Brazilian missed a crucial spot-kick for the Gunners ended in victory for Fleetwood, when Conor Haughey fired past Illan Meslier to make it five successful kicks out of five for the hosts. The second teenager to disgrace himself on the night, the young man from Norn Iron proceeded to drop a different kind of F-bomb in a post-match interview with Sky Sports. Asked what had been going through his mind before he took his penalty, Haughey replied: “Hit the top corner and run like f**k.”

Despite the post-watershed lateness of the hour, Sky’s pitchside reporter felt compelled to apologise to viewers for the youngster’s forthright response. While Arteta is left to focus on making sure his players get their act together ahead of Sunday’s trip to Liverpool, Fleetwood head coach, Matt Lawlor, can look forward to tonight’s quarter-final draw. “I’ve got no preference whatsoever,” he said. “We’ve got a big game at home [against Bristol Rovers] on Saturday and I want to win it. I would absolutely love to make an amazing night into an amazing week.” For Arsenal, on a night when heroes were hard to find, the dream of a domestic treble went its own way.

Tommy Robinson faces up to 10 years in jail after being found guilty of harassing journalists

The Guardian Wed, 28 Oct 2026 16:04:48 GMT

Judge says he will consider all options to sentence far-right activist who trial heard deployed ‘bullyboy, intimidatory tactics’

Tommy Robinson faces up to 10 years in prison after being found guilty of harassing two journalists to the point it caused them fear of violence.

Journalists from the Daily Mail and their family members fled their homes after “bullyboy, intimidatory tactics” were deployed by the far-right activist, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, his trial was told.

Robinson had shared pictures of the family of one of the journalists online and said he had “tagged and bagged” all three reporters who worked on an article about his alleged role influencing unrest that broke out after the 2024 Southport murders. The charges related to two of the journalists, Andrew Young and Jacob Dirnhuber.

Dirnhuber and his partner had to leave their home, while Young and his family were provided with a close protection officer after an alleged campaign of intimidation that also included a call to the editor of the Daily Mail in which Robinson said he would make the journalists and their families “famous”.

Robinson was found guilty on both counts against him on Wednesday at Southwark crown court. The jury had deliberated for two days and had to be directed by the judge that they could return a majority verdict rather than a unanimous one.

Journalists were given an escort out of the courtroom by security after one of them was threatened inside the court by one of Robinson’s supporters. The man was ejected from the press gallery and later from the courtroom.

Robinson, a former member of the British National party and co-founder of the English Defence League, had said before the trial that his legal bills were being paid for by the billionaire tech mogul and owner of X, Elon Musk.

He was accused of harassment causing fear of violence through posts shared with his hundreds of thousands of followers on X and by direct messages. He called Young on 5 August 2024 and told him that he would visit his house, saying: “I’m coming to get you.”

Robinson, who attended court each day with a large number of supporters, was said to have become enraged after the Mail tracked him down to a hotel in Cyprus, where he was commenting on events in the UK after the Southport murders, and published a story about him with the headline “Stoking race riots from his sunbed”.

Dirnhuber said in a witness statement he did not know how Robinson had obtained his address, or who he had shared it with, adding: “I was concerned about the risk of being intercepted on my way to work, either by Robinson for a livestreamed interview or by an unpredictable supporter of his hoping to cause me or my partner physical harm.”

Young said he felt his family was under threat and he was fearful of what might happen next. “It was clear to me that Tommy Robinson was following through on his threats. My main concern was that while he may not physically harm me, he had 800,000 followers on X at the time who might have been tempted to seek revenge on me, or my home, or my family for what I had written.”

A third Daily Mail journalist, George Odling, said in a witness statement that he, his wife and young child had to leave their home through a neighbour’s house because they feared being followed by Robinson’s supporters.

The trial heard that Robinson’s “angry” and “retaliatory” posts began on 5 August 2024, as he questioned the Daily Mail’s decision to photograph and write the story about him in Cyprus.

In a post on X, which has been viewed 244,000 times and made reference to the newspaper’s front page headline “Stoking riots from his sunbed”, he wrote: “Quick question, these lies have a direct result on threats to my family.

“Is it ok if I track down the journalists addresses + families details + dox them. Would that be journalism. This has been coordinated from the top down because my latest documentary humiliates their lies.

“They have purposely doxxed where my children are is it fair for me to do the same to them.”

Robinson said in evidence he had been in “a panic” after the Mail had in effect identified the hotel in Cyprus where he had gone with family and friends and published a photo of his ex-wife, which he said put her at risk. He said he had only wanted to question the journalists and claimed they knew he was “not coming to beat them up”.

After he was found guilty, the Crown Prosecution Service said Robinson had “weaponised social media”. Frank Ferguson, the head of the CPS’s special crime and counter-terrorism division, said: “Nobody should be made to fear violence because of the work they do. Journalists play an important role in a democratic society and should be able to carry out their professional duties without being subjected to harassment.

“We will always seek to work with the police to prosecute those who break the law and I hope these convictions provide reassurance that such behaviour will be treated seriously by the criminal justice system.”

Welcoming the verdict, a spokesperson for the Daily Mail said: “Yaxley-Lennon’s behaviour was reprehensible, and had grave consequences for our reporters and their families. Through his actions, Yaxley-Lennon sought to undermine our right to hold him to account. We stand by our journalists and their freedom to report legitimately in the public interest.”

Robinson is due back in court on 16 December for a sentencing hearing. Mr Justice Cavanagh said after the verdict he would be considering all options, including a custodial sentence, whether in full or suspended. Harassment causing fear of violence can carry a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison.

Will John Healey’s ‘breathing space’ budget deliver what Britain needs? Our panel responds

The Guardian Wed, 28 Oct 2026 15:39:33 GMT

Amid global economic storms, the new chancellor has promised to steer the course – with promises of more help to come. Will it be enough?

Polly Toynbee

Guardian columnist

First, he did no harm. Then he scattered sprinkles of feel-goods. He told the truth about the state we’re in, deep in an extra £14bn of expensive debt, and, though he put it politely, at the mercy of the monster in the White House’s whims on Iran and tariffs.

The losers were popular targets: the banks and gambling companies. But plainly bank threats to decamp partly paid off. Their shares leapt up on the news that their surcharge would rise to only 6%, not its original 8% before Tory reductions. They expected to pay more, and indeed they should. Gambling company shares jumped up too, with Rank up more than 10% on the day when the companies were only hit with five percentage points more tax on high-stakes machines, a missed chance, but better than nothing. The Treasury makes £4bn from gambling. Time to ban their advertising next.

The chancellor gave a gracious nod to his predecessor. He should be grateful, as she took the pain and he takes the gain for her £66.6bn in tax rises, in NI for employers and frozen income tax thresholds that slide by unseen, but yield mightily until 2031.

The public expected more personal taxes, according to Ipsos. It didn’t happen. Labour can take comfort that they think the Conservatives and Reform would both raise tax and cut public services.

Instead, help comes for their energy costs, one of the greatest causes of household debt, with bills set to rise brutally in January. Homes in council tax bands A-D get £100 and the VAT reduction has been extended until July, while abolished standing charges leave 60% of homes better off. But the rumbling discontent that has upended our politics since Brexit is easily explained by the unprecedented long fall in median household income, only in the last year rising back to levels six years ago.

Yet people’s priorities remain perverse: immigration stays top of their concerns, above inflation and the economy. Spending more on tougher border controls is second only to the NHS as the most popular expenditure. What do you do? Give in and let Shabana Mahmood be her harshest – or start telling people about the trade-off? Visas for work for another 200,000 migrants would bring the Treasury £18bn, says the Office for Budget Responsibility. Think what people could have for that.

Is this the “growth in every postcode and hope in every heart” Andy Burnham promises? No, not yet, not yet … Wait for his 10-year plan, spending review and an election with a new manifesto. And hope.

Hettie O'Brien

Writer on the Guardian’s morning newsletter First Edition, the Guardian Long Read, and the author of The Asset Class

While Keir Starmer promised to tread more “lightly” on voters’ lives, interpreting political disaffection as a sign that people wanted to hear less from their politicians, Andy Burnham has interpreted this loss of faith as a demand for more political action. But there was always a risk that without a theory of power, his premiership would come to resemble the Downing Street equivalent of the TV show Rip-Off Britain, giving voters “everyday fixes”, starter ISAs and cheaper gherkins while failing to change the economy or society as a whole.

The charitable reading of John Healey’s budget is that it was better than it could have been (and better than the Treasury, which briefed this as a “low-key” event, wanted us to expect). His energy package, including a £100 cut to bills for houses in council tax brackets A-D, will help ease the cost of living and should lower inflation. He also proposed a series of changes that should help to bring down energy bills in future. But there was no help for low-income renters, nor any plans for funding public services that are facing real-terms cuts. Bankers, meanwhile, will be breathing a sigh of relief after Healey imposed a temporary 6% tax on bank profits, below the pre-crisis level of 8%.

For a government that has promised to turn back 40 years of neoliberalism, you might have been hoping for something much more radical than this. Small, short-term fixes and making it easier to cancel your Netflix subscription don’t equate to a political philosophy, let alone a programme capable of convincing voters that difficult trade-offs – whether on defence spending or the costs of an ageing society – will be worth it. Governing, as Mark McVitie wrote recently, requires political imagination and a sense of where you want to end up. Let’s hope that Andy Burnham has more to offer than this.

Kevin Cashman

Researcher at Transition Security Project, a centre founded by Common Wealth and Climate and Community Institute

Just last month, the prime minister made the significant promise to “break with the direction of the past 40 years” and “build a new economy and a new politics”. John Healey’s budget, unfortunately, doesn’t do enough of either.

Department budgets were already slashed this summer to help finance the Ministry of Defence’s demand for an extra £15bn. Now, this budget adds £3bn more in cuts.

In July, Transition Security Project estimated that the defence investment plan, funded partly through £6.8bn in cuts, would result in more than 10,000 net job losses. With a further £3bn in cuts, those losses are now likely to exceed 15,000.

The reason is simply that military spending is a weaker driver of growth than the investment being sacrificed to fund it. Too much of the money leaves the country – flowing, especially, to the United States.

These cuts also undermine programmes that would help bring down the cost of living. The budget confirms a £1bn cut to Warm Homes, which supports heat pump grants. The additional help with household energy bills is welcome. But directing up to £5bn from the National Wealth Fund and British Business Bank towards defence reinforces the same misplaced priorities when these resources could have been invested in areas that help with living standards. Burnham does not have to accept these constraints. Healey has left the detailed funding route to the Nato spending targets until next year’s spending review. These targets – pushed by the US – imply a colossal transfer of wealth from the public to the military sector. Burnham should abandon these targets he inherited, which will steal more investment from every other department.

Healey was right that wars are driving up our energy bills and making Britain less safe. But let’s be honest about the role the government is playing. The US used British bases in its unprovoked attack on Iran, and our government is now backing Saudi Arabia’s war in Yemen. Diplomacy and de-escalation are part of a serious cost of living strategy – not bombing.

Rohan Sathyamoorthy

Writer from south-west London

Look hard enough at this budget, and there are some signs that the chancellor is serious about bridging the age divide: an increase in tax for Britain’s banks, increased investment in apprenticeships and a new scheme for first-time buyers will be a welcome relief for many young and working people who are tired of bearing a disproportionate share of Britain’s economic burden. However, the limitations of even these mild reforms are already apparent: bank stocks rose conspicuously this morning on news that the rise would be temporary and only a mere three percentage points. And although the first-time buyer ISA will help young savers in the immediate term, in the long run it is only continuing to subsidise the housing crisis at the expense of the taxpayer, rather than intervening directly in the market to bring prices back down to an affordable level.

Furthermore, while pensioners, businesses, workers, women, carers, families and even nightclubs all received explicit support from Healey, outrageously absent was any real help for young people, nor any mention of the student loan crisis. The only mention of young people not in employment, education or training was made in the context of reforming welfare. Instead of addressing the problems facing young people and making clear that he would tackle intergenerational fairness, Healey made his priority clear, with “the biggest increase in defence spending since the end of the cold war”.

Ultimately, it will be impossible to fully judge this budget until we see the one that succeeds it. This “breathing space” budget will be beneficial only if it really is just that – buying time for the government to solve the painful, unignorable issues still crippling Britain’s young people: jobs, student loans, soaring rents. If the mixed rhetoric today is anything to go by, I won’t be holding my breath.

Nik

Participant in the Changing Realities project

The chancellor said “hope starts with a home”, but for me, it’s the cost of my home that keeps me in poverty. I work multiple jobs just to pay my rent, and nothing in today’s budget will make that situation better. Where is the “breathing space” for families like mine, or hope for the future?

Families struggling through the storms of living on a low income deserve more than modest, micro-policies and everyday fixes to protect them from the incessant headwinds.

Extending the removal of VAT from electricity bills to next summer is being presented as help for households, but for rural families like mine, it offers little (or no) meaningful relief. I have no access to mains gas and can’t afford heating oil, so I depend on electricity to heat my home. Yet this measure does nothing to address the reality of living rurally without affordable alternatives. A record number of people now live in very deep poverty, with incomes that don’t cover the basics of food, housing or energy. We need meaningful, targeted support, not policies that offer some households a small saving while leaving others struggling to keep warm. In Cornwall, many homes rely on heating oil, and removing the kerosene tariff may help, but any savings depend on supplies holding up and suppliers passing them on.

The chancellor promised a distinctly Labour approach to welfare but I know many will feel incredibly fearful about the white papers to come later this year, after Alan Milburn and Stephen Timms deliver their reports on youth unemployment and disability benefits.

What we know from this budget is that families will be able to save about 40p on the weekly shop, assuming toffees and caramels are a part of your weekly essentials. Food poverty directly impacts health, productivity and social inclusion. I wish more had been done to help fill our fridges.

John McDonnell

Labour MP for Hayes and Harlington. He was shadow chancellor for Labour from 2015 to 2020

The chancellor has called his budget a “breathing space” budget and that’s exactly what it is. It’s less a break with Keir Starmer, but hopefully the start of a step away.

The range of small-scale cost of living assistance offered on energy and food costs are all welcome elements of relief, but the harsh reality is that they provide an extremely limited breathing space.

The government has to be extremely careful that the goodwill that Andy Burnham’s arrival has generated does not degenerate into disappointment and disillusionment. Reform UK may have dipped in the polls but the rise of the far right in Germany, France and Italy demonstrates all too clearly where that disappointment can lead to.

This budget indicates to people that the government appreciates their concerns and is on their side, but it is absolutely critical that the time this budget may buy is used to demonstrate that it also has the plan needed to tackle the financial pressures people are under.

Next year’s spending review provides that opportunity.

The government has committed to the large-scale capital investment programme in council housing, home insulation and alternative energy that can stimulate the growth promised in every postcode.

But there has to be demand in the economy too. That means putting money to spend in people’s pockets by modernising our taxation system to redistribute wealth and tackle the underinvestment in our public services, low pay and poverty that have held our economy back.

Nobody doubts the pressure John Healey has been under as a result of the crass geopolitical nightmares caused by Donald Trump’s attacks on Iran. Both Benjamin Netanyahu and Vladimir Putin have played Trump like a fiddle to their own advantage, and we are all now paying the economic price. With the potential change in the midterms, perhaps it’s also time for leaders to start talking less about defence spending and more about peace making.
