The best LED face masks in the UK, tested: 12 light therapy devices that are worth the hype

The Guardian Wed, 28 Oct 2026 15:00:52 GMT

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

They claim to reduce fine lines, blemishes and redness – but which stand up to scrutiny? After consulting dermatologists and putting them to the test, we have crowned a brand new number one

The best anti-ageing creams, serums and treatments

LED face masks are booming in popularity – despite being one of the most expensive at-home beauty products to hit the market. They claim to reduce the appearance of fine lines, stop spots and calm redness, with some even combining different types of light to enhance the benefits.

However, it’s wise to be sceptical about new treatments that are costly and non-invasive, and to do your research before you buy. With this in mind, I interviewed doctors and dermatologists to find out whether these light therapy devices work.

They’re not a miracle cure for deep-set wrinkles, but experts say the best light therapy masks can promote collagen production, improve elasticity and help smooth skin with sustained use. And while it may seem like a new technology, research from the 1990s shows the efficacy of light therapy in wound healing, acne treatment and skin rejuvenation.

Red and infrared light are safe to use on all skin types, but be warned that blue light can worsen hyperpigmentation on darker skin tones.

I’ve tested some of the most popular devices on the market – including infrared masks – to narrow down my favourite LED face masks for treating a range of skin concerns.

Best LED mask overallCurrentBody Series 3

Best budget LED face maskSilk’n LED face mask 100

Best LED mask for full facial coverageTherabody TheraFace mask Glo

Best LED device for acne-prone skinLustre Solo

Best LED mask for quick treatmentsDr Dennis Gross SpectraLite FaceWare Pro

Best LED mask for travelSilk’n LED face mask Pro

I’ve been reviewing health and beauty tech for the past five years. During this time I’ve witnessed many beauty fads come and go. Naturally tight-fisted and a sceptic, I was initially struck by the cost of these masks. How on earth can an elaborate LED light strip set you back more than £300?

But after testing multiple light therapy masks, I’ve come to understand the technology behind them – and, sadly, you won’t be able to engineer your own light therapy system with a costume mask and a set of LED string lights.

I don’t have many fine lines or wrinkles to test on, but I can comment on how blue-light treatment affects acne because I’ve suffered from it since I was a teenager – despite my mum’s assurances that it would clear up after puberty. The experts I spoke to agreed on the efficacy of red and infrared light for anti-ageing.

Light therapy masks are fantastic additions to a skincare routine, helping to smooth, firm and reduce blemishes. Since I started using one almost two years ago, my skin is calmer, less prone to redness, and has a more even tone.

However, LED masks can be expensive, and if you’re not disciplined enough to use one regularly, you won’t see results. Before you splash up to £500, keep in mind that light therapy masks are most effective when paired with a good skincare routine. It’s crucial to make sure skin is properly cleansed before treatment and protected from sun damage afterwards.

If you don’t already have a skincare routine nailed down, don’t buy a light therapy mask just yet. Consider starting out using a gentle cleanser and moisturiser, with an SPF for daytime. You could also incorporate targeted skincare serums, such as retinol and vitamin C, to help firm and brighten the skin without the need for an expensive light therapy mask.

Since LED treatments take a while to show visible results, it’s difficult to test multiple light therapy masks at once (at least, without spending a few years testing them), so I enlisted the help of dermatologists who were familiar with light therapy treatments long before they were commercially available.

I spoke to Dr Barbara Kubicka, an expert in aesthetic medicine; Dr Derrick Phillips, a consultant dermatologist and spokesperson for the British Skin Foundation; and aesthetic doctor Dr Priya Verma, an authority on the science of skin ageing.

I asked these experts to identify which light therapy mask features – such as bulb quality and quantity, light wavelength and treatment time – matter the most, to inform my choices. They also outlined the suitability of light therapy for different skin types and its associated risks.

Armed with their advice, I tested the fit, comfort levels and usability of 18 of the most popular light therapy masks and other targeted LED devices. Getting hands on with the masks allowed me to pinpoint any of the key features the experts recommended, as well as features I found helpful as a consumer.

I’ve been using a light therapy mask regularly for almost two years, so I can identify a good mask from a bad one. My tests also included monitoring results after four nightly sessions, with the obvious caveat that only very minimal changes could be observed after such a short-term treatment. I then tested my favourite masks over several months, too, helping me to verify any unique treatment claims – as well as giving me plenty of opportunities to scare my boyfriend by sneaking up on him wearing each one.

Only masks that use the brightest, flicker-free bulbs, fit comfortably and are easy to use made the final cut. After testing, I returned the masks sourced for this article to the manufacturers. Where that wasn’t possible, I cleaned the masks and donated them to the Redbridge Reach Out service, which supports anyone experiencing domestic abuse.

Most LED masks come with a few settings that treat the entire face for one skin concern. But many of us don’t have uniform faces: a dark spot here, a blemish there, fine lines elsewhere. One flat treatment might help with overall skin condition, but it can’t pinpoint a specific skin concern exactly where you need it.

The CurrentBody Series 3 is the only mask I’ve found that allows users to completely customise their treatments. It’s also the only mask I’ve tested that offers penetrating deep near-infrared lights across the whole face, making it the new LED mask to beat.

Why we love it The mask has 125 light points spread over the face, each of which can produce six light wavelengths: green for pigmentation, yellow for redness, blue for blemishes, red for wrinkles, near-infrared for firming and near-infrared to support deeper skin renewal. I was able to select exactly which light (or combination of lights) I wanted to shine from each light point on the face using the CurrentBody app. Since I primarily get spots on my chin, I targeted these breakouts while sticking to anti-ageing treatments elsewhere and threw in some yellow light to tackle redness in my cheeks.

I usually hate apps for beauty tech, but I found it refreshingly simple to use, without any ads or pop-ups. Tailoring the light colours I wanted was as easy as using a colouring book, and the app then automatically programmed the light levels to ensure the right dosage within the 10-minute treatment time. It paired seamlessly with the mask to run my custom treatment – the whole process took less than five minutes.

In terms of results, the redness in my cheeks had faded, my chin appeared to clear quickly after a particularly brutal hormonal breakout, and the rest of my skin looked glowier and healthier than usual after my six weeks of testing. And, if you aren’t fussed about personalising your treatments, the mask has four pre-programmed options for anti-ageing, blemishes, redness and dark spots.

It’s a shame that … it’s so expensive and, to accommodate its wider range of treatment options, its controller has a touchscreen that’s frustratingly easy to knock to pause or stop your treatment midway.

Number of LEDs: 750 at 125 light points Number of settings: four preset, with unlimited customisation Treatment time: 10mins Light wavelengths: red (633nm), near-infrared (830nm), deep near-infrared (1,072nm), blue (415nm), green (532nm), yellow (590nm) Timer countdown: yes

Read our full CurrentBody Series 3 LED mask review for more details

If you want to try light therapy without remortgaging the house, the Silk’n LED face mask 100 is a good choice. It has 100 LED bulbs with good facial coverage, is comfortable to wear, and offers a good range of light colours. It doesn’t have near-infrared lights like the pricier options, but it covers the basics at a decent price.

Why we love it This mask offers four colour modes: red, blue, yellow and purple. Red light helps stimulate collagen to reduce the appearance of fine lines, while blue light helps to soothe breakouts. The purple light comes from mixing the aforementioned blue and red lights, combining the effects of both to boost the skin’s overall evenness.

Although less widely researched (and with limited clinical evidence to suggest efficacy), the experts I spoke to said the yellow-light treatment could help improve hydration levels in the skin. I didn’t notice a huge hydration hit when testing this feature, so if your skin is crying out for hydration, I recommend using the other light settings alongside a hydrating serum.

Each colour can be selected individually for a 10-minute targeted session, or you can select automatic mode, which cycles through the colours over 15 minutes to provide all the benefits at once.

I found the Silk’n light therapy mask simple to use and comfortable to wear. Its flexible silicone build didn’t feel quite as sturdy as more expensive options, but I didn’t really notice this when using the mask. The built-in eye shields weren’t as bulky as others, but they still blocked out the light and protected my eyes well.

The automatic mode left my skin feeling completely comfortable, with a slightly glowier finish than usual – just what I’d expect from an entry-level mask such as this one.

It’s a shame that … there’s no timer and it has fewer than a seventh of the bulbs of the CurrentBody, with no near-infrared light treatment for effective collagen stimulation deeper in the skin. This means it’s better for light-touch anti-ageing, and for soothing, acne-busting blue-light treatments.

Number of LEDs: 100 Number of settings: five Treatment time: 10 or 15mins Light wavelengths: red (633nm), purple (463nm+633nm), blue (463nm), yellow (592nm) Timer countdown: no

Most face masks look a little creepy, but the TheraFace Mask Glo takes this to another level. It focuses on providing full facial coverage over the mouth and nose area, and its glowing red eyes might be the last thing you’d want to see staring back at you from across a dark room, but the results are fantastic. And, if its appearance gives you a shock, you can switch on its massage function to calm back down.

Why we love it The first thing to note about the TheraFace Mask Glo is its sturdy build, which feels surprisingly lightweight on the face thanks to the adjustable back and top straps and large silicone-padded eye area. These distribute the weight across the brow bone and undereyes and around the head so that everything feels comfortable, no matter the position you’re in. There’s also a removable inner eye insert that blocks light from your eyes without blocking light from reaching the undereye area, where it can help reduce the appearance of fine lines.

The mask has 168 light points that emit the three most well-researched light wavelengths: blue, red and near-infrared light. These can be selected as individual settings, or you can kick back while the automatic 12-minute treatment cycles through everything you need to target fine lines, firmness and breakout-causing bacteria. Alongside this, I found the steady vibration massage, located in the mask’s straps, oddly relaxing. Its aim is to gently stimulate the scalp, increase circulation and relieve tension, but if you find the massage uncomfortable, it can be switched off.

Another selling point is its wireless controls. It has two buttons, which scroll through the three treatment modes and the vibration massage functions. These are intuitive, and I liked that I could roam around freely instead of carrying around a wired controller for the 12-minute treatment.

It’s a shame that … its lack of mouth and nose holes means the mask steams up by the end of a session. Also, it doesn’t have a countdown, so the 12-minute treatment can feel long.

Number of LEDs: 504 at 168 light points Number of settings: three LED modes, plus an automatic cycle, and three massage functions Treatment time: 4-12mins Light wavelengths: red (633nm), near-infrared (830nm), blue (415nm) Timer countdown: no

Acne can be a real pain, and many cosmetic treatments that target it leave skin feeling irritated, dry and flaky. These nifty adhesive LED patches from Lustre use blue light, which the company claims reduces breakout-causing bacteria.

Why we love it Each Solo patch has 15 pure blue LEDs at the proven wavelength for treating acne, 415nm. The patches cover a targeted area of skin about 2.5 x 5cm, which is perfect for treating problem areas such as the chin, cheeks and forehead. Since they’re rechargeable and far smaller than a typical LED face mask, they’re highly portable, making it easy to stick to a treatment routine.

I found the targeted treatments very effective for minimising breakouts in my chin area – somewhere I often struggle with spots. Continued treatments saw fewer breakouts and faster healing.

The patches come with a supply of double-sided adhesive to fix each one to your skin, allowing you to move around freely during treatment. This also means, unlike typical light therapy masks, they can be safely fixed anywhere on the body.

If you’re worried that the adhesive will feel uncomfortable or be tricky to remove from breakouts, don’t be. The patches are so lightweight that the adhesive doesn’t need to be very strong. I found it easy and comfortable to peel off the patches after the recommended 20-minute treatment time.

It’s a shame that … you need to buy the sticky patches when they run out. These cost £18 for a pack of 60, or 30p each. They also look a bit like leeches – only you can decide if that’s more palatable than the Hannibal Lecter look of the full-face LED masks.

Number of LEDs: 15 Number of settings: one Treatment time: 20mins Light wavelengths: blue (415nm) Timer countdown: no

Most LED masks recommend 10- to 15-minute daily treatments for best results. If you’re short on time but still want to invest in a reliable face mask, the SpectraLite FaceWare Pro is my recommendation. It offers anti-ageing, anti-blemish and a combination of both treatments, with daily sessions taking just three minutes. That’s something even the most time-poor can commit to, and consistency is what gets you results.

Why we love it This is the most comfortable hard-shell LED mask I’ve tested. It’s lined with a thick, flexible but sturdy-feeling layer of silicone that provides cushioning on every part of the face. During use, it evenly distributed the mask’s weight across my nose, forehead and cheekbones, no matter if I was lying flat or sitting up.

I was surprised by this, since the mask’s battery is built into the forehead rather than in a separate remote – the Lustre Renew Pro Facewear reviewed below has a similar design but is less comfortable to wear. The SpectraLite FaceWare Pro perfects the hands-free design, making it comfortable, breathable and easy to control with one button. Mercifully, there’s no useless app.

In the mask, you’ll find 100 red LEDs (including red, near-infrared and amber) and 62 blue LEDs distributed over 80 light points on the face. These have been strategically positioned so that the blue lights cover the nose, forehead, chin and lower cheeks (oily areas where acne-causing bacteria thrive), while the red light is more evenly dispersed. There are separate red anti-ageing and blue acne-fighting modes, but I used the combination mode in my tests and was pleasantly surprised by how well the mask reduced blemishes while easing redness across my face.

The keen-eyed among you may notice that the three-minute treatments are significantly shorter than the 10- to 20-minute treatment times recommended by the experts I spoke with. However, according to the brand, its clinical studies have seen results from red-light treatments within 10 weeks of daily use, and blue light within two weeks. In my weeks testing this mask, my skin did appear smoother, brighter and clearer. If you’re hunting for a quick, comfortable mask without fancy features, such as app connectivity and additional colour options, this is a strong bet.

It’s a shame that … its straps aren’t the easiest to adjust, and the mask doesn’t shield the eyes as effectively as others. If you have sensitive eyes, opt for something that has built-in eye guards instead. It also doesn’t have a remote or a countdown, but the treatments are so quick that this isn’t much of an issue.

Number of LEDs: 162 Number of settings: three Treatment time: 3mins Light wavelengths: red (630nm), amber (605nm), near-infrared (880nm), blue (415nm) Timer countdown: no

For a long time, deep near-infrared light was reserved for the most expensive LED masks. So, when the Silk’n LED face mask Pro launched in October 2025, with 20 deep near-infrared lights included on the forehead and around the eyes and mouth, I was keen to try it. Even more so when I learned of its comparatively reasonable price.

While its treatments aren’t quite as streamlined as the CurrentBody Series 3 above, it offers a range of treatments and light wavelengths at half the cost. So, if you want a great value mask, or travel often and need a mask that packs down well, this is my recommendation.

Why we love it This mask packs in seven treatment options, which combine five wavelengths of light. A few of these treatments felt a little surplus to requirements, such as the stand-alone red- or amber-light treatments – I can’t fathom why you wouldn’t want to use the setting that includes near-infrared and deep near-infrared as well. But the treatments I used most often were effective. The red-light settings had a good calming effect on my skin, and when I paired this with a few minutes of the blue light, I noticed my blemishes reduced and healed faster.

All the controls for this mask are built into a small battery pack, which magnetically attaches to the front of the mask. While this means you don’t get to see a countdown or a screen displaying setting time, there are no wires to mess around with. The battery is incredibly lightweight and can last through a whole week of treatments without recharging.

I also liked this mask’s flexible straps and its adjustable chin strap. The Silk’n Pro packs down completely flat or folds into its carry case, not much larger than a box of tissues, for travel. This is incredibly useful if you’re frequently away from home.

It’s a shame that … the chin strap hangs away from the chin slightly, and I found the eye guards pressed hard into the bridge of my nose. I also found it confusing to select different treatments because the various configurations of red-toned light were indistinguishable from each other.

Number of LEDs: 480 at 120 light points Number of settings: seven Treatment time: 10mins Light wavelengths: red (633nm), near-infrared (830nm), deep near-infrared (1,072nm), blue (463nm), amber (605nm) Timer countdown: no

Best for: fine lines and blemishes

The Shark CryoGlow is the only LED face mask I’ve tested that offers built-in undereye cooling alongside targeted light therapy. It has three different wavelengths of light: blue, red and near-infrared, arranged into presets for “better ageing”, “blemish repair” and “skin sustain”. I found the lights incredibly bright during my tests – although for safety, they automatically dim when you remove the mask from your face – but I was happy with how the mask shielded my eyes.

During every treatment, you can choose to switch on the cooling undereye patches, which aim to de-puff and soothe your skin. The cooling can also be used on its own, without the LEDs. There are three levels, the coolest of which felt startlingly cold at first but did a great job of calming down my eyes on a particularly bad hay fever day. Likewise, the blemish mode did a brilliant job of calming spots and redness with sustained use. I also liked using the skin sustain mode for a quick pick-me-up to brighten skin before a night out.

It didn’t make the final cut because … it’s noticeably heavier than its silicone competitors, and other plastic masks that don’t have undereye cooling. The mask fits comfortably when you’re sitting up, but when lying down, the metal cooling patches pressed into the delicate area under my eyes. Similarly, the location of the cooling patches means the light can’t access fine lines under the eyes. Another unfortunate side-effect of the cooling is the whirring noise it makes – inaudible from far away, but pretty noisy when pressed on to your face. I think most people would be better off with the TheraFace Mask Glo.

Number of LEDs: 160; number of settings: four; treatment time: 4-8mins light therapy; 5-15mins undereye cooling; light wavelengths: red (630nm), near-infrared (830nm), blue (415nm); timer countdown: yes

Best for: anti-ageing

If the multiple settings in the Series 3 mask above offer more versatility than you’ll use, and you’re mainly hoping to achieve anti-ageing results, choose this mask. The CurrentBody Series 2 mask was my top choice on this page for a long time, and it’s still an incredibly comfortable, effective mask that offers red, near-infrared and deep near-infrared lights.

The deep near-infrared lights penetrate deeper than the other two types of light, CurrentBody claims. This leads to more effective treatment where it’s needed most – the deep near-infrared bulbs are positioned under the eyes and around the lips to better target areas where ageing is more pronounced.

I used this mask for three months, and was pleased to notice my skin looking calmer and more even-toned than usual, with less undereye inflammation. As it’s a red-light mask, it didn’t have much effect on my acne, but it did help to reduce redness.

It didn’t make the final cut because … as someone with temperamental skin, I think spending the extra £100 on the multiuse Series 3 is worth it. This mask offers only one treatment setting, and there isn’t a screen displaying the treatment time. Neither is a dealbreaker, but it’s nice to be able to choose different treatments, and at this price, I’d expect a countdown timer.

Number of LEDs: 236; number of settings: one; treatment time: 10mins; light wavelengths: red (633nm), near-infrared (830nm), deep near-infrared (1,072nm); timer countdown: no

Best for: treating multiple areas

The neck and decollete are often the first places to show signs of ageing, as the skin is thinner in those areas. Consequently, expensive neck light therapy masks have started to flood the market – but rather than requiring additional expensive kit, this Stylpro mask can be adjusted to treat multiple areas including the back, neck, scalp and face.

It’s incredibly versatile. It has red, deep red, near-infrared and blue light, which all combine into 11 programs to target different areas of concern on your body. The remote control has a huge screen, making it easy to select the desired programme and treatment zone. This also displays the mask’s battery life and treatment time.

In my tests, the straps did a great job of keeping the flexible silicone mask in place. Its eye shields were also brilliant at blocking out light, and the snap fasteners made it easy to adjust the mask between different treatment areas. To treat the back and neck area, I found you needed to lie down or sit up very straight to prevent it from slipping, but it was great to have the versatility.

It didn’t make the final cut because … when used in face mode, the mask hangs a few inches away from the chin area, which means the light has less direct contact there. Its eye guards also tended to gently pinch the bridge of my nose.

Number of LEDs: 137; number of settings: 11; treatment time: 12-15mins; light wavelengths: red (633nm), deep red (655nm), near-infrared (830nm), blue (415nm); timer countdown: yes

Best for: wireless custom treatments

Most light treatment masks have wired controls. That doesn’t mean you need to remain tethered to a single spot, but it does mean there’s a remote that you have to carry around with you. This mask from Lustre, on the other hand, is controlled via a mobile app. The two preset treatments can also be operated using a button on the mask.

It has two programmes, called Energise and Revitalise, and uses blue, red and near-infrared light. Unusually, you can choose which kind of light you want to use in four areas of your face: forehead, eyes, nose, and cheeks and chin. In my tests, I liked being able to treat spots on my chin with blue light while using red light on the rest of my face.

It didn’t make the final cut because … it’s not very comfortable. Since the battery is on the mask itself, it’s a little top heavy, and the eye protectors don’t do a great job of shielding your eyes.

Also, I hate having lots of apps on my phone – it’s up to you whether the wireless freedom is worth the app installation.

Number of LEDs: 80; number of settings: two presets, with in-app personalisation options across four facial zones; treatment time: 10mins; light wavelengths: red (630nm), near-infrared (830nm), blue (415nm); timer countdown: yes

Best for: targeted lip treatments

If your main area of concern is the lip area, you might not need to buy a full mask. The Silk’n LumiLips has 30 LEDs concentrated in the lip area, covering smile lines and the chin. It has five light wavelengths – amber, red, dark red, near-infrared and deep near-infrared. The only other masks in this roundup offering deep near-infrared light are more than £250, which gives you a good idea of how much value it offers.

The mask has two modes, both of which use dark red, near-infrared and deep near-infrared light. The red-light mode claims to promote lip volume and firmness, while the second mode adds in amber light to reduce pigmentation and redness. I love that the mask requires only a five-minute daily treatment, making its less-than-comfortable mouthpiece slightly more bearable.

It didn’t make the final cut because … it’s built like an adult pacifier and feels like one too. You have to bite down on the mouthpiece to keep it in place, which is far less comfortable than just wearing a mask with a strap around your head.

Number of LEDs: 30; number of settings: two; treatment time: 5mins; light wavelengths: amber (605nm), red (633nm), dark red (660nm), near-infrared (830nm), deep near-infrared (1,072nm); timer countdown: no

Best for: reviving and soothing the undereyes

LED face masks usually arrive with guards to protect your eyes from the light, which means they neglect to treat the delicate skin around the eyes – an area particularly prone to fine lines, wrinkles and discoloration.

The Peep Club heated eye wand is a nifty little gadget that was designed in collaboration with optometrists, primarily as a hot compress to help with dry, tired eyes. The LED+ model includes a small LED light, which glows red to reduce fine lines and amber to decrease the visible blood vessels that cause dark circles. There’s also green light for soothing inflammation, although the evidence around green light is shaky.

During testing, I found it soothed my irritated eyes after long days staring at a screen. The amber light setting seemed to reduce my dark circles, too, after a few weeks of consistent use. As recommended, I used it with the Peep Club coconut eye balm to give the wand a bit of slip, which avoided irritating the delicate skin under my eyes.

It didn’t make the final cut because … it’s not as convenient to use as a dedicated mask, since you have to glide it over the skin. Its LED light is small, so you need to dedicate a lot of time to treatment to get the best results. While I love using the coconut eye balm and a 40ml tub lasts a long time, it leaves an oily slip on the skin after treatment, and the need for this extra running cost may be off-putting.

Number of LEDs: not listed; number of settings: five, three with LED; treatment time: 5mins; light wavelengths: amber (605nm), red (633nm), green (525nm); timer countdown: yes

I’ve tested many more LED devices than can fit on this page, and while I don’t usually draw attention to bad products, I came across so many poorly designed models that I feel it necessary to shed light on the LED masks that overpromise and underdeliver.

First, we have the Revolution Pro Miracle LED face mask, which costs just £59.99 at full price. Believe me, I wanted this mask to be a winner, but its solid plastic structure, with no eye shielding or padding, made it so wildly uncomfortable to wear that it was an almost instant write-off. The straps are another problem; they come together around the bottom part of your head, causing the mask to constantly fall. It also seems built for very small faces, so it constantly slipped down my face, pinching my nose and making it difficult to breathe properly – even if I used it without the straps and lay flat during treatment. Throw in fewer LED bulbs than average and dim lights, and this mask is impossible to recommend.

A high price tag doesn’t guarantee how good the mask is either, as evidenced by the Foreo FAQ 202 LED mask, £719 at full price. Its light weight and comfort level, along with an array of treatment options via its app-based controls, meant it impressed initially. However, its silicone design felt incredibly flimsy, and after a week of use, it had already started peeling away from the central battery pack.

This might be forgivable if Foreo offered a full warranty and repair service. There’s a two-year warranty covering defects and faulty workmanship, but this does not cover “cosmetic deterioration caused by fair wear and tear, or damage caused by accident, misuse or neglect”. To access accidental damage coverage, you have to pay Foreo’s £9.99/month subscription. Even if you’re happy to risk it, at the time of testing in June 2026, you still had to shell out £4.99/month to access the mask’s full suite of preset treatments. Add to this the scale of advertising you’re bombarded with in the app – some of it unskippable. When you consider its price, this brazen money-grubbing leaves a very bad taste.

Through testing this family of devices, I had also been hoping to find an undereye brightening LED patch to usurp the Peep Club wand, which requires constant movement across the eye area. I had hoped that the Lustre GoGlow brightening and de-puffing patches would fit the bill. They come in a handy headphone-like charging case and have a clever wireless design. However, when positioned under the eyes as advertised, the light was incredibly bright, which made it tricky to see. The sticky pads, although small, were uncomfortable to remove, and my skin was left feeling irritated for a day afterwards. The search for the perfect undereye LED patch continues …

“LED (light-emitting diode) therapy is a non-invasive treatment that uses specific wavelengths of light to stimulate various cellular processes in the skin,” says aesthetic medicine expert Kubicka. “Depending on the colour or wavelength, LED light can target inflammation, promote collagen production, accelerate healing and even kill bacteria.”

Light therapy is a great addition to your skincare routine – for me, it’s helped reduce breakouts, improve healing and reduce the appearance of my acne scars. LED face masks are quick, gentle and non-invasive, and suitable for most skin types (although as mentioned above, blue light can worsen hyperpigmentation on darker skin tones, according to the experts I spoke with). The masks are effective and foolproof to use, and the daily treatments also force you to take a little time for yourself – perfect for a morning pick-me-up or an evening wind-down.

“Red-light therapy can reduce the appearance of fine lines and wrinkles through a process called photobiomodulation,” says consultant dermatologist Phillips. “It energises mitochondria, which are the batteries of the cells, powering the production of collagen and elastin by fibroblasts, the factories of the skin.”

Elastin and collagen are “the building blocks of firm, youthful skin”, says Kubicka. Stimulating the production of these molecules can “improve skin density, elasticity and overall smoothness” as long as you complete treatments regularly.

I don’t have many fine lines or wrinkles, but I’m keen to avoid more by using red-light therapy for “preventive ageing”. However, “most of the clinical evidence focuses on treating visible signs of ageing or repairing damaged skin, rather than long-term prevention in younger skin”, as aesthetic doctor Verma explains.

Still, Verma reassured me my efforts wouldn’t be in vain. “Using LED light consistently and appropriately may help support overall skin health […] especially when combined with sun protection and a good skincare routine.”

For more, read do you really need an LED face mask?

Several colours are available, with each wavelength said to target a different skin concern. These colours correlate to the visible light spectrum, and each can have a different effect on the skin.

Red light has a wavelength of between 630 and 700nm and is the most widely known form of light therapy, loved for its non-invasive potential anti-ageing benefits. Near-infrared light above 700nm “penetrates the skin more deeply to support tissue repair and reduce inflammation”, according to Kubicka. Blue-light therapy (415nm), on the other hand, has been proven to target acne-causing bacteria, leading to a reduction in breakouts over time. Kubicka also says blue light can help regulate oil production – another common problem for those with acne.

The effects of some types of light on the skin are better researched than others. Near-infrared, red light and blue light are backed by scientific studies that identify the biological processes that each type of light triggers in the body.

Meanwhile, research into green and yellow light is more limited. One study questions the efficacy of yellow-light therapy and claims that a previous study may have been influenced by the placebo effect. Similarly, a study on green light therapy suggests that more research is needed to provide a solid recommendation for use as an anti-ageing treatment.

The “how” is simple: always use light therapy masks on freshly washed, dry skin, before applying serums and creams. This will give the light the most direct access to the skin.

Despite what some instruction manuals advise, don’t jump into daily treatments straight away – you may end up with slightly irritated skin. Start by introducing treatments two to three times a week, and monitoring the impact on your skin. If you don’t notice any sensitivity, you can incorporate more treatments, if permitted by the manufacturer’s guidelines.

Once your skin is used to the treatment, “home devices should be used three to five times a week, for 10-20 minutes a session,” says Phillips. But treatment times vary between devices, so always follow the manufacturer’s instructions, and don’t expect instant results. If you’re hoping to reduce breakouts, you should “see a reduction in redness and the frequency of acne breakouts within two to four weeks”. Those using red light for anti-ageing benefits will need to wait a little longer: “It typically takes six to eight weeks to see visible changes.”

“LED light therapy is generally very safe when used correctly,” says Verma. This is because, unlike laser hair removal, it only uses low-level, non-thermal light. “The most common side effects are mild and temporary, such as slight redness, dryness or irritation.”

“People with known photosensitive disorders or taking medications that make them more sensitive to light (eg certain antibiotics) should consult their doctor,” says Phillips. He also warns that those with darker skin tones should exercise caution when using blue light, since “some blue wavelengths have been associated with hyperpigmentation”. The Lustre Solo patches recommended above offer exclusively blue light, but the other masks in this roundup have blue-light-free settings if you do find that it causes sensitivity.

There are hundreds of light therapy masks available at different prices, but the quality varies wildly. You may see results from a budget-friendly mask, such as the Silk’n LED face mask 100 reviewed above, but spending more will generally get you a larger quantity of bulbs that offer a greater range of wavelengths. You’re also more likely to get a mask with a better fit and coverage.

The best mask for you will depend on your skin concerns and budget. Those hoping to invest in a mask with anti-acne properties will be able to spend less, since blue light is more widely available, but if you’re looking for the best anti-ageing deep near-infrared light therapy, you will need to part with more cash.

High-end red-light therapy masks can cost upwards of £500; if you spend that much, just make sure you use it regularly, or you won’t see results.

Cleaning instructions for LED masks will differ slightly from brand to brand, based on the different materials used. As a general rule, you want to steer clear of using chemical or alcohol-based cleansers since these can damage a mask’s delicate silicone and padded components. Always check the instructions for your specific mask before jumping into cleaning.

The usual best practice is to use a non-abrasive cloth, such as microfibre, dampened with water to wipe down your mask after every use. Try not to use too much water and never submerge the mask, as doing so will damage the electrical components. Always make sure your mask is unplugged and switched off before cleaning, and wait for the mask to dry completely before storing, charging or switching it on.

Sarah Matthews is a consumer journalist who specialises in health and beauty reviews. In her four years of product testing, she’s worked her way through countless hair styling tools, hair removal, light therapy and skincare innovations. She’s seen beauty trends come and go, and can sniff out a fad from a gamechanger (that doesn’t mean she’s disciplined enough to always follow her own advice, though)

London Broncos to go without £1.3m RFL funding if they enter Super League next year

The Guardian Wed, 28 Oct 2026 14:22:09 GMT

Rugby Football League set to ratify elevation imminently

Partnership with NRL not expected now till 2028

London Broncos have agreed to a condition from the existing 14 Super League clubs that they must relinquish any rights to about £1.3m in central distribution funding if they are to enter the competition in 2027, with the Rugby Football League expected to ratify their elevation imminently.

A partnership between Super League and Australia’s National Rugby League (NRL), which would mean the latter taking administrative control of the English game and injecting tens of millions of pounds of much-needed financial support, is now not expected to begin until 2028. Despite that, the expansion of Super League to 15 teams to include London has moved a step closer.

Many of the existing top-flight clubs were aware the NRL would insist on London’s inclusion in Super League when a partnership eventually starts. It was initially suspected that would be in 2027, but the two competitions have failed to agree a deal in time, though the NRL will assist in ensuring four Super League games per week are shown on Dazn next year.

That partnership not beginning until 2028 appeared to have consigned London to another season in the Championship, which they won at a canter this year. But Super League clubs informed the Broncos they would still be willing to include them on the proviso they came in with zero distribution. The other 14 clubs currently get around £1.3m in central funding.

It is understood that London have now accepted those terms. They were only due to get around £140,000 in distribution had they remained in the Championship, such is the harsh financial reality of life outside Super League. But London were also fearful they would lose their best playing talent if they decided against agreeing to the stringent financial conditions.

York and Toulouse joined Super League with half the central distribution of the other teams, around £650,000, this year when the competition expanded to 14 teams. It will now grow again with London set to be included as a 15th team – with Super League clubs now ultimately expected to vote on expansion shortly.

Super League clubs cannot handpick new teams though, only decide on the size of the league. That decision will then go to the RFL, who will launch a process to decide the 15th team. The governing body would probably use the IMG gradings system which decides the makeup of Super League as a metric for London’s elevation.

Broncos actually finished 16th in this year’s gradings but the team that finished 15th, Barrow, have already said they are not ready for Super League. Their facilities also do not meet minimum standards – meaning the RFL can approach London as next in the pecking order and invite them into Super League.

Mark Carney is celebrated abroad – while he guts hard-won protections at home

The Guardian Wed, 28 Oct 2026 13:00:04 GMT

The Canadian prime minister’s reckoning with Trumpism in Davos clashes with his attacks on environmental, Indigenous and labour rights

The Canadian prime minister is a hero around the world for his Davos speech that reckoned with a reconfiguration of power in the shadow of Donald Trump.

But at home, Mark Carney is mirroring the US president by radically centralizing power within his office and cabinet and taking a hatchet to dozens of laws protecting environmental, Indigenous and labour rights, all in order to enact his economic agenda.

His global sale of Canadian land and resources comes just weeks after another major Canadian export – wildfire smoke – decimated First Nations communities in northern Ontario, leading to mass evacuations and warning the world of the impact of a fossil fuel economy.

The Building Canada Strong Act, Bill C-39, is a 250-page piece of omnibus legislation introduced on 21 September by the transport minister and House leader, Steven MacKinnon.

The new bill expands his previous legislation that created an expansive fast-tracking designation for “projects of national interest” to “regions of national interest”, which could exempt vast areas of Canada from labour and Indigenous rights, and environmental protections.

Geographic regions can be given this sweeping new designation by federal ministers, diminishing the sovereignty of parliament and bypassing local elected officials and affected citizens in these special economic zones.

Arms-length environmental review boards are also being done away with. Decision-making for new pipelines, nuclear facilities, highways and other major infrastructure has been shifted to the very bodies charged with promoting these sectors. The Canada Energy Regulator now directly assesses energy projects, while the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission directly approves nuclear/uranium projects.

Cabinet approval has also been removed entirely for most pipelines under the amended framework, now strictly reserved for pipeline projects requiring more than 300km of new right of way. Even if a significant pipeline is proposed, if it hews close to existing corridors, it is now exempt from federal cabinet oversight.

This is what Carney believes it takes to make good on his oft-repeated promise that Canada “has what the world wants”.

As Narwhal magazine reported, these changes follow lobbying by the oil and gas industry in the form of a literal wishlist of demands to speed up project reviews for fossil fuel projects. A public pressure campaign by the CEOs or executive chairs of 14 companies was released last March, calling on the prime minister to undo the former prime minister Justin Trudeau’s modest climate policies.

It is not only environmental protections that are impeding the economy Carney hopes will stabilize Canada’s GDP. The new bill also explicitly adds the power to end a legal strike in the Canada Labour Code.

For Indigenous peoples, the rollback is just as massive. They have fought for decades to constitutionally enshrine their rights to consultation on development affecting their lands.

But with fast-tracked projects and a new guarantee to industry of a one-year timeline for decisions, communities must determine all cumulative impacts in the early stages of assessment, virtually wiping out their opportunity to influence the project direction, given the time-consuming nature and costly nature of impact assessment.

What is the former central banker’s vision for Canada? To what image of nationalism is Carney hewing?

Carney’s approach has been called a “carve-out” system of legal exceptionalism. These aren’t the sensational executive orders of Trump’s bombastic political style, but more sophisticated and sly swipes at our existing framework of law.

Sign up to How We Win

Bernie Sanders, Robert Reich, Stacey Abrams, Mehdi Hasan, Paul Krugman and other bold thinkers on how to defeat Trumpism and build a better future. From our opinion desk.

after newsletter promotion

It is no coincidence that this omnibus legislation came down following the major Canada Investment Summit that Carney held in Toronto in September. It replaced what many feared was the worst rollback in rights Canadians had ever seen – Bill C-5 - with something even worse.

The leaked pitch book for the Investment Summit showed 167 projects being sold to the highest bidder among the 200+ private equity and sovereign wealth funds reps who attended. The projects include AI datacentres, publicly owned airports, defence manufacturing, and dozens of energy and mining projects.

Carney has claimed the summit raised over $500bn in new foreign investment commitments to Canada. But how will he accommodate the needs of capital to make these projects viable? The Building Canada Strong Act is the most crucial way, through regulatory concessions. But it’s part of a buffet of public wealth on the table.

Only one day after the summit, Carney introduced the Productivity Mega Deduction, allowing businesses to deduct the cost of a much broader range of assets right away, including pipelines, mining property, aircrafts and bridges. The effective tax rate went from 13% to 6.4% – the lowest of any major economy, including the US.

Carney also promised to distribute C$280bn in federal subsidies to industry by way of tax write-offs and shifting risk from capital to taxpayers via cheap credit and loans from the Canada Growth Fund, the Canada Infrastructure Bank, and Export Development Canada.

To survive Trump’s trade war, the doors of Canada have been flung open to a giant sale of resources to industrial projects that would not be viable without the public backstop of financing and corporate license to plunder.

Though Carney is popular, Canadians are waking up to this elitist agenda. Rather than rescuing Canada, it is endangering the survival of our country and people.

Shiri Pasternak is an associate professor in criminology at Toronto Metropolitan University and a member of the Infrastructure Beyond Extractivism research team, a collaboration between critical scholars and Indigenous land defenders across North America

‘I am mother, leader, warrior of the Amazon’: Nemonte Nenquimo on why the west needs to be rescued

The Guardian Wed, 28 Oct 2026 12:00:03 GMT

The Waorani leader says millennia of living in harmony with their surroundings give Indigenous groups unique insights into the consumerist west

Every Waorani child knows the story of the boa’s mouth. How the snake inches forward, watching, its movements almost imperceptible, before it strikes, swallowing its victim whole.

Nemonte Nenquimo knows the boa’s bite. Beguiled as a young girl by the blue eyes and bright dresses of an American missionary child in her Amazon village in Ecuador, she consented to be baptised and left home to study at a church school.

“My grandfather used to tell me that the global system of money and material things is like the boa. It attracts people, it bewitches,” the 41-year-old Indigenous activist says. “It’s a fact, I’ve lived it.”

The Nenquimo of today has travelled far from her teenage self. Feted by Time magazine as one of the world’s 100 most influential people, this vocal activist for Indigenous rights proudly identifies as a “mother, leader, and warrior of the Amazon”.

Dressed in ceremonial dress, her eyes masked behind an achiote-seed red dye and with a sacred palm-fibre band around her head, she was in Europe in September to collect the €1m Gulbenkian prize for humanity.

The prize recognises her leadership of the Ceibo Alliance, a coalition of four forest peoples spanning Ecuador, Peru and Colombia that she helped co-found back in 2014 and that fights to defend Amazonian lands and cultures.

Born into a Waorani community in the southern Ecuadorian Amazon, Nenquimo first grabbed international headlines when she issued an open letter to global leaders in which, among other stinging truths, she denounced the “white man that knows too little for the power that he wields”.

The viral letter was prompted by the Covid-19 pandemic, which claimed the lives of thousands of forest peoples across the Amazon, including that of the prominent Kayapó chief Paulinho Paiakan.

“The outside world comes with beautiful words, ‘We save, we bring a project of salvation’, [but] you’re not saving; you’re really killing my people, my ancestors, my territory,” she says.

Through the Ceibo Alliance, Nenquimo has done much to resist the outside world’s encroachment. The “pillaging” of the Amazon rainforest, a magnet for loggers, oil companies, cattle ranchers and goldminers over recent decades. Years ago, she spearheaded a successful legal case against the Ecuadorian government’s decision to license a 202,000-hectare (500,000-acre) plot of Waorani historic lands for oil exploration.

Other tactics deployed by the alliance include an “Indigenous guard” system, where volunteer patrols use drones, camera traps and other monitoring equipment to track illegal incursions into their land.

But opposition is fierce. Last year, following a nationwide protest organised by Ecuador’s main Indigenous group (Conaie), the Ceibo Alliance had its bank accounts frozen without warning.

Violence from drug gangs and illegal miners is also spilling over into Indigenous territories, Nenquimo warns. In neighbouring Colombia, for example – which includes territories of two of the Alliance’s people groups, the A’i Cofán and Siona – 39 land activists were murdered last year, almost one-third of all such killings globally.

Her fight extends beyond land protection. The incursion of cowori (the Waorani word for “white man”) is also undermining the rich linguistic, cultural and spiritual traditions of the forest peoples, she argues.

“Through their ‘salvation’, they make us disconnect from our own connection with the plants, with the spirit of the jaguar, with healing,” she says. “The Waorani people have even begun to stop taking ayahuasca, which is a sacred medicine for all Amazonian peoples.”

Yet, Nenquimo vehemently rejects any narrative of victimhood. She says that it’s the west that really needs rescuing. Moreover, the rainforest defender believes people groups like hers have answers to hand.

First, the west has an imperative to reconnect with Mother Earth. The forest, as Nenquimo is fond of saying, is her community’s “market, pharmacy, hardware store and place of worship”. To destroy it, therefore, is to jeopardise their survival.

“We are not destroyers. We do not pollute the river. Gold is what we have to leave. Petroleum is the blood of our ancestors,” she says. “The water you drink, the air you breathe – as Indigenous peoples, we are protecting it.”

Connecting with nature extends to connecting with those who inhabit and guard it, she adds. Millennia of living in harmony with their surroundings give Indigenous groups unique insights that the consumerist west would gain by rediscovering them. Hence her antipathy to international charities and other well-meaning groups that impose sustainability solutions born of their own market mentality, such as carbon credit schemes and “sustainable” commercial agriculture.

In her recent memoir, We Will Not Be Saved, Nenquimo goes further, arguing that “connectedness involves responsibilities”; not least for those in industrial economies to beware the boa and question their pursuit of relentless economic growth.

Learning to overcome the barriers that divide us is also critical, she maintains. As a union of distinct peoples with a history of inter-tribal conflict, the Ceibo Alliance demonstrates in microcosm what is possible when old enmities are left behind.

That journey begins with empathy, she says. In her memoir, she recalls realising that for the judges in her landmark court case to “truly see” her, she must also see them: “Not as enemies … not as caricatures of conquest but rather as people.”

Last, and arguably hardest, is finding the humility to genuinely listen and the strength to truly love. This Waorani leader has every reason to hate the cowori: under their hand, disease, pollution, deforestation and, in her own lived experience, sexual abuse have been inflicted upon her people.

If the world’s “developed” countries are to be saved – from the desire to take, to own, to control – then acknowledging that the planet’s last remaining “primitive” peoples might have something valuable to impart merits consideration, she suggests.

“If you don’t have a mind or heart to love, then what’s the point? It’s just being angry, wanting to devour, wanting to accumulate,” she says. “When we die, we will go with a light, peaceful spirit. We won’t have to suffer in our spirit.”

Airbnb feels like a soulless rip-off – and its hosts are revolting

The Guardian Wed, 28 Oct 2026 11:00:03 GMT

Excuse me if I feel no sympathy for the property owners who have threatened strike action because guests no longer have to do their chores. Whatever happened to the company’s initial guff about building community?

To Airbnb or not to Airbnb, that is the question. Would you like to help pay someone’s mortgage and clean their house and fork out an extortionate cleaning fee and abide by a 90-page list of house rules? Or would you like to check into a nice hotel where you get fresh towels and a tiny chocolate on your pillow?

Airbnb’s business is booming, so plenty of people are still choosing the first option. Nevertheless, the hospitality giant seems to have realised travellers are sick of being handed ridiculous chore lists, and is reining in some of its more tyrannical hosts. Last week Airbnb posted updated guidelines stating guests can no longer be asked to complete tasks that “require significant effort or time or would typically be performed by a cleaner”.

This entirely reasonable stipulation has gone down exactly how you’d expect from landlords who want to charge hotel-like fees without providing hotel-like services. Some hosts are desperately trying to find loopholes, while others are calling for a strike. “Even if we all unlist our properties for just a day or two, we can send a powerful message,” one budding revolutionary wrote in a Facebook group for Airbnb hosts. “Airbnb built its empire on OUR properties. It’s time we reminded them who actually holds the power.”

I’ve tried to avoid Airbnb ever since a stay where the coffee table was proclaimed off-limits for coffee cups and there was a snake in the basement. So I can’t say I have much sympathy for hosts who are melting down about not being able to force their guests to scrub the floors.

That said, I fully support a general Airbnb strike. Despite all the guff about building community, the platform is as soulless as every other tech company. It has enabled Israeli settlers to make money from illegal settlements built on stolen land, for example. And it has supercharged property speculation. In the name of maximising profits, it has also gone through the same enshittification as other once-shiny startups. What was once a fun and inexpensive way to travel often now feels like a bland rip-off.

So, please, disgruntled hosts, go ahead and remind Airbnb who actually holds the power. And don’t stop with Airbnb. If every one of those small-time property moguls channelled that same energy into protecting democracy rather than their bank balance, the world would be a far better place to live.

Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

A bitter night in Israel for all who craved a fresh start. Netanyahu survives for now – and we are more divided than ever

The Guardian Wed, 28 Oct 2026 10:08:29 GMT

Exit polls gave the opposition hope, but then reality dawned. With most votes going to rightwing parties, the prospects for the left and centre now look bleak

Following Israel’s nail-biting election, nearly every political community in the country experienced triumph and despair. The initial results swung wildly from the first exit polls to the slow real-vote count; the bloc of parties loyal to the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, might yet win, and each side feels that its fate hangs in the balance.

So far, only one certainty remains: Israel’s bitter divisions are deeper than ever.

At 10pm Jerusalem time, three television stations published their exit polls by veteran pollsters showing a stinging loss for Netanyahu’s current government. In all three, his current coalition won just 50 out of 120 parliamentary seats, with 70 for the opposition. It was small consolation for Netanyahu that his Likud party held a slight lead over the main challenger, the Yashar party led by former IDF chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot.

Millions of Israelis who voted for opposition parties felt exhilarated. Together, four Zionist lists within the opposition ran a two- or three-seat lead over Netanyahu’s bloc, though neither of those groupings was close to a 61-seat majority. Eisenkot gave a passionate speech about the defeat of the “coalition of failure”, by a “larger and stronger Zionist majority”. Former prime minister Naftali Bennett, another leading opposition figure, declared that the “alliance of those who served” had won – referencing Israelis who have served in the military, while Netanyahu’s government had shielded Israel’s ultra-Orthodox Jews from service during Israel’s longest and bloodiest war.

Those first polls also showed an unprecedented gain for parties representing Arab-Palestinian citizens of Israel, with 17 or 18 seats out of 120. That community, about one-fifth of the population, had a powerful turnout of more than 75%. In earlier years, their turnout rates had lagged behind those of Jewish voters. Many Arab citizens preferred to avoid legitimising elections in a country that has discriminated against them since its founding, alongside ongoing occupation and now full-blown war against Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza.

But the community was seized by the urgency of ousting ultra-nationalist, anti-Arab extremists in the current government. Calls to boycott elections nearly vanished, and the first results made Arab parties look like kingmakers for coalition bargaining.

Netanyahu’s camp would have been dejected at first. To be sure, two additional exit polls showed more flattering results for his bloc, but these were commissioned by right-leaning channels that many viewed as biased. Throughout the campaign, their poll findings had been outliers.

Then the counting began. Within hours, Netanyahu’s bloc staged a reversal, pulling significantly ahead of the four opposition Zionist parties many hoped would replace him. The Arab parties retained a strong showing but lower than the original heady projections. But three of the four Zionist parties preferred to exclude them for coalition-building purposes. As a result, even if the total opposition vote outweighs support for the outgoing government, Netanyahu might have done it again.

It is not yet clear if any one group of parties can reach a 61-seat majority. Negotiations to form a coalition will take dizzying twists in the coming weeks; maybe a minority government or a stalemate will be the unsatisfying result. But one thing is certain. Israel’s divisions have never been more profound. Blocs, camps and tribes have never been more irreconcilable.

The majority of Israelis who voted for any opposition party cannot fathom how they will survive under another extremist, anti-democratic, pro-war coalition led by Netanyahu and his theocratic allies.

Yet the clear majority of the voters supported ideologically rightwing parties, who hold perhaps 74 seats at present, including Netanyahu’s bloc and at least two clearly rightwing opposition parties led by Avigdor Lieberman and Bennett. The centre and left wing in Israel cannot fathom how they will survive under these nationalist, militarist, illiberal lawmakers with a firm majority in Knesset, regardless of the government.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Arab citizens could suffer the most severe disappointment. In return for their greatest-ever political participation, with the singular aim of ousting a government that loathes them, their efforts may have gone for nought.

Israel’s moderately leftwing Democrats party appears on course to reach around nine seats, more than twice the parliamentary strength of an equivalent party in the last Knesset. But for roughly 20% of all Israelis who call themselves leftwing, who dream of a country that no longer lords it over Palestinians and still dares to hope one day for peace, there is little horizon for hope.

Israel has always been famously divided, yet managed somehow to hold together. Now, the lively disagreements of the past have given way to fundamental, even existential questions about whether the people of Israel have anything in common with each other; and whether some will simply give up and go.

Dahlia Scheindlin is a political analyst in Tel Aviv

‘There is no inevitable dystopia’: Jeanette Winterson on AI and the future of humanity

The Guardian Wed, 28 Oct 2026 10:00:05 GMT

The author believes we are at a turning point as a species – and even in the shadow of big tech it’s up to us how we want to proceed

‘I am a storyteller by trade,” writes Jeanette Winterson on the first page of her 2021 book 12 Bytes, an idiosyncratic and thought-provoking series of essays in which she considered just how artificial intelligence might change everything about our lives. “And I know everything we do is a fiction until it’s a fact: the dream of flying, the dream of space travel, the dream of speaking to someone instantly, across time and space, the dream of not dying – or of returning.”

She had already been thinking about our possible futures for at least 15 years – her 2007 novel, The Stone Gods, for instance, imagined a post-climate catastrophe world populated by robots and humans who never age, while 12 Bytes was preceded by Frankisstein: A Love Story, which alternates a recreation of the summer Mary Shelley wrote Frankenstein with a trans doctor’s travels among present-day cryogenecists and AI-enabled robots.

When we meet, Winterson is just back from China, where, she tells me, her first novel, Oranges Are Not the Only Fruit, a fictionalised account of her childhood, has sold more than a million copies in the past six years; more than 200,000 mostly young women tried to come to see her speak. She thinks this is because, in a world of long work hours and looming AI-engendered precarity, this fictionalised account of her own escape from an entrapped childhood gives readers permission to imagine a different future for themselves. She has since written 13 novels for adults, as well as nonfiction, short stories, children’s books and screenplays. Now she wants to persuade the production company Goalhanger to give her a podcast. “I want to do one called The Rest is Human,” she says, sitting at a bare wooden table in her home, a Georgian set of rooms above a shop – which she also owns – in Spitalfields, east London. “To see what we retain for ourselves in this absolute scramble to outsource everything we thought we were.”

Because we are, she argues, at a turning point in our story as a species. Until the Industrial Revolution, change was all about “Mother Nature and the slow process of becoming”, but then we “massively intervened. And that’s a decisive moment.” Computing, 70 years ago, was another step. Artificial intelligence – which she would prefer to call alternative intelligence – is next, and “an evolutionary leap. That’s what this is. AI is much more than a tool.” Given this, a certain understanding of the irreducibly human – our feelings, our imaginations, our centuries of study of who we are and what we have done – must be central to how well or badly things might go.

She’s often strikingly optimistic about it. She imagines a relationship with AI, for instance, where you can “have a chat to your system. It’s going to look at everything. It’s going to go at such speed. It’s going to look at transport. It’s going to look at utilities. It’s going to look at employment, going to look at job hours, going to say, ‘What do these weird things called humans thrive on? What do they like? And have they always liked it?’ We could do this in a genuinely utopian way and say, ‘Right, we’re going to make it better.’” We are at a deeply significant moment of choice, she believes, that mirrors the choice we had in the Industrial Revolution – namely, “What future shall we build?”

But in failing to distribute its gains fairly, the Industrial Revolution ushered in an era of unprecedented wealth for the few and unprecedented levels of misery for the many – a state of affairs many predict is not only already echoed but will be dwarfed by the fallout from AI: a permanent underclass, entire continents left behind and starved of current sources of income. Not to mention the environmental impact of datacentres at a time when the world can least afford it.

The problem is not AI, she insists, but us. “There is no inevitable dystopia.” If things go wrong, it will be because of “old-fashioned thinking laid over this brand-new reality”. Specifically, “the idea of meaningless endless work being good for the soul is a 19th-century madness designed to keep people in their place. Most of what we fear about AI and jobs comes down to the political and economic choices our masters will make, just as they did in the Industrial Revolution.” She isn’t blindly optimistic. She does know that, “Yes, we are on track to mess up this chance to fundamentally change our relationship to the world of work” – but that’s because “our masters are using out-of-date, not-fit-for-purpose economic models”.

But it isn’t only the old winner-takes-all, “rational” ends-justify-the-means economic models that are the problem. Our flawed assumptions, and our prejudices, being the material on which large language models (LLMs) are trained, are built into the very fabric of AI. Not to mention the characters and the moral imaginations of those developing it. When we meet, Winterson is reading Jill Lepore’s The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State, and reiterates Lepore’s argument that we are now living “the sci-fi books that these [men who are] ruling the world read when they were 13. And she said, ‘We are now all under the covers with these boys and their flashlights. And the thing is, they didn’t read them as warnings about how to preserve what’s good in us. They read them as instruction manuals.’ It’s absolutely terrifying.”

One big thing they seem to have taken from these books, and Winterson cannot help but be fascinated by, is “the ultimate goal of Silicon Valley … to get out of the body and off the planet” – not least because she is so aware that humanism, in which everything is brought back to ourselves, our perceptions and our bodies, is historically so recent. People say, “These are machines, you can’t have relationships with them,” she says. “I look at them and say, ‘billions of people on this Earth right now are having their most profound relationship with a non-biological entity they call their sky god.’ Right? It’s always been so! We are absolutely primed not to worry about biology being everything about us. That’s why religion was invented – it is the world’s first disruptive startup. It’s there to say, this is not it. This is not the end, this doesn’t matter, this is a transition.”

So we’re literally making our own gods? “Totally! What tech is doing now is what religion has always wanted,” which is, at its most basic level, a solution to the problem of death. “I mean, has there ever been a time where religion and science are asking the same question, since the Enlightenment? They’re both saying, ‘Is consciousness obliged to materiality?’ And religion has always said no. And science has always said yes. And now science is saying, ‘Um, noooo.”’ You know, to me, where I come from” – a childhood of fundamentalist Christianity in 1960s Accrington, and training as a preacher – “this is completely fascinating.” Later, on email, she adds, “I love my body, but I would be happy to shape shift. Happy to slip out of it into pure consciousness one day and of course people say there is no consciousness without a body, and that was the scientific belief. But now? Haha.”

I would, I have to say, argue the opposite, that advances in neuroscience, immunology and psychotherapy mean it is more the scientific belief than ever. Not to mention the fact that AI is also entirely dependent on a physical system, otherwise known as datacentres. Although, as she points out it’s important to remember that “the machines don’t have a limbic system. They’re only neural networks. But we’ve got two systems – we’re like a hybrid car with two powertrains, so we’ve got the neural network, our rational processing self, and we’ve got the limbic system, which is much older and that’s the fight-flight-freeze, and where all our feelings come from.” Perhaps detaching from the limbic is the next stage, she says, and it definitely isn’t all good. “Maybe we’ll decide that we don’t need this feeling machine … that is where the tech bros are heading. I don’t know if you’ve ever sat in a room with some of these bigger guys, because it’s very interesting. They are not connected to their feelings. They find them kind of bothersome.”

This tech-enabled possibility of a kind of transcendence seems to have arrived alongside a requirement for faith – in the technology, in the future it is making, in the people building that future, in its predictions both of utopian heaven and various shades of hell, all by high priests who jealously guard access to what’s actually going on. “What we know about humans is they love monopolies,” says Winterson, “because it’s a concentration of power. Of course it can be corporatised, monopolised to such a degree that it becomes the worst prison imaginable,” as told in Joanna Kavenna’s brilliant 2019 dystopian novel Zed. “That is a real possibility,” she says. “And that’s why we need people who are sort of free-range humans, who can think.”

The problem then is how we support – or develop – such humans. “There are basically two ways to know you have a future,” claimed Alex Karp, the CEO of Palantir, recently. “One, you have some vocational training. Or two, you’re neurodivergent.” Daniela Amodei, the president of Anthropic and herself a literature graduate, when asked more or less the same thing, had a different take. “I actually think studying the humanities is going to be more important than ever,” she said, because “the things that make us human will become much more important instead of much less important.” Which makes the bonfire of the humanities in the UK somewhat concerning: in the year to December 2024, 4,000 jobs in the social sciences, humanities and arts were lost. Exeter University recently announced it would be cutting 150 roles, affecting eight in 10 academics in the faculty of humanities, arts and social sciences, while last month Nottingham said it would be ending its modern languages and its music degrees. At some universities the humanities, according to a report in this paper, risk being “extinguished” altogether.

Why save the humanities? One answer might be that they teach a sense of where we come from and who we are, which also feels threatened. “Massive numbers of students are going to emerge from university with degrees, and into the workforce, who are essentially illiterate,” one professor told New York magazine, responding to the first tranche of AI natives arriving in higher education. “Both in the literal sense and in the sense of being historically illiterate and having no knowledge of their own culture, much less anyone else’s.” It risked, a report from MIT claimed, being a kind of generational “cognitive surrender”.

Another is the processes by which people should be taught – reading, and being critical of what is read, and then having to write cogent defences of those critiques. Having to tussle your intuitions into an essay helps you to discover what – and how – you think, and how the ideas of others work. Winterson, who studied English at Oxford, and has been professor of new writing at the University of Manchester for 14 years, as well as teaching “a free-thinking class about creativity”, agrees. But she is dismissive of much of the current system. “Maybe I’m controversial here but I do think higher education needs a top-down restructure. I don’t think it’s viable and I don’t think it’s delivering in its present form.” The thing is, “We’ve got a market that doesn’t really know what education is for. Is it for jobs? Is it for personal growth? There are a lot of worthless higher education courses which are not helping, either. I think it’s always better, being a practical northern girl, to face the facts to start with.”

We need to think, she says, about “what’s reserved to us that isn’t going to be done bigger, better, faster, stronger by the machines. And that’s where higher education really comes in. The question that’s sitting on top of all these things about, ‘Why are these jobs going?’, ‘What’s happening in these courses that aren’t getting any applicants any more?’, is ‘What sort of humans will we need in the world to come? What are humans for? What are we going to do with us?’”. And that “takes us back to the idea of, well, OK, how do you develop a mind? How do you protect a mind? Because the mind is this massive, monstrous place where anything can happen.”

And for this, “a humanist education is essential. We have to centre the human here. By changing how we educate our kids from the start we can foreground creativity, play, problem-solving, thinking, because it’s fun to think, the arts because humans are naturally creative. Show me a child that doesn’t want to hear a story or do a dance or paint a picture or have an imaginary friend. This isn’t imposed and it isn’t elitism. It’s us.”

Even an hour a week, she thinks, would make a difference. “Let’s ask what you think about the world. ‘Why do you think that?’ It’s not costly. It’s actually about will.” Teach maths and arts and science, she suggests, at least to A-level, even if they aren’t examined. “Of course we will specialise. We need doctors and chemists but we also need what used to be called well-rounded people. Everything is interesting! Humans are born with a big brain. Mostly we don’t use it.”

Once past formal education, she would embed artists and public intellectuals at every level. “The arts aren’t a leisure industry,” as she puts it in 12 Bytes. “The arts have always been an imaginative and emotional wrestle with reality – a series of inventions and creations. A capacity to think differently, a willingness to change our understanding of ourselves. To help us to be wiser, more reflective, less frightened people. Artists make something out of nothing every day.”

We meet before Jacob Coxon quit his job at Anthropic to warn of a 10% chance AI might erase humanity, sending a wave of panic across the world. Afterwards, I check in about how positive Winterson is feeling now. The worst “could happen”, she repeats. But “the immensity of the good outcome is just as real as the totality of our failure to get this right”. Above all, “this is a human decision and a human predicament. This is our big chance. Maybe our last chance, just like Turing’s colleague Jack Good said when he called AI our last invention. It’s all to play for.”

We can only hope it’s not too late.

Jeanette Winterson’s most recent book is One Aladdin, Two Lamps. She also writes at jeanettewinterson. substack. com
