We are seeing the rise of psychopatriarchy everywhere

The Guardian Wed, 28 Oct 2026 10:00:03 GMT

Psychopatriarchy is jet fuel to racism, colonialism, imperialism and capitalism

For those of us who have spent our lives trying to dismantle this endlessly destructive paradigm of patriarchy, it has become increasingly clear in recent months that something more terrifying is afoot.

The wheels are off the cart. We are in the midst of a chaotic, demented acceleration of the most violent and cruel aspects of this system which has evolved into what I am calling Psychopatriarchy.

Psychopatriarchy is a reaction, a backlash against the progress we have made on all fronts: women’s rights, civil rights, immigrant rights, workers rights, trans rights etc.

It has birthed an authoritarian fascist reality, poisoning our social and psychological environment with terrorizing violence, cruelty and precarity. It has consolidated the billionaire class who are driven by the mindset summed up in the slogan “move fast and break things.” Or, one might say, grab things, rape things.

Psychopatriarchy is found in the 120 people who own more money than half the population on Earth, in the systems of oppression, surveillance and violence which become more and more sophisticated and widespread, in the few mainly white men with extreme wealth and power who are now merged with the government and own the systems of communication, AI, police or state militias like ICE.

Psychopatriarchy is a sanctioning of extreme hatred and violence against women from the top, many of whom are rapists, batterers, pedophiles and abusers or men who openly support them.

The president of the US is a civilly adjudicated sex abuser and has not only flippantly dismissed allegations of sexual violence made against others in his orbit, but made it fashionable and popular attitude for the men in his delusional cult.

He has created a suffocating atmosphere of misogyny and predation. We only have to look to the manosphere, or the rape academies online where millions of men exchange best practices for drugging and raping their wives, girlfriends, sisters or deepfake pornography which is destroying thousands of women’s lives or sex robots.

Or rape islands where some of the most powerful men in the world are alleged to have raped underage girls and not one has been prosecuted. Or universities where young men allegedly gang-rape an incapacitated woman or where young women can’t put down a drink at a party without fear of being drugged, where they are blamed for being assaulted.

Psychopatriarchy is women dying preventable deaths because abortion care is denied or delayed or the introduction of extreme constitutional amendments such as North Carolina House Bill 1232, where men might be legally allowed to kill women who have abortions. This bill will hopefully not pass, but the fact that it is even being considered is an example of how deeply far we have fallen.

Psychopatriachy is the open and unapologetic death of compassion; as Elon Musk said: “Empathy is the fundamental weakness of western civilization.” This means a kind of contempt for anything that appears to be emotional, alive, feminine, caring.

Strength in the form of dissociation is revered. When you feel nothing, no guilt, no shame, no horror at your actions, you can better serve your goals and the state. When you are ruled by your blind devotion to the president, the boss, the father, you become capable of doing anything in his name.

Psychopatriachy is renaming the Department of Defense the “Department of War”, well, the “High-T Department of War”, as Hegseth calls it, wanting all military personnel aged 30 and over to “have the right testosterone levels” to operate at their “absolute best” and to optimize “natural capabilities”, “longevity”, and “readiness”. Preparing a psycho army driven by chemicals beyond their control.

Psychopatriarchy is wanting to livestream a firing squad. It’s the endless genocide in Gaza, the outright murdering of babies, toddlers, mothers, fathers, journalists, doctors. It’s the US bombing a girls school in Iran and murdering 120 girl children and 26 teachers, and no one ever taking responsibility for one of the worst war crimes since Vietnam.

It’s illegally kidnapping presidents and randomly murdering people by bombing them in boats in the middle of the sea. It’s masked men dragging away wailing children from their parents.

It’s killing activists in the streets: Renee Good and Alex Pretti. It’s intimidating and threatening deportation to those who disagree with you: Ilhan Omar. It’s creating the conditions for the lynching of Black people across the United States.

It’s tearing down ancient grandmother trees to build walls to keep suffering people out or to landscape a golf course. It’s the coldhearted, discompassionate billionaire class taking everything, erasing everyone.

Psychopatriarchy is the decimation of all forms of accountability. Infinite impunity. No supreme court, no Department of Justice, no leaders, no Congress. Withdrawing or refusing to be part of any international courts or abiding by international law. When there is no accountability, when there is no place to turn for justice, a society loses its moral footing and begins to fall.

Psychopatriachy is not just a political notion. It’s a state of existence, a blight on the condition of humanity locking us into daily terror, cruelty, depression, malaise, a manufactured sense of powerlessness, alienation and a desire to disappear.

It is a kind of low-level anxiety, an ongoing foreshadowing or feeling of imminent destruction coming from multiple directions at once, and rather than reducing these threats (AI, nuclear weapons, climate catastrophes, pandemics), the psychopatriarchs are accelerating all these things. AI is charging forward with no regulation, escalating the nuclear arms race, increasing drilling of oil at breakneck speed.

Psychopatriarchy is jet fuel to all the other -isms: racism, colonialism, imperialism, capitalism.

It is propelled by its own mad trajectory. We can try to block it (courts); we can starve it (strikes); we can remove it (vote and get them out office). We can name and shame it (speaking out, marches and rallies), refuse to normalize it (write about it, make art about it); we can prosecute it.

We can create a parallel world that is so inviting, generous and caring that even those who are still struggling to break out of the cult will eventually be emboldened.

But what we cannot do is go to sleep, become small and still, with the childlike fantasy that they will not find us. What we cannot do is succumb to it or become them – numb, selfish, hollow and cruel.

Our feelings, our pain, our empathy, our rage, our love, our refusal to turn away will be our salvation. Psychosis is the inability to tell what is real from unreal. Our work is to say what we see and trust what we know, to keep speaking truth to power and go to any lengths to stay connected to reality and each other.

V (formerly Eve Ensler) is a playwright and activist and the founder of V-Day, a global movement to end violence against women and girls

The shocking rise of rib remodelling: ‘I wanted that hourglass shape’

The Guardian Wed, 28 Oct 2026 05:00:54 GMT

It involves the fracturing of a patient’s ribs, before they spend three months laced into a corset. Some of those who have had this cosmetic procedure say it is like being ‘hit by a bus’. Why is it becoming more popular?

Daniela Cesin was 14 when she began thinking about her looks. “I was a little bit chubby and I started to work out at home and lose weight. I saw the difference in my body: my abs, the muscles in my arms, and I started liking it,” she says. By 31, she had the slim, toned body she had hoped for, but something was still missing. “I wanted to have that guitar hourglass shape.”

In August, Cesin travelled from Miami, where she has lived for the past 15 years, to her native Venezuela for liposuction and a fat transfer to her hips. She met her cosmetic surgeon for the first time the day before the procedure, and he realised she didn’t have enough fat to go ahead with it. Instead, he offered to perform RibXcar: a rib remodelling surgery that would involve fracturing three of her lower ribs on each side and binding them in a corset for three months, to set the ribs in a new position and give her a wasplike waist.

“I was like: ‘No, no, no, I don’t want to do anything with the ribs,’” she says. The idea of breaking the bones around her vital organs sounded a lot more invasive than a breast augmentation, which she had 10 years ago, or a rhinoplasty (nose surgery) and blepharoplasty (eyelid surgery), which she had two years ago. Also, she had never heard of the procedure.

But after the consultation, she decided to trust her surgeon. Cesin had already paid for flights and taken three weeks off from her job as a sales director. The next day she was anaesthetised, and her surgeon used an ultrasound to locate the ribs, made six small incisions in her back, and inserted a vibrating tool to create greenstick fractures – an incomplete bone break – on each rib. When she came to she was wearing a black corset with small knobs on each side that she could tighten to her preferred measurements.

The recovery has been uncomfortable. It was initially hard to stand or lie down without help, and there was soreness from the incisions. The first week, Cesin barely slept. “Your body doesn’t get used to any position, so every hour I would wake up.” But the worst part has been eating while wearing her corset, which must remain on for 23 hours a day; this causes acid reflux. Despite her discomfort, when we speak six weeks after her surgery, she is pleased with the eight centimetres she has shaved off her waist.

Cesin is one of a small but growing number of women choosing to fracture their ribs for an hourglass shape. To achieve this look, women previously underwent riskier rib removal techniques, which reduce the protective bone barrier for the liver and spleen. Kazbek Kudzaev, a plastic surgeon in Russia, realised in 2017 that he could achieve similar aesthetic results when he moved the ribs with a drill until one side fractured, then bound the body in a corset while they healed. Since his discovery, surgeons in countries including Colombia, Korea and France have refined the technique. Today, it takes about an hour and is performed under general anaesthesia as a day-surgery treatment.

It is touted as a noninvasive procedure, but many of the women I interviewed described feeling as if they had been “hit by a bus” after surgery. And there are serious risks. These include standard surgical complications, such as allergic reactions to the anaesthesia, blood clots, wound infections and seromas (pockets of fluid that build up under the skin). But also more specific dangers, including a collapsed lung, known as a pneumothorax; and a haemothorax, where blood collects in the space between the chest wall and the lungs. Both of these are potentially fatal.

Sandip Hindocha, a consultant plastic surgeon at the Private Clinic on Harley Street in London, is sceptical about the procedure. “If a patient came to my clinic and said this is what I want to do, I’d be asking the question: ‘Why do you want to do that? And why do you want to make such a permanent change to your body?’”

He references a paper published in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery, which states that between 2018 and 2024, out of 2,351 patients who had rib remodelling, there was an overall complication rate of 3.7%. “That’s not a small number,” he says. “If we did a breast augmentation, you wouldn’t expect a complication rate like that.”

The British Association of Aesthetic Plastic Surgeons (BAAPS), doesn’t endorse the procedure. Former president Nora Nugent points out that it is relatively new, “with limited data available on long-term results and it requires advanced body contouring skills as well as the ability to treat any potential complications. It may be something that UK/BAAPS plastic surgeons bring into their practices in due course but it is not available at the moment.”

The procedure isn’t typically offered to cisgender women over the age of 40, because of the increased chance of them having osteoporosis, which can cause the bones to fully break rather than fracture. Another complication for patients is that gaining weight can cause your body to change shape again, so pregnancy can affect the results. The procedure “needs to be done with a surgeon who has a lot of experience in it,” says Hindocha. “Maybe a surgeon that also does chest wall reconstruction.”

In the UK, plastic surgeons are advised to give patients a cooling-off period of at least two weeks to weigh up the risks and potential consequences of having any procedure. But Hindocha worries that patients are sometimes opting for rib remodelling with less time for reflection, despite the permanence of the change. “If you put an implant in and later you don’t want it, you can, worst case scenario, remove it,” Hindocha says. Whereas the ribs are “a structural, rigid part of you that you cannot reverse.”

Throughout history, waistlines have expanded and shrunk. Between the 16th and 19th centuries, corset wearing and tight-lacing became a symbol of beauty for the “leisure class” (the restrictive garments made physical labour impossible). The engineered hourglass shape fell out of fashion in the 1920s, but made a comeback with Marilyn Monroe, before slender, androgynous frames gained popularity from the 60s to the 90s. In the 2010s, the extreme curves of the Kardashians became the defining silhouette.

In recent years, tinier, waif-like frames have become popular on TikTok and Instagram, but a highly defined waist is also considered desirable. This is thanks, among other things, to the multibillion-dollar shapewear industry; global access to Instagram and filters; and easily streamed online workout videos that focus on creating a slim, hourglass silhouette through targeted training. But now there are adverts on social media for permanent surgical options too.

In July, 10 Australian influencers, who have made names for themselves globally on shows including Married at First Sight and Below Deck, prompted headlines with a trip to Bali. They were there for a brand collaboration with a rib recontouring practice called Snatched Waist. The clinic they visited looked more like a spa than a surgeon’s office and, post-surgery, the influencers were soon lounging by the pool, showing off their narrow waists on Instagram.

Not everyone is sunbathing in a bikini after the procedure. When Sophia woke up from her rib remodelling procedure in November 2025, she expected to be transferred to her Beverly Hills hotel room, a little sore but ready for recovery. Instead, she was surrounded by emergency medical technicians, who were putting her on to a stretcher to take her to hospital by ambulance. The next thing she remembers is lying in a hospital bed, hooked up to an electrocardiogram and an intravenous drip.

A CT scan showed Sophia had suffered a pneumothorax: 25% of one of her lungs had collapsed. She was put on oxygen and monitored for six hours before being released. Although she had signed all the consent forms for the procedure, “it was completely shocking to me,” she says.

For at least a month, Sophia had a deep pain in her lung and some shortness of breath. She had to return to the hospital after some fluid build up, but eventually started feeling better. The pain from the surgery itself subsided after about three weeks: coughing and sneezing was no longer agonising. And she was able to return to her office job and hike in her corset at the weekends.

Sophia is transgender and chose the procedure to feminise her body, by narrowing her torso, which she felt was too wide. She began consultations for the procedure in August last year, with the surgeon planning to fracture ribs 10, 11 and 12. But by the time of her surgery in November, the surgeon felt confident he could achieve better results by going even further up the ribcage, ultimately operating on five ribs on each side. Sophia knew this would increase her risk of a pneumothorax, but was willing to take the chance.

“I didn’t start transitioning until I was 47 and I feel as if I’m playing catch up, because I’m so old, and testosterone was running rampant all those decades,” she says. “That’s why gender-affirming procedures are really important to me.” The final results weren’t what she had hoped for though. “It was a bit underwhelming.”

In September this year, she went for a second round of rib remodelling with Leif Rogers, a different surgeon in Pasadena and Beverly Hills, California. Rogers removed cartilage from the anterior side of her ribcage on ribs three to 10. On rib four, he cut sections out and secured them with titanium plates and screws. Sophia had a breast augmentation at the same time, as the inframammary incisions were already open. When she emails to update me a week and a half after her second surgery, although there has been no collapsed lung this time, she says: “Recovery has been significantly more painful, and I am experiencing more shortness of breath.”

Despite the risks, Rogers expects skeletal remodelling to take off: that includes rib remodelling, clavicle shortening and pelvic widening. “Versions of it have existed for quite some time,” he says. “Limb lengthening and shortening has been around for a long time. Of course, we change the bony skeleton of the face all the time, but other than that we haven’t changed the torso very much. The changing of the skeleton of the body is a little bit newer, as for a long time people used to just put their hands up and say: ‘Too bad, this is the way you’re built.’”

So why now? “The techniques have got way better. And there’s marketing for it out there.” In the US, he says, medical insurance often covers the procedure for transgender patients, “because they consider it a medical condition to have gender dysphoria. And I think on top of that, it’s just social media. Social media makes everything explode.”

Rogers says the Kardashians have been highly influential. “I think Kim was part of why we wanted a big butt, and then she lost a lot of weight, so everyone wants to be like Kim, right?” In 2022, Kim Kardashian attended the Met Gala after losing a considerable amount of weight, in a sparkling dress once worn by Monroe. Her slender figure coincided with a growing movement towards thinness, a rejection of the body positivity movement of the 2010s, and the advent of the Ozempic era, when the diabetes drug became popular as a weight-loss treatment. A controversial 2022 New York Post article was headlined: “Bye-bye booty: Heroin chic is back”. On TikTok, people had begun measuring their waists using A4 sheets of paper, phones and Apple headphone wires, showing off their Barbie-like proportions.

“We have always done very demanding things for beauty,” says Heather Widdows, a philosophy professor and author of the 2018 book Perfect Me, who mentions foot binding and extreme corsetry. “But they were always about adornment. I think what’s different with the global ideal now is that increasingly things are becoming normalised and naturalised. We’re seeing things that are purely about adornment being recategorised as health and hygiene, and then they become invisible, and if you don’t do them you start to look abnormal,” she says. “It becomes about standard presentation.”

As we move from a text-based culture to a visual culture, increasingly, “who we are is how we look,” she says, “and that is a form of identity that is a massive and dramatic change, but one that’s snuck up on us, that we don’t talk about enough. So the visual is becoming the dominant way of presenting ourselves, being ourselves and thinking about ourselves.”

Elizabeth Rivera trained in high level gyms alongside American football players, baseball players and Ms Bikini Olympia, to try to reach her beauty ideal. This was the X-frame specific to bodybuilders: broad shoulders, prominent glutes and a small waist. For her, she says: “That looks like health. That’s a visible indication of discipline.” Rivera was “busting ass”, trying to reach this aesthetic ideal, but “it was not working for me. And I was making myself very sick from overtraining.”

Rivera is a 35-year-old licensed masseuse and she has lipedema, a chronic condition that causes abnormal fat deposits, which can be painful and are resistant to diet or exercise. “Once I accepted that my inability to lose fat wasn’t my fault, I said: ‘OK, I can accept that.’ But I still would like to have a smaller abdomen. I still would like to have more of an hourglass. So surgery was the next option.” A friend had recently had her ribs remodelled, and Rivera was impressed with the results.

She stands up halfway through our Zoom call to show off her waist. It’s objectively tiny, and the effect is exaggerated by her breast implants and petite Brazilian butt lift (BBL). “I can go most places in Chicago [where she lives], and there’s no one shaped like me. And I’m not saying that in a bad way. I’m saying that because it looks more extreme with the ribs, it’s noticeable.”

In Miami where Cesin lives, she says she doesn’t feel her shape puts her in the minority. There, cosmetic surgery is widely accepted and expected. “The girls in Miami, all of them look the same, because it’s a lot of fillers, a lot of buttocks, a lot of surgery and BBLs,” she says, adding that it’s easy, as a result, to get carried away. But she doesn’t want to end up like that. “People say rib remodelling was a little bit extra, that I didn’t need to do anything, but it makes me happy, so that’s why I did it. But I’m done. No more surgeries.”

‘It’s the gay Titanic!’ Inside La Bola Negra, the maximalist queer spectacular bound for Oscars glory

The Guardian Wed, 28 Oct 2026 05:00:53 GMT

Oozing panache and bagging awards already, La Bola Negra is an eye-popping war and prejudice epic starring Penélope Cruz in a blond wig and Glenn Close speaking Spanish. We meet the ex-lovers who dreamed it up

When Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo – the directing duo known in their native Spain as “Los Javis” – began writing their queer epic La Bola Negra, they weren’t thinking about whether it would be stylish (which it is) or win numerous awards (which it has) or capture what they refer to as “the anti-fascist zeitgeist” (which it does). Instead, they thought only of scale. “I’m done with LGBTQ+ movies being niche,” says Ambrossi. “I was like, ‘Let’s make the biggest, gayest war movie ever.’” Job done.

At Cannes this year, the best director prize was awarded jointly to them and to Paweł Pawlikowski, who made the Thomas Mann road trip film Fatherland. La Bola Negra is now an Oscars frontrunner, with best picture and best director nominations all but guaranteed. Brimming with panache, the movie darts back and forth between three stories set in Spain: in 1932, a young man applying for membership of an exclusive casino is rejected on the grounds of his suspected homosexuality; in 1937, a callow nationalist soldier develops tender feelings for the injured republican prisoner under his watch; and in 2017, a queer historian inherits an unfinished story by Federico García Lorca. That story lends the movie its title and provides the thread that sews its strands together.

Throw in spectacular set pieces, Ken Russell-style visual flair, cameos from a blond-wigged Penélope Cruz and a Spanish-speaking Glenn Close, and the result is a maximalist collage where the Spanish civil war sits side-by-side with Grindr hook-ups. “We loved imagining scenes that you don’t usually have in queer movies,” says Ambrossi, citing the spectacular opening sequence in which a Spanish village is bombed by Italian fascists. “A lot of people have said they’ve been missing something like this. They want to buy popcorn and be given a big movie like Titanic.” His eyes widen. “This is the gay Titanic!”

Relaxing at a corner table in the restaurant of a London hotel, Los Javis represent a study in contrasts. Ambrossi is 42, dinky and loquacious, his impish face crowned with a laurel of curls. He leans forward as he talks, arms folded on the white tablecloth. The taller, taciturn Calvo, 35, is gravely handsome. Battling jet lag, he repeatedly stretches his limbs like a cat, sneaking a glance at himself in the mirror next to the table as he does so. Both men have black caterpillar eyebrows, as well as cheekbones that could double as clothing rails.

On this chilly autumn morning, Los Javis could do with some extra layers. They rub their bare arms furiously until an assistant arrives bearing hoodies. Then again, maybe the three of us have goosebumps not from the cold but from discussing their film. Ambrossi approves of this theory: “There’s a trend on TikTok where people video themselves – ‘This is us before watching La Bola Negra’ – and then it cuts to afterwards when they’re crying and hugging. All this togetherness from the cinematic experience is beautiful.” No wonder Los Javis insisted on an extended theatrical window for their film before selling the US rights to Netflix. La Bola Negra will remain in US cinemas for 47 days, a record for the streaming platform. Even Scorsese didn’t get that.

The movie also marks a personal breakthrough for the pair, who first met when they were actors. “Friends who read the script said to us, ‘Oh, you’re going there?’” recalls Ambrossi. “We’ve been writing together for 13 years about LGBTQ+ characters but it has always been, like, lesbians, trans women …” Previous collaborations include their 2017 debut film, Holy Camp!, which they adapted from La Llamada, their stage musical about a summer camp staffed by nuns. In one scene, God materialises to sing I Will Always Love You. Their 2023 series La Mesías (now streaming on Mubi) is a hypnotically bizarre tale of Christian pop stars, extraterrestrials and bad parenting. But no gay men.

What took them so long? “Sometimes you don’t want to talk about yourself,” offers Calvo, speaking up at last. “Many queer creators have projected themselves into other characters. Pedro Almodóvar, Lorca with The House of Bernarda Alba, Michael Patrick King with Sex and the City.” He flashes a rare smile. “Good show.”

Ambrossi identifies a psychological dimension to the delay: “It’s true you don’t want to be too on-the-nose. But you start wondering if there is also another reason.” In the 1932 strand of the film, the elite casino members use a system of black and white balls to vote on admitting newcomers. The black ball for no– la bola negra – becomes a symbol of queer generational shame and rejection that must be wrestled with. Is it shame, then, that kept Ambrossi from addressing his own sexuality in his work? “In my case, yes. I wasn’t ready to talk about desire or sex because I felt ashamed in some way.”

He and Calvo were already friends with their compatriot and hero Almodóvar, whose company El Deseo, meaning Desire, co-produced La Bola Negra. “I told Pedro, ‘I don’t deal well with desire.’ He looked at me and said, ‘You need to start.’ That’s when it clicked: if you don’t deal explicitly with desire, you are missing life.”

Perhaps that is why the word “explicit” crops up several times in Ambrossi’s conversation today: having been out as a gay man but under the radar in his work, he is eager now to emphasise the ways in which La Bola Negra is defiant or unequivocal. One aspect is the casting of gay actors in gay roles, most notably the Bambi-eyed singer Guitarricadelafuente, who makes his screen debut as the lovestruck soldier.

“It’s not that straight actors can’t play gay,” says Calvo. “There are no rules in art. But …” Ambrossi jumps in: “We like to do it this way. When I was 10, I watched Rupert Everett in My Best Friend’s Wedding. I wasn’t sure I was gay, but I knew he was like me. There was a truth in his eyes that I want to get in my movies.” He sighs. “Rupert Everett was so brave. He should have been James Bond.”

Calvo had an unhappy experience as a young gay actor. “I was a teenager playing a gay role on TV,” he says. “When it finished, I didn’t get many auditions. I was advised to cut my hair, not paint my nails.” A short back and sides didn’t help, though. “I guess people could still tell. So I decided to write roles for actors who don’t have space in the industry.”

Once the pair began dating as well as working together, the two-headed queer celebrity phenomenon of Los Javis was born. They were playwrights, film-makers, actors and reality TV participants, including regular judges on the Spanish version of Ru Paul’s Drag Race. Being an indispensable part of Spanish cultural life came at a price. Calvo points to this now as one of the reasons he and Ambrossi separated during the making of La Bola Negra. “People would talk to me in the plural all the time, ‘It was nice to meet you guys.’ I’d be like, ‘Huh? I’m standing alone here.’ I felt I’d lost my individuality.”

Spain didn’t cope well with the breakup. “It was a big deal,” Calvo admits. “There were cameras outside my door for a month.” Keen to move on, Ambrossi displays a flicker of irritation: “I think we’ve passed through this conversation. Imagine everyone talking about your ex forever! We love to write and direct together and we’re going to keep doing that.” The matter is closed.

After all the diversifying and cross-platforming, Los Javis have reached their Pokémon-style final evolution. “From now on, we want to focus on movies,” says Calvo. No regrets, though. “The other things were important in making a statement,” Ambrossi points out. “I grew up thinking directors should be serious and monolithic. We represented a new way.” Calvo lifts a finger: “A non-binary way,” he says. “We don’t see life as stiff. We mix genres. A more flexible time is coming. Take the work seriously but not yourself.”

Before they go, there is a line in La Bola Negra that I ask them to unpack. When the modern-day researcher Alberto asks the Lorca scholar played by Glenn Close for advice on what he should do with the pages of that incomplete story, she tells him: “You’ve inherited something and you don’t know what to do with it. You are truly a Spaniard.”

Calvo is happy to help. “In Spain, we always have to be reminded by foreigners that we have a rich, interesting culture and history,” he says. Ambrossi elaborates: “It is as if pride is shameful. When someone is doing well and winning awards all over Spain, people are like, ‘Hmm. That’s not very Spanish.’ Unless it’s football.” Where does that attitude come from? “Maybe religion,” muses Calvo. “Maybe dictatorship.”

Does it apply to them? Are they destined to underplay their triumphs for ever? They offer their best you’ve-got-to-be-kidding looks, then answer in unison: “Not us.”

La Bola Negra is in UK cinemas from 6 November.

Weil Gotshal, Once A Legal Powerhouse, Plans to Dissolve

The New York Times October 28, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The prominent law firm has been rocked by an exodus of high profile lawyers, a failed succession plan and a scuttled deal to merge with a rival firm.

By Lauren Hirsch

Weil Gotshal & Manges’s leadership team recommended on Wednesday that the law firm wind down after nearly a century of advising many of America’s largest corporations.

In a statement, Weil said that the recommendation to dissolve followed a “careful review of alternatives” and that the firm’s partners would vote on the matter in the coming days.

Weil’s dissolution would be a stunning collapse of one America’s most prominent white shoe law firms, delivering a painful blow to the firm’s 2,000 employees, including its roughly 1,200 lawyers, who will have to find work elsewhere.

Weil had in recent weeks hired advisers from the law firm Davis Polk & Wardwell to help it with a range of options, which this week turned to discussions about the possibility of winding down the firm.

Once one of the most sought after firms for top lawyers, Weil Gotshal has been rocked by an exodus of partners, including the chair of its global corporate practice. It has also been roiled by a failed succession plan for the firm’s next leader and a scuttled deal to merge with its rival Willkie Farr & Gallagher.

While other options remain on the table, including a possible rescue deal, the situation had become increasingly urgent as more lawyers continued to prepare to leave, according to two people with knowledge of internal discussions.

Weil said it would it continue serving clients during the wind down process, which would take place over the coming months.

Weil’s struggles reflect the broader changes sweeping through Big Law in recent years, in which the largest firms are sucking up talent and business. While firms once functioned as true partnerships centered on loyalty, they are now run more like sprawling businesses, trying to maximize profits by dominating every corner of the legal business from dealmaking and private capital to litigation.

Weil Gotshal was once the marquee for bankruptcy advice but has more recently had difficulty competing with giant law firms that can poach talent with lavish pay packages.

Amid these pressures, Weil has also struggled to determine the firm’s future leadership. Ramona Nee, its co-head of private equity, had been expected to take over as the firm’s leader from Barry Wolf, who is preparing to retire. But in August, Ms. Nee told the firm’s management that she was declining the top role, the two people said. Many partners learned of Ms. Nee’s decision this week.

The uncertainty had been weighing on the law firm’s lawyers, many of whom have been sending out a deluge of résumés over the past few days, according to three people with knowledge of the firm’s internal workings. At law firms, whose primary assets are its employees, downward spirals can happen fast: Once key partners lose confidence and start leaving, it can be near impossible to persuade them and other lawyers to stay.

Rivals had already been circling, scouring for lawyers they can pick up in the frenzy, two people familiar with the matter said.

Similar spirals have befallen major law firms before. At their worst, they have driven them into bankruptcy, as was the case with Dewey & LeBoeuf in 2012.

Weil had been trying to solidify a path forward through merger talks with Willkie, which would have given it combined might to compete against larger peers, the people said. But those talks recently fell through, igniting a series of meetings among the firm’s management committee to find another solution. Those meetings continued into Wednesday.

Spokespeople for Weil and Willkie did not immediately respond to a request for comment. A spokeswoman for Davis Polk confirmed that Weil had hired Neil Barr, its chair who advises on mergers, and Brian Resnick, a partner in its restructuring practice.

The Financial Times earlier reported its hiring of restructuring advisers.

Weil Gotshal was founded in 1931 by Frank L. Weil, Sylvan Gotshal and Horace S. Manges. Three decades later, Harvey Miller helped the firm climb the ranks to the uppermost echelons for firms by focusing on bankruptcy and restructuring, practices that rivals had historically shunned.

The bet proved lucrative as the firm went to on advise on the collapses of Drexel Burnham Lambert, Texaco and the Macy’s department store chain with hard-nosed tactics that earned it the nickname “We’ll Getcha & Mangle Ya.” The firm rode that expertise through the financial crisis, notching more than a billion fees in 2009, advising the likes of Lehman Brothers and General Motors.

But as the country emerged from the depths of the recession, Weil Gotshal’s restructuring prowess alone was no longer enough to keep it competitive. The Chicago law firm Kirkland & Ellis led the way in running a firm like a big business. Kirkland and others that followed in its footsteps, including Latham & Watkins and Simpson Thacher & Bartlett, poached star partners promising big paychecks and the ability to create their own mini kingdoms within their firms.

“They just were sort of treading water,” Bruce MacEwen, a lawyer and consultant to law firms, said of Weil.

Some smaller firms responded to the emergence of these giants by prioritizing niche specialties. But specialization, Mr. MacEwen said, also frequently requires significant layoffs, a path that longtime firm leaders, like Weil’s Mr. Wolf, are not often keen to do.

That left Weil vulnerable to poaching. Among the top partners the firm has lost over the past several years: Ray Schrock, who was a co-chair of its bankruptcy practice; Michael Aiello, the chair of its global corporate practice; and Christopher Machera, a co-head of Weil’s U. S. private equity practice.

Lauren Hirsch is a Times reporter who covers deals and dealmakers in Wall Street and Washington.

Fed Holds Rates Steady Despite ‘Elevated’ Inflation

The New York Times October 28, 2026

Kevin Warsh, the Federal Reserve chairman, gave an upbeat assessment of the economy but stressed that inflation was too high. He said the Fed would hold fewer rate-setting votes starting next year.

Note: Data represents the lower, upper and midpoint of the federal funds target rate range.

Source: Federal Reserve.

Jacqueline Gu/The New York Times

Colby Smith

Colby Smith covers the Federal Reserve.

The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady on Wednesday, despite no recent progress on getting inflation down to the central bank’s 2 percent target.

Officials voted 10-2 to keep rates at the range of 3.75 percent to 4 percent. That range was reached in September after policymakers decided unanimously to raise rates for the first time since 2023.

Lisa D. Cook, a Fed governor who President Trump has tried to fire, issued her first-ever dissent on the Fed’s monetary policy settings in favor of a quarter-point increase on Wednesday. She was joined by Beth M. Hammack, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland, who has dissented repeatedly this year.

In a statement accompanying the rate decision, the Fed conveyed that it had more work to do to quell inflation, which it described as “elevated.”

At a news conference after the decision, Kevin M. Warsh, the Fed chairman, started with an upbeat assessment of the economy, but stressed that inflation was still too high.

He also said the central bank would cut the number of meetings at which it votes on interest rates. Mr. Warsh said the Fed would still meet eight times in 2027, but one of those meetings would focus “exclusively on broad monetary policy strategy” and would not include a vote on interest rates. Starting in 2028, the Fed plans to dedicate two meetings to such broader strategy.

The Fed gathered days before midterm elections that will decide whether Republicans retain control of Congress and how much scope President Trump will have to enact his agenda in the second half of his term. Affordability issues are central for voters after nearly six years in which inflation has overshot the Fed’s target.

“Politics played no role in the decision,” Mr. Warsh said when asked about the midterms.

Mr. Warsh, who took over as chairman of the Fed in May, has made taming inflation the top priority of his four-year term.

Since officials at the Fed met in September, inflation data has been far from reassuring. Price pressures appear to be broadening out after shocks caused by Mr. Trump’s tariffs and the U. S.-Israel war with Iran. Energy prices have shot higher, threatening to spill over into other goods and services.

The economy has continued to grow at a solid pace despite these headwinds, fueled by an investment boom stemming from companies scrambling to expand their artificial intelligence capabilities. Wage gains have failed to keep up with rising prices, however, meaning Americans are earning less for an hour of work.

U. S. government borrowing costs have risen sharply, making not only mortgages and other consumer loans more expensive, but also financing for companies. Certain A. I. companies, which have issued a significant amount of debt to fund their expansion plans, appear particularly exposed.

As a result, financial conditions, which track the availability of credit across the economy, appear slightly less accommodative. To what extent this will help the Fed tame inflation depends in large part on whether these conditions tighten further.

Ms. Hammack’s dissent on Wednesday was widely expected given her views that the Fed’s policy settings are not restraining the economy. Ms. Cook’s dissent was notable in that she is locked in a legal battle with Mr. Trump, who has sought to pressure the Fed into lowering rates. Ms. Cook became a target in the summer of 2025 when the president seized on unproven allegations that she committed mortgage fraud before joining the central bank.

Mr. Trump renewed that effort after the Supreme Court ruled against him on the matter earlier this year. The White House started its own investigation into Ms. Cook and summoned her in for an in-person hearing.

Joe Rennison

The S&P 500 ended the day 0.3 percent higher, after a volatile period of trading while Warsh was speaking. Easier monetary policy, with rates expectations falling, is usually bullish for the stock market.

Ben Casselman

Starting next year, the Federal Reserve will reduce the number of meetings at which it sets interest rates, Kevin M. Warsh, the central bank’s chairman, announced Wednesday.

The Fed’s 12-member policy committee currently holds eight regularly scheduled meetings a year, a cadence it has maintained since the 1980s. Mr. Warsh, who took over as the Fed’s leader in May, raised the idea of reducing the number of meetings at the committee’s closed-door session in July, a discussion first reported by The New York Times and later confirmed in the publicly released minutes of the meeting.

In a news conference on Wednesday, Mr. Warsh said the Fed would meet eight times next year as usual. But only seven of those meetings will include a vote on interest rates. The eighth “will focus exclusively on broad monetary policy strategy,” he said.

In 2028, the Fed expects to hold just six rate-setting meetings, with two meetings dedicated to discussions of longer-run strategy, Mr. Warsh said.

“Getting policy right involves assessing near-term developments at timely, regular and information rich intervals,” Mr. Warsh said, “but it’s equally important we reserve time and space as an intellectually diverse group for strategic deliberations, for thinking anew about big questions, looking out over longer time horizons.”

Some economists have criticized the idea of holding fewer meetings, arguing it could make it harder for the Fed to respond quickly to changes in inflation and the labor market. The move also fits a pattern during the early months of Mr. Warsh’s chairmanship toward providing less information to investors and the public, reversing a decades-long trend toward greater openness.

Other economists, however, have defended the idea. They argue that providing more time between meetings will make it easier for policymakers to identify meaningful shifts in economic conditions. And they note that the Fed can hold emergency meetings if necessary, as it has done numerous times in the past.

Mr. Warsh’s biggest announcement of the day pertained to how often the Fed will vote on interest rates in the coming years, an idea that The New York Times first reported the chairman raised in July. In 2027, the Fed plans to hold seven policy meetings, with one dedicated to discussing “broad monetary policy strategy.” In 2028, there will be six policy meetings and two on strategy.

Mr. Warsh repeatedly mentioned a shift in financial conditions since September, which he suggested helped the Fed in the pursuit of its inflation goal on the margins. Credit conditions have “tightened for some businesses and households, much as we would expect,” he said. “Market participants are becoming somewhat more discerning in their capital allocations, and while overall financial conditions are tighter, I’m unwilling and unable to call them tight. But broadly, these developments go in the direction of achieving a longer, more durable period of economic growth and price stability.”

The Fed’s meeting is days before the midterm elections, but Mr. Warsh emphasized that politics played no role in Wednesday’s decision to hold rates steady. But the political backdrop has been hard to ignore, especially because of Mr. Trump’s repeated attacks on the Fed for not complying with his demands for lower rates. Though consumer prices continued to climb last month, the Fed held interest rates steady on Wednesday, after a quarter-point increase last month. But a December rate increase is possible — and that could make borrowing ahead of the holiday shopping season more expensive.

Credit card rates, which closely track the Fed’s moves, have risen for the past three months to their highest level in nearly a year. The rate on a new credit card offer climbed to an average of 23.96 percent in October, according to LendingTree, which analyzes about 220 of the most popular cards from more than 50 issuers.

“Higher credit card rates just make it that much harder to contend with rising prices,” said Matt Schulz, chief consumer finance analyst at LendingTree, the online loan marketplace.

That makes good debt hygiene even more important: making timely payments, keeping debt levels manageable or paying off balances when possible. “These steps can also improve access to more favorable financing options should interest rates moderate in the future,” said Charlie Wise, head of global research and consulting at TransUnion, one of the big three credit bureaus.

After the Fed’s quarter-point increase in September, its benchmark rate is now in a range of 3.75 to 4 percent. Many consumer products, like credit cards, personal loans and small business loans, are pegged to the prime rate, which tracks the Fed’s actions, and serves as a base line to set rates.

Other rates don’t move in lock step with the Fed’s actions, but are still influenced by them. Rates on 30-year, fixed-rate mortgages, for example, generally track the yield on 10-year Treasury bonds. As of Thursday, 30-year fixed-rate loans averaged 7.32 percent, according to Freddie Mac, down from 7.40 percent last week but up substantially from 6.19 percent a year ago.

Elevated rates have helped savers, however, who have collected more in interest on high-yield savings accounts and money market funds.

The average interest rate for the 100 biggest money market funds tracked by Crane Data now stands at 3.73 percent, up from 3.51 percent at the end of August.

When Kevin M. Warsh, the Federal Reserve chairman, takes the podium for his post-meeting news conference on Wednesday, he is sure to be asked a slew of questions about the thorniest issues facing the U. S. economy.

But there is also an uncomfortable political quandary that he might not be able to avoid: a renewed attempt by President Trump to fire one of Mr. Warsh’s colleagues.

In recent weeks, the White House has redoubled its efforts to oust Lisa D. Cook, a Fed governor, over allegations of mortgage fraud that she has consistently denied. The matter is set to come to a head on Nov. 5, when the administration aims to grill Ms. Cook at an unorthodox, private hearing that her lawyers have said is politically tainted.

Caught in the middle is Mr. Warsh, who has tried to walk a fine line between defending the Fed’s independence, maintaining a good relationship with the president and steering clear of one of the most sensitive issues ever to face his institution. His next steps will carry great weight, given the stakes for the nation’s central bank and its more than century-old mission to set monetary policy free from political influence.

For the moment, Ms. Cook continues to serve on the board, and she issued a surprising dissent on Wednesday voted instead for a quarter-point increase. But her fate otherwise is unclear.

Her lawyers told the White House she could not appear for the November hearing, citing scheduling conflicts and foreign travel. Since then, her lawyers and White House officials have repeatedly declined to say if they were discussing moving the different hearing date or another option entirely.

Nevertheless, the hearing itself is an outgrowth of Mr. Trump’s first attempt to fire Ms. Cook, which she successfully sued to block in a case that reached the Supreme Court. In a June ruling, the justices took no position on the charges against her, but they did say that Mr. Trump should have afforded Ms. Cook a proper chance to respond to them.

Throughout that drama, Mr. Warsh has largely refrained from commenting on the charges against his colleague — or on the president’s general attempts to pressure the Fed into lowering interest rates.

At one point during his confirmation hearing to become chairman, Mr. Warsh was explicitly asked about Ms. Cook’s lawsuit against the president. It had named the Fed board as well as Jerome H. Powell, then the leader of the central bank, as defendants, citing the fact that the Fed could have been required to carry out the firing.

Asked if as chairman he would defend Ms. Cook’s tenure, Mr. Warsh revealed little about his thinking.

“If I stand for anything, it’s the Fed should stay in its lane,” he said, citing the fact that the case at that time had not yet been decided.

He added: “It’s inappropriate for me to weigh in on that, especially because, in the event that I am confirmed, I could be a party to that matter.”

Colby Smith

Colby Smith covers the Federal Reserve.

The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady on Wednesday, despite no recent progress on getting inflation back down to the central bank’s 2 percent target.

Officials voted 10-2 to keep rates at the previous range of 3.75 percent to 4 percent. That level was reached in September after policymakers decided unanimously to raise borrowing costs for the first time since 2023.

Lisa D. Cook, a Fed governor whom President Trump has tried to fire, issued her first-ever dissent on the Fed’s monetary policy settings, voting in favor of a quarter-point increase. She was joined by Beth M. Hammack, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland, who has dissented a number of times this year.

In a statement accompanying the rate decision, the Fed conveyed that it still had more work to do to quell inflation, which it described as “elevated.”

“The accumulation of more information will help the committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the committee’s 2 percent goal,” it said. That message aligned with comments from top policymakers in the lead-up to October’s meeting. Several officials signaled their support for another rate increase later this year, even as they argued that there was no urgency to deliver increases at back-to-back meetings.

The central bank gathered just days before midterm elections that will decide whether Republicans will retain control of Congress and in turn, how much scope President Trump will have to enact his agenda in the second half of his term. Affordability issues are front and center for voters after nearly six years in which inflation has overshot the Fed’s target.

Kevin M. Warsh, who took over as chairman of the central bank in May, told reporters that politics did not factor into the Fed’s decision on Wednesday. Instead, he suggested that the Fed had the flexibility to wait and accumulate more information before its next meeting in December. He pointed to the fact that the public does not appear to be losing confidence in the Fed’s ability to eventually achieve its 2 percent target and that there were not yet signs that the economy was overheating.

“Is the economy running too hot? Is the economy too strong? That isn’t the judgment of most of my colleagues,” said Mr. Warsh.

Mr. Warsh also leaned into the fact that financial conditions, which track the availability of credit across the economy, appear slightly less accommodative than they have in the past.

U. S. government borrowing costs have risen sharply in recent months, making not only mortgages and other consumer loans more expensive, but also financing for companies. Certain artificial intelligence companies, which have issued a significant amount of debt to fund expansion plans, appear particularly exposed, sparking a sell-off in technology stocks as recently as last week.

On Wednesday, the short-dated, two-year Treasury yield fell to 4.72 percent while the 10-year Treasury yield rose before settling around 5.02 percent. The move in the 10-year was driven by a rise in the break-even inflation rate, which is a market measure of investors’ inflation expectations.

Mr. Warsh stopped short of describing financial conditions as “tight,” but he noted that “market participants are becoming somewhat more discerning in their capital allocations.”

Later in the news conference, he said this shift wasn’t something that the Fed was “uncomfortable with.”

“It tells me the policy is working, and I think we can do that and make the economy more durable, have it last longer, and still achieve stable prices,” he said.

The chairman was on the defensive on Wednesday because the incoming inflation data since the central bank’s last meeting has been far from reassuring. Price pressures appear to be broadening out after a series of recent shocks caused first by Mr. Trump’s tariffs and later by the U. S.-Israel war with Iran. Energy prices have shot higher across the board, threatening to spill over into other goods and services.

The economy has continued to grow at a solid pace despite these headwinds, fueled in large part by an investment boom stemming from companies scrambling to expand their A. I. capabilities. Prices for computer chips and other crucial components have risen sharply, contributing to higher inflation. Wage gains have failed to keep up with rising prices, however, meaning Americans are earning less for an hour of work.

Asked specifically about A. I., Mr. Warsh pushed back on the idea that the sector is insensitive to higher rates, citing recent market ructions in that space. Investors were “discriminating between the kinds of investments they want to make,” he noted.

Mr. Warsh also stressed the productivity gains that he expects the proliferation of this technology to continue to fuel. “Economic growth is higher, but that doesn’t tell me that economic growth is somehow causing inflation and making our job harder.” he said.

Ms. Cook’s dissent was notable for two reasons. She is the first governor on the Fed’s board to vote against a policy decision since Mr. Warsh took over as chairman. She is also locked in a legal battle with Mr. Trump, who has long sought to pressure the Fed into lowering rates. Ms. Cook became a target in the summer of 2025 when the president seized on unproven allegations that she committed mortgage fraud before joining the central bank.

Mr. Trump has renewed that effort after the Supreme Court ruled against him on the matter earlier this year. The White House has launched its own investigation into Ms. Cook and summoned her in for an in-person hearing. Mr. Warsh on Wednesday said the Fed would not be involved in those proceedings.

The chairman on Wednesday also announced a major change to how often the Fed will vote on interest rates going forward, an idea that The New York Times first reported the chairman raised with colleagues in July. In 2027, the Fed will hold seven policy meetings where rates will be set, and one dedicated to discussing “broad monetary policy strategy.” In 2028, there will be six policy meetings, and two focused on strategy. For decades, the Fed has met eight times a year to set interest rates.

Sydney Ember

Karla Guity and her family pay just $1,800 a month for a three-bedroom house with a yard in Shoreline, Wash., just north of Seattle. The modest rent meant she did not have to work when her two daughters were young. She loves the neighborhood and the local schools.

She also worries she will never be able to leave.

Although Ms. Guity, 33, and her husband want to own their own home in the area, buying would be too much of a financial stretch as long as mortgage rates remained high. The possibility that a monthly mortgage payment would exceed $6,000 was enough to convince her that her family would stay renters for much longer than she had once thought.

“We’re depending on the graces of the landlord,” she said.

Higher mortgage rates are compelling aspiring homeowners across the country to continue renting, tightening competition for rentals and putting upward pressure on rents for the first time in years. According to private-sector data from real estate sites including Zillow and Apartment List, rents have steadied in recent months after a prolonged softening driven by a glut in new apartment buildings that sprouted up after the pandemic. Government data also show sturdier rent growth.

Note: Data for October 2025 is unavailable because of the government shutdown.

Source: Bureau of Labor Statistics.

By The New York Times

The upswing in rents could pose a challenge for the Federal Reserve in its fight against persistent price increases. Though the Fed held rates steady at its meeting on Wednesday, investors anticipate the central bank will raise borrowing costs once more before year-end, which would keep mortgage rates elevated.

“We’re not in deceleration world anymore, probably not going to get a lot of disinflationary pressures from rents,” said Jonathan Millar, senior U. S. economist at Barclays. “If anything, the risks are that we may be going the other direction.”

The emerging signs of strength in the rental market follow a roller coaster of a period. During the depths of the pandemic, housing demand soared, fueled by a desire for more space, the ability to work from home and swelling savings. Without the supply to match, both home prices and rents skyrocketed in much of the country.

That demand for housing, coupled with rock-bottom interest rates, encouraged residential builders to flood growing cities, especially in the Sun Belt, with new rental properties. The mushrooming housing stock, along with generous incentives to attract renters, decreased landlords’ pricing power and compelled them to slash rents rapidly in many big cities nationwide. Rents in cities including Austin, Texas, and Phoenix plummeted in the years after the pandemic.

Then rising interest rates starting in 2022 made it more expensive to finance large construction projects, which slowed the building frenzy. Tariffs and supply chain troubles have pushed up material costs, and a labor shortage, exacerbated by President Trump’s immigration policy, has also weighed on construction. Higher mortgage rates and lofty home prices are making home buying increasingly inaccessible for a vast number of people. Homeowners who secured ultralow rates during the depths of the pandemic are reluctant to sell, further slowing the housing market.

At the same time, the labor market, which has been characterized by relatively few layoffs and a low unemployment rate, is allowing many workers to continue spending.

The result is that fewer new rental units are becoming available just as more people are clamoring for them. National rents rose 2.7 percent in September, according to the Zillow Observed Rent Index, compared with 2 percent a year earlier.

“Higher mortgage rates put pressure on the rental market not only from renters who are kind of stuck in there creating that demand,” said Molly Boesel, senior principal economist at Cotality, a housing market data provider. “But you also have that making it more difficult for builders to finance new apartments, so you could see a drastic slowdown in supply on the multifamily side.”

Most private rent indexes track new leases, which tend to adjust more quickly to market conditions. The rush of new apartment buildings in recent years, many of which reduced rents to lure tenants, caused rents in a number of cities to drop. Renters who renewed their leases continued to see their rents go up.

Lance Swank, the chief executive of the Sterling Group, a multifamily builder in Mishawaka, Ind., said his company had taken advantage of low interest rates to ramp up construction. When it became clear that a wave of new rental developments was about to inundate the market, his company decided to scale back.

“We became much more selective,” he said.

Mr. Swank, whose company builds and owns rental communities in the Midwest and Southeast, said he had also noticed the effects of rising mortgage rates on certain tenants. While renters in luxury apartments seemed less influenced by higher rates, fewer renters were moving out of his company’s lower-tier housing, he said.

“It’s just a math equation for people,” he said. “It’s what they can afford.”

It is not clear how much momentum the rental market is gaining. Yet the fact that it appears to be on slightly stronger footing at all has defied some economic projections.

Most notably, Stephen Miran, who served briefly as a Fed governor, said in a speech last year that he expected that the Labor Department’s measure of rent inflation would fall below 1.5 percent in 2027, from its level at the time of about 3.5 percent. One reason he cited was stricter immigration policy, which he believed would reduce the demand pressure on rents.

“One might characterize this view on rental inflation as optimistic,” he said in the speech. “However, I believe forecasters have underappreciated the significant impact of immigration policy on rent inflation — both on the way up and, now, on the way down.”

Complicating the picture for the Fed is a lag between moves in rental market data and government data. Typically, the Consumer Price Index, released by the Bureau of Labor Statistics, takes time to catch up to market rents, partly because the government surveys any given rental property only once every six months. That means that if rent goes up the month after a survey, it will take another five months for it to show up in the data.

At the moment, however, rent inflation appears to be moving in step with market rents. One possibility for the alignment is that landlords are eager to raise rents, said Mark Franceski, the chief strategist at Middleburg, a developer of rental housing.

“Whether growth is flattening or accelerating, they seem to be moving in the same direction,” he said. “This is becoming less of a renters’ market and more of a landlords’ market.”

Forecasters broadly believe that the factors pressuring rents upward are not going away in the near term. The slowdown in residential building will limit housing availability. Mortgage rates, which are unlikely to fall substantially any time soon barring a recession, will keep pushing more people into the rental market.

“In theory, higher rates make it more restrictive: You slow growth, that lowers inflation,” said Chris Salviati, the chief economist at Apartment List.

“There is the counterargument that because you’ve got higher rates, you’re going to have less building, and then you’re going to have less supply,” he added. “And that will increase the pressure on shelter rents and make inflation worse.”

Siri Kahn, 32, pays $2,325 a month for a one-bedroom apartment on the North Side of Chicago. Though she and her husband have been saving money for 10 years to buy a home with enough room to start a family, they still can’t afford the down payment on a two-bedroom house in the city, she said. Moving to the suburbs would mean they would have to pay for gas to drive to their jobs instead of using public transportation.

While their most recent rent increase was manageable, they are bracing themselves for their rent to eventually rise above what they can bear.

“It’s only a matter of time until we are forced out of renting,” she said.

Advertisement

Colby Smith

Colby Smith covers the Federal Reserve.

Kevin M. Warsh wants inflation to move more swiftly back to the Federal Reserve’s 2 percent target. But on Wednesday, the central bank chairman and his colleagues are widely expected to hold interest rates steady.

The discrepancy is poised to be a focal point at the latest meeting, which is taking place just days before midterm elections that will decide who controls Congress in the latter half of President Trump’s second term.

Since officials voted unanimously in September to raise rates by a quarter point to 3.75 percent to 4 percent, the incoming inflation data has been anything but reassuring. Energy prices are up across the board as the war with Iran has dragged on. The range of goods and services growing costlier appears to be broadening out. And a splurge in spending tied to the proliferation of artificial intelligence shows little sign of abating.

The Fed’s other priority, the labor market, has also remained stable, despite monthly growth downshifting in September, in a sign that the Fed’s policy settings are not excessively onerous for the economy.

Numerous Fed policymakers have already indicated their support for a rate increase at their final gathering of the year in December in pursuit of a “timelier” return to the 2 percent target after six years of overshooting it. So the question for Mr. Warsh at Wednesday’s news conference is, why wait?

“The economics support another rate increase,” said Loretta Mester, who ran the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland for a decade until 2024. “By not moving in October, I’m a little skeptical whether a timely path is substantially different from just being on a downward path to 2 percent.”

Mr. Warsh had the last word ahead of the upcoming rate decision. Speaking in Bangkok at the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank this month, the chairman did little to change the narrative that had been laid out by a number of his fellow policymakers in the weeks prior. The overarching message was that the central bank had more work to do to tame inflation, but that there was no urgency to raise rates at consecutive meetings.

Among the officials to push for patience was John C. Williams of the New York Fed and Philip N. Jefferson, the vice-chair, both of whom are part of an internal policy-steering committee, known as the troika, that Mr. Warsh leads.

Those comments represented exactly the kind of guidance that Mr. Warsh had long denounced. Onstage in Bangkok. Mr. Warsh went so far as to say that it was a “new chapter at the Fed, and we’re not in that business anymore.”

But for a broad swath of economists and investors, the primary reason that a rate increase was not penciled in for October in the face of hotter-than-expected inflation data was precisely because of the steer that Mr. Warsh’s colleagues provided. What has also helped in the interim is recent jitters in financial markets amid concerns about the sustainability of the A. I. boom. That has made financial conditions, which measure the availability of credit in the economy, only slightly less accommodative than before.

But looking solely at the inflation data, Riccardo Trezzi, a former Fed economist who runs the research firm Underlying Inflation, said a rate increase was clearly justified on Wednesday.

“There is zero evidence of cooling down,” he said of current price pressures. Mr. Trezzi estimates that the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, which strips out volatile food and energy items, will reach 3.4 percent in December. At the same time last year, it stood at 3 percent. Overall inflation, as measured by the Personal Consumption Expenditures price index, is projected to reach 3.8 percent, according to Mr. Trezzi’s calculations, nearly double the 2 percent target. P. C. E. data for September will be out on Thursday, the day after the Fed’s decision.

“There’s a disconnect in terms of how the Fed sounds at the moment,” he said. “They still have to make up their minds whether they’re really serious about disinflating the U. S. economy.”

The issue for the Fed is that the primary sources of resurgent inflation are out of their control. Beyond the Iran war and Mr. Trump’s tariffs, both of which have bid up price pressures, many of the biggest A. I. companies that are fueling growth also appear impervious to higher rates.

Perhaps the biggest propellant of demand right now is the sharp rise in wealth across the country being generated from stock market gains, said Marc Sumerlin of Evenflow Macro, an economic consulting firm.

In the last four quarters, households’ net worth rose roughly $20 trillion, according to Fed data as of September. While most of these gains have accrued to high-income households, the bulk of consumer spending is driven by this group.

Estimates vary about how much the Fed will need to squeeze the economy in the coming months to begin to turn the tide on inflation. Some believe price pressures will begin to ease as the impact of Mr. Trump’s tariffs and the energy shock fade, obviating the need for an aggressive response from the Fed. But for others, a more forceful approach might be required.

“If you want to lower inflation now, you have to lower demand because raising supply takes time,” Mr. Sumerlin said.

The first of two wild cards is how financial conditions evolve in the coming months. U. S. government bond yields are sharply higher today than just a few months ago for a variety of reasons. Some of that reflects changing expectations about how much the Fed will need to raise rates as growth has picked up. There is also intensifying competition between governments and companies for capital as large A. I. companies borrow aggressively to fund their expansions.

Investors also appear to be demanding extra compensation to hold longer-dated debt versus shorter-term ones amid ever-present concerns about Washington’s fiscal profligacy and whipsawing worries about the Fed’s ability to operate independently, said Ellen Zentner, chief economic strategist at Morgan Stanley Wealth Management.

Rising yields on the margins will help the Fed in its pursuit of its inflation goal, but that will not supplant entirely the work the central bank has to do when it comes to raising rates to at least a neutral level that neither speeds up nor slows down the economy, Ms. Zentner said.

The second wild card is how the public perceives the Fed’s grip on inflation. Concerns about price pressures in the year ahead have mounted, but longer-term metrics look more benign.

For now, that has afforded the Fed some flexibility around when it must deliver additional increases, said Raphael Bostic, who served as president of the Atlanta Fed for nine years until February. But, “there are limits,” he warned.

“The danger always is that every additional month that inflation is way higher than your target is another month where people say, ‘maybe this is the new normal,’” Mr. Bostic said.

Ben Casselman

Ben Casselman is the chief economics correspondent.
