Last week provided a final snapshot of the state of the economy before voters head to the polls for next month’s midterm elections.

The flood of government data clarified a familiar picture — and thus a grim one for President Trump and incumbent Republicans.

True, much of the data pointed to strength, or at least stability. Retail sales rose at a healthy pace in September. Filings for unemployment benefits remained low. Industrial output hit a postpandemic high.

But there was no relief on the issue that matters most to many voters, inflation. Consumer prices rose last month at their fastest rate since May, outpacing wage growth for the sixth month in a row. Producer prices, too, came in hot, as did prices for imported goods. And gasoline — the most visible price in the economy, and one that few Americans have any choice about paying — stayed above $4 a gallon nationally, where it has been for most of the past six months.

Little wonder, then, that measures of consumer sentiment have worsened, and that polls show voters are poised to punish Republicans for failing to keep the economic promises they made on the campaign trail two years ago.

The cost of living “is going to be the first issue on the scorecard in 2026,” said John W. Lettieri, president of the Economic Innovation Group, which last week published a survey of voter attitudes on the economy. “The results are not good on that top issue.”

Still, the state of the economy is more nuanced than the dour mood of voters might suggest. Economists point to areas of weakness and others of strength, and say the outlook — for inflation and more broadly — is highly uncertain.

Note: Inflation data is the year-over-year change in the Consumer Price Index. Wages are year-over-year changes in average hourly earnings. October 2025 is missing from the inflation data because of the government shutdown.

Source: Bureau of Labor Statistics.

Ben Casselman/The New York Times

Inflation, as measured by the Consumer Price Index, had fallen to about 3 percent when Mr. Trump returned to office, from a peak of 9 percent in 2022. Most economists expected it to drop further.

Instead, progress stalled in 2025, partly because of Mr. Trump’s tariffs, which drove up prices of many imported goods. Then, just as the tariff effect was beginning to fade, Mr. Trump led the United States into war with Iran, which pushed energy prices and inflation back up. Consumer prices were up 3.7 percent in September from a year earlier.

“Voters had the sense that President Biden’s policies were leading to higher prices, and voters have the sense that President Trump’s policies are leading to higher prices now,” said Michael Strain, an economist at the American Enterprise Institute, a conservative think tank. “In both cases, I think voters made the right judgment.”

Gas prices are just the most visible piece of a broader affordability challenge. Record prices for diesel fuel are threatening to ripple through to food and other goods. The artificial intelligence boom has led to a surge in demand for computer chips and related equipment, which has raised costs for smartphones, tablets and other consumer electronics. And some economists say they believe companies are still waiting to pass along some of the cost of tariffs to customers.

Higher inflation has also forced the Federal Reserve to reverse course and begin raising interest rates again, which is making it more expensive to borrow money as many Americans are relying on debt to make ends meet. Mortgage rates have jumped this year, dashing hopes of a rebound in the housing market and pushing homeownership further out of reach for many families.

Then there is the other side of the affordability equation: income. Wage growth slowed to just 3 percent in September, down from nearly 4 percent a year earlier. The combination of higher prices and weaker earnings growth means that, at least by one measure, the average worker has experienced no wage growth, adjusted for inflation, since the beginning of Mr. Trump’s second term.

Notes: Data is seasonally adjusted. Resignations exclude retirements. The layoff category reached to nearly 9 per 100 workers during the pandemic.

Source: Bureau of Labor Statistics

Ben Casselman/The New York Times

American households, at least in the aggregate, have weathered higher prices better than many economists predicted. That is partly because the job market has held steady — workers may not be getting big raises, but at least most of them have jobs.

The unemployment rate, at 4.2 percent in September, remains low, and has been at or below 4.5 percent for five years — a record. Layoffs, despite fears of job losses from A. I., remain low by historical standards. Nearly 81 percent of adults of prime working age, 25 to 54, were employed in September, close to a 25-year high.

But while the labor market is solid, it is hardly robust. Companies are not cutting jobs, but they are not adding many, either — a “low-hire, low-fire” stasis that makes it hard for anyone who needs a job to find one. The average unemployed worker has been looking for a job for nearly six months.

The slow pace of hiring also makes it harder for people to change jobs, or threaten to, in search of higher pay. The rapid rate of job-switching after the pandemic, sometimes referred to as the “great resignation,” helped many workers keep up with higher prices. The slower pace of turnover now may be part of the reason wage growth has slowed. It is particularly hard on younger workers, who typically change jobs frequently as they seek a foothold on the career ladder.

“You have to scramble pretty hard to find another job that is better than your current job,” said Skanda Amarnath, executive director of Employ America, a research group focused on the labor market. “There’s a level of fragility in that. How am I supposed to feel like I can get ahead if I’m not earning a higher wage increase?”

Notes: Data is presented as a seasonally adjusted annual rate, adjusted for inflation. “Computing equipment” includes computers and peripherals equipment and communication equipment categories.

Source: Bureau of Economic Analysis.

Ben Casselman/The New York Times

Strong retail sales data last week was the latest evidence that Americans are spending despite their dour mood. Consumer spending, adjusted for inflation, grew at a 3.8 percent annual rate in the second quarter, and most forecasters expect strong numbers for the third quarter as well.

Business investment, too, has been robust, with companies pouring money into equipment and software. Corporate profits continue to set records, helping to push the stock market — despite some jitters — to fresh highs.

But much of that strength stems from sectors connected to A. I., and the trillions of dollars in infrastructure needed to enable it.

Seemingly insatiable demand for microchips, data centers and the electricity to power them is responsible for much of the increase in investment. The companies that benefit from that demand, like Nvidia, the chipmaker, are helping to fuel the surge in corporate profits. And the market’s gains are helping to prop up consumer spending, especially among the wealthy households that own most stocks.

That could leave the economy vulnerable if investors lose confidence in the A. I. boom. There are hints that could already be happening. Shares of CoreWeave and other data center operators have tumbled amid questions about whether their enormous spending will ever pay off. In a research note published on Friday, Torsten Slok, the chief economist at Apollo Global Management, warned that a pullback in investor enthusiasm for A. I. could expose “a stagflationary environment in which growth slows even as price pressures persist.”

At the same time, a growing number of economists and technologists, including leaders of the A. I. companies themselves, are warning the technology could lead to widespread job losses. To many workers, that has created the impression that A. I. portends something of a Catch-22 for their well-being: If A. I. achieves its promise, it could put them out of work. If it falls short, the bursting bubble could wipe out their retirement portfolios and cause a recession.

“For two or three years, we have been waiting with bated breath for this A. I. bubble to pop or for this mass displacement to occur,” said Elizabeth Pancotti, vice president at Groundwork Collaborative, a progressive research organization.

That is adding to a more general sense of economic uncertainty that is eroding voters’ confidence. And it has been a long time since most Americans felt stable.

“The thing that people want more than anything, more than economic opportunity or economic growth, they want economic stability,” Ms. Pancotti said.

New York Times economics reporters want to understand how Americans are navigating employment and the rising cost of living. We may want to use your experience in a story, but we would only do so with your permission.

‘A Twisted Tangle of Metal and Wreckage’: Spain Train Crash Kills at Least 68

The New York Times October 28, 2026

Deadly Train Crash in Spain

Advertisement

Supported by

The accident, the second in less than a year on the same busy rail line, was one of the deadliest in the country’s history.

By Jason HorowitzJosé Bautista and Carlos Barragán

Jason Horowitz reported from Madrid, and José Bautista from the scene of the crash in Spain.

Traveling home on a high-speed train from Madrid to Seville in Spain, Fernando Seco was annoyed when congestion caused the train to stop about a half-hour after its 8 a. m. departure Wednesday. Not long after, it restarted, picked up speed and slammed into another train stopped on the tracks.

Mr. Seco, 62, and other panicked passengers climbed out of their carriage at the back of the train and into a field in central Spain. They saw the derailed carriages of the train they had barreled into in an embankment farther ahead. A rail beam, he said, had “pierced right through a carriage from bottom to top, like carving meat.”

He and others rushed to those carriages and found the dead and injured, those “trapped in a twisted tangle of metal and wreckage.”

The scene was eerily quiet because people were either dead or so hurt they couldn’t speak. He said survivors used parts of the destroyed train as makeshift stretchers to extract the injured from the wreckage. That’s when the screaming started. Doctors among the passengers treated people in what became a field hospital among almond groves.

At least 68 people died in the crash. More than 50 others were injured, some critically.

Spain is living through a recurring nightmare. For the second time in less than a year, a high-speed crash between the same two train operators on the same busy line from Madrid to Seville threw the country into official days of mourning, shook its confidence in the security of it once-vaunted rail system and undercut its international image as a modernizing tourist mecca helping to thrust Europe forward.

In January, a collision between two high-speed trains near Adamuz, farther south, left 46 dead in what had been the country’s worst rail disaster since 2013. The crash on Wednesday surpassed that toll and became one of the deadliest train crashes in Spanish history. And coming a month before national elections in an already bitter campaign, it heaped more pressure on a left-wing government that often seems in a state of perpetual crisis.

“It’s not possible for a country like Spain to suffer two high-speed train accidents in one year,” Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez told reporters at the scene of the crash. Even though the two episodes seemed unrelated, they showed that Spanish rail’s security systems needed to be reinforced, he said.

As he joined Spain’s king, international leaders, his election opponent and local officials in expressing condolences to the families of the victims, he said the country would turn its focus to why the crash had occurred.

His government had already given an explanation. Óscar Puente, Spain’s transportation minister, told reporters that the horrific crash appeared to have resulted from an “inexplicable” decision by train traffic control operators in Madrid.

After watching a reconstruction of the crash and listening to relevant audio recordings of communications between the control center and the trains involved, Mr. Puente recounted the unfolding of a national disaster.

About 8:30 a. m., half an hour after the latter train — run by the national operator, Renfe — departed, the aging safety system along that section of the railway went down. Its failure forced the six trains traveling in that area to stop.

Following protocol, Mr. Puente said, a train traffic control center in Madrid took over. It allowed the Renfe train to resume its journey. “Was that the correct decision?” Mr. Puente asked. He clearly did not think it was.

He said one conductor of a train not involved in the crash had even corrected the operator at the control center, saying that the trains were not supposed to resume normal operation and had to proceed at low speeds of about 40 kilometers an hour (about 25 miles an hour) that would allow their drivers to stop within the visible distance ahead. Mr. Puente recounted that the Madrid operator, who was not identified, replied, “Oh, yes.”

According to Mr. Puente, the railway control operator told the Renfe train conductor to resume regular travel “despite there being another train ahead of it.” The minister called the instruction “incorrect.” The Renfe train traveled 15 miles, or about 25 kilometers, before rear-ending the other train, which had remained stopped on the tracks.

Mr. Puente said the stopped train, which was run by the private company Iryo, had apparently received instructions to move on, as well. According to the Spanish newspaper El País, which on Wednesday evening obtained audio of the exchanges between the conductors and the operators in Madrid, the operator authorized the driver of the Iryo train to resume “normal speed.” But seven minutes later the Iryo driver called to report that she could not restart the train. The Madrid operators failed to tell the driver of the Renfe train, which was closing in, that it needed to brake.

At the moment of impact, Antonio de la Corte, 77, was napping in the third carriage in the back of the Renfe train. “Bam!” he said, recalling that he was immediately awakened, lurched forward and banged his knees while his brother, with whom he was traveling, hit his head. A rail shot through the inside of his train car like a skewer, killing people seated to his right, he said.

As he and his brother climbed down to the field, farmhands cut the fences around the embankment so passengers could take shelter in the fields of alfalfa and almond trees. Word of the disaster quickly spread, and Yahadi Mohamed Maulud, 41, a resident in the nearby town of Yébenes, loaded his car with water bottles and rushed to help.

“We found a massacre,” he said, describing torn limbs and one woman, drenched in blood, searching for her brother. He said he was one of the first people on the scene and helped move the injured passengers on makeshift stretchers.

Soon, a long procession of ambulances, police cars and fire trucks arrived under the whir of rescue helicopters flying low overhead. Dozens of Civil Guard officers, many wearing the white protective suits and masks used by forensic investigators, inspected the scene and gathered evidence.

Broken cables and fallen utility poles were scattered around. The derailed carriages looked pulverized, a heap of charred wheels, smoldering metal and crushed luggage. Some workers hovered over still bodies covered in Mylar blankets as firefighters used cranes to lift the wreckage in search of survivors and more dead.

As family members and friends rushed to sports pavilions to which survivors, including Mr. Seco, had been evacuated in Urda, a group of Roman Catholic priests approached the crash site.

“We came to pray for the dead,” said the Rev. Luis Lucendo, 63, a parish priest in the nearby town of Villacañas. “One man told us that his wife had died, and I was able to make the sign of the cross over her,” he said.

Mr. Maulud, who had brought water and other supplies, was also in Urda, watching the scenes of both thankful reconciliation and grief behind his cigarette smoke. He frequently took the train himself for business in Madrid, he noted.

Then he added, “I’m never getting on that train again.”

Jason Horowitz is the Madrid bureau chief for The Times, covering Spain, Portugal and the way people live throughout Europe.

You Can’t Stop A. I. But You Can Bargain With It.

The New York Times October 28, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Video

By Jillian WeinbergerBinyamin Appelbaum and Steph Khoury

Workers are increasingly worried that artificial intelligence will take their jobs. Back in the late 1950s, on the San Francisco docks just down the street from what’s now Anthropic’s headquarters, a longshore labor leader named Harry Bridges faced a similar fear: that a new technology would make jobs disappear. The Opinion video above details the story of how Bridges fought to make technological change work for his longshoremen — and how workers today can use his playbook.

Below is an edited transcript of this video. We recommend watching it in its original form for the full effect. You can do so using the video player above.

Jillian Weinberger: Are you worried about A. I. taking your job? Yeah, us too.

Maybe older workers might be able to retire. And maybe younger workers could pivot. But what about the rest of us? Are we screwed? Well, this guy might just have a solution. His name is Harry Bridges.

He actually worked in San Francisco, down the street from what’s now Anthropic, OpenAI and Perplexity. He’s long dead, but he also lived through a technological revolution. And for him, that piece of technology was — the box.

OK, so this box. It was actually a container. And it revolutionized Harry’s world.

You see, Harry was a longshoreman, those guys who used to move lots of stuff from the ships to the docks. It was the 1950s, and the box threatened his way of life. It was about to put a lot of the longshoremen out of work.

Archival documentary clip: Salt-resistant aluminum alloy containers are automatically loaded and unloaded by a specially designed crane, with minimum use of manpower.

With the box, all the bosses needed was a man in a booth, rather than a gang of longshoremen on every pier. For Harry, the container was the A. I. of the 1950s. He was a union leader.

Archival clip of Harry Bridges: I know that every half penny or penny that they grant to the union workers in increased wages, that’s that much less profit. That brings about a conflict of interest. And that is generally known as the class struggle.

He wanted to protect workers. But Harry realized that he couldn’t stop the technological revolution in front of him. The containers were coming. There was too much money to be made. So Harry wanted a piece of that profit for the workers.

And he did have some leverage. The shipping companies still needed some workers to transition to the box. So Harry negotiated with the bosses. His men agreed — they wouldn’t fight the box. And the companies agreed to keep the current workers on until they retired, even if they didn’t have much work to do.

Most of the union was all for it. But some of the men were upset with Harry. The box would completely change the industry and a way of life on the waterfront. And they were right.

Today’s waterfront looks and feels totally different. But history shows that if the longshoremen had tried to resist, they would have lost. So Harry proactively made a deal. And just maybe, you should be thinking along the same lines.

Harry got what he did, in part, because he represented all of the longshoremen on the West Coast. And he negotiated with all of the shipping companies at once.

Today, that’s nearly impossible. Look around: Most Americans aren’t in unions. But there is a solution. It’s fun. It’s sexy. It’s — sectoral bargaining. OK, it’s an insanely wonky name for a really smart idea.

Here’s what it would look like: Take all the fast-food workers in the country — Wendy’s, Burger King, McDonald’s — it doesn’t really matter who they work for, they all work in a single sector. And their representative negotiates a deal with all the fast-food companies — kind of like our old pal Harry. Think it can’t work? Meet Dennis Dacke.

Labor organizer Dennis Dacke: [Waving] Hello!

Weinberger: He represents service workers in Germany — Lufthansa flight attendants, H&M retail workers, even Hamburg longshoremen. He negotiates sectoral bargains that require employers to use A. I. to help workers do their jobs — not replace them.

If they can’t do that, they need to train workers for other jobs. And any workers they still need to eliminate get a pile of money as they walk out the door. And all of that is possible because the deal binds the whole sector. It sets a minimum standard for everyone. Sounds great, right? But here’s the problem: In the United States, for most workers, sectoral bargaining is illegal. Until that changes, states should follow the example of Massachusetts.

The federal labor law prohibiting sectoral bargaining doesn’t apply to contractors. And in 2024, Massachusetts voted to allow it for ride-share drivers. Those workers now have a better chance to negotiate with companies like Uber and Lyft, and to fight for their share of the profits A. I. will likely bring in. We think Harry would approve.

Archival clip of Bridges: What’s good for the workers, I think, will have a beneficial effect on all other people in the country.

Most people I know are worried about A. I. eventually taking their job. I am, too, so I decided to investigate how previous generations of workers have dealt with technological threats. I was thrilled to learn about Harry Bridges and the longshoremen. The deal Bridges made for his men as containerization came in gives me hope that those of us warily watching the A. I. models improve can do the same today.

The director of Opinion Video is Jonah M. Kessel. The director of audio engineering is Isaac Jones. The deputy director of Opinion Shows is Alison Bruzek. Dolores Huerta, Labor Leader and Force for Civil Rights, Has Died

The New York Times October 28, 2026

Dolores Huerta (1930-2026)

She founded the United Farm Workers with Cesar Chavez. In early 2026, she told The Times that she had been raped by him decades earlier. She was 96.

Dolores Huerta at a women’s march in Utah in 2017. Credit... By Getty Images

Supported by

By Robert D. McFadden

Dolores Huerta, who with Cesar Chavez founded what became the United Farm Workers and led strikes and boycotts in the 1960s and ’70s that unionized many California table-grape growers, changing laws and the lives of thousands of migrant laborers, died on Wednesday at her home in Bakersfield, Calif. She was 96.

The cause of death was cancer, Erik Olvera, a spokesman for her family, said.

Ms. Huerta, who became a kind of Mexican American folk hero, depicted in murals and ballads, was the union’s vice president for nearly four decades and, until Mr. Chavez’s death in 1993, his second-in-command. He was the charismatic — and, it was later revealed, abusive — leader; she, the skilled organizer who coordinated walkouts and boycotts under a black Aztec eagle banner and negotiated pathbreaking contracts with agribusiness.

But there was a long-hidden dark side to her years by Mr. Chavez’s side. She was, by her account, raped by him — an assault she never spoke about publicly until early 2026, when she was interviewed by The New York Times as it was reporting on the extensive evidence that Mr. Chavez had also groomed and molested underage girls as young as 12.

“I saw him, again, as my boss, as my hero, as, you know, somebody that would do the impossible,” Ms. Huerta told The Times. “I never talked about it to anybody, and the reason I didn’t is because I just didn’t want to hurt the movement.”

On picket lines and in civil disobedience protests, Ms. Huerta and Mr. Chavez practiced the nonviolent civil rights strategies of the Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. She was arrested 22 times, roughed up by strikebreakers and once severely beaten by a police officer, suffering broken ribs and a ruptured spleen that left her disabled for months.

The mother of 14 children, Ms. Huerta sometimes changed diapers between organizing meetings and nursed her babies during breaks in negotiations. Her children often lived with friends and supporters, ate donated food and coped with frequent moves. Most grew up to become activists and professionals, including a lawyer, a physician, performing artists, a therapist, business administrators and a chef.

Ms. Huerta also championed immigrants’ and women’s rights and was an ally of progressive Democrats like Gov. Jerry Brown of California, who signed legislation she sought; Senator Robert F. Kennedy, whose murder she witnessed; and President Barack Obama, who awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom, America’s highest civilian honor, in 2012.

Mr. Chavez and Ms. Huerta founded the National Farm Workers Association in 1962 with little but a dream of an organization to help migrant laborers who toiled long hours at backbreaking work for low wages and with no job security, and to challenge abuses, including exposure to toxic pesticides, by powerful California growers.

“People thought we were crazy,” Ms. Huerta told The Salt Lake Tribune years later. “They asked: ‘How are you going to organize farm workers? They are poor, powerless immigrants. They don’t have any money and they can’t vote.’”

How The Times decides who gets an obituary. There is no formula, scoring system or checklist in determining the news value of a life. We investigate, research and ask around before settling on our subjects. If you know of someone who might be a candidate for a Times obituary, please suggest it here.

But by 1965, they had 1,200 members and enough clout to join Filipino workers in a strike against table-grape growers in the Delano area of the San Joaquin Valley, and later in the Coachella Valley of Southern California. It was a bitter fight. The growers brought in strikebreakers, and the local police ignored repeated acts of harassment and violence.

When one grower began selling grapes under another’s label, Ms. Huerta and Mr. Chavez called for a boycott against the offender’s products. The F. B. I. placed both labor leaders under surveillance for suspected Communist ties.

But the strike won the support of some other unions, including the United Auto Workers, and of Senator Kennedy, who attended a rally in Delano on March 10, 1968. “The world must know,” he said, addressing the crowd of 4,000, “that the migrant farmworker, the Mexican American, is coming into his own right.”

The senator then handed Mr. Chavez a piece of bread. Mr. Chavez had been fasting for 25 days, taking only water, and weighed 140 pounds, having lost 35. Accepting the bread, Mr. Chavez broke his fast. It was a crucial moment for both sides in the strike.

The union had recently declared a national boycott of all California table grapes, and Ms. Huerta was already in New York City organizing what became one of America’s most successful produce boycotts, a cause célèbre that, polls showed, drew the support of 17 million households and thousands of food stores.

Table-grape sales plummeted. Several growers caved and signed contracts. In 1970, the Delano growers capitulated en masse. Most of the industry soon followed, granting first-time benefits to workers.

Membership in the renamed United Farm Workers Organizing Committee swelled to a record high of 80,000; as an affiliate of the A. F. L.-C. I. O., it became the United Farm Workers in 1972. Later strikes against lettuce and table-grape growers and the Gallo Winery led to another triumph: passage by California’s Legislature in 1975 of the nation’s first major farm-labor law outside Hawaii.

Signed by Governor Brown, the Agricultural Labor Relations Act guaranteed California farm workers the right to organize unions and required employers to bargain for contracts in good faith. Migrant workers became eligible for medical insurance, employer-paid pensions and other benefits, including mechanisms to challenge abusive working conditions.

In retrospect, it was the high point for the union. Its membership fell sharply in later years as growers signed with the rival Teamsters union, as strikes and boycotts lost their cachet and as the U. F. W. was hit by internal squabbles and, in an increasingly conservative nation, was no longer seen as a social cause, but as a conventional labor union struggling for political and popular support.

Ms. Huerta continued her activism. She spent four months in Washington lobbying lawmakers to pass the Immigration Reform and Control Act of 1986, landmark legislation that granted amnesty to millions of undocumented immigrants.

But at a news conference scheduled to celebrate the victory, Ms. Huerta was nowhere to be seen, having not been told of the event. To her, it was a reflection of the sexism and machismo culture that permeated the union.

“I realized afterward they just wanted to get me out of the way so they could take credit for the work,” she said of her male co-workers in remembering the news conference. “Straight male-chauvinist trick.”

She did not describe the internal atmosphere publicly until she was interviewed by The Times for its 2026 investigation, when she also revealed Mr. Chavez’s abuse. Ms. Huerta said that he raped her inside a vehicle in a secluded California grape field in 1966, when she was 36 and he was 38 or 39. She decided not to report the assault to the police because of their hostility toward the movement, she told The Times, and because she feared that no one in the union would believe her.

She said that two of her children were the products of sexual encounters with Mr. Chavez, including the rape — baby girls who, by her arrangement, were raised by others. She said she had not been aware of his abuse of underage girls.

“Unfortunately, he used some of his great leadership to abuse women and children,” she said.

Reporting by The Times also showed that many other women in the union faced sexual assault and harassment from men they worked with, including senior managers. Interviews with former union associates and an examination of archived records suggested that a number of women complained at the time that Ms. Huerta often failed to support them and rebuffed their complaints of sexism.

Dolores Clara Fernández was born in Dawson, N. M., on April 10, 1930, the second of three children of Juan Fernández and the former Alicia Chávez Hernandez. Her father, a coal miner, became a union leader and a member of the New Mexico Legislature.

After her parents divorced, she and her two brothers were raised by their mother and a grandfather in Stockton, Calif. Her mother worked as a waitress, a cannery worker and a cook before buying and operating a hotel, where she sometimes housed and fed migrant workers at no charge.

“My mother was a strong woman and she didn’t favor my brothers,” Ms. Huerta told Susan Ferriss and Ricardo Sandoval-Palos for “The Fight in the Fields” (1997), a companion book to a PBS documentary of the same name. “There was no idea that men were superior. At home, we all shared equally in the household tasks.”

After graduating from Stockton High School in 1947, she earned a teaching certificate at Stockton College (now San Joaquin Delta College). She taught in an elementary school, but quit in frustration. “I couldn’t stand seeing kids come to class hungry and needing shoes,” she told The San Diego Union-Tribune.

In 1950, she married Ralph Head, a high school classmate. They had two daughters; the marriage ended in divorce. She had five children with her second husband, Ventura Huerta, whose surname she kept after their divorce. She later had four children with Richard Chavez, a brother of Cesar Chavez’s, in a long-term domestic partnership with him.

Her survivors include 13 of her children, 24 grandchildren, 23 great-grandchildren and seven great-great-grandchildren.

Ms. Huerta was in her 20s when she became involved in community organizing, working for the Community Service Organization, a Latino civil rights group in California founded in 1947. She met Mr. Chavez in 1955, at a fund-raising dinner in Oakland, where she was introduced to him by a C. S. O. co-founder, Fred Ross Sr., a veteran grass-roots organizer who had mentored him.

In 1960, she organized the Agricultural Workers Association, two years before she and Mr. Chavez formed the National Farm Workers Association. It was in 1960, Ms. Huerta told The Times in 2026, that Mr. Chavez first made a sexual advance toward her. She described feeling pressured to have sex with him in a hotel room during a working trip in San Juan Capistrano, Calif.

Their encounters and the confrontations she witnessed in the fields were not the only moments of violence that affected Ms. Huerta. She stood with Senator Kennedy in 1968 as he celebrated his victory in the California presidential primary from a stage at the Ambassador Hotel in Los Angeles, then joined his entourage passing through a basement pantry, where he was shot by an assassin.

In 1988, at a demonstration against Vice President George H. W. Bush, then a presidential candidate, outside a San Francisco hotel where he was speaking, Ms. Huerta was seriously injured in an unprovoked attack by a police officer wielding a baton. She won a settlement with the city for $825,000, money that she used to benefit migrant workers. The city also agreed to change crowd-control procedures.

After her recovery, she took a leave from the union and traveled for two years for the Feminist Majority Foundation to promote women candidates for public office. She later became a mentor to many elected officials, including Hilda L. Solis, a four-term congresswoman who was President Obama’s labor secretary from 2009 to 2013 and the first Hispanic woman to serve as a cabinet officer.

Ms. Huerta stepped down as an officer of her union in 1999 after 37 years. In 2002, she became founding president of the Dolores Huerta Foundation, which helps communities organize health, environmental, educational and economic projects.

Her portrait was known to hang in some U. S. embassies. She was showered with awards, including 15 honorary degrees, and at the 2008 Democratic National Convention in Denver, she formally placed Hillary Clinton’s name in nomination for president.

Ms. Huerta is widely believed to have coined the phrase “Sí se puede” (“yes we can”), still a common chant at Democratic campaign rallies and marches, and which Mr. Obama adopted as his presidential campaign slogan. (He acknowledged it was hers in his remarks about her at the Medal of Freedom ceremony.)

Her life was extolled in “Dolores,” a 2017 documentary by Peter Bratt. In 2019, Gov. Gavin Newsom of California proclaimed an annual Dolores Huerta Day to commemorate her “lifelong pursuit of justice.” In a 2020 interview with The Times, she was asked why movements like hers transcended borders.

“I think it’s because of the people who are involved,” she said. “And this is the reason I, at the age of 90, continue to work. When people come together and take collective action, whether it’s in a march, whether it’s in a union election or, most important, come together to vote, this is how we make change.”

Manny Fernandez and Sarah Hurtes contributed reporting.

Robert D. McFadden was a Times reporter for 63 years. In the last decade before his retirement in 2024 he wrote advance obituaries, which are prepared for notable people so they can be published quickly upon their deaths.

Flávio Bolsonaro Lands in Miami After Fleeing Brazil

The New York Times October 28, 2026

Brazil’s Presidential Election

Advertisement

Supported by

Mr. Bolsonaro, who lost Sunday’s presidential election, fled Brazil for the United States via Argentina after the police canceled his passport in relation to an investigation.

By Ana IonovaEdward WongAlice Maciel and Lucía Cholakian Herrera

Ana Ionova and Alice Maciel reported from Brasília, Brazil, Edward Wong from Washington, and Lucia Cholakian Herrera from Buenos Aires.

Flávio Bolsonaro, the presidential candidate defeated in Brazil’s elections, landed in Miami on Wednesday, according to a U. S. official, fleeing his country after Brazilian authorities asked him to surrender his passports as part of a money-laundering investigation.

Mr. Bolsonaro arrived in the United States after apparently vanishing for a whirlwind 24 hours during which it was largely unclear where he was and how, or if, he would reach the United States.

The State Department plans to issue visas allowing him and his family to enter the country, a senior department official said on Tuesday. The official spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive diplomatic matters.

Just after 9:30 a. m., Mr. Bolsonaro could be seen leaving a plane at a private airport outside Miami along with his family, according to news media video footage. The group was ushered into an S. U. V. shortly after exiting the airport, hidden under umbrellas.

The U. S. government’s assistance to Mr. Bolsonaro could escalate tensions between the Trump administration and President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva of Brazil, who has accused President Trump of interfering in his country’s internal affairs.

What you should know about anonymous sources. The Times makes a careful decision any time it shields the identity of a source. The information the source supplies must be newsworthy, credible and give readers genuine insight.

Mr. Bolsonaro, a right-wing senator and the son of a former president serving a lengthy sentence for attempting a coup, lost Sunday’s presidential vote to Mr. Lula. After initially contesting the result, he conceded but claimed Mr. Lula had won through unfair tactics.

Mr. Trump has also criticized the election, saying it appeared to have been “rigged.”

Following his loss, Mr. Bolsonaro seized on a change in the voting hours on Sunday to demand the election be annulled because of foul play. But the change affected only 0.03 percent of the vote and Brazil’s electoral authorities said it did not make any difference to the result, which saw Mr. Lula win by a margin of 4.4 million votes over Mr. Bolsonaro.

Mr. Bolsonaro eventually dropped those complaints, but still insisted Mr. Lula had unfairly used government funds to win, citing the leftist president’s move to raise a welfare stipend in the last stretch of the campaign. (Mr. Lula’s government claimed the increase was an overdue inflation adjustment.)

Mr. Bolsonaro crossed from Brazil to Argentina by land on Tuesday night with his wife and two daughters, Argentina’s National Directorate of Migration said Wednesday. It said that he then boarded a private fight to Guayaquil, Ecuador. He then took another flight to the United States.

Earlier on Tuesday, Brazilian authorities had canceled Mr. Bolsonaro’s passports because he is being investigated over his links to a Brazilian lawyer accused of laundering more than $1 billion through a scheme involving online gambling.

Separately, Mr. Bolsonaro is also the subject of a police inquiry over millions of dollars he raised from a disgraced banker at the center of a huge corruption scheme to finance a biopic of his father, Jair Bolsonaro. The elder Mr. Bolsonaro was convicted of attempting a coup after losing the presidential election in 2022 to Mr. Lula and is serving his prison sentence under house detention.

Besides canceling his passports, Brazilian authorities also issued an alert to immigration authorities barring Mr. Bolsonaro’s exit from the country. It was not immediately clear how he was able to cross the border into Argentina.

The Brazilian federal police said it had no official record of Mr. Bolsonaro exiting the country. The agency also said, in a statement, that the restrictions on Mr. Bolsonaro’s travel and documents did not necessarily make him a fugitive or allow for his arrest. The police are now “investigating the circumstances surrounding the senator’s failure to comply with court orders.’’

Argentina’s federal police also said they had not registered his entry.

Still, the nation’s immigration authorities said in a statement overnight that Mr. Bolsonaro, his wife and two daughters entered the country at 22:50 p. m. on Tuesday. They made the journey in a van, crossing what is known as the “Friendship Bridge,” connecting Foz do Iguaçu in southern Brazil to Puerto Iguazú in Argentina.

The group crossed the border “with valid travel documentation and without any legal impediment to entering the country,” the Argentine immigration agency said in a statement. Beside his Brazilian documents, Mr. Bolsonaro also holds Italian citizenship and the authorities had also asked him to turn over his Italian passport.

Some 40 minutes later, Mr. Bolsonaro and his entourage embarked on a plane owned by Baires Fly, a private company that has transported Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, in the past. Once in Ecuador, they took another plane early on Wednesday morning that was headed to Miami.

Public U. S. government records suggest that Mr. Bolsonaro entered the United States with a canceled Brazilian diplomatic passport.

At home, Mr. Bolsonaro’s abrupt and mysterious departure left many of his political allies perplexed. Ahead of his escape to the United States, his party had urged him to concede and harness the vast support he had drawn in Sunday’s election to lead the right-wing opposition in Brazil.

Reporting was contributed by David C. Adams Emma Bubola Lucía Cholakian Herrera Thayz Guimarães and Karla Adam.

Ana Ionova is a correspondent for The Times, covering Brazil and neighboring countries.

Edward Wong reports on global affairs, U. S. foreign policy and the State Department for The Times.

Apple Unveils Its First Touch-Screen Laptop Computer

The New York Times October 28, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Steve Jobs and Tim Cook both dismissed the idea, but Apple’s new chief executive is reimagining some of the company’s most important products.

By Kalley Huang and Brian X. Chen

Kalley Huang reported from Los Angeles and Brian X. Chen from San Francisco.

Apple on Wednesday unveiled a touch-screen laptop, a product that past company leaders once bluntly dismissed.

At an event in Los Angeles, John Ternus, Apple’s newly minted chief executive, introduced a version of the MacBook Pro that users will be able to control by touching its screen with their fingers, similar to an iPhone.

The new Mac is the latest step into a new era for the consumer electronics giant. After years of sticking to its knitting, Apple is starting to reimagine some of its key products, from the iPhone to laptop computers.

The touch-screen laptop is the third new product for the company since Mr. Ternus succeeded Tim Cook in September. Last month, the company unveiled its first foldable smartphone, the iPhone Duo. And earlier this month, it introduced a new tablet for the home, called the HomeView.

Mr. Ternus, who first helped design screens for Macs and later led hardware engineering at Apple, is leaning into his 25-year history at the company while demonstrating that he is willing to rethink decisions made by his predecessors.

In 2010, a year before his death, Steve Jobs dismissed the idea of a touch-screen laptop, calling it “ergonomically terrible.” Two years later, Mr. Cook, Mr. Jobs’s successor, doubled down when investors asked whether the MacBook and iPad would someday merge into one product. He compared the idea to combining a toaster with a refrigerator.

But on Wednesday, Mr. Ternus presented a touch-screen as the natural next step for the Mac.

“As we like to do around here, we asked ourselves: How do we make the MacBook Pro even better?” Mr. Ternus said. “This display provides so much more than touch.”

The new Mac will start at $2,899 and be available on Nov. 6. Apple also upgraded its chips and microphones and added a brighter and more vivid screen to the laptop. It is thinner and lighter than its predecessor.

In demonstrations on Wednesday, Apple showed off how its touch-screen laptop could be used for work like graphic design and music production. It also emphasized the performance of the laptop at researching and running artificial intelligence.

Apple has made an about-face on products before. In 2010, Mr. Jobs mocked competitors who were making miniature tablets and said they should be sold with sandpaper so people could file their fingers down to use them. But two years later, Mr. Cook introduced the iPad mini, a product that he said he personally believed in.

Apple was not the first to create any of its new products. The biggest makers of personal computers — Lenovo, HP and Dell — each sell their own touch-screen laptops. But touch-screen laptops have yet to become mainstream. In the first half of this year, touch-screen laptops accounted for 16 percent of all laptop shipments, according to IDC, which tracks consumer electronics markets.

Still, with the new MacBook Pro, Apple is betting that it can win the market with a more polished device and a supply chain that can quickly deliver millions of products.

Like nearly all consumer electronics companies, Apple is raising prices because the components it uses are becoming more expensive, thanks in part to the A. I. boom that is causing demand for memory chips to skyrocket. Apple raised the prices of its Macs in June, with the base model of the MacBook Pro increasing $300 to $1,999.

A splashy new feature can be an incentive for consumers to overlook higher price tags, said Jitesh Ubrani, a director of consumer devices research at IDC. He added that the touch-screen laptop might appeal to people in creative businesses who spend more time editing photos and videos.

“One way to justify that price increase is to give more features,” Mr. Ubrani said. “You could add to that and make it seem like a better value.”

But for Apple, which once said its process for designing products had “1,000 noes for every yes,” churning out many new types of products creates new risks.

The company now sells six types of Macs, six types of iPhones and four types of iPads, each with minor distinctions and with many options on features like screen size, storage capacity and the type of glass for a screen. That can confuse consumers.

Michael Gartenberg, a consumer technology analyst who worked in product marketing at Apple from 2013 to 2016, said Apple’s current product strategy reminded him of the 1990s, when Apple was run by John Sculley and nearing bankruptcy. At the time, the company offered a wide range of computers. When Mr. Jobs became chief executive again, he killed most of the products to focus on just a few.

Today, Apple is one of the most profitable companies in the world, with a market capitalization of $5 trillion. But the new strategy, Mr. Gartenberg said, is still “such a nontraditional Apple way of doing things.”

“It sort of feels like it’s a thousand yeses for every no,” Mr. Gartenberg said. “Whatever we’ve got cooking in the lab, just put them out there.”

Kalley Huang is a Times reporter in San Francisco, covering Apple and the technology industry.

Brian X. Chen is the lead consumer technology writer for The Times. He reviews products and writes Tech Fix, a column about the social implications of the tech we use.

Veterans’ complaints about the rules of engagement have reached Pete Hegseth and a generation of new recruits.

Shawn Ryan (right), once a member of the U. S. Navy SEALs and now a podcast host, interviewing Christian Craighead (left), a former British soldier who has appeared numerous times on Ryan’s show, in Franklin, Tenn., in September. Credit... Victor J. Blue for The New York Times

Supported by

By Wesley Morgan

Wesley Morgan interviewed more than a dozen U. S. Special Operations veterans over three months and traveled to Kalispell, Montana.

In July, nearly an hour into recording the 458th episode of his podcast, “Cleared Hot,” Andy Stumpf asked his guest, Matt Bissonnette, why he got out of the military.

Bissonnette, like many of Stumpf’s guests — and like Stumpf himself — is a former member of the U. S. Navy SEALs. In 2011, Bissonnette damaged his back when the helicopter he was in crash-landed during the mission to kill Osama bin Laden in Pakistan, and he left the service the following year, opting out of SEAL Team 6’s punishing pace of annual deployments. Even before the back injury, though, Bissonnette had been thinking about leaving, he said. On each deployment to Iraq and Afghanistan, new restrictions were being imposed on his unit — to his mind, putting him and his teammates in greater danger — and he had had enough of it.

“I saw the rules of engagement changing in Afghanistan,” Bissonnette explained. In the early years, he said, Team 6 had been left alone to do what it did best: sneaking into militants’ hide-outs undetected and killing whoever made any move to resist. But during President Barack Obama’s surge in Afghanistan, there was a shift to a “hearts and minds” counterinsurgency; senior officers began to emphasize capturing over killing, insisting that targeted commanders be given every chance to surrender.

“Why are you sending a very-high-end top-tier unit to go basically surround the mud hut and have an interpreter on a bullhorn say, ‘Hey, come out!’” Bissonnette complained. “Why are we putting ourselves in additional risk?”

Stumpf calls his podcast “Cleared Hot” after military lingo for authorizing pilots to open fire, and he tries to make his guests feel as if they’re cleared to talk about subjects they normally wouldn’t with a journalist. His is one of more than a dozen podcasts hosted by former “operators,” as modern commandos refer to themselves, who are retelling the story of America’s post-9/11 wars for a generation of men and boys too young to have fought in them. What written memoirs were to the post-Vietnam generation, these shows have become to the post-Afghanistan generation, holding sway over audiences who tune in religiously and who aspire to join the Special Operations forces themselves. The largest podcast in this space, “The Shawn Ryan Show,” sometimes comes in second only to “The Joe Rogan Experience” on the Spotify charts.

On these shows, the conversation might be about anything — CrossFit, mental health, testosterone — but a collective narrative about the fight against terrorism surfaces again and again. Some hosts and many guests argue that the United States was defeated in Afghanistan because our presidents and generals, more concerned with politics and optics than the realities of the battlefield, imposed crippling restrictions on Special Operations. Freed from constraints, they say, the lethal raiding machine that Team 6 was a part of — with its exquisite training, cutting-edge technology and overwhelming firepower — might have simply killed its way to victory.

That argument has become influential in the Trump administration, affecting how Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has directed the military to operate in the Caribbean, Yemen and Iran. Hegseth, who stays plugged in with the most popular shows and was an occasional guest before taking charge of the Pentagon, has brought it out of the podcast world and into the national discourse. “We wonder why the war never ends and why it perpetuates itself,” Hegseth said on “Shawn Ryan” in 2024. “Because we’ve written rules that are impossible, that are written for us to lose. They’re written for our guys to be in handcuffs.”

Stumpf, a youthful-looking 49-year-old with salt-and-pepper hair and a cheerful interviewing style, is at pains not to endorse that message. He hopes to convey to listeners that the wars were futile and wore down the souls of those who fought them, but he did not push back when Bissonnette criticized the restrictions. Minutes later, Bissonnette made clear that he thought the war in Afghanistan had lost focus long before the surge, when the Bush administration decided to keep fighting against the homegrown Taliban after largely driving Al Qaeda out of Afghanistan. Neither man felt the two conflicts had accomplished much they could be proud of. “I wonder often about the long-term impact of the things that we broke, and the history books, and how they will judge us,” Stumpf said.

I had traveled to Kalispell, Mont., outside Glacier National Park, to sit in on Stumpf’s episode with Bissonnette. I’d been a guest on “Cleared Hot” five years earlier, when Stumpf invited me on to discuss a book I wrote about the war in Afghanistan. Since then, his operation had become more polished: He’d hired a producer, and his recording studio was furnished with military-themed décor, like replicas of M4 rifles and the emblem of SEAL Team 6’s Gold Squadron, the unit he fought with until 2005, when he took a bullet to the hip.

Stumpf had recently learned to fly helicopters, and he was planning to give Bissonnette a lift to the airport in Missoula, saving him a two-hour drive. Buckling into the little four-seat aircraft and taking off into the mountains, the three of us discussed the memories of Iraq and Afghanistan that helicopter flights evoked. Two decades ago in Baghdad, as a passenger, Stumpf relished such flights; he loved to sit in the open door of the Black Hawk ferrying him and other operators out on their night raids, his foot resting on the aircraft’s front wheel.

On the way back to Kalispell, over the cockpit intercom, I asked Stumpf which of the two narratives about Afghanistan he heard most often from his guests and other Special Ops veterans: that the war had been an exercise in futility, or that it might have been won if the United States had taken the gloves off.

“Unfortunately, the second,” he answered.

How veterans tell their stories about past wars has an inevitable influence on how their successors fight future ones. Many Special Ops veterans who enlisted in the decade before the Sept. 11 attacks were motivated to do so by Vietnam memoirs they read as adolescents — not the meditative antiwar ones by draftees and literary-minded officers but the exciting ones by that generation’s commandos. More than a dozen SEAL Vietnam memoirs were published in the 1990s. As a child in Alaska, Bissonnette tore through “Men in Green Faces,” a former SEAL’s fictionalized account of hunting Viet Cong in the Mekong Delta. “The world has changed and it’s a different medium, but the stories are the same,” Bissonnette told me. “It’s access into a world you’ve heard about, read about, dreamed about.”

Stumpf was one of the pioneers of operator podcasting, starting “Cleared Hot” in 2017, four years after he left the Navy. He had been working for the chief executive of CrossFit and leaning into professional skydiving. He set a world record — gliding more than 18 miles in a flying-squirrel-like wingsuit — that landed him the first of several appearances on “Joe Rogan,” the emerging titan of the form. Podcastland seemed like “a weird world,” Stumpf remembered, but Rogan encouraged him to start his own show. Stumpf had all kinds of guests — a NASCAR driver, extreme athletes, a former Scientologist turned activist against the cult — but war content proved the most popular.

Since then, operator podcasts have proliferated: “Combat Story” in 2020, “Frog Man Friday” in 2021, “Green Beret Chronicles” in 2022, “Tier-1” and “Lesser Known Operators” in 2025. Some, like “The Team House,” stick to stories of war and deployments, avoiding culture-war content, but many wander naturally into political and men’s lifestyle topics. “I’ve never seen you more lean,” Mike Glover, a retired Green Beret who served in Delta Force, told Stumpf near the beginning of his appearance on “Cleared Hot” in July, and asked what peptides he was using. (Sometimes a cocktail marketed as Wolverine, Stumpf answered, paired with kettlebell workouts and testosterone.)

Podcasts allow a parasocial dynamic that old war memoirs didn’t: For those who want personal advice from their heroes, the DM button on Instagram is right there. “Fanboys are a thing,” said Brent Tucker, a Delta Force veteran in Florida who hosts the “Tier-1” podcast. “I’ve met a few who I think know more about my career than I do.” Fans of the podcasts discuss different elite units and former operators as though they were their favorite sports teams and players. They pick apart what they see and hear in minute detail, cross-referencing missions described in different episodes and cataloging rifles, body armor, insignia and camouflage patterns. “What we got from the audience was, ‘Hey, man, it feels like I’m in the team room with you guys,’” said Glover, who originally focused on war stories on his show, “Mike Force,” before switching to wilderness survival and disaster preparedness content.

Much of this is frustrating to veterans from conventional military units — infantrymen, tankers, logisticians — who made up the majority of the United States’ troop presence and took the majority of casualties during the war’s first decade or so, up through the surge in Afghanistan. Special Ops stories tend to be about capturing or killing bad guys, not the slower, more patient work the infantry did patrolling neighborhoods day after day, trying to gain locals’ trust and locate I. E. D. s and ambushes. It’s the SWAT team’s story compared with the beat cop’s, and the operator podcasts can seem to erase the less glamorous side of the war altogether.

One 21-year-old fan, who asked to be identified by only his first name, Owen, told me that he stumbled onto the operator podcasts as a high schooler and that they turned his life around: He started to run and lift weights and took up mixed martial arts. “I’d be on the bus staring into the window listening to hours of podcasts, telling my friends information they didn’t care about Iraq,” he remembered. “I’d never felt so motivated about something.” Joining an elite unit like the SEALs or Rangers “felt like all I wanted to do.”

When Owen learned after graduating from high school that his vision was too poor to qualify for an elite unit even if corrected with laser surgery, he dropped the idea of enlisting altogether. “With the Special Operations guys on podcasts telling their side of GWOT,” he said, using the common Pentagon acronym for the global war on terrorism, “you would think there’s no conventional troops. I think I was a casualty of that. I definitely didn’t want to go into the conventional military.”

Even many Special Ops veterans disapprove of the podcast scene, maintaining that at least until everything is formally declassified in the coming decades, and maybe even after, “quiet professionals,” as special operators term themselves, should keep their war stories within the fraternity. Some Team 6 and Delta Force veterans who have gone on podcasts say others from their old units have pressured them to take down their episodes and declared them persona non grata, no longer welcome at official reunions and ceremonies. The ship has sailed, though: More than 70 Team 6 and Delta Force veterans of the post-9/11 era have talked about their service on podcasts. Stumpf sees no shame in that: The idea of all the secrecy is to protect current operations and tactics, not hide history. The phrase is not “silent professional,” he says.

Former commanders who oversaw operators like Stumpf, Bissonnette and Glover tended to react with exasperation when I asked them about the podcasts. Rich Clarke, who as a colonel commanded a task force of SEALs and Rangers in Afghanistan, told me that, as a Ranger commander, he’d insisted that new Ranger officers read books on Iraq and Afghanistan by journalists and academics. But in his final military job, as the general in charge of all Special Operations forces, he found that when he asked junior and midlevel officers what they were reading, he would often get blank stares; he got better results asking what podcasts they were tuning in to. He tells young listeners to “take them with a grain of salt,” he told me. “But senior guys like me who dismiss these podcasts do so at our own peril.”

By far the most popular of the operator podcasts is “The Shawn Ryan Show,” some episodes of which have cleared seven million views on YouTube alone. Ryan, whose real name is Sean Ryan Palmisano, was in the SEALs for four years (not long enough to try out for Team 6) and did two tours in Iraq and Afghanistan before joining the C. I. A. as a security contractor. After discussing his attempted suicide on another SEAL podcast, Ryan started his own in 2019. His aim was to give Special Ops veterans a venue to tell stories about the wars and their psychological toll. “All of our best friends are dead, most of them from suicide,” he told me.

His recording studio, on a sprawling compound outside Nashville, features deep purple backdrops, black leather armchairs and, although he no longer drinks, a wall of more than a hundred liquor bottles — everything from whiskeys and tequilas to Hpnotiq, the turquoise liqueur famous from hip-hop music videos.

Compared with the animated, jovial Stumpf, Ryan, a 44-year-old with broad features and a shaved head, is a minimally expressive interviewer. He often asks combat veterans who go on his show what it felt like the first time they killed someone. He does not generally press guests on whether the stories they tell are true, and his meteoric rise seems, in part, to stem from his willingness to dive into partisan politics and conspiracy theories: He’s into U. F. O. s and numerology and has claimed that the military mandated the coronavirus vaccine as part of a “woke agenda” to drive combat veterans out of the ranks. He publicly supported Donald Trump during the 2024 campaign.

Ryan now has around 20 employees, according to his chief of staff. He does brand collaborations with tactical gear and security companies, as well as with purveyors of wellness and workout supplements: Laird Superfood’s Shawn Ryan Bundle includes prebiotic greens and “performance mushrooms.” During some recent episodes, Ryan has given guests high-end assault rifles — gifts, he said, from the gun manufacturer Sig Sauer. In 2022, Ryan talked about his experience traveling to Tijuana, Mexico, for treatment with ibogaine, a psychedelic derived from the root of an African shrub, helping the drug go mainstream among veterans struggling with PTSD, brain injuries and alcoholism. “We shot that to the moon,” Ryan said. In April, Trump issued an executive order fast-tracking psychedelics like ibogaine for clinical trials.

He does the same thing for fellow veterans’ brands. When a former SEAL turned craft ice cream maker, Chris Fettes, went on the show last year, Fettes talked about his own brush with suicide after shooting two Afghan boys he thought were combatants and about how ibogaine helped him. But Ryan also coached him to say that he was looking for distribution for his ice cream. Less than a year later, Fettes is in talks with supermarket chains. Fettes’s flavors, with names like Cookie Commandough, “will be right next to Ben and Jerry’s,” Ryan said proudly.

Just before the 2024 presidential election, Hegseth went on “Shawn Ryan” and walked Ryan through what he called one of his proudest accomplishments. In 2018 and 2019, Hegseth used his platform at Fox News to defend a series of veterans who had been either accused or convicted of war crimes, including Mathew Golsteyn, a Green Beret whose team killed a captive suspected of being a Taliban bomb maker and covered up the death, and Eddie Gallagher, a SEAL member whose prosecution for allegedly killing a wounded ISIS prisoner and shooting at civilians the Navy had flubbed, resulting in acquittals on the major charges but a conviction on a lesser one.

Trump, Hegseth explained to Ryan, would reach out after watching Hegseth’s segments about the cases. “He’d call me and be like, you know, ‘They did some nasty, they did some tough things, these are rough guys,’” Hegseth said, mimicking the president’s voice. Because of Hegseth’s advocacy, Trump gave all of them presidential pardons or other forms of clemency. (Gallagher had been an early guest on Ryan’s show in 2020, and the host has made clear that he thinks the men were railroaded.)

“Rules of engagement are a huge problem,” Hegseth went on, invoking a popular rationalization for defeat in guerrilla wars that was also widespread after Vietnam. “Why have we spent the last 20 years fighting enemies that don’t abide by the rules at all? And these are rules written by, like, dudes in cloak rooms in Europe after World War I, because they thought that they could fight polite wars.”

Speaking to Tucker Carlson recently, Ryan claimed some credit for Trump picking Hegseth for defense secretary less than a week after the episode aired. At the Army-Navy football game the next month, Ryan recalled, he was in the V. I. P. box with the president- and vice president-elect when Hegseth mouthed, “Thank you,” pointing to him. “It inflated my ego,” Ryan told Carlson. “I’m like, Holy [expletive], this show has power.”

At the Pentagon, Hegseth has doubled down on the same rhetoric. Last fall, shortly after launching an air campaign of contested legality against suspected drug-smuggling boats in the Caribbean, Hegseth promised an assembly of hundreds of generals and admirals that he was working to “untie the hands of our war fighters.” In March, as he launched the bombing of Iran, he announced that this war would feature “no stupid rules of engagement.”

U. S. military rules of engagement are grounded in the internationally recognized laws of war, for which Hegseth has also expressed scorn; when he started referring to the Pentagon as the “Department of War,” he called for “maximum lethality, not tepid legality.” Asked whether Hegseth considers the military bound by those laws, Sean Parnell, a Pentagon spokesman, said in a statement that the department “follows U. S. law in everything it does,” but in the next sentence, he reiterated the claim that “previous administrations handcuffed our warriors with bureaucratic caution and fear of overzealous lawyers.”

Soldiers, of course, don’t always abide by the laws of war, but for obvious reasons, violations tend to occur in secret and be kept secret. As the Afghanistan and Iraq wars recede further into history, though, Stumpf has found his guests more willing to speak openly about acts that once were only whispered about.

Last January, SEAL Team 6’s highest-profile veteran, Robert J. O’Neill, flew to Montana to go on “Cleared Hot” and address a years-old dispute that had escalated in the podcast world in recent months: Was he really, as he has long claimed, the one who killed Osama bin Laden, or was he stealing the credit from an unnamed teammate?

Two dozen members of Team 6’s Red Squadron had been on the Bin Laden raid, but only a handful entered the room where the fatal shots were fired. There is no public, official military account of the shooting, but O’Neill and Bissonnette described different versions in dueling memoirs: O’Neill’s 2017 book had him as the killer, while Bissonnette’s, in 2012, credited the point man — the first SEAL member up the stairs — who remains anonymous. Two years ago, Brent Tucker, the Delta Force veteran who hosts “Tier-1,” resurfaced the old controversy from the memoirs for the podcast generation; O’Neill is now suing Tucker for defamation.

As Stumpf probed his guest’s account of the raid, O’Neill claimed that the anonymous point man had taken the first shot at Bin Laden but missed; to spare him embarrassment, O’Neill said, he and the point man agreed, upon landing back in Afghanistan, to leave that detail out of the immediate postmission “debrief” to senior officers, which would form the basis for all subsequent internal military accounts of the mission.

Stumpf paused and let out a curse and a short sigh. “What this means is, in the official debrief, the truth wasn’t told,” he finally said. Lies of omission were still lies, he pointed out, and during his time in Gold Squadron, the idea of debriefs had been that you told the whole truth and nothing but the truth, so everyone could learn from any mistakes. “At the JSOC level, don’t you think we should be better than that?” Stumpf asked, referring to the Joint Special Operations Command, the parent organization of Team 6, Delta and the Rangers.

“I also don’t think we should have [expletive] tattletales at the JSOC level, which we do,” O’Neill shot back.

O’Neill then made a further admission: He and some of his teammates had routinely lied by omission in their reports about raids in Iraq and Afghanistan, agreeing on a “clean” version of what happened to recount to their commanders.

What else was O’Neill saying that he and other SEALs had been dishonest about, Stumpf asked. Well, O’Neill said, when they’d shot a bazooka-like recoilless rifle at a mosque, for example, “we kind of left that out of the debrief.”

Stumpf asked O’Neill about what operators derisively call the “catch and release” system. Many insurgents understood that U. S. policy set a relatively high evidentiary bar for placing them in long-term military detention; if it wasn’t met after two or three weeks, they either had to be released or handed over to Afghan and Iraqi judicial systems, whose officials were subject to intimidation and bribery. Had O’Neill seen militants released only for SEALs to have to risk their lives going after them again?

Animated, O’Neill said that he had. “I’ve had Al Qaeda just tell me that in English: ‘They’re going to send me to Abu Ghraib. I’ll be out in 30 days.’ That’s why you change a [expletive] debrief,” O’Neill said. “I’ll tell you that much, I don’t think he made it to Abu Ghraib.”

Stumpf paused. What O’Neill seemed to have described — the killing of a prisoner who had already surrendered — would constitute a war crime. He understood the temptation to cover certain things up, he said, but he didn’t condone it: “Rob, I’m going to tell you, man — I don’t know if there’s ever a good argument to change the debrief.”

“Guess what?” O’Neill said. “You don’t want to see how justice is served, but it is.”

Stumpf moved on with the interview, but he wasn’t blind to the significance of what O’Neill had said. “I was wondering whether or not he remembered this was going to go on the internet,” Stumpf told me later.

When I interviewed O’Neill recently, with his lawyer present, he seemed to have forgotten what he’d said in Stumpf’s studio in January. “That sounds pretty bad,” he acknowledged when I read his words back to him. But, O’Neill said, it never actually happened: “I love my children too much to murder somebody and go to jail.” He did vaguely remember a conversation with an English-speaking member of Al Qaeda, he told me, but he had never executed a prisoner, had never seen a teammate do so and wasn’t sure why he said that to Stumpf, other than that he might have been “trying to sound tough” to a fellow SEAL member. He later said firing the recoilless rifle at the mosque had been authorized.

The temptation to kill surrendering enemies is a persistent feature of war. By the time of the surge, that temptation had become acute for some Special Ops personnel in Afghanistan. Veterans of JSOC raids had described such killings to me, typically citing catch-and-release as the motive, but always on condition of anonymity; the British and Australian governments are currently investigating suspected prisoner executions by members of their own elite units, which worked closely with JSOC.

Stumpf told me he never witnessed or heard contemporaneously about such an illegal killing, perhaps because he’d left Team 6 for other SEAL units with different missions early in the war, before deep frustrations took hold. But based on private conversations with veterans of the units since starting his podcast, he told me, he believes that minorities within both Team 6 and Delta had taken to executing prisoners.

“We can sit here and pretend that these units didn’t figure out their own solution to the catch-and-release problem,” Stumpf said, but they did. And with a defense secretary at the Pentagon who both hero-worships Special Operations and is openly scornful of rules of engagement and the laws of war, the odds that anyone from the units will be retroactively investigated or prosecuted over it seem minuscule. O’Neill is far from the only Team 6 or Delta veteran to have complained about catch-and-release and the rules of engagement on podcasts, sometimes describing ways they broke, bent or bypassed various restrictions.

Some Special Ops veterans who felt handcuffed in Afghanistan have praised the Trump administration’s bellicosity, expressing hope that unrestrained bombing will quickly achieve the kind of victory in Iran they couldn’t in Afghanistan. Others have condemned the Iran operation, with one Team 6 veteran recently calling it “unjust” on Ryan’s show. Ryan himself has come out hard against it: “Everybody knows they’re fighting for Israel,” he told Tucker Carlson in July. “We’re not defending our country.”

Stumpf falls in the same camp. The idea that another level of violence could have brought the Taliban to its knees, or will force Iran to surrender, is a powerful one among his peers, he acknowledged. “Powerful doesn’t mean true, though,” he told me in July in his recording studio. “What’s to be gained by a secretary of defense — or secretary of war, whatever — saying something like that? I don’t know the upside to that.” Setting aside legality, it seemed clear to Stumpf, now watching from afar like everyone else, that Hegseth’s new wars — Iran, the Caribbean and Pacific boat strikes — weren’t going much better than Iraq and Afghanistan had.

That morning, Stumpf had invited his guest for the day, Mike Glover, the fellow podcaster who served in Delta, to host a talk at a coffee shop he co-owns in Kalispell. The shop is an outpost of Black Rifle Coffee Company, a war-and-hunting-themed chain that a friend of Stumpf’s founded over a decade ago as a conservative-coded alternative to Starbucks.

Inside, among the stacks of coffee grounds in camouflage-print bags with names like “Silencer Smooth” and “Gunship,” teenagers were chatting over frozen drinks. On the patio, Glover lectured about survival and self-defense in your S. U. V. or pickup: what medical gear to keep in the trunk, where to keep your pistol for easiest access and so on. Both men had advertised the “mission-essential gear meet-and-greet” on social media, with the promise of free giveaways of gear and a copy of Stumpf’s new book, “Drownproof,” a motivational volume blurbed by Rogan.

About two dozen people showed up, many of them listeners of one or both men’s podcasts. A young infantryman on vacation in Kalispell, who wouldn’t give his full name because he isn’t authorized to speak to the media, told me that the podcasts are popular in his unit, where many soldiers, including himself, aspire to join the Green Berets or the Rangers. “Everyone pretty much tries to go and tune in to ‘The Shawn Ryan Show,’ that’s the big one,” he said.

But several attendees told me it wasn’t the war stories they listened for. Shawn Holmes, a longtime listener who works in the oil industry in Canada, had come wearing a “Cleared Hot” T-shirt; he drove down to Kalispell anytime Stumpf held an event, he said, and what resonated with him was “the never-quit mentality, the never giving up no matter what,” which Stumpf and other operator podcasters embodied to him. Holmes had “Team Never Quit” — the name of another SEAL podcast — tattooed on his forearm, and said he’d drawn inspiration from the shows to motivate his team in the oil fields.

Stumpf says he’s humbled by the DMs — and sometimes handwritten letters — that he gets from fans saying that his show has helped them. “The positive side,” he said, “is that people without somebody to ask in their life, or positive role models in their life, can find them.” But he wondered aloud what effect the podcasts’ drama and rehashing of old battles would have on young men listening and their conceptions of the military. A small group of middle-aged men who had highly unusual military careers, including himself, “have a vast influence over very young, impressionable minds that will be considering military service in the future,” he acknowledged during his conversation with Glover.

As with other parts of the manosphere, there are persistent allegations of domestic drama and dysfunction that fans can treat like ugly soap operas in the comments. Pair all that with support for Hegseth’s “handcuffed” narrative of why America lost in Afghanistan, and it’s easy to question whether the operator podcasts are setting good examples for boys and young men.

Stumpf doesn’t worry about that, he told me. He hopes that young viewers of “Cleared Hot” will come away understanding that their operator heroes wrestle with alcoholism and drug habits, failed marriages and suicidal ideation. The point, he said, is to “hear people who they may deify take the suit of armor off and talk about the realities, not just of the job but of the cost of the job as well.”

Toward the end of the Vietnam War, the filmmaker François Truffaut observed that, despite the intentions of antiwar directors, “every film about war ends up being pro-war.” Young soldiers, and would-be soldiers, that is, inevitably experience war movies — whether 1970’s “Patton” or 2001’s “Black Hawk Down” — less as warnings than as advertisements. Might the same be true of podcasts like his? I asked Stumpf. That no matter how much their makers emphasize suicide and war’s dark aftermath, it’s the stories of riding in the open doors of helicopters to raid insurgent hide-outs that stick with young listeners.

“Some people aren’t going to get the message, and that’s OK — I don’t think there’s any way to stop that,” Stumpf answered. “Maybe the move is just to tell the truth about your experiences, and then you have to hand it off to the viewer or reader or listener in the hopes that it’s received the way you want it to be.”

Wesley Morgan is the author of “The Hardest Place: The American Military Adrift in Afghanistan’s Pech Valley.” He last wrote for the magazine about the C. I. A.’s Afghan paramilitary forces.
