Don’t Cry for the Cheesecake Factory. It’s Weathered Worse.

The New York Times October 28, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

Long before its baroque décor and class identity became midterm talking points, this durable restaurant chain survived some withering critiques.

By Kim Severson

First, the man responsible for the way the Cheesecake Factory looks wants you to know he isn’t mad. And his feelings aren’t hurt.

Rick McCormack is the designer behind the eclectic décor of murals, towering columns and oversize amber light fixtures that gives each Cheesecake Factory the vibe of a postmodern suburban Versailles.

When he first learned that former President Barack Obama had told a political rally on Saturday that President Trump’s golden glow-up of the Oval Office looked “like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory,” he was surprised. And when the White House responded by denouncing Mr. Obama as an elitist — setting off an internet dumpster fire about class optics in America — Mr. McCormack just shook his head.

“I’m not emotionally attached to the Cheesecake Factory design, but don’t we have bigger issues in the country?” he said in an interview on Tuesday.

Then he thought about the bigger picture. Yes, like Cracker Barrel and Starbucks before it, the Cheesecake Factory has found itself an unwitting player in the culture wars. And yes, he said, the whole thing seems silly.

But on the positive side, the midterm dust-up has focused the attention of an entire nation — at least those following politics — on his true love, restaurant design.

“No design is universally loved,” said Mr. McCormack, 69. “I realize that. That is one thing I like about design. That makes the world of design go around.”

The Cheesecake Factory — which began in 1978 in an epicenter of elitism, Beverly Hills, Calif. — is a fortress, accustomed to absorbing attacks perhaps not as clever but equally forceful.

A writer for Vice once called it “the culinary embodiment of the Kardashians.” The Centers for Science in the Public Interest has assailed its portion sizes, calling its food “heart attacks disguised as dinner.”

The chain’s look, dreamed up by its founder and chief executive, David Overton, and refined over 16 years by Mr. McCormack, has long had its own band of critics.

“If you want a fully immersive ‘postmodern design hellscape’- themed dining experience, I highly recommend dinner at The Cheesecake Factory,” the game developer and commentator Max Krieger wrote in a 2017 rant on Twitter. “The interior is a world of aesthetic chaos that feels like a mix between a Fry’s Electronics, an overgrown Panera, and a laser tag arena.”

Whatever. It worked. The Cheesecake Factory has defined the term “upscale casual dining,” and has done such a good job reading the psyche and the appetite of the American diner that it reported on Tuesday that its revenue had risen to $1.03 billion, from $907.2 million a year earlier.

Sales from locations that had been open at least a year were up more than 15 percent over last year. (A competitor, Texas Roadhouse, reported 6 percent growth.) The Cheesecake Factory expects to add 26 new restaurants to its roster of 218 this year.

Mr. Overton grew up in Detroit, where his mother, Evelyn, sold cheesecakes to restaurants that she baked in the family’s basement, using a recipe she had clipped from a newspaper.

He moved to San Francisco, dropped out of law school and started playing drums for a rock band whose leader wrote the Jimi Hendrix hit “Hey, Joe.” In the early 1970s, he persuaded his parents and sister to move west and open a cheesecake bakery in North Hollywood called the Cheesecake Factory.

It wasn’t making much money, so Mr. Overton decided to turn it into a restaurant. In 1978, he opened a small spot a block from Rodeo Drive in Beverly Hills’ Golden Triangle.

He was such a novice that he served hash browns because he didn’t know how to make French fries. As business grew, he studied the menus at upscale restaurants like Wolfgang Puck’s Spago, trying veal dishes and figuring out how to make them with less-expensive chicken. He doubled down on portion sizes and sauces.

The menu kept growing into the 250-item behemoth it is today. (Ellen DeGeneres once called it “the only menu visible from space.”) Mr. Overton said it appealed to “palate of the common man.” “I’m not a gourmet,” he told the “Today” show. “I don’t like a lot of things, but what I like millions of people like, thank goodness.”

Mr. McCormack came along in 1992, and stayed until he opened his own design firm in 2008. He embraced Mr. Overton’s design sensibility, which drew on Victorian-era San Francisco and quirky ideas like the tall columns topped with palm fronds that he had seen at bathhouses. And, of course, each restaurant featured a glass case near the front filled with cheesecake.

“We were going for a little bit of an exotic or European feel,” Mr. McCormack recalled. Hand-painted plaster walls, limestone floors and booths in dark wood made it feel fancy.

“You’d see families coming in celebrating life’s milestones in a nice environment without having to spend every penny,” he said.

In the song “Childs Play,” the singer Drake calls it “a place for families that drive Camrys and go to Disney.”

This week, Mr. Trump and his allies hailed the Cheesecake Factory as America’s great middle-class restaurant and proof of how out-of-touch Mr. Obama is with the mainstream.

Democrats responded that Mr. Trump was the elitist, pointing out that the Cheesecake Factory isn’t exactly a bargain. Spaghetti and meatballs go for $25.95, and a burger close to $20. A slice of cheesecake is $10.95.

At a Cheesecake Factory in Atlanta on Tuesday night, many of the staff hadn’t heard about Mr. Obama’s remarks. But they laughed when they did.

One waiter, who asked not to be identified, pointed out that Cheesecake Factory stock was performing better than some of the market giants. (Indeed, the restaurant’s share price has risen 100 percent this year, compared with 15 percent for Amazon’s, and 18 percent for Apple’s.)

Over the years, the maximalist design that marked the early restaurants has been toned down, a casualty of economics and scale. But the Atlanta restaurant still has the high ceilings, giant murals and that amber glow.

“It does kind of look like Trump Tower in here,” the waiter said.

My teenager, like millions of others, is obsessed with The Cheesecake Factory. It is, in many ways, a ridiculous place, with a giant menu and huge slices of brownie-stuffed cheesecake and more calories in one entree than some people should eat in an entire day. But it’s also a lot of fun. Are you a Cheesecake Factory lover or a hater?

An earlier version of this article misstated the growth of the Cheesecake Factory’s share price this year. It has increased 100 percent, not 122 percent.

Kim Severson is an Atlanta-based reporter who covers the nation’s food culture and contributes to NYT Cooking.

McMahon Spends $43,000 for New Furniture as She Looks to Close Her Department

The New York Times October 28, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

The education secretary says her old furniture “cannot be configurationally or aesthetically integrated” into new office space.

By Michael C. Bender

Reporting from Washington

Linda McMahon, the education secretary, plans to spend $43,000 on new furniture for her government office, a work space makeover that comes as she lobbies Congress to shut down her department.

Ms. McMahon’s team has informed Congress that her current furniture is worn out and “cannot be configurationally or aesthetically integrated into the agency’s new office space,” according to Education Department records reviewed by The New York Times that have not been publicly disclosed.

A senior official at the Education Department said the costs included a new desk, conference table, chairs and other items. Ms. McMahon’s communications department did not respond to a request for a detailed breakdown of the $43,278.64 in expenses.

The education secretary, a former professional wrestling executive, announced in March that she was moving the department out of the seven-story, concrete-and-glass building in southwest Washington where federal education employees have worked since construction was completed in 1961.

The department’s new headquarters will occupy a smaller space, one block south, in a privately owned building that was once home to the now-shuttered U. S. Agency for International Development, which the Trump administration closed last year.

Ms. McMahon has said that the move would save about $5 million in annual operating costs following “unprecedented progress in reducing the federal education footprint,” a reference to her work toward President Trump’s campaign promise to close the Education Department.

After this article was published, Senator Patty Murray of Washington, the top Democrat on the Appropriations Committee, and Senator Tammy Baldwin of Wisconsin, the top Democrat on the Senate’s education appropriations subcommittee, sent a letter to Ms. McMahon urging her to “reconsider this wasteful purchase.”

“The American people are sick of the corruption, sick of the waste and sick of the hypocrisy coming out of all corners of this administration,” Ms. Murray and Ms. Baldwin wrote.

Federal law requires the executive branch to operate the department. The Republican-controlled Congress has not approved legislation to close it, and the Senate’s education committee has advanced legislation to block the administration from transferring major Education Department offices to other agencies.

Still, Ms. McMahon has supervised a systematic dismantling of her department during her nearly 20 months as education secretary, firing hundreds of workers and dispatching the department’s most significant functions to the Labor Department, Justice Department and other parts of the executive branch. Her decision to move special education services to the Health and Human Services Department has drawn sharp rebukes from advocates for disabled students.

The Education Department employs about 2,300 workers, according to federal work force data, down from about 4,100 at the start of Mr. Trump’s second term. In March, Ms. McMahon said 70 percent of the department’s existing headquarters was vacant.

In its new location, the department will occupy 80 percent less space than it did in its previous building, which has about 386,600 square feet of usable space, according to the General Services Administration, which manages federal property.

In response to questions about Ms. McMahon’s office purchases, Savannah Newhouse, the Education Department’s press secretary, said the agency was “saving taxpayers millions of dollars.”

“Believe it or not, just like in the private sector, new federal offices need places to sit, write and meet,” Ms. Newhouse said of the new furniture.

Rachel Gittleman, the president of the American Federation of Government Employees Local 252, which represents more than 2,000 current and former Education Department workers, said Ms. McMahon’s furniture purchase was “incredibly wasteful.”

“It’s not only insulting to the civil servants trying to administer the Department of Education’s programs through two years of chaos but also to the students and parents depending on the department and to the taxpayers funding it,” Ms. Gittleman said.

During President Trump’s first term, several cabinet officials faced ethics and spending questions involving office furniture and costly renovations.

In 2017, Ben Carson, the housing secretary, planned to spend $31,500 on a custom mahogany dining room set for his office as his agency cut programs to support the homeless, elderly and poor. Mr. Carson ultimately canceled the purchase.

In 2018, Scott Pruitt resigned from the top job at the Environmental Protection Agency after facing heavy criticism over spending, including $43,000 on a secure, soundproof phone booth in his office.

The Government Accountability Office, a congressional watchdog agency, said the purchase broke the law because the E. P. A. hadn’t notified Congress of cumulative office expenditures exceeding $5,000. Congress has long included the cap on office redecorating to limit spending on executive office upgrades.

Ms. McMahon’s department notified Congress of her redecorating plans in September, according to the records The Times reviewed.

On her first day as education secretary, Ms. McMahon informed staff that their “final mission” was to help shutter the agency. But during Mr. Trump’s first term, the administration spent millions on renovating the education building to consolidate workers under one roof.

That remodeling cost nearly $50 million, which the administration justified at the time with a similar goal of saving money in the long run.

The first $36.7 million was budgeted to consolidate work spaces into a more modern open-concept floor plan and upgrade to the electrical and HVAC systems in 2019, according to G. S. A. records. The government funded another $12.5 million in 2020 to expand the open-concept plans to additional floors in the building.

The federal government now needs to spend about $13 million renovating the department’s new space, according to two people familiar with the planning.

After Ms. McMahon moves into her new office, plans call for the Energy Department to take over the “Lyndon Baines Johnson Department of Education Building,” as it was officially named under legislation unanimously approved by Congress and signed by President George W. Bush in 2007.

But first, the Energy Department will need to make its own renovations to the education building, which was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2017.

The House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee has estimated that remodeling will cost $215 million.

Michael C. Bender is a Times correspondent in Washington.

What to Know About Brazil’s Election and Flávio Bolsonaro’s Departure

The New York Times October 28, 2026

Brazil’s Presidential Election

Advertisement

Supported by

President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s re-election ended a string of victories by right-wing candidates in Latin America. His opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, fled Brazil for the United States.

By Ana IonovaAdam B. Ellick and Yan Zhuang

President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva was re-elected as Brazil’s leader on Sunday, after a dramatic reversal from the country’s first round of voting secured a victory that defied a right-wing wave that has swept through Latin America.

His opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, fled the country in the aftermath of the vote and landed in Miami on Wednesday with his family. The State Department plans to issue them visas, a senior department official said on Tuesday.

Mr. Lula received 51.8 percent of the vote, compared with 48.2 percent for Mr. Bolsonaro. His win ended a string of seven consecutive presidential election wins by right-wing candidates in the region, delivering a setback to a movement encouraged by President Trump.

Mr. Bolsonaro’s political party raised questions about the results of the election, even after indicating that it would accept them. Mr. Bolsonaro refused to acknowledge defeat before leaving Brazil.

Mr. Bolsonaro fled on Tuesday, a day after the Brazilian police ordered him to hand over his passports because he was being investigated in a money-laundering case.

Mr. Bolsonaro has denied doing business with a lawyer accused of laundering more than $1 billion and called the investigation political persecution. He had previously said he had “never considered” leaving Brazil and that he would turn over his documents.

Here’s what to know:

Within days of Mr. Lula’s election victory, his opponent was no longer in Brazil. Mr. Bolsonaro crossed into Argentina by land on Tuesday night with his wife and two daughters, according to Argentine officials. He left soon after on a private flight to Guayaquil, Ecuador, the National Directorate of Migration of Argentina said Wednesday. He then took another flight to the United States.

Mr. Bolsonaro arrived in Miami on Wednesday morning, with news media cameras capturing his arrival at the Opa-locka airport. The State Department plans to issue visas allowing him and his family to enter the country, said a senior department official who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive diplomatic matters.

Mr. Lula became the first presidential candidate since 1989 to win after finishing second in the opening round. In just three weeks, he added more than 10 million votes, gaining ground across the country.

He also accomplished what no candidate had done since Brazil restored direct presidential elections in 1989: winning after finishing second in the opening round this month. In each of the nine preceding elections, the first-round leader won the presidency, either outright or in a runoff.

Mr. Lula tried and failed to overcome such a deficit in 1989. After finishing second to Fernando Collor de Mello, he rallied support from defeated rivals and surged in the polls. He ultimately lost in the runoff, 53 percent to 47 percent.

His victory on Sunday added another reversal to an extraordinary political career. Mr. Lula, 81, helped found the Workers’ Party under military rule and lost three presidential elections before winning in 2002. Jailed and barred from running in 2018, he returned to defeat Jair Bolsonaro in 2022 after his corruption convictions were annulled the previous year. He has now won an unprecedented fourth term.

Mr. Lula framed his candidacy as a way to defend democracy, protect Brazil’s sovereignty and prevent the Bolsonaro family’s return to power. Flávio Bolsonaro, 45, promised to restore his father’s conservative agenda while casting himself as a more moderate successor.

The result also halted a regional advance by the right. Although Mr. Trump did not openly champion either candidate in Brazil, as he had in two other elections in Latin America, his administration tried in subtle ways to bolster Mr. Bolsonaro’s campaign. Mr. Trump told reporters on Monday that “it looked like another rigged election,” without offering evidence to substantiate the claim.

Mr. Lula, who has repeatedly defied Mr. Trump, said the surge of rallies in the past week “was a demonstration that this country refuses to be anyone’s backyard.” It was an apparent reference to the United States, which has been trying to exert new levels of control over Latin America through measures such as tariffs, sanctions and election intervention.

Mr. Lula’s margin of victory, 3.6 percentage points, was wider than it was four years ago. Few pollsters had predicted his comeback.

At a news conference, Mr. Bolsonaro refused to recognize the result and said he would seek to have the election annulled. He described a court’s decision to extend voting hours as a “dirty trick,” adding, “What happened today was not normal, and it was even unacceptable.”

Both candidates had requested the additional time. Mr. Bolsonaro said that flooding in a part of the country where he had strong support would unfairly hurt him, while Mr. Lula accused public officials of deliberately slowing public transportation in areas where he had won in the first round of voting.

A judge decided minutes before polls closed to extend hours at all polling stations. But by the time of the announcement, some polling centers had already closed and their voting machines had shut down, preventing them from reopening.

To seek to have the election annulled, Mr. Bolsonaro’s party will need to petition the authorities for a review of the results. Since Brazil’s return to democracy, no presidential election has been annulled.

In the 2014 election, the losing party requested an audit, but the review found no evidence of fraud and the results were upheld. In 2022, the Liberal Party similarly challenged Jair Bolsonaro’s election loss but failed to provide evidence to support its accusations and was fined by a court.

Flávio Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party has two possible paths to challenge the result, said Raquel Machado, a professor at the Federal University of Ceará. It could seek a technical audit to determine whether unequal voting conditions affected the outcome, potentially leading to an annulment of the election. Or it could pursue an abuse-of-power case through the Superior Electoral Court’s inspector general, which could disqualify Mr. Lula and his running mate, Geraldo Alckmin, even after they take office.

But Professor Machado noted that many polling stations had closed by the time the Supreme Court’s order was made public and that there had been no significant influx of voters after 5 p. m. local time.

Mr. Lula’s Workers’ Party could bring its own challenge over restrictions on public bus services on Election Day.

The results were a surprise to investors, who saw Mr. Bolsonaro as the more market-friendly of the two candidates. After Mr. Lula’s win, Brazil’s benchmark stock index fell more than 10 percent as trading began on Monday. The currency, the real, was down more than 8 percent against the dollar, on course for its sharpest single-day weakening against the dollar since 1999.

Adeel Hassan and Silvia Ribeiro contributed reporting.

Ana Ionova is a correspondent for The Times, covering Brazil and neighboring countries.

Adam B. Ellick is The Times’s Brazil bureau chief, based in São Paulo.

Yan Zhuang is a Times reporter in Seoul who covers breaking news.

Kennedy to Allow Broad Use of Unapproved Peptide Injections

The New York Times October 28, 2026

U. S. Health Policy

Advertisement

Supported by

In a unilateral declaration by the health secretary, several injections promoted by online influencers will become widely available. The F. D. A. had advised against the move.

By Christina Jewett

Reporting from Washington

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said on Wednesday that he would allow widespread patient access to unapproved peptide injections made popular by internet influencers, sparking serious concern among drug safety experts.

The plan would bypass the most standard Food and Drug Administration safeguards for approving drugs, such as tests to see if the compounds work better than a placebo and whether they might cause cancer or birth defects. To do so, Mr. Kennedy announced “enforcement discretion,” meaning he will tacitly allow companies to produce the unproven injections without going through the usual review process.

Mr. Kennedy, who has said publicly that he has benefited from using peptides, propelled the matter forward, declaring on podcasts early this year that the F. D. A. would lift restrictions to widespread use.

But in a highly unusual turn of events, the document released Wednesday suggested that his action was unilateral and couched the decision as Mr. Kennedy’s alone. F. D. A. scientists previously advised against widespread use of the peptides, and none were present in at least one meeting Tuesday finalizing the policy.

“The secretary has determined that the policy advances patient choice and freedom while appropriately protecting patient safety,” the document posted on the H. H. S. website said.

Emily Hilliard, a spokeswoman for the Department of Health and Human Services, said the new policy requires “patient-specific prescriptions, traceable ingredients, quality testing and safety reporting to hold compounders accountable and give patients an alternative to unregulated sellers.”

She said the policy was aimed at “confronting the risks of black-market peptides,” adding: “The policy does not grant F. D. A. approval or establish clinical safety and effectiveness.”

Peptides are short chains of amino acids that give the body basic instructions. F. D. A.-approved peptide compounds include insulin to manage diabetes and GLP-1 drugs, a diabetes treatment that is widely used for weight loss.

But there are many other peptide compounds without scientific evidence of efficacy or safety. The six peptides that Mr. Kennedy said on Wednesday he would now allow to be used include epitalon, marketed for longevity, and BPC-157, marketed as the “wolverine” peptide and purported to help with muscle repair. Unlike the GLP-1 drugs, no major pharmaceutical company has performed the costly and regulated studies on those drugs that are required for approval.

Allowing widespread use of the unapproved peptides is consistent with the “medical freedom” movement espoused by Mr. Kennedy’s supporters, which tends to eschew widely studied vaccines and embrace the right to use treatments with little evidence of effectiveness.

The new policy comes with some criteria that are meant to add public protections, such as requiring that peptides be made at an FDA-registered facility, although the step basically only requires a manufacturer to notify the agency of its address. The policy also calls for adverse event reporting to the F. D. A. and product labels that list the active ingredient, strength and a unique identifier for the manufacturing facility.

The compounding pharmacies that will blend the drugs are not household names, but many of them work with telehealth companies that have said they are interested in dispensing the peptides, such as Hims & Hers and Noom.

Dr. Janet Woodcock, who retired in 2024 from the F. D. A. after 40 years in drug oversight, said that the move harks back to the days of folk medicine endorsed by word of mouth, which caused harm and led to the founding and strengthening of the F. D. A.

“It does undermine the idea that you would test drugs for safety and effectiveness before they were widely made available,” she said.

As unapproved injections, the peptides would not have fundamental agency safeguards in place, such as the type of safety review that flagged thalidomide, a drug that caused devastating birth defects in Europe but was not approved as a morning sickness remedy by a careful F. D. A. reviewer.

The new policy states that Mr. Kennedy has “determined that this limited enforcement-discretion policy will discourage the continued, widespread use of certain research-use-only peptides supplied by foreign manufacturers that pose a safety risk to U. S. patients.”

To bypass approval, earlier this year the F. D. A. started a process to add the peptides to a list of products that could be compounded by bespoke pharmacies to meet the needs of individual patients. In July, a compounding committee met to consider adding seven peptides to the list.

During the hearing, F. D. A. officials and patient safety advocates aired concerns about the lack of basic information about the peptides, such as their effect on the immune system or potential to fuel tumor growth. Agency scientists formally advised the committee not to add the peptides to the list.

Other people at the hearings testified about their positive experience using peptides and about the risks inherent in dispensing any drug, approved or otherwise. The committee, which Mr. Kennedy’s department had filled with a majority of people who prescribed peptides or worked in drug compounding, voted in favor of adding the six compounds to the list.

The agency did not take that step, though. Dr. Woodcock said the decision to put so-called enforcement discretion in place “is just a policy of looking the other way.”

Although some panelists at the July meeting aired their concerns about bad actors prescribing unsafe peptides, it is not clear whether the policy change will curtail their operations.

“I think what it translates to for the average consumer and someone looking for these peptides is there’s been a tacit recommendation from the F. D. A. and that it’s OK,” said John Hertig, chairman of the Collaborative for Evidence-Based Medicines. “When really there hasn’t been the diligence and the review and the scientific rigor that we deserve as the American public, in terms of what we ingest or inject.”

The peptides that the F. D. A. panel reviewed this summer are promoted as supporting a wide range of conditions. One of the most popular, BPC-157, is also marketed as helping with joint healing. Another, semax, is purported to treat mental health and neurological conditions like migraine, anxiety and Parkinson’s disease.

There is little research, especially in humans, on these peptides to back up these claims. Critics have raised concerns that people will turn to these unproven therapies instead of medications that are F. D. A.-approved and have a track record of safety and efficacy.

Some of the peptides also target fundamental biological processes, which could potentially lead to dangerous side effects. Epitalon is promoted as a longevity peptide for its reported ability to lengthen telomeres — the caps on the end of chromosomes that shorten with age and have been studied in relation to longevity. But long telomeres have also been linked to cancer, raising concerns that epitalon could potentially be carcinogenic.

Other peptides allowed on Wednesday include KPV, a cream or gel marketed for wound healing and inflammatory skin conditions. Another called MOTS-c is created from mitochondria DNA and is suggested to play a role in cellular metabolism, although no data in humans supports the claim. TB-500, another peptide, was developed as a veterinary drug to improve greyhound and horse performance in races.

Dana G. Smith contributed to this report.

Christina Jewett covers the Food and Drug Administration, which means keeping a close eye on drugs, medical devices, food safety and tobacco policy.

What We Know About the Deadly Train Crash in Spain

The New York Times October 28, 2026

Deadly Train Crash in Spain

Advertisement

Supported by

A train accident near Toledo, Spain, which killed at least 68 people, was one of the deadliest in the country’s history.

By Jonathan Wolfe

Follow live updates on the crash.

A high-speed passenger train rear-ended another on Wednesday near Toledo, Spain, killing at least 68 people and injuring dozens, according to local emergency officials.

It was one of the deadliest train crashes in the country’s history.

The collision comes months after another deadly train crash in southern Spain that involved the same carriers, killing 46 people in January.

The accident on Wednesday was the third fatal train crash in Spain this year, adding to deep concern about the safety of the country’s extensive rail system.

Around 9 a. m., a train belonging to the private rail operator Iryo was stopped on the tracks near Toledo when a train operated by Spain’s national rail company, Renfe, barreled into it. Both trains were covering the route between Madrid, the capital, and the southern city of Seville.

Óscar Puente, Spain’s transportation minister, said in a news conference that the crash appeared to result from what he called an “inexplicable” decision by traffic control operators to tell the Renfe train to continue its journey when the other train was stopped farther along the tracks.

Passengers involved in the crash told local news outlets that the impact tossed people around cabins. Some crawled out of windows and lay in a nearby field, where local workers, who had heard the crash, rushed to help them.

Video filmed inside one of the train cars and verified by The New York Times showed smoke rising from a charred, mangled carriage on the slope by the rail line.

On Wednesday afternoon, the trains were surrounded by ambulances, police cars and fire trucks, with helicopters flying low overhead. Dozens of Civil Guard officers, some wearing white protective suits, were inspecting the scene.

Both trains appeared to have sustained substantial damage, according to images from the scene. The nose of the Renfe train, which was traveling to Seville, appeared destroyed. Three rear carriages of the Iryo train appeared to have been derailed, two of them overturned.

More than 50 people were injured in the crash, according to local officials. Some 397 passengers were aboard the Renfe train and about 150 aboard the Iryo train, local news outlets reported.

Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez traveled to the scene of the crash on Wednesday.

“It’s not possible for a country like Spain to suffer two high-speed train accidents in one year,” he said, adding that while Wednesday’s accident and a fatal January crash on the same line seemed unrelated, Spanish rail’s security systems clearly needed to be reinforced.

With national elections set for the end of November, the crash has the potential to become an issue in an already bitter campaign, in which opponents have attacked the competence of the left-wing government of Mr. Sánchez.

“I am very concerned about the information we are receiving regarding another train accident,” the conservative opposition leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, wrote on social media. “The priority now is to assist the victims and support their families. My full support goes to the emergency teams working on the ground.”

The collision on Wednesday came months after a deadly collision involving the same carriers that killed 46 people.

In that accident, in January, a train belonging to Iryo derailed near the town of Adamuz as it traveled north toward Madrid from Málaga. Two of its rear cars fell onto the opposite track and were struck by a southbound train operated by Renfe.

An official report on what caused that accident is not yet completed, but preliminary investigations pointed to a broken rail as the likely cause.

In 2013, 80 people were killed when a high-speed train carrying more than 200 passengers derailed near Santiago de Compostela in northwest Spain and slammed into a concrete wall. The driver of the train admitted to speeding before the accident and was also on a call with a railway official before the crash.

The accident on Wednesday was the third fatal crash in Spain this year. Days after the accident in January, a commuter train near Barcelona struck a collapsed retaining wall and derailed, killing one person.

Reporting was contributed by José Bautista from the scene near Toledo, Jason Horowitz from Madrid, James McManagan from London and Carlos Barragán from New York.

Jonathan Wolfe is a Times reporter based in London, covering breaking news.

Inside Democrats’ Secret Effort to Stack Alaska’s Ballot

The New York Times October 28, 2026

Latest polls

Senate

House

Governor

Pres. approval

Advertisement

Supported by

Times Exclusive

Operatives aligned with Mary Peltola, the Democratic nominee for Senate, spent months recruiting candidates to peel votes from Senator Dan Sullivan, the Republican.

By Kellen Browning

In the summer of 2025, a staffer for Mary Peltola, the Alaska Democrat who was eyeing a run for Senate, received unusual instructions from top campaign aides: Find as many people named Dan Sullivan in Alaska as you can.

The staffer complied, combing through voter records to produce a list of Dan Sullivans from across the state.

This was no random request. Dan S. Sullivan is the name of the state’s Republican senator. And if the Peltola campaign or its allies could track down and persuade another Dan Sullivan to run for Senate, the confusion could cost the senator crucial votes on the state’s unusual, four-person ballot.

The plan worked. This spring, a retired teacher from a tiny fishing village along the Alaska Panhandle, reachable only by air and sea, announced his candidacy for Senate. His name was Dan J. Sullivan.

The Peltola campaign has repeatedly denied any involvement in his candidacy. But The Times has found, based on interviews and text messages, along with documents prepared for a potential lawsuit against the campaign, that not only did Ms. Peltola’s team work with people trying to recruit Mr. Sullivan to run for Senate, but the effort was much broader. The group worked to coax other would-be spoilers into the race, to dilute the incumbent’s support and help catapult the Democrat to victory.

The endeavor, which was internally called the ballot composition project, involved secret trips to far-flung Alaskan communities and the appearance of a mysterious Midwestern operative, who traversed the state using a fake name and made his pitch to would-be candidates over beers at brew pubs.

It also involved the Peltola campaign’s lawyers, as well as senior aides at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, which directs the party’s campaign strategy in Senate races across the country. From Washington to Anchorage, those advisers participated in regular conversations about the effort and even considered forming a new political party to draw conservatives onto the ballot.

Ballot-stacking tactics are common in politics and generally considered legal — and have been employed by both parties in Alaska. But this operation, which has not been reported before, reveals the lengths to which Democrats went to seek advantage in a Senate race that could determine control of the chamber.

“Alaskan voters need to know,” said Elisa Rios, Ms. Peltola’s former campaign manager and longtime aide, who was fired amid a staff shake-up in August, and agreed to a series of interviews with The Times since then. “There was a lot of speculation, and voters should get the full picture when making their decisions.”

Ms. Peltola was not directly involved in the project, Ms. Rios said, but she was “definitely aware.”

The operation had impact. On Tuesday, Ms. Peltola will be the only Democrat on the ballot, facing off against the two Mr. Sullivans and a long-shot candidate named Gerald Heikes who was also recruited into the race, according to The Times’s reporting. Polls give Ms. Peltola a strong chance of winning.

The Justice Department, meanwhile, filed a lawsuit in federal court at President Trump’s behest last week seeking to block certification of the election results if votes for the other Mr. Sullivan cost Senator Sullivan the win.

Both the Peltola campaign and the D. S. C. C. denied participating in efforts to recruit spoilers to the ballot in Alaska. Neither group addressed a detailed list of questions provided by The Times.

“The Alaskans for Mary campaign has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign and did not recruit any candidates into the race,” the campaign wrote in a statement.

The D. S. C. C. sent a similar response, saying it had “no involvement” in recruiting Mr. Sullivan “or any other Republican candidate.”

This article is based on interviews over the past two months with 12 people who participated in or were told of the plan, or were would-be candidates that the team tried to recruit. The Times also obtained dozens of text messages that provided updates on the progress of the effort. The reporting included the extensive interviews with Ms. Rios, during which she shared details of the operation.

Last week, as The Times prepared to publish this article, Ms. Rios, who had been planning to file a wrongful termination lawsuit against the Peltola campaign, contacted The Times and said she wanted to take back her previous statements.

“As discussed on our call earlier today, I am confirming that I have retracted all statements made regarding the 2026 Alaska Senate Race in connection with any article you may or may not be writing,” Ms. Rios wrote. “I am not willing to be a source for any story in any capacity.”

It is rare for a source to seek to retract comments made in previous interviews, and The Times’s standards do not obligate reporters to comply with such requests. The Times had never agreed that those previous interviews could not be published, and informed Ms. Rios last week that they would be a part of this story.

In addition, Ms. Rios’s interviews were consistent with The Times’s other reporting. She has not filed a lawsuit against the campaign.

The operation began in the summer of 2025 to lure potential spoiler candidates onto the state’s unusual four-person ballot, Ms. Rios said. In one early meeting, she said, aides with the D. S. C. C. introduced a veteran Democratic operative named Jerid Kurtz to Ms. Rios and Anton McParland, who at the time was Ms. Peltola’s chief of staff. Mr. Kurtz, a native of Ohio, was introduced as a specialist in secret ballot maneuvers, Ms. Rios said.

Months later, in early 2026, Mr. Kurtz participated in a video call with members of the ballot composition team, Ms. Rios said. He told the group he had made contact with one of the Dan Sullivans. This Mr. Sullivan lived in the tiny village of Petersburg, and Mr. Kurtz described him as amenable to running if it would help Ms. Peltola, Ms. Rios said.

Mr. Kurtz “told us when he found him,” she said. He said Mr. Sullivan “said he hated Trump, and if it was going to help Mary, he liked Mary. He didn’t have any interest in being a politician, but if this could help.”

Mr. Sullivan, who has maintained that he entered the race of his own volition, did not respond to repeated requests for comment over the past week.

According to Federal Election Commission records, a pro-Peltola super PAC called 49th State PAC paid Wingspan Strategies, a firm co-owned by Mr. Kurtz, about $87,000 this fall. The PAC said in a statement this week it had “never hired or paid Jerid Kurtz for performing any services.”

Mr. Kurtz did not respond to repeated requests for comment. In recent days, he removed his LinkedIn profile from public view and made his X account private.

Text messages viewed by The Times show officials with the D. S. C. C. and the Peltola campaign communicating for months about the project. Mr. McParland asked for updates from “Jarid,” “Jared” or “our friend,” and D. S. C. C. officials quickly scheduled calls, the messages showed. (Mr. McParland, who was demoted to a consulting role in August, did not respond to multiple requests for comment.)

Ms. Rios regularly participated in the calls. She said the members sometimes chatted casually, and Mr. Kurtz occasionally grew animated when describing his tactics, saying he used pseudonyms and cover stories to keep his activities under wraps.

In late May, just before Mr. Sullivan filed his papers to run, Mr. Kurtz spoke by phone to a Peltola campaign aide, saying he had just gotten off a plane in Petersburg, according to Ms. Rios and another person familiar with the conversation.

The Peltola aides worried at times that Mr. Kurtz’s efforts would be discovered, such as when he posted an image of the Anchorage airport on his Instagram account.

“I am hearing that our friend in the state is being noticed,” Mr. McParland wrote in a text message in January reviewed by The Times. Andrew Piatt, the D. S. C. C.’s director of campaigns, replied: “We will check in.”

Alaska’s voting system makes it especially easy to add spoilers to the ballot. The state holds nonpartisan primaries, so candidates can claim any party affiliation on the ballot without being vetted by parties themselves. That allowed Mr. Sullivan of Petersburg, a longtime supporter of Ms. Peltola and other Democrats, to land a spot on next week’s ballot.

Republicans have also taken advantage of this system. When Ms. Peltola ran for re-election to the House two years ago, the state Republican Party backed an effort to help a Democrat — an inmate who ran his campaign from a New York prison — stay on the ballot.

This year, as soon as Mr. Sullivan entered the race, Republicans denounced him as a Democratic plant, but they haven’t been able to prove it. They attempted to remove him from the ballot, arguing that he was not a “good faith” candidate and citing his registration switch from unaffiliated to Republican just before the deadline to run.

In June, the Alaska Supreme Court brushed aside that argument, ruling there was no basis for removing Mr. Sullivan in either state law or the U. S. Constitution.

The lawsuit from the Justice Department, meanwhile, is still making its way through the court. Election law experts say the case is dubious, given that states control the administration of elections under the Constitution, and the suit seeks to challenge an election that hasn’t happened yet.

While the Justice Department is focused on the two Dan Sullivans, The Times found other Alaskans the team sought to recruit as spoilers. Not all of them, of course, shared a name with the Republican senator. Some would simply add more options to the ballot and potentially siphon support from the incumbent.

Matthew Salisbury of Anchorage said he got a call out of the blue last December from an unfamiliar Google Voice number with an Ohio area code.

A one-time candidate for the U. S. House, Mr. Salisbury said in an interview that the caller identified himself as Zane — no last name — and asked him if he would consider running in the upcoming Senate race. Zane also wanted to meet him in person.

Over beers at an Irish pub in Anchorage, and over more meetings and calls in subsequent months, Zane continued to press Mr. Salisbury to run for Senate. He said he was looking for independent-minded candidates, and that his backers would support Mr. Salisbury with outside spending. He seemed friendly and intelligent, Mr. Salisbury recalled, but never provided more details about his background or political party, and he wouldn’t say who was paying for the effort.

“I’m not naïve,” said Mr. Salisbury, who didn’t end up running for Senate. “I had to have that general idea that they’re not in it for me.”

When The Times sent Mr. Salisbury a photograph of Mr. Kurtz, Mr. Salisbury identified him as the man who called himself Zane. Efforts to reach the Google Voice number were unsuccessful, as were attempts to reach Mr. Kurtz at the email address he used with Mr. Salisbury, which includes the word “buckeye.” Public records show that Mr. Kurtz is from Ohio, known as the Buckeye State.

In late May, Mr. Kurtz, still posing as Zane, texted Mr. Salisbury that he had also tried to recruit several “upper level candidates, including a few of the folks currently in the gov race,” to no avail.

And he wanted Mr. Salisbury’s opinion on a recent news story, writing: “You see this craziness with another Dan Sullivan? What’s your read on that?”

Throughout the spring, the campaign swapped leads with the D. S. C. C. on potential candidates and continued to participate in efforts to shape the ballot.

In one exchange of text messages obtained by The Times, Peltola advisers seemed to make fun of voters while watching a focus group, surmising the participants would be susceptible to being tricked into voting for a ballot spoiler.

“Do we have a scheme for you,” wrote a consultant for the Peltola campaign. A pollster on the chat wrote that one voter seemed like the perfect audience “for our ballot strategy plan :)”

The team’s spirits rose with the results of the Aug. 18 primary, as both Dan Sullivans advanced to the four-way general election. But there was one problem: The fourth spot on the ballot had gone to a Democrat who could siphon some votes away from Ms. Peltola that fall.

That Democrat, a progressive named David Leslie, quickly faced calls from his party to withdraw. One of those callers, Mr. Leslie said in an interview, was Jerid Kurtz. Mr. Kurtz met with Mr. Leslie in person, at a cafe in Fairbanks, according to a person familiar with the exchange.

Mr. Leslie soon agreed to drop out.

“I’m really proud of the action you took today,” Mr. Kurtz wrote to Mr. Leslie on Aug. 31, the day he dropped out, in a text message viewed by The Times.

Mr. Leslie’s exit cleared the way for another Republican to take his spot on the ballot, potentially dividing the G. O. P. vote even further: Gerald Heikes.

Mr. Heikes, a drywall contractor, said in an interview that he was recruited to run for Senate this spring “by a guy from the Midwest.” The man, whose name Mr. Heikes did not remember, first reached him on the phone, then met with him at a deli in his hometown of Palmer, Alaska. Mr. Heikes did not think he resembled the photo of Mr. Kurtz.

“He said, ‘Hey, if you go and file to run for Senate, we’ll back you — we can’t give you money or anything, but we’ll make things happen for you,’” Mr. Heikes said.

Mr. Heikes, who has said before that he believed God was telling him to run for office, decided after the meeting to run for the Senate.

There were also efforts to support the new candidates financially. Back in March, Peltola campaign employees had dinner with a local political consultant named Jim Lottsfeldt. Mr. Lottsfeldt, who works with super PACs aligned with Ms. Peltola, agreed to lead an effort to boost the long-shot Senate candidates with outside spending, said Ms. Rios, who was among the attendees.

“We were talking about how we would balance the different distinct universes and create basically a Republican war in the primary,” Ms. Rios said.

Federal filings from Alaska Values, a new super PAC supporting Mr. Heikes, show that Mr. Lottsfeldt had requested advertising time from Alaska radio stations this month.

In an interview, Mr. Lottsfeldt denied any knowledge of or involvement in the effort, and said no such topic was discussed at the dinner. He argued that Ms. Rios was a source of “disgruntled, anti-Mary Peltola stuff that I think is often not true.”

He also denied an association with the Alaska Values PAC, but could not explain how his name ended up on the filings, suggesting it must have been an error.

“These forms have auto-whatever, it’s quite possible that my name was on it from a blank form and then it got moved over,” Mr. Lottsfeldt said. “Even if I had requested some time, OK, so what? There’s nothing illegal about that, there’s nothing suspicious about that.”

Even as the Peltola campaign and D. S. C. C. officials denied participation in the operation, the texts and documents reviewed by The Times show it involved the party’s Senate committee and its top law firm. At one point, when Peltola campaign aides toyed with an audacious idea to establish a right-wing state party that could challenge the incumbent senator, they contacted D. S. C. C. officials.

“Imagine if there was a MAGA party!” Mr. McParland, of the Peltola campaign, wrote in January.

“Smart,” replied Mr. Piatt, the D. S. C. C.’s director of campaigns. “Let’s see.”

Jacquelyn Lopez, an attorney with the Elias Law Group, the firm that represents both the committee and the Peltola campaign, was part of this effort, according to Ms. Rios. In a text message from April viewed by The Times, a campaign consultant asked Ms. Rios: “Do we need to follow up with Jackie about maga party stuff?”

In another message from that month that misspelled Mr. Kurtz’s first name, Mr. McParland wrote: “Jackie is calling Jarid.” Ms. Lopez did not respond to a request for comment.

The MAGA party plan fizzled out in May.

But in June, the D. S. C. C. celebrated alongside the campaign when an Alaska court cleared the way for the other Dan Sullivan to stay on the ballot.

“Other Dan won, will be on ballot,” Shelbi Dantic, a D. S. C. C. employee, wrote in an internal group chat.

Three people — two Peltola aides and a member of the D. S. C. C. staff — reacted with heart emojis.

Nathaniel Herz contributed reporting from Alaska, and Matt Zdun, Theodore Schleifer, Emily Davies and Beth Reinhard contributed reporting from New York and Washington. Georgia Gee and Julie Tate contributed research.

Kellen Browning is a Times political reporter based in San Francisco.

4 Takeaways From the Incomplete Israeli Election

The New York Times October 28, 2026

Israel’s Election

Advertisement

Supported by

news analysis

Votes are still being counted, and much is in flux. But as the stage was set for bitter talks over forming a government, nearly all sides could face disappointment.

By David M. Halbfinger

Reporting from Jerusalem

The results of Israel’s pivotal parliamentary election will not be finalized at least until Thursday and it could be weeks until it is clear what kind of government will be formed and who will lead it. But some conclusions are already inescapable.

Arab citizens of Israel turned out to vote in record numbers. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party gobbled up many votes that his right-wing and Orthodox Jewish coalition partners had expected would be theirs. And the pre-election polls failed to anticipate both phenomena.

Much could still change. But with most of the votes counted by Wednesday afternoon, here are some initial takeaways.

Mr. Netanyahu’s coalition appears to have shrunk considerably from the 64 parliamentary seats that it won in 2022: The latest results show it with around 54, well short of a majority in the 120-member Knesset, or Parliament. But he could wind up in better position to form a government than his chief rival, Gadi Eisenkot.

Mr. Eisenkot, a former Israeli military chief of staff, had two goals in the election: to lead the Jewish opposition parties to an outright majority or at least get very close to one, and to make sure his own party, Yashar, got more votes than any other. He failed on both counts, the initial results indicate.

Reuven Hazan, a political science professor at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, said that it had been hard to imagine better conditions for Mr. Eisenkot’s alliance ahead of the election. Mr. Netanyahu and his coalition were weighed down by anger over the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023 attacks and their failure to do more to free Israeli hostages; by anger over ultra-Orthodox Jewish draft-dodging in wartime; and by outrage over the government’s efforts to neuter the judiciary and allow growing settler violence against Palestinians in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, he said.

“The anti-Netanyahu camp had an election handed to them on a silver platter, and they still lost,” Mr. Hazan said. “Israelis have sent an ambiguous message: ‘We don’t really like the current government, but we don’t see a viable alternative.’”

As votes were being counted on Wednesday afternoon, Likud was poised to be the largest party in the larger of the two blocs of Jewish-led parties, meaning Mr. Netanyahu could well be given the chance to form a government, Mr. Hazan said.

The long-serving Israeli premier may try to peel away some of Mr. Eisenkot’s putative partners in order to achieve a majority of 61 seats in Parliament. A number of them are as right-wing as he is, though all have more or less ruled out entering a Netanyahu-led government.

He could also try to form a national unity government with Mr. Eisenkot — perhaps with the assistance of President Trump, who has praised Mr. Netanyahu as a “warrior prime minister” and has made clear he wants Israel to join the United States in another round of war against Iran.

Perhaps the most mind-bending option available to Mr. Netanyahu, given that he ran a scaremongering campaign that demonized Arab lawmakers and stoked fears of Arab voter turnout, would be to recruit an Arab party to join him in a government. He nearly did so once before, in 2022.

“It could very well be that they become indispensable,” said Dahlia Scheindlin, a pollster and political analyst, said of Arab lawmakers. “And Netanyahu has certainly demonstrated his willingness to do anything to stay in power.”

Speaking of Jewish opposition parties in isolation ignores the fact that, when Arab parties are included, Mr. Netanyahu’s rivals appeared headed toward a significant majority in Parliament, with about 66 seats to roughly 54 for the prime minister’s bloc.

“There is no need to go with the racist assumption that you need not count the Arabs,” said Gayil Talshir, a political scientist at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem who is advising the opposition.

That means the Knesset in effect will be controlled by the anti-Netanyahu opposition, regardless of who ends up being prime minister. If the vote breakdown roughly holds, Ms. Talshir said she expected Mr. Eisenkot and his Jewish and Arab allies to elect a new parliamentary speaker, begin repealing unpopular laws and at least try to form a government — perhaps including some combination of Arab and ultra-Orthodox lawmakers.

“I’m not saying it’s a good scenario to take the Knesset and not be able to form the government,” Ms. Talshir said. “It’s a disaster. But this is the hand they’re dealt, and they have to play it.”

Tuesday’s election appears to have had many losers. Mr. Netanyahu’s support shrank and Mr. Eisenkot came up short of his goal. The ultra-Orthodox parties were projected to lose seats, according to the latest returns, and two right-wing nationalist parties failed to make gains, despite four years in which they drove the Netanyahu government’s extreme policies in the West Bank.

The biggest ostensible winners were the Arab voters who voted in record numbers. But they could well wind up the most disappointed citizens of all, if the Jewish opposition leaders prove unwilling or unable to form a majority in an alliance with the Arab parties.

“They’re saying, ‘We believe in Israeli democracy, we believe in the system, we want to be part of the system, and we want to be treated better,’” Mr. Hazan said. “And if Netanyahu forms a government, they’ll get none of that.”

David M. Halbfinger is The Times’s Jerusalem bureau chief, leading coverage of Israel, Gaza and the West Bank. He also held that post from 2017 to 2021. He was the politics editor from 2021 to 2025.

Byron Donalds Holds Slim Lead in Florida’s Race for Governor

The New York Times October 28, 2026

Latest polls

Senate

Governor

Supported by

New polls in Florida, South Carolina and Minnesota illuminate the head winds that Republicans are facing.

The New York Times/Siena poll

Oct. 19-26

Among likely voters. Shaded areas represent the margin of error.

Based on New York Times/Siena polls of 813 voters in Florida, 707 voters in South Carolina and 752 voters in Minnesota conducted Oct. 19 to 26. Question wording has been condensed.

Jillian Vordick/The New York Times

By Emily Cochrane and Ruth Igielnik

Less than a week before Election Day, Republicans hold a slim lead in the Florida governor’s race, according to new polls from The New York Times and Siena University.

Representative Byron Donalds, a Republican who would be Florida’s first Black governor if elected, is ahead of his Democratic opponent, David Jolly, by only four percentage points, 48 percent to 44 percent.

The poll in Florida, along with polls in South Carolina and Minnesota, illuminate the head winds that Republicans are facing nationally. The current Republican governor of Florida, Ron DeSantis, won his re-election campaign four years ago by more than 19 percentage points. But Mr. Jolly, who previously represented the state in Congress as a Republican, has ground to make up.

Seven percent of Florida voters remain undecided, a higher percentage than that of any of the other governor and Senate races polled across the three states.

In South Carolina, Alan Wilson, the Republican candidate for governor, is ahead by seven percentage points. And in Minnesota, the Democrat running for governor, Senator Amy Klobuchar, is comfortably positioned with an 18-point advantage over Lisa Demuth, the Republican.

Mr. Donalds has hustled across Florida, working to win over Black voters who often support Democrats. He is also handily out-raising Mr. Jolly. But Mr. Jolly, a critic of President Trump who left the Republican Party in 2018 and registered as a Democrat in early 2025, is making it a race.

Florida has not elected a Democratic governor this century, although Mr. DeSantis won his first campaign for governor by the slimmest of margins in 2018 against a progressive Black Democrat, Andrew Gillum.

The new poll suggests that the governor’s race is slightly more competitive than the Senate race in the state. Senator Ashley Moody, the Republican incumbent, is ahead of Angie Nixon, a state representative and democratic socialist who stunned the Democratic establishment with her primary win, by six percentage points.

Mr. Donalds is slightly more popular with voters in Florida than Mr. Jolly is, according to the poll, with 44 percent of voters viewing him favorably. Mr. Jolly is viewed favorably by 36 percent of voters, but about one-third of voters have not heard of him or did not offer an opinion.

The poll results signal that the Democratic enthusiasm in other reliably conservative states may help Democrats close what would otherwise be wider gaps in races like the ones in Florida and South Carolina.

Mr. Wilson, the Republican nominee in South Carolina and the state’s attorney general, is ahead of Jermaine Johnson, the Democratic nominee who is a state representative, 51 percent to 44 percent.

While Mr. Wilson has a comfortable lead, that margin is far narrower than expected in a state that Mr. Trump won by about 18 percentage points in 2024. But Mr. Wilson is still ahead with the state’s traditional Republican constituencies such as voters over 65, men and white working-class voters.

Democrats in South Carolina may also be getting a boost from the Senate race playing out there, which has unexpectedly tightened. The poll found the Senate race as effectively tied between Senator Darline Graham, the sister of Senator Lindsey Graham who was appointed to his seat after he died, and Annie Andrews, the Democratic nominee.

Mr. Trump is scheduled to rally in South Carolina to shore up support for Ms. Graham.

In Minnesota, Ms. Klobuchar, who has won by wide margins every time she has run for Senate in the state, is ahead in the poll with men and women, across every age group, and among both college-educated voters and those without a college degree.

Despite some Democratic concerns that the Senate race in Minnesota would become competitive, Peggy Flanagan, the Democratic lieutenant governor aiming to replace the retiring Democratic senator Tina Smith, also has a comfortable lead.

Here are the key things to know about these New York Times/Siena polls:

The margin of sampling error among likely voters is between plus or minus 3.9 and 4.3 percentage points in each state. In theory, this means that the results should reflect the views of the overall population most of the time, though many other challenges create additional sources of error.

You can see full results and a detailed methodology here. If you want to read more about how and why we conduct our polls, you can see answers to frequently asked questions and submit your own questions here.

Emily Cochrane is a national reporter for The Times covering the American South, based in Nashville.

Ruth Igielnik is a Times polling editor who conducts polls and analyzes and reports on the results.

This Is What the GOP’s Final Midterms Push Looks Like

Wired October 28, 2026

Republicans are spending the final week ahead of the midterm elections defending historically red Senate seats that have suddenly become competitive, according to federal filings and sources familiar with the matter.

A significant focus is now on four Senate races in ​K​ansas, ​South Carolina, ​Nebraska, and even ​Mississippi, all traditionally red seats, in what’s ​an ominous development for Republicans in their effort to at least keep control of the upper chamber.

Trump operatives tell Inner Loop that they do not expect ​Democrats to win those Senate seats and that they have ​mainly directed GOP outside groups to spend there to ​​help boost incumbents that only have a narrow lead.

But ​t​he operatives also concede that they are having to divert an increasing amount of resources ​to those states—states that president Donald Trump carried by double digits in 2024 and where Republicans never dreamed of having to spend tens of millions of dollars.

In total, in the penultimate week of the campaign, the Senate Republican–aligned Senate Leadership Fund spent $14 million across those four states, according to a WIRED review of federal filings. The biggest spend has been in Kansas, where SLF has abruptly dumped more than $5 million.

Trump operatives say Kansas has been a major headache since the start of October, when Trafalgar Group​, a GOP pollster, found Democratic candidate Adam Hamilton one point ahead of ​incumbent GOP senator Roger Marshall.

Marshall, a doctor, has had an unusually tough race following a slew of negative stories about how he pursued legal action against his patients with unpaid bills and how much time he spends in Florida. Some political operatives have also complained that he has not taken his race seriously, sources say.

​But the last-minute spending is also coming in places like South Carolina, where SLF spent another roughly $5 million to help incumbent Darline Graham, who has struggled to galvanize Trump's base despite having the president’s endorsement that propelled her to victory in the primary.

SLF also spent nearly $3 million in Nebraska to help Republican incumbent senator Pete Ricketts, who has been behind in some polls, and in Mississippi, the fund put just under $1 million toward Republican incumbent senator Cindy Hyde-Smith.

The final sprint has highlighted the fraught predicament for Republicans, who are having to patch a seemingly ever-growing number of vulnerabilities.

Trump's campaign schedule has also added several deep-red states that are flashing warning signs, in addition to the expected campaign stops in battleground states. Last week, Trump went to Kansas and South Carolina. This week, he has been in Mississippi and will return to Kansas and South Carolina, as well.

Still, several Trump operatives tell Inner Loop they have been encouraged by the fact that Democratic candidates lately have not expanded their leads in several key Senate races—a concern that has cropped up among some Senate Democratic leadership aides.

Chief among their concerns is Michigan, the best GOP pickup opportunity. Many of the most viable paths to Democrats taking the Senate majority pass through the state, but Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed has suffered lingering issues with key voting blocs.

Black voters turned out in droves to help Barack Obama carry the state in 2008 and 2012, and the conventional wisdom in Washington is that El-Sayed will need similar support in order to keep the seat blue, one of the Democratic aides tells Inner Loop.

But the trouble for El-Sayed, they add, has been the decades-long animosity between Arab and Black communities in Michigan, a divide that was further strained during the primary when supporters of his challenger, Haley Stevens, ran ads featuring Barack Obama praising her earlier work during the financial crisis.

In an effort to rebuild at least part of that coalition, Obama held a joint rally with El-Sayed in Detroit over the weekend, which aides are hoping could persuade some voters. Operatives aren’t sure if it’ll be enough.

We will have to see how it pans out. See you next week, on the other side!

This is an edition of Hugo Lowell’s Inner Loop newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

Most Servers on the Planet Are Vulnerable to This Firmware Code-Execution Flaw

Wired October 28, 2026

Defenders across the world face the burden of responding to yet another botched code-execution vulnerability, this time in boot-time firmware used by most of the world’s server vendors and data centers.

The vulnerability, with a severity rating of 9.5 out of 10, resides in the TianoCore EDK II, an open source codebase that hardware makers and cloud providers use to create the UEFI firmware that runs during the boot-up sequence. Last year, a representative of the UEFI Forum called EDK2 the “preeminent solution / implementation of the UEFI specifications.” Virtually all UEFI suppliers (sometimes still called IBVs or independent BIOS vendors), including AMI, Insyde, and Phoenix, use the reference code extensively. Project Mu, Microsoft’s hardened EDK2 fork, used the code containing the vulnerable component as well.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-97631, is a memory-corruption flaw in an ICMP component that attackers can exploit to execute malicious code that runs before the operating system and firmware can implement defenses like Secure Boot, which establishes a chain of trust for all code, including the Trusted Platform Module (TPM), loaded during boot. While final payloads delivered by CVE-2026-97631 have no persistence—meaning they run only once—they can give attackers a wide opening to install other payloads that also run each time early in the boot process.

The parties that discovered CVE-2026-97631—Alex Matrosov of Anthropic and Dan Holmes of Google—had arranged for it to stay under wraps until a coordinated disclosure that was scheduled for January. AMI, a maker of motherboards and other hardware, published this pull request last month that detailed the vulnerability and included a code fix. Once the post came to the attention of the discovering parties, TianoCore Project members published a public advisory last week.

With publicly available patch code, it will be trivial for advanced hackers to learn how the vulnerability is triggered and to build working exploits. Further compounding the urgency, patching UEFI code vulnerabilities in millions of end devices sold and used by thousands of hardware makers and cloud providers is cumbersome and time-consuming. Word of the vulnerability comes six days after another botched disclosure, this one involving a critical code-execution vulnerability in the PHP programming language.

“This vulnerability in the ICMP parser of the EDK2 network stack is interesting in terms of how it affects the chain of trust and the broader ecosystem,” said HD Moore, creator of Metasploit and chief research officer at security firm Dragos. “An attacker intent on compromising a nearby endpoint or server could use this bug to hijack program flow at a point where the boot process still has access to sensitive components, like the endpoint’s TPM. This could be used to break disk encryption for cases where an attacker has short-term network access (and it would be even easier in a theft scenario).”

CVE-2026-97631 is a 16-year-old buffer overflow in the PXE-Base Code driver (NetworkPkg/UefiPxeBcDxe), which is responsible for allowing servers, storage equipment, and other devices to boot using code downloaded from a local network. During this process—known as the pre-execution environment boot—the driver uses a network listener to monitor for ICMP errors. Because the driver doesn’t enforce a memory copy limit of 504 bytes, overwriting adjacent data, a malicious insider or a hacker who has gained low-level access to a local network can send an error message that appends code past this limit. The IUEFI module running on the CPU then becomes corrupted.

As the official advisory puts it:

During network boot, the PXE Base Code driver (NetworkPkg/UefiPxeBcDxe) keeps a receive request open for ICMP error messages and copies each received message into the fixed 504-byte field Mode. IcmpError of its private context structure. The copy loop’s bounds handling is incorrect in both the IPv4 and IPv6 handlers (PxeBcIcmpErrorDpcHandle and PxeBcIcmp6ErrorDpcHandle): for a message longer than 504 bytes it still copies bytes into the field, and it advances the destination pointer by the cumulative rather than the per-fragment length, so an oversized message writes attacker-controlled bytes past the field. Nothing earlier on the receive path restricts the message length.

The malicious error can be delivered through a simple unicast sent from any network distance to a target device’s IP address, as long as it’s sent during the PXE boot sequence. An attacker can deliver a denial-of-service by causing the boot sequence to hang. When the attacker knows what the target firmware build is, it can plant a “counterfeit event” that executes the malicious code on the CPU in its UEFI firmware environment. The code runs in ring 0, a CPU’s most privileged execution level. Because exploits bypass attestation processes designed to cryptographically prove to remote servers that the hardware is secure, they present a key opportunity for elevating limited privileges.

CVE-2026-97631 joins a long list of previously discovered vulnerabilities in UEFI or code that works closely with it. The most severe of them, LogoFail, stemmed from logo images included in the UEFI of just about every hardware maker. Rendering bugs allowed attackers to subvert the chain of trust UEFI enforces and go on to install malicious components before the OS loaded or Secure Boot ran. PixieFail was a vulnerability similar to CVE-2026-97631. It, too, was the result of faulty PXE boot flaws in EDK2. Following discovery of the vulnerability, researchers embarked on multiple fuzzing projects designed to surface other critical flaws in the open source code library. It appears those efforts failed to find this latest flaw.

Other recently discovered UEFI flaws include:

Like CVE-2026-97631, exploitation or use of these payloads is appealing because it allows attackers to infect machines early in the boot process, before TPM and other defenses load, so they can inflict maximum damage. Given the ubiquity of CVE-2026-97631, Moore said it’s likely a “forever” bug that will live on in end-of-support systems.

There are important caveats and limitations to exploiting this latest vulnerability. As noted, some level of control over a local network is a prerequisite. That likely limits exploitation to insiders or attackers, such as nation-states or ransomware operators, who manage to gain low-level access inside a network and are looking for a way to elevate system rights. There’s no evidence yet that CVE-2026-97631 provides an initial entry point into a network. There are other hurdles to clear.

“For exploiting the vulnerability itself, an attacker needs to guess specific addresses within the target system, so it’s not something that you can throw a single exploit at any target and get RCE across a diverse range of devices, but it needs to be tuned for each target model/version/configuration since the addresses will change based on those,” Jesse Michael, a principal researcher at firmware security firm Eclypsium, told Ars.

“Unlike some of the previous, high-profile vulnerabilities like BootHole, Black Lotus, and Baton Drop, this vulnerability can be fixed with a basic code fix, which will require deploying a BIOS/UEFI update, but they don’t need to deal with revocations, pk/kek/db/dbx key management updates, or making sure to update OS and provisioning media like you do with Secure Boot bypasses in the bootloader itself.”

CVE-2026-97631 doesn’t affect home and small office users, or any other users who boot their devices solely from disk drives. Instead, it applies only to organizations with machines that boot from local networks, or conceivably from Internet-connected resources. Even then, the targeted firmware must rely on EDK2, as opposed to a different reference implementation, and use the PXE functionality (which is turned on by default).

In an email, Intel said that none of its “commercial products currently under security support” are known to be affected. “Intel does not include the affected EDK2 functionality in its reference code, though it may be integrated by an OEM board vendor or system manufacturer,” the company added. It advised customers to check with their system manufacturer for specific guidance. Publicly available Intel reference code, however, makes reference to EDK2. Further, TianoCore has said that each Intel-supplied UEFI development kit “is a fully validated implementation … for a specific revision of the EDK II source.” Many other Intel documents reference EDK2 as well.

Arm, meanwhile, responded to a list of questions with: “CVE-2026-97631 is not directly applicable to Arm’s product portfolio.” Like Intel, firmware the company makes available also borrows heavily from EDK2. TianoCore has also documented Arm’s reliance on EDK2.

While it’s possible some platforms are free of EDK2 code, it’s prudent for users of all servers to investigate if CVE-2026-97631 affects them.

Questions sent to AMD, Phoenix Technologies, AMI, Microsoft, and Amazon—likely some of the other biggest organizations affected—went unanswered when this post went live. Without concrete answers to questions about the use of EDK2 by organizations like these, it’s impossible to say what or how devices are affected and what actions, if any, these organizations, or their users, should take. Representatives from the TianoCore Project also didn’t respond.

Some readers are likely to be unhappy at the lack of detail. Sometimes—particularly in cases involving botched disclosures that break embargoes months before they’re scheduled to lift—there’s no escaping the lack of actionable information in initial reporting.

Those affected should check with the maker of the firmware being used to boot their systems and ask for guidance. Beyond that, they should consider turning off network boot capabilities at least temporarily if possible. Firmware configurations should always enable security features such as TPM and Secure Boot whenever possible, although those defenses don’t protect against this particular threat. It’s also a good idea to monitor logs for signs of exploitation attempts.

This story originally appeared on Ars Technica.
